Therefore his people turn back to them, and find no fault in them. And they say, How can God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High?

The ESV notes that verse 10 is difficult in Hebrew, but the drift is plain and it is the worst part: God's own people are drifting after them and finding nothing to criticise. Success is its own argument, and a congregation watching it long enough begins to want it.

And the creed of the arrogant is the creed of Psalm 10 again, in a politer form: How can God know? Not denial — a shrug about whether he is paying attention.

Behold, these are the wicked; always at ease, they increase in riches.

He sums up the evidence like a man laying a file on a table. Always at ease. Increasing. That is the case, and it is a good case.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — Until I Went into the Sanctuary
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All in vain have I kept my heart clean and washed my hands in innocence (vv. 13-14). If I had said, I will speak thus, I would have betrayed the generation of your children (v. 15). Thinking it through was a wearisome task, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end (vv. 16-17). Truly you set them in slippery places ... How they are destroyed in a moment ... Like a dream when one awakes (vv. 18-20), and he sees what envy had made of him: I was brutish and ignorant; I was like a beast toward you (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: He kept his doubts to himself, and then went to church, and the perspective changed.

verseByVerse.quote: All in vain have I kept my heart clean and washed my hands in innocence. For all the day long I have been stricken and rebuked every morning. If I had said, "I will speak thus," I would have betrayed the generation of your children. But when I thought how to understand this, it seemed to me a wearisome task, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All in vain have I kept my heart clean and washed my hands in innocence. For all the day long I have been stricken and rebuked every morning.

Here is the conclusion he nearly drew, and it should be quoted to anyone who thinks this kind of doubt is unusual among believers. All in vain. I have kept myself clean for nothing. The two lives are laid side by side — they are at ease and increasing; I am disciplined and stricken — and the arithmetic comes out wrong.

Every morning is the detail that hurts. Not one great calamity: a daily, grinding correction, while the people who ignore God are fat and sleek.

If I had said, I will speak thus, I would have betrayed the generation of your children.

And this is the sentence that saved him, so dwell on it. He did not stop feeling it. He stopped short of saying it publicly — because he could see what it would do to younger believers if a man like him stood up and announced that serving God was a waste of time.

That is not dishonesty. It is the difference between bringing your doubt to God and broadcasting it to people who are not carrying it. There is a place to say all in vain, and it is this psalm, addressed to God. There is a place not to say it, and it is in front of the young.

But when I thought how to understand this, it seemed to me a wearisome task, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end.

He tried to think his way out, and it exhausted him. The problem is not solvable by harder thinking, and anyone who has lain awake trying to reason themselves back into contentment knows why.

What changed everything was a place: until I went into the sanctuary of God. He went to worship. He was not given new information about the wicked, and he did not receive an explanation of the general problem. He stood where God is worshipped and saw the same facts from a different end — their end.

Take that as the most practical thing in the psalm. When the arithmetic of your life will not come out, the answer is not more calculation in private. It is the sanctuary: the place where God is at the centre of the room and the timescale is eternity.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly you set them in slippery places; you make them fall to ruin. How they are destroyed in a moment, swept away utterly by terrors! Like a dream when one awakes, O Lord, when you rouse yourself, you despise them as phantoms. When my soul was embittered, when I was pricked in heart, I was brutish and ignorant; I was like a beast toward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly you set them in slippery places; you make them fall to ruin. How they are destroyed in a moment, swept away utterly by terrors! Like a dream when one awakes, O Lord, when you rouse yourself, you despise them as phantoms.

The word truly comes back from verse 1, and the whole picture inverts. He thought they were standing and his own feet were slipping (v. 2). It is the other way round: they are the ones on the slippery ground.

And the timing changes everything. In a moment — not a slow decline but a collapse. Like a dream when one awakes: vivid, absorbing, and then you open your eyes and there is nothing there. That is what he had been envying.

When my soul was embittered, when I was pricked in heart, I was brutish and ignorant; I was like a beast toward you.

He looks back at himself with real shame, and the words are strong: brutish, ignorant, like a beast. Envy had reduced him to an animal that sees the food and nothing else — no past, no future, no God.

Notice too that he calls it embittered and pricked. That is what unrelieved envy turns into: not a doctrine but a soreness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–28 — Whom Have I in Heaven but You?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nevertheless, I am continually with you; you hold my right hand. You guide me with your counsel, and afterward you will receive me to glory (vv. 23-24). Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever (vv. 25-26). But for me it is good to be near God (vv. 27-28).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who nearly walked away ends up saying the most extravagant sentence in the Psalter.

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, I am continually with you; you hold my right hand. You guide me with your counsel, and afterward you will receive me to glory. Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever. For behold, those who are far from you shall perish; you put an end to everyone who is unfaithful to you. But for me it is good to be near God; I have made the Lord GOD my refuge, that I may tell of all your works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nevertheless, I am continually with you; you hold my right hand.

The greatest word in the psalm is nevertheless. He has just called himself a beast, and the next sentence begins: and yet. Not "therefore God cast me off"; not "so I pulled myself together". While he was brutish, ignorant and bitter, he was continually with God — and the hand-holding is God's doing. You hold my right hand, the way you take the hand of a child who is not paying attention near a road.

You guide me with your counsel, and afterward you will receive me to glory.

Two tenses. Guidance now; glory afterwards. And the verb receive is the hope of 49:15, the one used of Enoch, whom God took (Gen 5:24). An Old Testament believer, with the resurrection still in shadow, says that the end of his story is being collected by God.

That is what the sanctuary gave him. Not fewer troubles: a longer line. Everything in verses 4-12 was true and measured against the wrong span.

Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you.

The most extravagant sentence in the Psalter, from the man who forty lines ago was eaten up with wanting what other people had. Heaven itself would not interest him without God in it, and earth has nothing he would swap for him.

And here is the cure for envy, which is not being told to stop wanting. It is wanting something else so much that the old cravings lose their grip. Nobody argues themselves out of envy; they are drawn out.

My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.

He grants the worst case: body and courage both giving out. And beneath the failing heart is another heart's strength — the ESV notes the Hebrew is rock. And my portion, which is the Levite's word from Psalm 16: no land, no share, God instead.

For behold, those who are far from you shall perish ... But for me it is good to be near God; I have made the Lord GOD my refuge, that I may tell of all your works.

The psalm ends by redefining wealth. The question was never who has more; it is who is near. It is good to be near God — that is the whole of his estate, and it is enough.

And the last clause turns him outward: that I may tell of all your works. The man who kept quiet in verse 15 to protect the young now has something to say to them. The doubt he refused to broadcast became a testimony worth publishing, which is why this psalm exists.

73.title: Until I Went into the Sanctuary
73.overview: Asaph opens with his conclusion — God is good to the pure in heart — and then admits how nearly he walked away: he envied the arrogant when he saw the prosperity of the wicked (vv. 1-3). They have no pangs, are fat and sleek, exempt from ordinary trouble, wearing pride like jewellery, setting their mouths against heaven and asking How can God know?, while God's own people drift after them (vv. 4-12). All in vain have I kept my heart clean (vv. 13-14). He would not say it aloud, for the sake of the young (v. 15); thinking it through exhausted him, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end (vv. 16-17) — slippery places, ruin in a moment, a dream on waking (vv. 18-20). He was brutish and beastlike, nevertheless God held his right hand and will receive him to glory (vv. 23-24). Whom have I in heaven but you? (vv. 25-26). It is good to be near God (vv. 27-28).
73.theology:
The crisis is envy, not persecution (v. 3) — the Psalter's recurring problem (37; 49; cf. Job 21:7; Jer 12:1) — and the psalm is honest that it nearly ended his faith (v. 2).

Prosperity is shown making its owners worse, not better (vv. 6-9), and the drift of God's own people after them is the darkest detail (v. 10).

Two things saved him. He would not broadcast the doubt, for the sake of younger believers (v. 15) — the difference between bringing doubt to God and unloading it on people not carrying it. And he went into the sanctuary (v. 17), where he received no new information but a different end of the same facts: the problem was not solvable by harder thinking.

Nevertheless (v. 23) is the hinge of grace: while he was brutish, God was holding his hand. Receive me to glory (v. 24) recalls Enoch, whom God took (Gen 5:24; cf. 49:15).

The cure for envy is not the suppression of desire but a greater one (v. 25), and wealth is redefined as nearness (v. 28). The doubt he refused to publish becomes the testimony this psalm is.
73.examples:
He tells you the ending first, because the middle is dark.

Almost and nearly: an inch from walking away.

Everyone gets their share of trouble, and these people seem skipped.

Pride worn like jewellery; a tongue that struts.

The worst detail: God's people drifting after them.

What saved him was not saying it out loud.

Not new information — the same facts from the other end.

Nevertheless: held while he was behaving like an animal.

Nobody argues himself out of envy; he is drawn out.

74.text: A Maskil of Asaph. 1O God, why do you cast us off forever? Why does your anger smoke against the sheep of your pasture?2Remember your congregation, which you have purchased of old, which you have redeemed to be the tribe of your heritage! Remember Mount Zion, where you have dwelt.3Direct your steps to the perpetual ruins; the enemy has destroyed everything in the sanctuary!4Your foes have roared in the midst of your meeting place; they set up their own signs for signs.5They were like those who swing axes in a forest of trees.6And all its carved wood they broke down with hatchets and hammers.7They set your sanctuary on fire; they profaned the dwelling place of your name, bringing it down to the ground.8They said to themselves, "We will utterly subdue them"; they burned all the meeting places of God in the land.9We do not see our signs; there is no longer any prophet, and there is none among us who knows how long.10How long, O God, is the foe to scoff? Is the enemy to revile your name forever?11Why do you hold back your hand, your right hand? Take it from the fold of your garment and destroy them!12Yet God my King is from of old, working salvation in the midst of the earth.13You divided the sea by your might; you broke the heads of the sea monsters on the waters.14You crushed the heads of Leviathan; you gave him as food for the creatures of the wilderness.15You split open springs and brooks; you dried up ever-flowing streams.16Yours is the day, yours also the night; you have established the heavenly lights and the sun.17You have fixed all the boundaries of the earth; you have made summer and winter.18Remember this, O LORD, how the enemy scoffs, and a foolish people reviles your name.19Do not deliver the soul of your dove to the wild beasts; do not forget the life of your poor forever.20Have regard for the covenant, for the dark places of the land are full of the habitations of violence.21Let not the downtrodden turn back in shame; let the poor and needy praise your name.22Arise, O God, defend your cause; remember how the foolish scoff at you all the day!23Do not forget the clamor of your foes, the uproar of those who rise against you, which goes up continually!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — There Is No Longer Any Prophet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O God, why do you cast us off forever? Remember your congregation and Mount Zion; the enemy has destroyed everything in the sanctuary (vv. 1-3). They roared in the meeting place, took axes to the carved wood, set the sanctuary on fire and burned every meeting place in the land (vv. 4-8). We do not see our signs; there is no longer any prophet, and there is none among us who knows how long (v. 9). How long, O God ... Why do you hold back your hand? (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The building is ashes, the prophets have stopped, and nobody can say how long it will last.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, why do you cast us off forever? Why does your anger smoke against the sheep of your pasture? Remember your congregation, which you have purchased of old, which you have redeemed to be the tribe of your heritage! Remember Mount Zion, where you have dwelt. Direct your steps to the perpetual ruins; the enemy has destroyed everything in the sanctuary! Your foes have roared in the midst of your meeting place; they set up their own signs for signs. They were like those who swing axes in a forest of trees. And all its carved wood they broke down with hatchets and hammers. They set your sanctuary on fire; they profaned the dwelling place of your name, bringing it down to the ground. They said to themselves, "We will utterly subdue them"; they burned all the meeting places of God in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O God, why do you cast us off forever? Why does your anger smoke against the sheep of your pasture? Remember your congregation, which you have purchased of old ... Remember Mount Zion, where you have dwelt. Direct your steps to the perpetual ruins; the enemy has destroyed everything in the sanctuary!

It is called a Maskil of Asaph, and it reads like instruction: somebody thought the congregation needed teaching how to pray in the worst year of its history, and this is the lesson.

This psalm is prayed in a ruin. The temple has been burned, and the congregation is asking God to come and walk through the rubble — direct your steps to the perpetual ruins, as you would ask someone to come and see what has happened to a house.

The arguments are all about ownership. The sheep of YOUR pasture, YOUR congregation, which you purchased and redeemed, and Zion where YOU have dwelt. They are not claiming to deserve rescue. They are pointing out whose property has been damaged.

Your foes have roared in the midst of your meeting place; they set up their own signs for signs. They were like those who swing axes in a forest of trees. And all its carved wood they broke down with hatchets and hammers. They set your sanctuary on fire; they profaned the dwelling place of your name, bringing it down to the ground.

The detail is that of a man who watched it. Soldiers shouting in the holy place; their own emblems planted where the signs of God's presence had been; and then the carved panelling — Solomon's cedar work, gourds and open flowers, a century of craftsmanship — attacked by men with axes as though they were clearing woodland. The ESV notes verse 5 is obscure in Hebrew; the picture is not.

Kings had burned the temple before, and the history books record it flatly: he burned the house of the LORD (2 Kgs 25:9). This is what it sounded like from inside.

verseByVerse.quote: We do not see our signs; there is no longer any prophet, and there is none among us who knows how long. How long, O God, is the foe to scoff? Is the enemy to revile your name forever? Why do you hold back your hand, your right hand? Take it from the fold of your garment and destroy them!
verseByVerse.commentary:
We do not see our signs; there is no longer any prophet, and there is none among us who knows how long.

This is the worst verse in the psalm, and it is not about the building. Three losses in one line. The visible signs of God's presence are gone. There is no prophet — nobody through whom God is currently speaking. And nobody can even say how long it will go on, which removes the last comfort available to people in trouble.

A congregation can survive a disaster if God is still talking. What this verse describes is disaster plus silence plus no end date, and any believer who has lived through a season when God seemed to have stopped speaking will recognise it.

How long, O God, is the foe to scoff? Is the enemy to revile your name forever? Why do you hold back your hand, your right hand? Take it from the fold of your garment and destroy them!

The image in verse 11 is extraordinary. The ESV notes the Hebrew is from your bosom: God is pictured with his right hand tucked inside his robe, like a man standing with his hands in his pockets while his house burns. Take it out, they say.

It is very bold and it is prayer. They are not describing God as he is; they are describing how his inaction looks, and asking him to change it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — Yet God My King Is from of Old
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Yet God my King is from of old, working salvation in the midst of the earth. You divided the sea by your might; you broke the heads of the sea monsters ... You crushed the heads of Leviathan (vv. 12-14). He split open springs and dried up rivers; Yours is the day, yours also the night ... You have fixed all the boundaries of the earth; you have made summer and winter (vv. 15-17).
verseByVerse.theology: With nothing left to point at in the present, he points backwards — to the sea, and to the calendar.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet God my King is from of old, working salvation in the midst of the earth. You divided the sea by your might; you broke the heads of the sea monsters on the waters. You crushed the heads of Leviathan; you gave him as food for the creatures of the wilderness. You split open springs and brooks; you dried up ever-flowing streams. Yours is the day, yours also the night; you have established the heavenly lights and the sun. You have fixed all the boundaries of the earth; you have made summer and winter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet God my King is from of old, working salvation in the midst of the earth.

Yet — and the psalm turns. But notice what it turns to, because this is the most instructive thing in it. There is no new promise here, no prophecy, no assurance about the future. He has nothing in the present to point at. So he points backwards.

You divided the sea by your might; you broke the heads of the sea monsters on the waters. You crushed the heads of Leviathan; you gave him as food for the creatures of the wilderness.

The sea divided is the exodus, and the monsters are the chaos powers of the old stories — the ESV notes they may simply be the great sea creatures — with Leviathan, the great sea dragon of Job 41 and Isaiah 27, broken and left out for scavengers. Egypt and the deep are remembered as one defeat.

You split open springs and brooks; you dried up ever-flowing streams. Yours is the day, yours also the night; you have established the heavenly lights and the sun. You have fixed all the boundaries of the earth; you have made summer and winter.

And then he goes wider still: water out of a rock, the Jordan dried up, day and night, sun and stars, the coastlines, the seasons. In a country where the sanctuary is a burnt-out shell, the sun still comes up and summer still follows spring, and he takes that as evidence.

This is how faith works when there is nothing in front of it: it reaches for what God has already done and what he is still visibly doing. The temple is gone; the calendar is his. Anyone praying in a ruin can still say verse 16.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — Do Not Forget the Life of Your Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Remember this, O LORD, how the enemy scoffs (v. 18). Do not deliver the soul of your dove to the wild beasts; do not forget the life of your poor forever (v. 19). Have regard for the covenant, for the dark places are full of violence (v. 20); let the downtrodden not be shamed (v. 21). Arise, O God, defend your cause ... Do not forget the clamor of your foes ... which goes up continually! (vv. 22-23).
verseByVerse.theology: The last claim they have is the covenant, and the psalm ends with the noise still going on.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember this, O LORD, how the enemy scoffs, and a foolish people reviles your name. Do not deliver the soul of your dove to the wild beasts; do not forget the life of your poor forever. Have regard for the covenant, for the dark places of the land are full of the habitations of violence. Let not the downtrodden turn back in shame; let the poor and needy praise your name. Arise, O God, defend your cause; remember how the foolish scoff at you all the day! Do not forget the clamor of your foes, the uproar of those who rise against you, which goes up continually!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember this, O LORD, how the enemy scoffs, and a foolish people reviles your name. Do not deliver the soul of your dove to the wild beasts; do not forget the life of your poor forever.

Your dove is the tenderest thing said about Israel in this psalm — not an army, not a nation: a bird with no defence at all, against wild animals. And the request is modest to the point of pathos: not victory, only that God should not forget.

Have regard for the covenant, for the dark places of the land are full of the habitations of violence.

Here is the one claim they have left, and it is the right one. Not their record — the burned temple is a judgment on that. The covenant: the agreement God made and bound himself to. When a believer has nothing else to plead, what remains is that God has given his word.

And the second half of the verse is a phrase for any age: the dark corners of a country fill up with violence when the light goes out. Where God is not feared, somebody always builds a house in the shadows.

Let not the downtrodden turn back in shame; let the poor and needy praise your name. Arise, O God, defend your cause; remember how the foolish scoff at you all the day! Do not forget the clamor of your foes, the uproar of those who rise against you, which goes up continually!

Notice whose cause it is: defend YOUR cause. Having appealed to God's ownership of the sheep, the city, the covenant, they end by handing him his own reputation as the reason to act.

And the psalm stops there. No answer comes, no fire falls, no promise is given. The last word is the noise of the enemies, still going up continually. Scripture leaves it unresolved because that is where the people who first sang it were living — and a congregation that has only psalms with happy endings has nothing to sing in a year like theirs.

74.title: Have Regard for the Covenant
74.overview: Prayed in the ruins of the burned temple. Why has God cast off the sheep of his pasture? Remember the congregation you purchased, and come and walk through the rubble (vv. 1-3). The enemy roared in the meeting place, took axes to the carved panelling, burned the sanctuary and every meeting place in the land (vv. 4-8). We do not see our signs; there is no longer any prophet, and there is none among us who knows how long (v. 9); why is God's right hand tucked inside his robe (vv. 10-11)? Yet God my King is from of old — he divided the sea, crushed Leviathan, split open springs, made day and night, sun and seasons (vv. 12-17). Remember the scoffing; do not give your dove to the beasts; have regard for the covenant; arise and defend your cause (vv. 18-23).
74.theology:
Every argument in the lament is about ownership — your sheep, congregation, Zion, sanctuary, name — not about merit (vv. 1-8).

Verse 9 names the worst loss: disaster plus silence plus no end date. A congregation can survive a catastrophe while God is still speaking.

The turn at v. 12 is the psalm's great lesson: with nothing to point at in the present, faith reaches for what God has already done (the sea, Leviathan) and what he is still visibly doing (day and night, sun and seasons). The sanctuary is ash; the calendar is his.

Israel is your dove (v. 19), and the only claim left is the covenant (v. 20) — God's own word, not their record. Where God is not feared, the dark places fill with violence.

The psalm ends unanswered, with the enemies' noise going up continually (v. 23): a church whose hymnbook has only resolved endings has nothing to sing in such a year.
74.examples:
Come and walk through the rubble.

Solomon's carved cedar, attacked as though it were woodland.

No signs, no prophet, and nobody who knows how long.

God's right hand tucked inside his robe.

Nothing to point at in the present, so he points backwards.

The temple is gone; the seasons are still his.

Your dove: a bird with no defence, against wild animals.

The last claim is the covenant, not the record.

75.text: To the choirmaster: according to Do Not Destroy. A Psalm of Asaph. A Song. 1We give thanks to you, O God; we give thanks, for your name is near. We recount your wondrous deeds.2"At the set time that I appoint I will judge with equity.3When the earth totters, and all its inhabitants, it is I who keep steady its pillars. Selah4I say to the boastful, 'Do not boast,' and to the wicked, 'Do not lift up your horn;5do not lift up your horn on high, or speak with haughty neck.'"6For not from the east or from the west and not from the wilderness comes lifting up,7but it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another.8For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, well mixed, and he pours out from it, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs.9But I will declare it forever; I will sing praises to the God of Jacob.10All the horns of the wicked I will cut off, but the horns of the righteous shall be lifted up.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — At the Set Time That I Appoint
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: We give thanks to you, O God ... for your name is near (v. 1). Then God speaks: At the set time that I appoint I will judge with equity. When the earth totters, and all its inhabitants, it is I who keep steady its pillars (vv. 2-3). I say to the boastful, Do not boast, and to the wicked, Do not lift up your horn ... or speak with haughty neck (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: God's first word about judgment is about its timing, and his second is to the people currently getting away with it.

verseByVerse.quote: We give thanks to you, O God; we give thanks, for your name is near. We recount your wondrous deeds. "At the set time that I appoint I will judge with equity. When the earth totters, and all its inhabitants, it is I who keep steady its pillars. Selah I say to the boastful, 'Do not boast,' and to the wicked, 'Do not lift up your horn; do not lift up your horn on high, or speak with haughty neck.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
We give thanks to you, O God; we give thanks, for your name is near. We recount your wondrous deeds.

The reason given for the thanks is unusual: your name is near. Not that the trouble has ended — that God is not far off. And the congregation's activity is recounting: going over the deeds again, out loud, together.

At the set time that I appoint I will judge with equity. When the earth totters, and all its inhabitants, it is I who keep steady its pillars.

God speaks, and his first sentence is about the diary. At the set time that I appoint — the delay everyone complains about in these psalms is here revealed as an appointment already in the book. Judgment is not late; it is scheduled.

And while the world wobbles, someone is holding it up. It is I who keep steady its pillars: the tottering is real, and so is the hand under the floor. God is not merely going to judge the world at the end; he is keeping it standing in the meantime.

I say to the boastful, Do not boast, and to the wicked, Do not lift up your horn; do not lift up your horn on high, or speak with haughty neck.

The horn is the ancient image of strength — what a bull has and uses. To "lift up the horn" is to throw your weight around, and the psalm adds the physical detail of the haughty neck, the posture of a man who has stopped looking up because he has decided there is nothing above him.

Note who is being addressed. God is speaking directly to the people who are currently getting away with it, and what he says is a warning rather than a sentence. Even here, the door is open.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–10 — The Cup in the Hand of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For not from the east or from the west and not from the wilderness comes lifting up, but it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another (vv. 6-7). For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, well mixed, and he pours out from it, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (v. 8). But I will declare it forever ... All the horns of the wicked I will cut off, but the horns of the righteous shall be lifted up (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: Promotion comes from no direction on the compass, and there is a cup being kept for those who rose without him.

verseByVerse.quote: For not from the east or from the west and not from the wilderness comes lifting up, but it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another. For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, well mixed, and he pours out from it, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs. But I will declare it forever; I will sing praises to the God of Jacob. All the horns of the wicked I will cut off, but the horns of the righteous shall be lifted up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For not from the east or from the west and not from the wilderness comes lifting up, but it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another.

The psalm rules out three directions of the compass — east, west, the southern desert — and leaves the fourth unspoken, because north is where God's mountain is. Promotion does not come over any horizon. There is no geography of advancement, no useful direction to look in.

Putting down one and lifting up another is the great levelling sentence, and Scripture keeps saying it. Hannah sang, The LORD makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and he exalts (1 Sam 2:7). Mary sang, he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate (Luke 1:52). Every career, every dynasty, every collapse: one hand.

For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, well mixed, and he pours out from it, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs.

The image is of a cup that has been standing ready — well mixed, prepared with care, foaming at the brim. Judgment in this psalm is not an outburst; it is something poured out from a vessel that has been in God's hand the whole time.

Jeremiah was told to take this cup round the nations and make them drink (Jer 25:15). John saw it at the end (Rev 14:10). And in a garden one night a man who had never lifted his horn asked whether that cup could pass from him, and then drank it. The wicked drain it down to the dregs in this psalm; at Golgotha someone else did, for people who deserved it.

But I will declare it forever; I will sing praises to the God of Jacob. All the horns of the wicked I will cut off, but the horns of the righteous shall be lifted up.

The psalm ends with the horn image resolved. The same verb does both jobs: the horns that were lifted up get cut off, and the horns of people who never raised theirs are lifted — by God, which is the only way anyone in this psalm rises at all.

75.title: It Is God Who Executes Judgment
75.overview: Thanks are given because God's name is near (v. 1). Then God himself speaks: At the set time that I appoint I will judge with equity, and while the earth totters he keeps its pillars steady (vv. 2-3); he warns the boastful not to lift up their horn or speak with haughty neck (vv. 4-5). Promotion comes from no direction of the compass: it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another (vv. 6-7). In his hand is a cup of foaming wine which the wicked will drain to the dregs (v. 8). The psalmist will sing forever, for the horns of the wicked will be cut off and the horns of the righteous lifted up (vv. 9-10).
75.theology:
God's first word about judgment concerns timing: the delay is an appointment, not a failure (v. 2). Meanwhile he holds the tottering world up (v. 3).

He addresses the people currently getting away with it, and speaks warning rather than sentence (vv. 4-5): the raised horn and the stiff neck are the posture of a man who has stopped looking up.

There is no geography of advancement (v. 6). Every rise and fall is one hand's work (v. 7), as Hannah and Mary both sang (1 Sam 2:7; Luke 1:52).

The cup has been standing ready, carefully mixed (v. 8; cf. Jer 25:15; Rev 14:10) — and in Gethsemane one who never lifted his horn asked whether it might pass, and drank it instead.

The same verb cuts off and lifts up (v. 10): the only way anyone rises in this psalm is by God's hand.
75.examples:
Thanks because the name is near, not because the trouble ended.

Judgment is not late; it is in the diary.

The tottering is real, and so is the hand under the floor.

A haughty neck: the posture of a man who has stopped looking up.

Three directions ruled out, and no useful horizon left.

A cup mixed in advance and kept in his hand.

Someone else drained it in a garden.

Horns cut off, horns lifted: the same hand.

76.text: To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments. A Psalm of Asaph. A Song. 1In Judah God is known; his name is great in Israel.2His abode has been established in Salem, his dwelling place in Zion.3There he broke the flashing arrows, the shield, the sword, and the weapons of war. Selah4Glorious are you, more majestic than the mountains full of prey.5The stouthearted were stripped of their spoil; they sank into sleep; all the men of war were unable to use their hands.6At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, both rider and horse lay stunned.7But you, you are to be feared! Who can stand before you when once your anger is roused?8From the heavens you uttered judgment; the earth feared and was still,9when God arose to establish judgment, to save all the humble of the earth. Selah10Surely the wrath of man shall praise you; the remnant of wrath you will put on like a belt.11Make your vows to the LORD your God and perform them; let all around him bring gifts to him who is to be feared,12who cuts off the spirit of princes, who is to be feared by the kings of the earth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — There He Broke the Flashing Arrows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Judah God is known; his name is great in Israel. His abode has been established in Salem, his dwelling place in Zion (vv. 1-2). There he broke the flashing arrows, the shield, the sword, and the weapons of war (v. 3). More majestic than mountains full of prey, he stripped the stouthearted of their spoil; they sank into sleep and the men of war could not use their hands; at your rebuke, O God of Jacob, both rider and horse lay stunned (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The city whose name means peace is where God snaps the weapons, while the soldiers sleep.

verseByVerse.quote: In Judah God is known; his name is great in Israel. His abode has been established in Salem, his dwelling place in Zion. There he broke the flashing arrows, the shield, the sword, and the weapons of war. Selah Glorious are you, more majestic than the mountains full of prey. The stouthearted were stripped of their spoil; they sank into sleep; all the men of war were unable to use their hands. At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, both rider and horse lay stunned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Judah God is known; his name is great in Israel. His abode has been established in Salem, his dwelling place in Zion.

Salem is the old name of Jerusalem, the city of Melchizedek (Gen 14:18), and it means peace. The psalm uses the ancient name deliberately, because of what happens in the next verse: the city called Peace is where God destroys the weapons.

There he broke the flashing arrows, the shield, the sword, and the weapons of war.

Four items, itemised like an inventory after a battle, and every one of them is broken rather than captured. This is Psalm 46's God, who breaks the bow and shatters the spear. He does not disarm his enemies by taking their equipment for his own use; he ends its usefulness.

Glorious are you, more majestic than the mountains full of prey. The stouthearted were stripped of their spoil; they sank into sleep; all the men of war were unable to use their hands. At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, both rider and horse lay stunned.

The detail is eerie, and it reads like an eyewitness account of the morning after. The stouthearted — the elite, the brave ones — have been robbed of the plunder they came for. Hands that were trained for war cannot be used. Men and horses lie stunned.

And nobody on Israel's side has done anything. They sank into sleep: the great victory happened while the soldiers were unconscious. Jerusalem watched this at least once, when an Assyrian army camped outside her walls and the city woke to find it dead (2 Kgs 19:35).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Surely the Wrath of Man Shall Praise You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But you, you are to be feared! Who can stand before you when once your anger is roused? (v. 7). From the heavens you uttered judgment; the earth feared and was still, when God arose to establish judgment, to save all the humble of the earth (vv. 8-9). Surely the wrath of man shall praise you; the remnant of wrath you will put on like a belt (v. 10). Make your vows and perform them, and bring gifts to him who cuts off the spirit of princes (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: God rises to judge, and the sentence says what that is for: to save the humble.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, you are to be feared! Who can stand before you when once your anger is roused? From the heavens you uttered judgment; the earth feared and was still, when God arose to establish judgment, to save all the humble of the earth. Selah Surely the wrath of man shall praise you; the remnant of wrath you will put on like a belt. Make your vows to the LORD your God and perform them; let all around him bring gifts to him who is to be feared, who cuts off the spirit of princes, who is to be feared by the kings of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you, you are to be feared! Who can stand before you when once your anger is roused?

The question is not rhetorical decoration. Everyone in the psalm who tried to stand is lying down.

From the heavens you uttered judgment; the earth feared and was still, when God arose to establish judgment, to save all the humble of the earth.

Two things to notice. First, what God does is utter — the weapons in verse 3 were broken by a sentence, and the whole earth went quiet the way a room does when someone in authority speaks.

Second, and more important, the purpose clause: God arose to establish judgment to save all the humble of the earth. Judgment and salvation are not two separate divine activities; they are the same act seen from two sides. The stopping of the violent is the rescue of the people underneath them. Anyone who wishes God were less severe should ask what that would mean for the humble of the earth, who are relying on exactly this.

Surely the wrath of man shall praise you; the remnant of wrath you will put on like a belt.

Here is the great sentence of the psalm, and it is one of the boldest claims in Scripture. Human rage — which intends nothing but destruction — will end up adding to God's praise. Not that God approves of it, and not that it becomes harmless; but when it has done its worst, the result will be his glory.

The church's founding example is the cross. Peter preached it exactly this way: Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and also crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). The wrath of man did its very worst and produced the salvation of the world. Paul generalises it: God works all things together for good for those who love him (Rom 8:28).

And the second half of the verse is stranger and better: the remnant of wrath you will put on like a belt. Whatever rage is left over, after it has been made to serve his purposes, God fastens round himself as an ornament. The ESV notes the word may be extremity. Either way, the leftovers of human fury end up as part of God's dress.

Make your vows to the LORD your God and perform them; let all around him bring gifts to him who is to be feared, who cuts off the spirit of princes, who is to be feared by the kings of the earth.

The right response to all this is two practical things: keep your promises to God, and bring him something. And the psalm ends by naming the audience it wants: the kings of the earth. The God who breaks arrows in the city of peace, and who cuts off the spirit of princes — deflating them, taking the wind out — is the one every government should be afraid of, and generally is not.

76.title: The Wrath of Man Shall Praise You
76.overview: God is known in Judah and lives in Salem — the old name of Jerusalem, which means peace — and there he broke the flashing arrows, the shield, the sword, and the weapons of war (vv. 1-3). The elite were stripped of their plunder, sank into sleep, and could not use their hands; rider and horse lay stunned at his rebuke (vv. 4-6). Who can stand before him (v. 7)? From the heavens you uttered judgment; the earth feared and was still, when God arose to establish judgment, to save all the humble of the earth (vv. 8-9). Surely the wrath of man shall praise you; the remnant of wrath you will put on like a belt (v. 10). So make vows and keep them, and bring gifts to the God whom the kings of the earth should fear (vv. 11-12).
76.theology:
The city called Peace is where God breaks the weapons (vv. 2-3; cf. 46:9): they are destroyed rather than captured. The victory is won while Israel's soldiers are asleep (v. 5; cf. 2 Kgs 19:35).

God's judgment is spoken, and the earth goes quiet (v. 8).

Verse 9 states the purpose: God arose to judge to save all the humble of the earth. Judgment and salvation are one act seen from two sides — stopping the violent is rescuing those underneath them.

Verse 10 is among the boldest claims in Scripture: human rage, intending only destruction, ends up adding to God's praise — the cross being the founding example (Acts 2:23; cf. Rom 8:28) — and the surplus is worn like a belt.

The response asked for is vows kept and gifts brought (v. 11), and the audience named is the kings of the earth, before the God who cuts off the spirit of princes (v. 12).
76.examples:
The city whose name means peace, and the broken arrows in it.

Weapons ended, not confiscated.

Trained hands that cannot be used.

The victory won while the soldiers slept.

The earth going quiet the way a room does.

Ask what a less severe God would mean for the humble.

Human fury doing its worst, and producing salvation.

The leftovers of rage worn as a belt.

77.text: To the choirmaster: according to Jeduthun. A Psalm of Asaph. 1I cry aloud to God, aloud to God, and he will hear me.2In the day of my trouble I seek the Lord; in the night my hand is stretched out without wearying; my soul refuses to be comforted.3When I remember God, I moan; when I meditate, my spirit faints. Selah4You hold my eyelids open; I am so troubled that I cannot speak.5I consider the days of old, the years long ago.6I said, "Let me remember my song in the night; let me meditate in my heart." Then my spirit made a diligent search:7"Will the Lord spurn forever, and never again be favorable?8Has his steadfast love forever ceased? Are his promises at an end for all time?9Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has he in anger shut up his compassion?" Selah10Then I said, "I will appeal to this, to the years of the right hand of the Most High."11I will remember the deeds of the LORD; yes, I will remember your wonders of old.12I will ponder all your work, and meditate on your mighty deeds.13Your way, O God, is holy. What god is great like our God?14You are the God who works wonders; you have made known your might among the peoples.15You with your arm redeemed your people, the children of Jacob and Joseph. Selah16When the waters saw you, O God, when the waters saw you, they were afraid; indeed, the deep trembled.17The clouds poured out water; the skies gave forth thunder; your arrows flashed on every side.18The crash of your thunder was in the whirlwind; your lightnings lighted up the world; the earth trembled and shook.19Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters; yet your footprints were unseen.20You led your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — My Soul Refuses to Be Comforted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I cry aloud to God ... In the day of my trouble I seek the Lord; in the night my hand is stretched out without wearying; my soul refuses to be comforted (vv. 1-2). Remembering God makes him moan; you hold my eyelids open; I am so troubled that I cannot speak (vv. 3-4). He considers the days of old and searches (vv. 5-6): Will the Lord spurn forever ... Has his steadfast love forever ceased? ... Has God forgotten to be gracious? (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Six questions a believer is allowed to ask out loud, in a night God is keeping him awake through.

verseByVerse.quote: I cry aloud to God, aloud to God, and he will hear me. In the day of my trouble I seek the Lord; in the night my hand is stretched out without wearying; my soul refuses to be comforted. When I remember God, I moan; when I meditate, my spirit faints. Selah You hold my eyelids open; I am so troubled that I cannot speak. I consider the days of old, the years long ago. I said, "Let me remember my song in the night; let me meditate in my heart." Then my spirit made a diligent search: "Will the Lord spurn forever, and never again be favorable? Has his steadfast love forever ceased? Are his promises at an end for all time? Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has he in anger shut up his compassion?" Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
I cry aloud to God, aloud to God, and he will hear me. In the day of my trouble I seek the Lord; in the night my hand is stretched out without wearying; my soul refuses to be comforted.

He is praying with his voice and with his body — my hand is stretched out all night, and it does not get tired. What has given up is something else: my soul refuses to be comforted.

Notice that he says it about himself. This is not a complaint that people are comforting him badly. He knows that consolation is being offered and that something in him will not take it. Anyone who has been in that state knows how accurate the word refuses is.

When I remember God, I moan; when I meditate, my spirit faints.

And here is the frightening part. The things that normally help are making it worse. Thinking about God produces a groan; meditating leaves him fainting. The medicine has stopped working.

You hold my eyelids open; I am so troubled that I cannot speak.

He names God as the cause of his insomnia — not the enemy, not anxiety: you hold my eyelids open. And the man who was crying aloud in verse 1 has now lost his words altogether.

I consider the days of old, the years long ago. I said, Let me remember my song in the night; let me meditate in my heart. Then my spirit made a diligent search.

He goes looking in the past, and specifically for a song — something he used to sing in nights like this. The ESV notes the Hebrew lacks I said; the searching is the point. And what the diligent search turns up is not comfort but six terrible questions.

Will the Lord spurn forever, and never again be favorable? Has his steadfast love forever ceased? Are his promises at an end for all time? Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has he in anger shut up his compassion?

Read them slowly, because the Psalter has put them in the hymnbook and they are asked by a believer. Has the covenant love stopped? Have the promises expired? Has God forgotten to be gracious — not refused, forgotten, as a man forgets a habit? Has compassion been locked up somewhere out of reach?

These are the questions people are ashamed to say aloud in church, and here they are, set to music and handed to the choirmaster. God is not injured by them. What he has actually done with them is preserve them, so that the next believer awake at four in the morning knows he is not the first.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — I Will Remember the Deeds of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then I said, I will appeal to this, to the years of the right hand of the Most High (v. 10). I will remember the deeds of the LORD; yes, I will remember your wonders of old. I will ponder all your work, and meditate on your mighty deeds (vv. 11-12). Your way, O God, is holy. What god is great like our God? He works wonders and redeemed his people with his arm (vv. 13-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Four deliberate verbs, applied by a sleepless man to himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said, "I will appeal to this, to the years of the right hand of the Most High." I will remember the deeds of the LORD; yes, I will remember your wonders of old. I will ponder all your work, and meditate on your mighty deeds. Your way, O God, is holy. What god is great like our God? You are the God who works wonders; you have made known your might among the peoples. You with your arm redeemed your people, the children of Jacob and Joseph. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I said, I will appeal to this, to the years of the right hand of the Most High.

Here is the turn, and the ESV notes that the verse can be read two ways. Either it is the decision the translation gives — I will appeal to this, I will take my stand on the years when God's right hand was at work — or it is the bottom of the pit: "This is my grief: that the right hand of the Most High has changed."

The two readings are not as far apart as they look. Either he says "God's right hand has altered, and that is what is killing me", and then immediately goes to work on the memory of that hand; or he says "the years of that right hand are my appeal". Both hinge on the same thing: the hand of God in the past, brought into the present.

I will remember the deeds of the LORD; yes, I will remember your wonders of old. I will ponder all your work, and meditate on your mighty deeds.

Four deliberate verbs — remember, remember, ponder, meditate — all in the future tense, all first person. Nobody does this for him. This is a man in the dark administering the only treatment available: going back over what God has actually done.

And it is exactly what he was doing in verse 3, when remembering God made him moan. The difference is the object. There he remembered God in the abstract and it hurt; here he remembers deeds, wonders, work, mighty deeds — specific things God did on particular days. Vague thoughts about God will not hold a man up at night. Facts will.

Your way, O God, is holy. What god is great like our God? You are the God who works wonders; you have made known your might among the peoples. You with your arm redeemed your people.

The questions of verses 7-9 are not answered one by one. They are simply left behind, because the man asking them has started looking at something else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–20 — Your Way Was Through the Sea
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the waters saw you, O God ... they were afraid; indeed, the deep trembled; clouds poured, thunder crashed, lightning lit the world and the earth shook (vv. 16-18). Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters; yet your footprints were unseen. You led your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron (vv. 19-20).
verseByVerse.theology: The great rescue left no tracks — and the psalm ends there, with the flock and the shepherds.

verseByVerse.quote: When the waters saw you, O God, when the waters saw you, they were afraid; indeed, the deep trembled. The clouds poured out water; the skies gave forth thunder; your arrows flashed on every side. The crash of your thunder was in the whirlwind; your lightnings lighted up the world; the earth trembled and shook. Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters; yet your footprints were unseen. You led your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the waters saw you, O God, when the waters saw you, they were afraid; indeed, the deep trembled. The clouds poured out water; the skies gave forth thunder; your arrows flashed on every side. The crash of your thunder was in the whirlwind; your lightnings lighted up the world; the earth trembled and shook.

This is the exodus, and he tells it as a thunderstorm. Exodus 14 says a strong east wind drove the sea back; this psalm hears the thunder and sees the lightning going off like arrows, with the sea itself frightened at the sight of God.

The man who could not speak in verse 4 is now describing the biggest thing that ever happened to his people, in detail, at length. That is what the four verbs of verse 11 produced.

Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters; yet your footprints were unseen.

And here is the verse the whole psalm has been walking towards. God went through the sea — and left no tracks. The ESV notes the Hebrew is that his footprints were unknown.

Hold that against verses 7-9. He could not see what God was doing; he asked whether God had stopped caring; and the greatest rescue in the history of his nation had been carried out by a God who leaves no footprints. The absence of evidence in the sand was never evidence of absence. He had been walking there the whole time.

That is the answer to the six questions, and it is not an explanation. It is a fact about how God works: invisibly, in deep water, and afterwards you find that a nation got across.

You led your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron.

The psalm ends abruptly, on a quiet domestic image after all that thunder. No footprints, but there were two men walking in front with the people following, and the psalm calls that God's leading. He guides by ordinary hands — a brother and a brother, a pastor, a friend — and the flock gets home.

And it ends there, with no word about the psalmist's own trouble. Nothing in his situation is said to have changed. He simply stops talking about himself and finishes looking at the sea.

77.title: Your Footprints Were Unseen
77.overview: He cries aloud, stretches out his hand all night, and his soul refuses to be comforted; remembering God makes him moan, and God holds his eyelids open (vv. 1-4). Searching the past brings up six questions: has the Lord spurned forever, has his steadfast love ceased, are his promises at an end, has God forgotten to be gracious, has he shut up his compassion (vv. 5-9)? Then the turn: I will appeal to this, to the years of the right hand of the Most High (v. 10), and four deliberate verbs — remember, remember, ponder, meditate (vv. 11-12). God's way is holy; he works wonders and redeemed his people with his arm (vv. 13-15). The exodus is retold as a thunderstorm, with the waters afraid and the deep trembling (vv. 16-18), and it ends: Your way was through the sea ... yet your footprints were unseen. You led your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron (vv. 19-20).
77.theology:
My soul refuses to be comforted is said by the sufferer about himself (v. 2), and God is named as the one holding his eyes open (v. 4). Even prayer and meditation can make things worse for a time (v. 3).

The six questions of vv. 7-9 are preserved in the hymnbook: God is not injured by them, and their preservation tells the next believer awake at four in the morning that he is not the first.

The turn (v. 10) is textually two-sided, but either reading hinges on the right hand of God remembered — and the cure is self-administered in four deliberate verbs (vv. 11-12). What changed was the object: remembering God in the abstract hurt (v. 3); remembering his deeds held.

The questions are never answered one by one; they are left behind.

Verse 19 is the psalm's answer in a fact rather than an explanation: at the exodus God left no footprints. The absence of visible tracks was never evidence of absence — and he led that invisible way by two ordinary men (v. 20).
77.examples:
A hand stretched out all night that does not get tired.

The medicine that has stopped working.

Naming God as the cause of the insomnia.

Six questions set to music and handed to the choirmaster.

Remember, remember, ponder, meditate — self-administered.

Vague thoughts about God will not hold you at night; facts will.

A rescue that left no tracks in the sand.

Invisible leading, by way of two men walking in front.

78.text: A Maskil of Asaph. 1Give ear, O my people, to my teaching; incline your ears to the words of my mouth!2I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter dark sayings from of old,3things that we have heard and known, that our fathers have told us.4We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD, and his might, and the wonders that he has done.5He established a testimony in Jacob and appointed a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers to teach to their children,6that the next generation might know them, the children yet unborn, and arise and tell them to their children,7so that they should set their hope in God and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments;8and that they should not be like their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation, a generation whose heart was not steadfast, whose spirit was not faithful to God.9The Ephraimites, armed with the bow, turned back on the day of battle.10They did not keep God's covenant, but refused to walk according to his law.11They forgot his works and the wonders that he had shown them.12In the sight of their fathers he performed wonders in the land of Egypt, in the fields of Zoan.13He divided the sea and let them pass through it, and made the waters stand like a heap.14In the daytime he led them with a cloud, and all the night with a fiery light.15He split rocks in the wilderness and gave them drink abundantly as from the deep.16He made streams come out of the rock and caused waters to flow down like rivers.17Yet they sinned still more against him, rebelling against the Most High in the desert.18They tested God in their heart by demanding the food they craved.19They spoke against God, saying, "Can God spread a table in the wilderness?20He struck the rock so that water gushed out and streams overflowed. Can he also give bread or provide meat for his people?"21Therefore, when the LORD heard, he was full of wrath; a fire was kindled against Jacob; his anger rose against Israel,22because they did not believe in God and did not trust his saving power.23Yet he commanded the skies above and opened the doors of heaven,24and he rained down on them manna to eat and gave them the grain of heaven.25Man ate of the bread of the angels; he sent them food in abundance.26He caused the east wind to blow in the heavens, and by his power he led out the south wind;27he rained meat on them like dust, winged birds like the sand of the seas;28he let them fall in the midst of their camp, all around their dwellings.29And they ate and were well filled, for he gave them what they craved.30But before they had satisfied their craving, while the food was still in their mouths,31the anger of God rose against them, and he killed the strongest of them and laid low the young men of Israel.32In spite of all this, they still sinned; despite his wonders, they did not believe.33So he made their days vanish like a breath, and their years in terror.34When he killed them, they sought him; they repented and sought God earnestly.35They remembered that God was their rock, the Most High God their redeemer.36But they flattered him with their mouths; they lied to him with their tongues.37Their heart was not steadfast toward him; they were not faithful to his covenant.38Yet he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity and did not destroy them; he restrained his anger often and did not stir up all his wrath.39He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again.40How often they rebelled against him in the wilderness and grieved him in the desert!41They tested God again and again and provoked the Holy One of Israel.42They did not remember his power or the day when he redeemed them from the foe,43when he performed his signs in Egypt and his marvels in the fields of Zoan.44He turned their rivers to blood, so that they could not drink of their streams.45He sent among them swarms of flies, which devoured them, and frogs, which destroyed them.46He gave their crops to the destroying locust and the fruit of their labor to the locust.47He destroyed their vines with hail and their sycamores with frost.48He gave over their cattle to the hail and their flocks to thunderbolts.49He let loose on them his burning anger, wrath, indignation, and distress, a company of destroying angels.50He made a path for his anger; he did not spare them from death, but gave their lives over to the plague.51He struck down every firstborn in Egypt, the firstfruits of their strength in the tents of Ham.52Then he led out his people like sheep and guided them in the wilderness like a flock.53He led them in safety, so that they were not afraid, but the sea overwhelmed their enemies.54And he brought them to his holy land, to the mountain which his right hand had won.55He drove out nations before them; he apportioned them for a possession and settled the tribes of Israel in their tents.56Yet they tested and rebelled against the Most High God and did not keep his testimonies,57but turned away and acted treacherously like their fathers; they twisted like a deceitful bow.58For they provoked him to anger with their high places; they moved him to jealousy with their idols.59When God heard, he was full of wrath, and he utterly rejected Israel.60He forsook his dwelling at Shiloh, the tent where he dwelt among mankind,61and delivered his power to captivity, his glory to the hand of the foe.62He gave his people over to the sword and vented his wrath on his heritage.63Fire devoured their young men, and their young women had no marriage song.64Their priests fell by the sword, and their widows made no lamentation.65Then the Lord awoke as from sleep, like a strong man shouting because of wine.66And he put his adversaries to rout; he put them to everlasting shame.67He rejected the tent of Joseph; he did not choose the tribe of Ephraim,68but he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loves.69He built his sanctuary like the high heavens, like the earth, which he has founded forever.70He chose David his servant and took him from the sheepfolds;71from following the nursing ewes he brought him to shepherd Jacob his people, Israel his inheritance.72With upright heart he shepherded them and guided them with his skillful hand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — That the Next Generation Might Know
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Give ear, O my people, to my teaching ... I will open my mouth in a parable (vv. 1-2). What the fathers told them we will not hide ... but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD (vv. 3-4), so that the next generation might know them, the children yet unborn, and set their hope in God and not forget the works of God ... and that they should not be like their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation (vv. 5-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Seventy-two verses of national history, and the stated reason is the children.

verseByVerse.quote: Give ear, O my people, to my teaching; incline your ears to the words of my mouth! I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter dark sayings from of old, things that we have heard and known, that our fathers have told us. We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD, and his might, and the wonders that he has done. He established a testimony in Jacob and appointed a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers to teach to their children, that the next generation might know them, the children yet unborn, and arise and tell them to their children, so that they should set their hope in God and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments; and that they should not be like their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation, a generation whose heart was not steadfast, whose spirit was not faithful to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give ear, O my people, to my teaching; incline your ears to the words of my mouth! I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter dark sayings from of old.

It is a Maskil, and it reads as instruction — the longest such psalm in the Psalter. Asaph is teaching, and the classroom is the whole congregation with its children in it.

Matthew quotes verse 2 of Jesus' parables: I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world (Matt 13:35). A dark saying is not obscure for the sake of it; it is a truth that has to be worked at, and history is exactly that — the facts are public and the meaning has to be taught.

Things that we have heard and known, that our fathers have told us. We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD.

Here is the chain: the fathers told us, and we will not hide it from their children. Three generations in one sentence, with the psalmist's generation in the middle as the link that could break.

He established a testimony in Jacob and appointed a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers to teach to their children, that the next generation might know them, the children yet unborn, and arise and tell them to their children, so that they should set their hope in God and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments.

Four generations now, and the teaching is commanded. And read the stated purpose, because it is the whole reason this long psalm exists: so that children would set their hope in God, not forget, and keep his commandments. Hope, memory, obedience — in that order.

And that they should not be like their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation.

Which tells you what kind of history lesson is coming. It is not a heritage pageant. The point of telling children about their ancestors is so that they will not repeat them.

That is a rare and healthy thing in a national story. Israel's songbook contains a seventy-two verse account of her own failures, taught to her children on purpose, and the church that sings it should be equally honest about its own past.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–39 — Can God Spread a Table in the Wilderness?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ephraim turned back on the day of battle and forgot God's works (vv. 9-11). He divided the sea, led them with cloud and fire, and split rocks for water (vv. 12-16) — yet they demanded food and asked, Can God spread a table in the wilderness? (vv. 17-20). He rained down manna, the bread of the angels, and meat like dust (vv. 21-29), and judgment fell while the food was in their mouths (vv. 30-33). When he killed them they sought him, but they flattered him with their mouths (vv. 34-37). Yet he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity and did not destroy them (vv. 38-39).
verseByVerse.theology: Wonder, forgetting, rebellion, judgment — and then the verse the whole psalm turns on.

verseByVerse.quote: The Ephraimites, armed with the bow, turned back on the day of battle. They did not keep God's covenant, but refused to walk according to his law. They forgot his works and the wonders that he had shown them. In the sight of their fathers he performed wonders in the land of Egypt, in the fields of Zoan. He divided the sea and let them pass through it, and made the waters stand like a heap. In the daytime he led them with a cloud, and all the night with a fiery light. He split rocks in the wilderness and gave them drink abundantly as from the deep. He made streams come out of the rock and caused waters to flow down like rivers. Yet they sinned still more against him, rebelling against the Most High in the desert. They tested God in their heart by demanding the food they craved. They spoke against God, saying, "Can God spread a table in the wilderness? He struck the rock so that water gushed out and streams overflowed. Can he also give bread or provide meat for his people?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Ephraimites, armed with the bow, turned back on the day of battle. They did not keep God's covenant, but refused to walk according to his law. They forgot his works and the wonders that he had shown them.

Ephraim is named first and will be named last (v. 67). They were armed — the ESV notes the Hebrew is armed and shooting — and they ran anyway. The equipment was not the problem.

And the diagnosis is given at once: they forgot his works. Forgetting is the sin this psalm is written against, and it is not a lapse of memory but a failure to keep rehearsing what God has done, which is why the remedy in verses 4-6 is telling the story.

In the sight of their fathers he performed wonders in the land of Egypt ... He divided the sea and let them pass through it, and made the waters stand like a heap. In the daytime he led them with a cloud, and all the night with a fiery light. He split rocks in the wilderness and gave them drink abundantly as from the deep.

Four wonders in four verses: the plagues, the sea, the pillar, the rock. Paul says of the rock that they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ (1 Cor 10:4) — and then warns the Corinthians, using this very history, not to repeat it.

Yet they sinned still more against him ... They tested God in their heart by demanding the food they craved. They spoke against God, saying, Can God spread a table in the wilderness? He struck the rock so that water gushed out ... Can he also give bread or provide meat for his people?

The question is the most revealing sentence in the psalm. Can God spread a table in the wilderness? They ask it with wet mouths. The water from the rock is still running while they wonder aloud whether God can manage food.

That is how unbelief works, and it is recognisable in ourselves. It does not deny the last mercy; it simply cannot see how the next one could possibly arrive. Every Christian who has thanked God for one answered prayer on Sunday and panicked about the next thing on Monday has asked verse 19.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, when the LORD heard, he was full of wrath; a fire was kindled against Jacob; his anger rose against Israel, because they did not believe in God and did not trust his saving power. Yet he commanded the skies above and opened the doors of heaven, and he rained down on them manna to eat and gave them the grain of heaven. Man ate of the bread of the angels; he sent them food in abundance. He caused the east wind to blow in the heavens, and by his power he led out the south wind; he rained meat on them like dust, winged birds like the sand of the seas; he let them fall in the midst of their camp, all around their dwellings. And they ate and were well filled, for he gave them what they craved. But before they had satisfied their craving, while the food was still in their mouths, the anger of God rose against them, and he killed the strongest of them and laid low the young men of Israel. In spite of all this, they still sinned; despite his wonders, they did not believe. So he made their days vanish like a breath, and their years in terror. When he killed them, they sought him; they repented and sought God earnestly. They remembered that God was their rock, the Most High God their redeemer. But they flattered him with their mouths; they lied to him with their tongues. Their heart was not steadfast toward him; they were not faithful to his covenant. Yet he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity and did not destroy them; he restrained his anger often and did not stir up all his wrath. He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, when the LORD heard, he was full of wrath ... because they did not believe in God and did not trust his saving power. Yet he commanded the skies above and opened the doors of heaven, and he rained down on them manna to eat and gave them the grain of heaven. Man ate of the bread of the angels.

Watch the sequence: anger, and then bread. He was full of wrath, and he opened the doors of heaven and fed them anyway. The bread of the angels is the psalm's own phrase for manna, and Jesus took the argument up in Capernaum: their fathers ate manna and died, and he is the bread that came down from heaven (John 6:31-35).

He caused the east wind to blow ... he rained meat on them like dust, winged birds like the sand of the seas ... And they ate and were well filled, for he gave them what they craved. But before they had satisfied their craving, while the food was still in their mouths, the anger of God rose against them.

This is one of the most sobering passages in the Old Testament. They got exactly what they asked for — he gave them what they craved — and it killed them. A granted request can be a judgment. Some prayers are answered as a severity.

In spite of all this, they still sinned; despite his wonders, they did not believe ... When he killed them, they sought him; they repented and sought God earnestly. They remembered that God was their rock ... But they flattered him with their mouths; they lied to him with their tongues. Their heart was not steadfast toward him.

And here is the anatomy of shallow repentance. Under judgment they sought God earnestly — and it was flattery. They said the right things because they were frightened, and the psalm, which can see the heart, calls it lying. Anyone can produce religion in a crisis; the question is what happens when the pressure lifts.

Yet he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity and did not destroy them; he restrained his anger often and did not stir up all his wrath. He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again.

Here is the verse the whole psalm turns on, and it repays reading twice. After the craving, the lying and the flattery: YET HE, BEING COMPASSIONATE, ATONED for their iniquity. The word is the Day of Atonement word: God covered it himself.

He restrained his anger often — often, because they needed it often. And the reason given is not anything in them but a fact about them: he remembered that they were but flesh. He knows what he is dealing with. Nobody in this psalm gets away with anything, and nobody is treated as though he were stronger than he is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–55 — He Made a Path for His Anger
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How often they rebelled against him in the wilderness, not remembering the day he redeemed them (vv. 40-42). The plagues are retold: rivers to blood, flies and frogs, locusts, hail and frost on vines and cattle, a company of destroying angels, and every firstborn struck down (vv. 43-51). Then he led out his people like sheep and guided them in the wilderness like a flock, brought them to his holy land and settled the tribes (vv. 52-55).
verseByVerse.theology: The same God made a path for his anger in Egypt and led his people out like a flock.

verseByVerse.quote: How often they rebelled against him in the wilderness and grieved him in the desert! They tested God again and again and provoked the Holy One of Israel. They did not remember his power or the day when he redeemed them from the foe, when he performed his signs in Egypt and his marvels in the fields of Zoan. He turned their rivers to blood, so that they could not drink of their streams. He sent among them swarms of flies, which devoured them, and frogs, which destroyed them. He gave their crops to the destroying locust and the fruit of their labor to the locust. He destroyed their vines with hail and their sycamores with frost. He gave over their cattle to the hail and their flocks to thunderbolts. He let loose on them his burning anger, wrath, indignation, and distress, a company of destroying angels. He made a path for his anger; he did not spare them from death, but gave their lives over to the plague. He struck down every firstborn in Egypt, the firstfruits of their strength in the tents of Ham. Then he led out his people like sheep and guided them in the wilderness like a flock. He led them in safety, so that they were not afraid, but the sea overwhelmed their enemies. And he brought them to his holy land, to the mountain which his right hand had won. He drove out nations before them; he apportioned them for a possession and settled the tribes of Israel in their tents.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How often they rebelled against him in the wilderness and grieved him in the desert! They tested God again and again and provoked the Holy One of Israel. They did not remember his power or the day when he redeemed them from the foe.

Grieved him is the striking word: God is not merely offended but pained. And the root of it is named for the third time — they did not remember.

He turned their rivers to blood ... He sent among them swarms of flies ... He gave their crops to the destroying locust ... He destroyed their vines with hail ... He let loose on them his burning anger, wrath, indignation, and distress, a company of destroying angels ... He struck down every firstborn in Egypt.
