Anyone comparing this with Exodus will notice that the psalm names seven plagues rather than ten and puts the flies before the frogs. It is not trying to be a chronicle. It is a sermon on a well-known story, preaching the point rather than filing the report — which is what the psalm said it would do in verse 2, opening its mouth in a parable.

The plagues are retold at length, and the reason is verse 42: they had forgotten them. This is memory-work. A generation that cannot remember what God did to Egypt will ask whether he can manage a table in the wilderness.

Then he led out his people like sheep and guided them in the wilderness like a flock. He led them in safety, so that they were not afraid, but the sea overwhelmed their enemies. And he brought them to his holy land, to the mountain which his right hand had won.

And the list ends on the firstborn, the firstfruits of their strength in the tents of Ham — the night Israel walked out. Every household in Egypt lost its eldest son; and centuries later God did not spare his own.

Notice the change of register. After the destroying angels and the firstborn, the picture is a shepherd moving sheep. The same hand did both, on the same night, and the psalm sets them side by side without apology.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 56–72 — He Chose David His Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Yet they tested him again, twisted like a deceitful bow, and provoked him with high places and idols (vv. 56-58). He forsook his dwelling at Shiloh, gave his power to captivity and his people to the sword; priests fell and widows did not mourn (vv. 59-64). Then the Lord awoke as from sleep, like a strong man shouting because of wine, and routed his adversaries (vv. 65-66). He rejected Ephraim and chose Judah, Mount Zion, and David his servant ... from following the nursing ewes, to shepherd Israel with an upright heart (vv. 67-72).
verseByVerse.theology: Even the sanctuary was no guarantee — and the psalm ends with a shepherd taken out of a field.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet they tested and rebelled against the Most High God and did not keep his testimonies, but turned away and acted treacherously like their fathers; they twisted like a deceitful bow. For they provoked him to anger with their high places; they moved him to jealousy with their idols. When God heard, he was full of wrath, and he utterly rejected Israel. He forsook his dwelling at Shiloh, the tent where he dwelt among mankind, and delivered his power to captivity, his glory to the hand of the foe. He gave his people over to the sword and vented his wrath on his heritage. Fire devoured their young men, and their young women had no marriage song. Their priests fell by the sword, and their widows made no lamentation. Then the Lord awoke as from sleep, like a strong man shouting because of wine. And he put his adversaries to rout; he put them to everlasting shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet they tested and rebelled against the Most High God and did not keep his testimonies, but turned away and acted treacherously like their fathers; they twisted like a deceitful bow.

A bow that has warped will not shoot where it is aimed — it looks like a weapon and cannot be relied on. That is the psalm's picture of a people who still have the forms of faith. And the phrase like their fathers is the thing verse 8 was trying to prevent.

For they provoked him to anger with their high places; they moved him to jealousy with their idols. When God heard, he was full of wrath, and he utterly rejected Israel. He forsook his dwelling at Shiloh, the tent where he dwelt among mankind, and delivered his power to captivity, his glory to the hand of the foe.

Shiloh is the psalm's most frightening word. It was where the tabernacle stood for generations, and the day came when the ark was captured and the place was finished (1 Sam 4). Jeremiah would later stand in the temple gate and tell people to go and look at what was left of it.

God abandoned his own sanctuary. The building was never a guarantee; it was a privilege, and it could be withdrawn. Any congregation that assumes God is obliged to stay because of the address should read verse 60.

He gave his people over to the sword ... Fire devoured their young men, and their young women had no marriage song. Their priests fell by the sword, and their widows made no lamentation.

Four flat sentences about what a national catastrophe actually is: no weddings, no funerals conducted properly, a generation of young men gone. The detail about the widows not lamenting is the worst — there was no one left to do it, or no time.

Then the Lord awoke as from sleep, like a strong man shouting because of wine. And he put his adversaries to rout; he put them to everlasting shame.

The image is startling and the psalm means it to be. God has looked, for a long time, like a man asleep; and then he is suddenly up and roaring like a soldier who has had a drink. It is the answer to Psalm 44's Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? — not a rebuke of the question but a picture of what the waking looks like when it comes.

verseByVerse.quote: He rejected the tent of Joseph; he did not choose the tribe of Ephraim, but he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loves. He built his sanctuary like the high heavens, like the earth, which he has founded forever. He chose David his servant and took him from the sheepfolds; from following the nursing ewes he brought him to shepherd Jacob his people, Israel his inheritance. With upright heart he shepherded them and guided them with his skillful hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He rejected the tent of Joseph; he did not choose the tribe of Ephraim, but he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loves. He built his sanctuary like the high heavens, like the earth, which he has founded forever.

The psalm began with Ephraim running away (v. 9) and ends with Ephraim set aside. Shiloh was in Ephraim's territory; Zion is in Judah's. God moved house, and the move was a judgment on one tribe and a mercy to the whole nation.

He chose David his servant and took him from the sheepfolds; from following the nursing ewes he brought him to shepherd Jacob his people, Israel his inheritance. With upright heart he shepherded them and guided them with his skillful hand.

Seventy-two verses of rebellion end with a young man being fetched out of a field. The detail is lovely and deliberate: from following the nursing ewes — the ewes with lambs, the slowest and most demanding animals in the flock, which a shepherd walks behind at their pace. That is the training God chose for a king.

And the last two words of the psalm are about competence: upright heart and skillful hand. Integrity and craft together — neither is enough alone, and both were needed to lead the people this psalm has just described.

The psalm ends here, and it ends early. David is not the end of the story; the shepherd taken from the sheepfolds is a picture waiting for the one who would call himself the good shepherd and lay down his life for the sheep. The children being taught this psalm were being prepared for him.

78.title: Tell to the Coming Generation
78.overview: A history lesson given so that children will not repeat it. What the fathers told us we will not hide from the next generation, so that they will hope in God, not forget his works, keep his commandments, and not be like their stubborn fathers (vv. 1-8). Ephraim ran from the battle and forgot God's works (vv. 9-11). He split the sea, led them with cloud and fire and gave water from the rock — and they asked whether he could spread a table in the wilderness (vv. 12-20). He rained manna and meat, and judgment fell while the food was in their mouths (vv. 21-33); under judgment they flattered him with their mouths (vv. 34-37) — yet he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity (vv. 38-39). The plagues are retold because they had forgotten them (vv. 40-51), and he led his people out like sheep into the land (vv. 52-55). They provoked him with idols, and he forsook Shiloh and gave his people to the sword (vv. 56-64). Then the Lord awoke like a strong man shouting (vv. 65-66), rejected Ephraim, chose Judah and Zion, and took David from the sheepfolds to shepherd Israel (vv. 67-72).
78.theology:
The psalm's stated purpose is the education of children (vv. 4-8): hope, memory, obedience — and explicitly so that they will not repeat their fathers. Israel's songbook contains seventy-two verses of her own failures, taught on purpose.

The recurring sin is forgetting (vv. 11, 42), which is not a lapse of memory but a failure to rehearse what God has done — hence the remedy of telling the story.

Can God spread a table in the wilderness? (v. 19) is asked with water from the rock still running: unbelief does not deny the last mercy, it cannot imagine the next.

A granted craving can be a judgment (vv. 29-31), and repentance under pressure can be flattery (vv. 34-37).

Verse 38 is the pivot: God atoned for their iniquity himself, restrained his anger often, and did so because he remembered they were flesh.

Shiloh proves that a sanctuary is a privilege and not a guarantee (v. 60; 1 Sam 4). The psalm ends with Judah chosen and a shepherd taken from the nursing ewes, with an upright heart and a skilful hand (vv. 70-72) — a picture waiting for the good shepherd.
78.examples:
A national story told so the children will not repeat it.

Armed and shooting, and they ran anyway.

They asked whether God could manage food, with wet mouths.

Anger, and then bread through the doors of heaven.

Given exactly what they craved, and it killed them.

Earnest repentance that the psalm calls flattery.

A warped bow: still a weapon, and useless.

God moved out of his own house.

Fetched from behind the ewes with lambs.

79.text: A Psalm of Asaph. 1O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have laid Jerusalem in ruins.2They have given the bodies of your servants to the birds of the heavens for food, the flesh of your faithful to the beasts of the earth.3They have poured out their blood like water all around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.4We have become a taunt to our neighbors, mocked and derided by those around us.5How long, O LORD? Will you be angry forever? Will your jealousy burn like fire?6Pour out your anger on the nations that do not know you, and on the kingdoms that do not call upon your name!7For they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his habitation.8Do not remember against us our former iniquities; let your compassion come speedily to meet us, for we are brought very low.9Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of your name; deliver us, and atone for our sins, for your name's sake!10Why should the nations say, "Where is their God?" Let the avenging of the outpoured blood of your servants be known among the nations before our eyes!11Let the groans of the prisoners come before you; according to your great power, preserve those doomed to die!12Return sevenfold into the lap of our neighbors the taunts with which they have taunted you, O Lord!13But we your people, the sheep of your pasture, will give thanks to you forever; from generation to generation we will recount your praise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — They Have Laid Jerusalem in Ruins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have laid Jerusalem in ruins (v. 1). The bodies of God's servants are food for birds and beasts, their blood poured out like water with no one to bury them (vv. 2-3), and the neighbours mock (v. 4). How long, O LORD? Will you be angry forever? (v. 5). Pour out your anger on the nations that do not know you, who have devoured Jacob (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The same catastrophe as Psalm 74, seen from the street: unburied dead, and neighbours enjoying it.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have laid Jerusalem in ruins. They have given the bodies of your servants to the birds of the heavens for food, the flesh of your faithful to the beasts of the earth. They have poured out their blood like water all around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have laid Jerusalem in ruins.

Two possessives in one sentence, and both of them belong to God: your inheritance, your holy temple. The land was never simply Israel's real estate; it was the property God had assigned himself, and the building was the place he had put his name. So the opening line is not "look what they did to us". It is a report of trespass filed with the owner.

That is a useful thing to notice about how a believer laments. The first move is not to catalogue the damage to oneself but to say what has been done to God.

They have given the bodies of your servants to the birds of the heavens for food, the flesh of your faithful to the beasts of the earth. They have poured out their blood like water all around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.

This is Psalm 74's disaster seen from outside the building. There the axes were in the sanctuary; here the bodies are in the streets. Jeremiah had warned that it would come to this — the dead bodies of this people will be food for the birds of the air, and for the beasts of the earth (Jer 7:33) — and in a culture where burial was the last duty owed to anyone, there was no one to bury them is a sentence about total collapse. Not even the funerals could be managed.

And again, whose bodies? Your servants ... your faithful. The psalm does not say the dead were innocent; it will shortly admit the opposite. It says they were his. People who belonged to God died badly and were left unburied, and the psalm insists on putting that on God's own ledger rather than filing it under the general misery of history. Blood like water is the image of something poured out and not collected — spilled, wasted, soaking away. Verse 10 will ask about that blood again; it does not soak away as far as God is concerned.

verseByVerse.quote: We have become a taunt to our neighbors, mocked and derided by those around us. How long, O LORD? Will you be angry forever? Will your jealousy burn like fire? Pour out your anger on the nations that do not know you, and on the kingdoms that do not call upon your name! For they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his habitation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have become a taunt to our neighbors, mocked and derided by those around us.

On top of the deaths, the jeering. The neighbouring peoples — Edom, Moab, Ammon, the ones who shared the borders — are enjoying it. Anyone who has suffered a public disaster and then had to endure the commentary on it knows why this verse is in the psalm at all. The shame is a separate wound from the loss, and it is felt for longer.

How long, O LORD? Will you be angry forever? Will your jealousy burn like fire?

Notice where the question is aimed. Before they say one word about the Babylonians, they address God's anger. They know whose hand is behind this, and they say so. That is the difference between a lament and a complaint about circumstances: they are not asking why such things happen, but how long God will remain angry.

Jealousy is the covenant word, taken from marriage. It is not petty; it is what love does when it has been betrayed and still refuses to let go. A God who could watch his people go after other gods with mild interest would not be a God anyone could pray to. But the fire is hard to live in, and the honest prayer is how long — which assumes, quietly, that it will not be forever.

Pour out your anger on the nations that do not know you, and on the kingdoms that do not call upon your name! For they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his habitation.

Jeremiah prayed these two verses almost word for word (Jer 10:25), which tells us this was a prayer the faithful shared and repeated in those years, not one man's outburst.

The request is that the anger be redirected, and the charge is specific: the nations did not merely defeat Israel, they devoured her. God may use a nation as a rod and still judge the rod for the way it swung — which is exactly what Isaiah says about Assyria, that when the Lord has finished his work on Zion he will punish the speech of the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria (Isa 10:12). Being an instrument of judgment is not a defence.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — For the Glory of Your Name
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not remember against us our former iniquities; let your compassion come speedily to meet us, for we are brought very low (v. 8). Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of your name; deliver us, and atone for our sins, for your name's sake! (v. 9). Why should the nations say, Where is their God? (v. 10). Let the prisoners' groans come before him (v. 11) and the taunts be returned sevenfold (v. 12). But we your people, the sheep of your pasture, will give thanks to you forever (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: They do not claim innocence. They ask for atonement, and the only reason they give is God's own name.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not remember against us our former iniquities; let your compassion come speedily to meet us, for we are brought very low. Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of your name; deliver us, and atone for our sins, for your name's sake!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not remember against us our former iniquities; let your compassion come speedily to meet us, for we are brought very low.

Here is what separates this psalm from Psalm 44. There a nation protested that it had done nothing to deserve the catastrophe. Here there is no protest at all. They ask only that the iniquities not be remembered against them — and the ESV notes that the phrase may be rendered "the iniquities of former generations", in which case they are carrying an account their fathers ran up.

Both readings are honest, and neither claims to deserve anything. We are brought very low is the whole of their case. When a man has stopped arguing his record and started describing his condition, he has begun to pray properly.

Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of your name; deliver us, and atone for our sins, for your name's sake!

Twice in one verse the same ground: for the glory of your name ... for your name's sake. They have nothing else to put forward. Not their usefulness, not their record, not even the sincerity of their repentance —God's own reputation is the entire argument. That is not a trick for getting round a reluctant God; it is the deepest reason anything is ever done, and the only ground that never depends on the state of the person pleading.

And in the middle of it comes the request that carries the most weight in the psalm: atone for our sins. They ask God to do the covering himself. The altar is rubble, the priesthood is scattered, the sacrifices have stopped — there is no atonement available to them through any channel God had provided. This is the Old Testament at the end of its own resources, asking God to supply what his own system no longer can. The answer, when it came, was that God put forward his Son as a propitiation by his blood, and did it to show his own righteousness (Rom 3:25-26). For his name's sake, exactly as they asked.

verseByVerse.quote: Why should the nations say, "Where is their God?" Let the avenging of the outpoured blood of your servants be known among the nations before our eyes! Let the groans of the prisoners come before you; according to your great power, preserve those doomed to die! Return sevenfold into the lap of our neighbors the taunts with which they have taunted you, O Lord! But we your people, the sheep of your pasture, will give thanks to you forever; from generation to generation we will recount your praise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why should the nations say, Where is their God?

It is the taunt from Psalm 42, where one man heard it all day long; now whole nations are saying it. And the psalm uses it as an argument. God's reputation is genuinely bound up with what happens to his people, and the believer is allowed to say so out loud in prayer.

Let the avenging of the outpoured blood of your servants be known among the nations before our eyes!

The blood of verse 3 comes back, and they ask that its avenging be public and in their lifetime. John heard the same prayer at the far end of the Bible, from martyrs under the altar: O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth? (Rev 6:10). They were told to rest a little longer. It is the same question, the wait is longer than anyone wants, and it has an answer.

Let the groans of the prisoners come before you; according to your great power, preserve those doomed to die!

A groan is what is left when speech has gone, and the psalm asks for the groan to be admitted as evidence. Those doomed to die are, in the Hebrew idiom, the sons of death — men already assigned to execution. The prayer for them is not comfort but preservation, and the measure asked is your great power. Nothing smaller will reach into that cell.

Return sevenfold into the lap of our neighbors the taunts with which they have taunted you, O Lord!

Two things keep this from being simple spite. The repayment is asked of God, not taken by the person praying; and the insult is not described as theirs. The taunts were shouted at the survivors, and the psalm says they taunted you. What is said about a believer's God, in his hearing, while he is down, is registered in heaven as an insult to God himself.

But we your people, the sheep of your pasture, will give thanks to you forever; from generation to generation we will recount your praise.

The ending is quiet and stubborn. Nothing has been restored. The temple is still defiled, the bodies are still unburied, the prisoners are still in their cells and the neighbours are still laughing — and the last word of the psalm is thanks, and a promise that the children will be told.

They call themselves the sheep of your pasture, which is where Psalm 74 ended and Psalm 100 will begin: not a strong name, and not one they gave themselves. A flock has nothing but its shepherd, which is precisely the position they are in. And the commitment to recount your praise from one generation to the next is what Psalm 78 said the whole enterprise was for. A congregation in the wreckage, with no altar and no city, decides that the telling will go on anyway. That decision is the only thing they have left to give, and they give it.

79.title: Where Is Their God?
79.overview: The nations have entered God's inheritance, defiled the temple and left Jerusalem in ruins; bodies lie unburied and blood has been poured out like water, while the neighbours jeer (vv. 1-4). How long, O LORD? Will you be angry forever? — and let the anger be poured on the nations who devoured Jacob (vv. 5-7). Do not remember against us our former iniquities (v. 8). Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of your name; deliver us, and atone for our sins, for your name's sake! (v. 9). Why should the nations ask Where is their God? (v. 10)? Let the prisoners' groans be heard and the taunts returned sevenfold (vv. 11-12). But we your people, the sheep of your pasture, will give thanks to you forever (v. 13).
79.theology:
The lament addresses God's anger before it mentions the enemy (v. 5): the people know whose hand is behind the catastrophe. God may use a nation as a rod and still judge it for how it struck (vv. 6-7).

Unlike Psalm 44, this psalm makes no claim of innocence. It asks that iniquities — their own, or their fathers' (see the ESV's note at v. 8) — not be held against them, and offers only we are brought very low.

The single ground of appeal is stated twice in one verse: God's own name (v. 9). And the central request is that God atone for their sins himself, since the altar is rubble and the priests are dead — the Old Testament asking for what its own system can no longer supply (cf. Rom 3:25-26).

The taunt Where is their God? is used as an argument (v. 10), and the cry for avenged blood is heard again from the martyrs (Rev 6:10). Vengeance is asked of God, not taken (v. 12), and insults aimed at God's people are registered as aimed at him.

Nothing is restored by the end; the congregation simply commits to keep telling the story (v. 13).
79.examples:
Psalm 74 from inside the temple; this one from the street.

Not even the funerals could be managed.

The deaths, and then the commentary on them.

They ask how long God will be angry, not why it happened.

No claim of innocence — only we are brought very low.

Atonement requested, with the altar in ruins.

Taunts aimed at the people, registered as aimed at God.

In the wreckage, a promise to keep telling the children.

80.text: To the choirmaster: according to Lilies. A Testimony. Of Asaph, a Psalm. 1Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, you who lead Joseph like a flock. You who are enthroned upon the cherubim, shine forth.2Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh, stir up your might and come to save us!3Restore us, O God; let your face shine, that we may be saved!4O LORD God of hosts, how long will you be angry with your people's prayers?5You have fed them with the bread of tears and given them tears to drink in full measure.6You make us an object of contention for our neighbors, and our enemies laugh among themselves.7Restore us, O God of hosts; let your face shine, that we may be saved!8You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it.9You cleared the ground for it; it took deep root and filled the land.10The mountains were covered with its shade, the mighty cedars with its branches.11It sent out its branches to the sea and its shoots to the River.12Why then have you broken down its walls, so that all who pass along the way pluck its fruit?13The boar from the forest ravages it, and all that move in the field feed on it.14Turn again, O God of hosts! Look down from heaven, and see; have regard for this vine,15the stock that your right hand planted, and for the son whom you made strong for yourself.16They have burned it with fire; they have cut it down; may they perish at the rebuke of your face!17But let your hand be on the man of your right hand, the son of man whom you have made strong for yourself!18Then we shall not turn back from you; give us life, and we will call upon your name!19Restore us, O LORD God of hosts! Let your face shine, that we may be saved!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Shepherd of Israel, Shine Forth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, you who lead Joseph like a flock. You who are enthroned upon the cherubim, shine forth (v. 1); before Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh, stir up your might and come to save (v. 2). Restore us, O God; let your face shine, that we may be saved! (v. 3). How long will he be angry with his people's prayers? They have been fed on the bread of tears and are laughed at by their neighbours (vv. 4-6). Restore us, O God of hosts; let your face shine, that we may be saved! (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: A shepherd who seems to have stopped listening is asked, twice, simply to turn his face towards his flock.

verseByVerse.quote: Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, you who lead Joseph like a flock. You who are enthroned upon the cherubim, shine forth. Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh, stir up your might and come to save us! Restore us, O God; let your face shine, that we may be saved!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, you who lead Joseph like a flock. You who are enthroned upon the cherubim, shine forth. Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh, stir up your might and come to save us!

The names locate the psalm. Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh are the northern tribes, and Benjamin sat on the border. It is a prayer for the north, and the likeliest setting is the long collapse that ended when the king of Assyria captured Samaria and carried the population away (2 Kgs 17:6) — probable, though the psalm never says so.

But the three tribe names are not random. In the wilderness Ephraim, Manasseh and Benjamin camped together on the west side of the tabernacle (Num 2:18-24), and on the march they set out directly behind the Kohathites carrying the holy things (Num 10:21-24). These were the tribes who walked behind the ark. So you who are enthroned upon the cherubim — the ark's God — is asked to go before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh the way he once did, and stir up the strength they used to follow.

The prayer reaches for the oldest memory the people have of God leading them. When the present is broken, the believer goes back to the beginning and asks God to be what he was then.

Restore us, O God; let your face shine, that we may be saved!

This is the refrain, and it will come three times. Let your face shine is the priestly blessing that was spoken over Israel every day: the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you (Num 6:25). They are asking for the blessing they used to hear at the tabernacle door.

And notice the order. The ESV notes that restore us may be rendered "Turn us again". They do not ask first for the Assyrians to go home. They ask God to turn them, and to turn his face. Everything else — that we may be saved — follows from the face. A person who has God's face turned towards him is safe whatever else is standing on his land.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD God of hosts, how long will you be angry with your people's prayers? You have fed them with the bread of tears and given them tears to drink in full measure. You make us an object of contention for our neighbors, and our enemies laugh among themselves. Restore us, O God of hosts; let your face shine, that we may be saved!
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD God of hosts, how long will you be angry with your people's prayers? You have fed them with the bread of tears and given them tears to drink in full measure.

A startling complaint: God is angry not merely with the people but with your people's prayers. The praying itself seems to provoke him. Every believer who has prayed for a long time and found the heaven brass has felt this — that the praying is not neutral, that it seems to make things worse — and the psalm lets it be said.

The bread of tears is a diet. Grief has become what they eat in the morning and drink at night, and in full measure is a measuring word: the portion has been weighed out, generously, as if a host were serving it. The phrase is bitter and precise, and it puts the serving in God's hands.

You make us an object of contention for our neighbors, and our enemies laugh among themselves.

The neighbours squabble over the carcass and laugh about it privately. Two kinds of contempt: the open quarrel over who gets what, and the joke told behind the hand.

Restore us, O God of hosts; let your face shine, that we may be saved!

The refrain again, and it has grown by one word. The first time it was O God; now it is O God of hosts. By the end of the psalm it will be O LORD God of hosts. The circumstances do not improve between the refrains, but the name they call on gets larger each time. That is how lament climbs: not by the situation changing, but by the God addressed coming more fully into view.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — You Brought a Vine out of Egypt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it (v. 8). God cleared the ground; it took root, shaded the mountains and cedars, and reached from the sea to the River (vv. 9-11). Why then have you broken down its walls, so that all who pass along the way pluck its fruit? (v. 12). The boar from the forest ravages it (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The vine was God's own planting, and the question is why the gardener has pulled down his own wall.

verseByVerse.quote: You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it. You cleared the ground for it; it took deep root and filled the land. The mountains were covered with its shade, the mighty cedars with its branches. It sent out its branches to the sea and its shoots to the River.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it. You cleared the ground for it; it took deep root and filled the land.

Now the whole history of Israel is told in one image. The exodus was a transplanting: God dug a vine out of Egyptian soil, carried it, cleared a site, and set it in. Every verb is God's — brought, drove out, planted, cleared. The vine did nothing except take root.

The image had a long life in the prophets. Isaiah sang of a vineyard God dug it and cleared it of stones, and planted it with choice vines (Isa 5:2), and Jeremiah heard God say, I planted you a choice vine, wholly of pure seed (Jer 2:21). In both, the vine went wrong. This psalm does not yet say so; it is remembering the planting.

The mountains were covered with its shade, the mighty cedars with its branches. It sent out its branches to the sea and its shoots to the River.

The vine grew until it shaded the hill country and climbed the cedars, and its reach ran from the Mediterranean to the River — the Euphrates, as the ESV notes. That was the boundary God had promised Abraham, and under David and Solomon it was reached. The verse is the high-water mark of the kingdom, described as a garden that got out of hand in the best way.

verseByVerse.quote: Why then have you broken down its walls, so that all who pass along the way pluck its fruit? The boar from the forest ravages it, and all that move in the field feed on it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why then have you broken down its walls, so that all who pass along the way pluck its fruit? The boar from the forest ravages it, and all that move in the field feed on it.

Why then. If you did all that, why this? A vineyard in the hill country had a stone wall or a hedge round it to keep out passers-by and animals, and the wall is gone. Every traveller helps himself, and the wild boar, the most destructive animal in the country, is rooting through the vines.

The psalm asks why; Isaiah had already given the answer from the other side. In his song God says, I will break down its wall, and it shall be trampled down (Isa 5:5) — because he looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed (Isa 5:7). The broken wall was not an accident of history. It was a decision.

This psalm never mentions that reason, and it does not claim innocence either. It simply brings the ruin to the gardener and asks him to look at it. There are times when a believer knows perfectly well why the wall came down, and still the right prayer is not an explanation but an appeal: this was yours; see what has become of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–19 — The Man of Your Right Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Turn again, O God of hosts! Look down from heaven, and see; have regard for this vine (v. 14), the stock his right hand planted; it has been burned and cut down (vv. 15-16). But let your hand be on the man of your right hand, the son of man whom you have made strong for yourself! (v. 17). Then we shall not turn back from you; give us life, and we will call upon your name! (v. 18). Restore us, O LORD God of hosts! Let your face shine, that we may be saved! (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The ruined vine and the man at God's right hand are described in the same words: the hope for the one rests on the other.

verseByVerse.quote: Turn again, O God of hosts! Look down from heaven, and see; have regard for this vine, the stock that your right hand planted, and for the son whom you made strong for yourself. They have burned it with fire; they have cut it down; may they perish at the rebuke of your face!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turn again, O God of hosts! Look down from heaven, and see; have regard for this vine, the stock that your right hand planted, and for the son whom you made strong for yourself.

The refrain asked God to turn us; here they ask God himself to turn again. Both are needed. A people will not turn back unless God turns them, and it will do them no good unless God has turned his face towards them first.

Look down ... and see is a request to be noticed. The vine is described by what God did to it — the stock that your right hand planted — and then, suddenly, the picture shifts to a person: the son whom you made strong for yourself. The vine is Israel, God's son (Exodus calls Israel that), and the image and the reality begin to blur.

They have burned it with fire; they have cut it down; may they perish at the rebuke of your face!

The vine has not merely been raided; it has been cut down and the stumps burned. And the face that they have been asking to shine on them is the same face they ask to rebuke the destroyers. God's face does two things: it shines on those it favours, and it withers those it rebukes. The whole psalm turns on which way the face is turned.

verseByVerse.quote: But let your hand be on the man of your right hand, the son of man whom you have made strong for yourself! Then we shall not turn back from you; give us life, and we will call upon your name! Restore us, O LORD God of hosts! Let your face shine, that we may be saved!
verseByVerse.commentary:
But let your hand be on the man of your right hand, the son of man whom you have made strong for yourself!

This is the hinge of the psalm. Verse 15 spoke of the son whom you made strong for yourself; verse 17 speaks of the son of man whom you have made strong for yourself, the man of your right hand. The vine and the man are described in the same words. The hope for the ruined vine is placed on a single figure standing at God's right hand.

In its first setting this meant the king, the one who represented the nation and in whom it stood or fell. But the psalm is asking for more than any king of Israel ever delivered, and the later Scriptures fill in the man. God said to David's Lord, Sit at my right hand (Ps 110:1). Jesus told a parable of a vineyard whose owner had still one other, a beloved son, and sent him (Mark 12:6). And on the night before he died, he said, I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser (John 15:1).

That is the answer to this psalm. The vine that was burned and cut down is replaced by a vine that cannot fail, because the vine is now the Son himself and his people are branches in him. The man at God's right hand was cut down too, and did not stay down.

Then we shall not turn back from you; give us life, and we will call upon your name!

Here is what the man at God's right hand produces: a people who shall not turn back. The whole history of the vine was turning back. What they could not do in their own strength, they will do when God's hand is on his man. And the request give us life is exactly right — a cut-down, burned vine does not need improvement. It needs to live.

Restore us, O LORD God of hosts! Let your face shine, that we may be saved!

The third refrain, and the name has reached its full size: O LORD God of hosts, the covenant name and the title of the commander of heaven's armies together. Nothing in the vineyard has been repaired between verse 3 and verse 19. But the one they are speaking to has grown in their sight, and the man of his right hand has come into view. The shining face of God, which Aaron could only pronounce over the people, is now seen in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4:6), and in that face the prayer is answered for everyone who is a branch in the true vine.

80.title: Let Your Face Shine
80.overview: Asaph calls on the Shepherd of Israel, enthroned on the cherubim, to shine forth before Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh — the tribes that marched behind the ark — and save them (vv. 1-2). The refrain Restore us, O God; let your face shine, that we may be saved! sounds three times (vv. 3, 7, 19), the divine name growing each time. God seems angry with his people's very prayers; they eat the bread of tears and are mocked (vv. 4-6). Israel was a vine God brought out of Egypt and planted until it reached from the sea to the River (vv. 8-11) — so why has he broken down its walls for every passer-by and the wild boar (vv. 12-13)? Turn again; see the vine his hand planted, now burned and cut down (vv. 14-16). Let your hand be on the man of your right hand, the son of man whom you have made strong for yourself (v. 17); then they will not turn back, and God will give them life (vv. 18-19).
80.theology:
The refrain asks first for God to turn his people and to turn his face towards them; salvation follows from the face (v. 3). Let your face shine recalls the priestly blessing (Num 6:25). Its three occurrences add to the divine name each time — lament climbing not by circumstances changing but by God coming more fully into view.

The vine is wholly God's work (vv. 8-11), and the broken wall (v. 12) is the judgment Isaiah announced from God's side (Isa 5:5-7). The psalm neither explains nor protests; it brings the ruin to the gardener.

The vine (v. 15) and the man at God's right hand (v. 17) are described in identical terms, so the hope for the people rests on one representative figure — first the king, finally the Son at God's right hand (Ps 110:1), the beloved son sent to the vineyard (Mark 12:6), and the true vine (John 15:1). Only then does a people become one that shall not turn back (v. 18).
80.examples:
The three tribes that walked behind the ark.

The priestly blessing, asked for from the ruins.

Angry with the prayers themselves.

Tears served in full measure, like a host's portion.

The refrain grows by a word each time.

Every traveller helping himself; the boar in the vines.

The vine and the man described in the same words.

A burned vine does not need improving. It needs life.

81.text: To the choirmaster: according to The Gittith. Of Asaph. 1Sing aloud to God our strength; shout for joy to the God of Jacob!2Raise a song; sound the tambourine, the sweet lyre with the harp.3Blow the trumpet at the new moon, at the full moon, on our feast day.4For it is a statute for Israel, a rule of the God of Jacob.5He made it a decree in Joseph when he went out over the land of Egypt. I hear a language I had not known:6"I relieved your shoulder of the burden; your hands were freed from the basket.7In distress you called, and I delivered you; I answered you in the secret place of thunder; I tested you at the waters of Meribah. Selah8Hear, O my people, while I admonish you! O Israel, if you would but listen to me!9There shall be no strange god among you; you shall not bow down to a foreign god.10I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.11"But my people did not listen to my voice; Israel would not submit to me.12So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels.13Oh, that my people would listen to me, that Israel would walk in my ways!14I would soon subdue their enemies and turn my hand against their foes.15Those who hate the LORD would cringe toward him, and their fate would last forever.16But he would feed you with the finest of the wheat, and with honey from the rock I would satisfy you."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — I Hear a Language I Had Not Known
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sing aloud to God our strength; shout for joy to the God of Jacob! (v. 1). Tambourine, lyre and harp; the trumpet at the new moon and the full moon, because it is a statute God decreed when he went out over Egypt (vv. 2-5). Then: I hear a language I had not known (v. 5), and God speaks: I relieved your shoulder of the burden; in distress you called, and I delivered you; I tested you at the waters of Meribah (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: In the middle of the festival the music stops and a voice speaks that the singer did not expect to hear.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing aloud to God our strength; shout for joy to the God of Jacob! Raise a song; sound the tambourine, the sweet lyre with the harp. Blow the trumpet at the new moon, at the full moon, on our feast day. For it is a statute for Israel, a rule of the God of Jacob. He made it a decree in Joseph when he went out over the land of Egypt. I hear a language I had not known:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sing aloud to God our strength; shout for joy to the God of Jacob! Raise a song; sound the tambourine, the sweet lyre with the harp. Blow the trumpet at the new moon, at the full moon, on our feast day.

The psalm opens loud. Singing aloud, shouting, tambourines, lyre and harp, and over them the trumpet — the ram's horn — blown at the new moon and again at the full moon. The law told Israel to blow the trumpets at your appointed feasts and at the beginnings of your months (Num 10:10), and the likeliest occasion for this psalm is the autumn, when the new moon of the seventh month opened the season and the full moon brought the Feast of Booths. It is a festival with the whole band playing.

For it is a statute for Israel, a rule of the God of Jacob. He made it a decree in Joseph when he went out over the land of Egypt.

The joy is commanded. That sounds odd until you notice why: the festival was a decree from the exodus, instituted to make Israel remember what God did when he went out over the land of Egypt (the ESV notes "against" as a possible rendering). Worship that is ordered by God is not the enemy of joy. It is the thing that keeps a people coming back to the reason for joy when they would otherwise forget it.

I hear a language I had not known:

And suddenly the music stops. Somebody — a Levite, a prophet in the choir — hears a voice he was not expecting, a speech he does not recognise as his own. For the rest of the psalm, God is the speaker.

This is the most important line in the psalm, and it is a warning to every congregation that sings well. The trumpets and the harps are not the point. The point of the festival is that God speaks into it, and the speech he gives is not the pleasant sort they had been singing.

verseByVerse.quote: "I relieved your shoulder of the burden; your hands were freed from the basket. In distress you called, and I delivered you; I answered you in the secret place of thunder; I tested you at the waters of Meribah. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
I relieved your shoulder of the burden; your hands were freed from the basket.

God's first words are a reminder, and they are physical. In Egypt the Israelites carried bricks and clay in baskets on their shoulders. God had promised to bring them out from under the burdens of the Egyptians (Exod 6:6), and here he remembers doing it: the weight lifted off the shoulder, the hands let go of the basket. The ESV notes the Hebrew says "his" shoulder — Israel spoken of as one man, one pair of hands.

Whatever God is about to say in rebuke, he begins with what he has done. He does not open his complaint against his people with their sin; he opens with the moment he took the load off them.

In distress you called, and I delivered you; I answered you in the secret place of thunder; I tested you at the waters of Meribah.

Three memories in order. They cried out in Egypt, and he delivered. He answered them at Sinai, from the secret place of thunder — the cloud on the mountain where the people saw the thunder and the flashes of lightning and begged Moses, do not let God speak to us, lest we die (Exod 20:18-19). And he tested them at Meribah, where they had quarrelled and said, Is the LORD among us or not? (Exod 17:7).

The last memory is the uncomfortable one. At Meribah God gave them water from a rock, and the name of the place is a monument to their quarrelling. The rescue and the rebellion sit in the same sentence, which is exactly where the rest of the psalm is going.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–16 — Oh, That My People Would Listen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hear, O my people, while I admonish you! O Israel, if you would but listen to me! (v. 8). No strange god; I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it (vv. 9-10). But my people did not listen to my voice ... So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts (vv. 11-12). Oh, that my people would listen to me — he would subdue their enemies and feed you with the finest of the wheat, and with honey from the rock I would satisfy you (vv. 13-16).
verseByVerse.theology: God offers to fill any mouth opened to him, and the saddest judgment in the psalm is that he let his people have what they preferred.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, O my people, while I admonish you! O Israel, if you would but listen to me! There shall be no strange god among you; you shall not bow down to a foreign god. I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear, O my people, while I admonish you! O Israel, if you would but listen to me!

Hear, O Israel was the first line of the confession every Israelite knew (Deut 6:4), and God speaks it himself. The tone is not a lawgiver's; it is a parent's. If you would but listen to me is the voice of someone who has said it many times and is still saying it.

There shall be no strange god among you; you shall not bow down to a foreign god. I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.

This is the Ten Commandments, heard again at the festival — the first commandment and the preface that comes before it at Sinai: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt (Exod 20:2). The order matters. Rescue first, then the command. God does not say "keep my law and I will save you"; he says "I saved you, so have no other god". Grace comes before obedience in the very structure of the covenant.

Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.

And then, straight after the command, the most generous sentence in the psalm. The picture is a nest of young birds with their beaks stretched open. The only thing required is the open mouth — the posture of need, expecting to be fed.

That is what having no other god looks like from the inside. It is not a narrowing of life but a refusal to go and feed anywhere else, because the God who brought you out of Egypt has promised to fill whatever you open to him. Most of our spiritual poverty is not that God gives too little. It is that we open our mouths too little, or open them towards someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: "But my people did not listen to my voice; Israel would not submit to me. So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But my people did not listen to my voice; Israel would not submit to me. So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels.

After the offer, the history. They did not listen; they would not submit. It was not that they could not hear the voice. They heard it and preferred not to.

And the judgment is terrible precisely because it is so quiet. God does not strike them. I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels. He let them have what they insisted on. The worst thing God can do to a person who will not listen is to stop contending with him and let him walk his own way to the end of it.

Paul describes exactly this judgment falling on the whole human race: God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts (Rom 1:24). Stephen said it of Israel in the wilderness: God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven (Acts 7:42). If you find that you can now do without distress what once troubled your conscience, the honest question is whether this verse has begun to happen.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, that my people would listen to me, that Israel would walk in my ways! I would soon subdue their enemies and turn my hand against their foes. Those who hate the LORD would cringe toward him, and their fate would last forever. But he would feed you with the finest of the wheat, and with honey from the rock I would satisfy you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh, that my people would listen to me, that Israel would walk in my ways! I would soon subdue their enemies and turn my hand against their foes.

And yet God has not finished speaking. Having handed them over, he grieves. Oh, that my people would listen to me is the sound of divine longing, and it is the same voice that wept over Jerusalem: How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! (Matt 23:37); Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! (Luke 19:42).

The enemies they are struggling against would be soon subdued. The fighting they were losing was never the real problem. The listening was.

Those who hate the LORD would cringe toward him, and their fate would last forever. But he would feed you with the finest of the wheat, and with honey from the rock I would satisfy you.

The psalm ends not on the judgment but on the table that was set and refused. The finest of the wheat — the best flour, the richest bread, the same gift later praised in Psalm 147:14. And honey from the rock, the phrase Moses used in his song: he suckled him with honey out of the rock (Deut 32:13). At Meribah (v. 7) the rock gave water to a quarrelling people. God says he would have made it give honey.

The ESV notes the Hebrew at the last line is "him", Israel as one person again, and the grammar slides between he and I, as though the speaker cannot keep still. The psalm is left open, which is why it could be sung at every festival. Psalm 95 makes the same move, and Hebrews preaches it to Christians: Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Heb 3:7-8). The mouth can still be opened. The table is still set.

81.title: Open Your Mouth Wide
81.overview: A festival call: sing aloud, play tambourine, lyre and harp, and blow the trumpet at the new moon and the full moon, because God decreed the feast when he went out over Egypt (vv. 1-5). Then I hear a language I had not known (v. 5), and God speaks for the rest of the psalm. He lifted the burden off Israel's shoulder, delivered them in distress, answered from the thunder of Sinai and tested them at Meribah (vv. 6-7). Hear, O my people: no strange god, for I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it (vv. 8-10). But they would not listen, so I gave them over to their stubborn hearts (vv. 11-12). Oh, that my people would listen to me — he would subdue their enemies and feed them with the finest of the wheat and honey from the rock (vv. 13-16).
81.theology:
The festival exists so that God can speak into it (v. 5); the music is not the point.

God's address begins with rescue, not rebuke (vv. 6-7), and the commandment is prefaced by redemption (v. 10; Exod 20:2): grace precedes obedience in the structure of the covenant. The first commandment is paired with the widest promise — open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.

Judgment can take the form of God handing people over to what they insist on (v. 12; Rom 1:24; Acts 7:42). Yet God grieves over the refusal (v. 13), in the same voice that wept over Jerusalem (Matt 23:37; Luke 19:42).

The psalm ends on the table that was refused (v. 16), and remains an open invitation: Today, if you hear his voice (Heb 3:7).
81.examples:
The whole band playing, and then a voice no one expected.

The shoulder freed from the brick-basket.

Rescue and rebellion in the same sentence: Meribah.

Grace first, then the commandment.

Young birds with their beaks wide open.

The quietest judgment: getting what you insisted on.

God grieving: Oh, that my people would listen.

Honey from the rock that once gave water to a quarrel.

82.text: A Psalm of Asaph. 1God has taken his place in the divine council; in the midst of the gods he holds judgment:2"How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked? Selah3Give justice to the weak and the fatherless; maintain the right of the afflicted and the destitute.4Rescue the weak and the needy; deliver them from the hand of the wicked."5They have neither knowledge nor understanding, they walk about in darkness; all the foundations of the earth are shaken.6I said, "You are gods, sons of the Most High, all of you;7nevertheless, like men you shall die, and fall like any prince."8Arise, O God, judge the earth; for you shall inherit all the nations!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — God Stands Up in the Council
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has taken his place in the divine council; in the midst of the gods he holds judgment (v. 1). How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked? (v. 2). Give justice to the weak and the fatherless; maintain the right of the afflicted and the destitute. Rescue the weak and the needy; deliver them from the hand of the wicked (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: The judges are put on trial, and the charge is what they did for people who could not pay them.

verseByVerse.quote: God has taken his place in the divine council; in the midst of the gods he holds judgment: "How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked? Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has taken his place in the divine council; in the midst of the gods he holds judgment:

The scene is a courtroom, and the surprise is who is in the dock. God stands up among the gods — not to preside over a case brought by them, but to judge them.

Who are they? Careful readers have understood the word in two ways. One reading takes them to be human rulers and judges, called gods because they sit in God's place when they decide cases; Jesus himself spoke of them as those to whom the word of God came (John 10:35). The other takes them to be heavenly powers to whom the nations were entrusted — Moses spoke of God fixing the borders of the peoples according to the number of the sons of God (Deut 32:8), and Paul of the cosmic powers over this present darkness (Eph 6:12), who stand behind unjust human rule.

The two readings are not far apart in practice. Either way, those who hold authority over others hold it from God, and either way God calls them to account in person.

How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked?

The charge is partiality. A court that favours the man with money, connections or a loud voice is not simply inefficient; it is a lie told in God's name. The law had said it plainly: You shall not be partial in judgment ... for the judgment is God's (Deut 1:17).

verseByVerse.quote: Give justice to the weak and the fatherless; maintain the right of the afflicted and the destitute. Rescue the weak and the needy; deliver them from the hand of the wicked."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give justice to the weak and the fatherless; maintain the right of the afflicted and the destitute. Rescue the weak and the needy; deliver them from the hand of the wicked.

This is the job description, and every name on it is someone who cannot pay. The weak, the fatherless, the afflicted, the destitute, the needy — people with no family to speak for them, no money to hire an advocate, no standing to make an official nervous. The test of any authority is what it does for them.

Notice the verbs: give, maintain, rescue, deliver. Justice is not merely refraining from harming the poor. It is actively pulling them out of the hand of the wicked. A judge who keeps his own hands clean while the powerful strip the weak has not done what God appointed him for.

When Jehoshaphat appointed judges he told them, Consider what you do, for you judge not for man but for the LORD (2 Chr 19:6). Every parent, employer, elder and manager holds some small share of this authority. The psalm asks what that authority has done for the person in the room who has least power.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — Like Men You Shall Die
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They have neither knowledge nor understanding, they walk about in darkness; all the foundations of the earth are shaken (v. 5). I said, You are gods, sons of the Most High, all of you; nevertheless, like men you shall die, and fall like any prince (vv. 6-7). Arise, O God, judge the earth; for you shall inherit all the nations! (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Whatever authority God lends is lent to mortals, and the psalm ends by asking the only true Judge to take the bench himself.

verseByVerse.quote: They have neither knowledge nor understanding, they walk about in darkness; all the foundations of the earth are shaken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have neither knowledge nor understanding, they walk about in darkness; all the foundations of the earth are shaken.

God turns from addressing the judges to describing them, and the verdict is blindness. They do not know, they do not understand, they stumble about in the dark — the very people appointed to bring things to light.

And the effect reaches further than one court. All the foundations of the earth are shaken. Justice is one of the things the world stands on. When those at the top judge corruptly, it is not just a few cases that go wrong; the ground under everyone shifts. Anyone who has lived under a corrupt system knows the feeling — nothing can be relied on, because the thing that should hold is rotten.

verseByVerse.quote: I said, "You are gods, sons of the Most High, all of you; nevertheless, like men you shall die, and fall like any prince."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I said, You are gods, sons of the Most High, all of you; nevertheless, like men you shall die, and fall like any prince.

God does not withdraw the title he gave. I said, You are gods — the dignity of the office was real; they did sit in his place. But the title was lent, and it came with a mortality clause. Nevertheless, like men you shall die. The ESV notes another way of reading the end of the verse: "fall as one man, O princes". Either way, those who judged as if answerable to no one will fall, and fall together.

Jesus quoted this verse when a crowd picked up stones because he had called himself the Son of God. Is it not written in your Law, I said, you are gods? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came — and Scripture cannot be broken — do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, You are blaspheming, because I said, I am the Son of God? (John 10:34-36).

The argument runs from the lesser to the greater. If Scripture, which cannot be set aside, gives the name gods to unjust men who merely received God's word, how can it be blasphemy for the one the Father sanctified and sent to call himself God's Son? They were called gods and died like men. He was the Son and died for men, and did not stay dead.

verseByVerse.quote: Arise, O God, judge the earth; for you shall inherit all the nations!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Arise, O God, judge the earth; for you shall inherit all the nations!

The psalmist has watched the council and drawn the only conclusion left: the lesser judges have failed, so let the true Judge stand up and do it himself. And the reason he gives is ownership. You shall inherit all the nations — they are his, not the property of the powers that mismanaged them.

The inheritance has a name attached to it elsewhere in the Psalter: the Father says to his Son, Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage (Ps 2:8). At the cross Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame (Col 2:15), and the day is coming when the saints will judge the world (1 Cor 6:2).

That is the comfort of this psalm for anyone who has been on the wrong end of a corrupt decision — a court, a tribunal, an office that looked the other way. There is a council above that one, and the Judge of it has already stood up. The prayer Arise, O God, judge the earth is not a cry into the void. It is a request for something he has promised to do, and has begun.

82.title: Arise, O God, Judge the Earth
82.overview: God takes his place in the divine council and puts the gods on trial (v. 1): How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked? (v. 2). Their commission was to give justice to the weak and fatherless, maintain the right of the afflicted and destitute, and rescue the needy from the wicked (vv. 3-4). Instead they walk in darkness, and the foundations of the earth are shaken (v. 5). I said, You are gods ... nevertheless, like men you shall die (vv. 6-7). The psalmist ends: Arise, O God, judge the earth; for you shall inherit all the nations! (v. 8).
82.theology:
The gods have been read as human judges exercising God's authority (John 10:35) or as heavenly powers set over the nations (Deut 32:8; Eph 6:12); on either reading authority is held from God and answerable to him in person.

Partiality in judgment is a lie told in God's name (v. 2; Deut 1:17). Justice is active rescue of those who cannot pay (vv. 3-4), and its corruption shakes the foundations of the world (v. 5).

The dignity of the office was real but lent, with mortality attached (vv. 6-7). Jesus argued from v. 6 that if Scripture, which cannot be broken, calls such men gods, it is not blasphemy for the one the Father sent to call himself the Son of God (John 10:34-36).

The failure of lesser judges leads to the plea for God to judge; the nations are his inheritance (v. 8), given to the Son (Ps 2:8), whose cross disarmed the powers (Col 2:15).
82.examples:
The judges in the dock.

A job description made entirely of people who cannot pay.

Clean hands are not enough; justice pulls the weak out.

When the courts rot, the ground under everyone shifts.

A lent title with a mortality clause.

Jesus: if they were called gods, what of the one the Father sent?

There is a council above the one that failed you.

83.text: A Song. A Psalm of Asaph. 1O God, do not keep silence; do not hold your peace or be still, O God!2For behold, your enemies make an uproar; those who hate you have raised their heads.3They lay crafty plans against your people; they consult together against your treasured ones.4They say, "Come, let us wipe them out as a nation; let the name of Israel be remembered no more!"5For they conspire with one accord; against you they make a covenant—6the tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagrites,7Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, Philistia with the inhabitants of Tyre;8Asshur also has joined them; they are the strong arm of the children of Lot. Selah9Do to them as you did to Midian, as to Sisera and Jabin at the river Kishon,10who were destroyed at En-dor, who became dung for the ground.11Make their nobles like Oreb and Zeeb, all their princes like Zebah and Zalmunna,12who said, "Let us take possession for ourselves of the pastures of God."13O my God, make them like whirling dust, like chaff before the wind.14As fire consumes the forest, as the flame sets the mountains ablaze,15so may you pursue them with your tempest and terrify them with your hurricane!16Fill their faces with shame, that they may seek your name, O LORD.17Let them be put to shame and dismayed forever; let them perish in disgrace,18that they may know that you alone, whose name is the LORD, are the Most High over all the earth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Against You They Make a Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O God, do not keep silence; do not hold your peace or be still, O God! (v. 1). God's enemies make an uproar and plot against his treasured ones: Come, let us wipe them out as a nation; let the name of Israel be remembered no more! (vv. 2-4). Against you they make a covenant (v. 5) — Edom, the Ishmaelites, Moab, the Hagrites, Gebal, Ammon, Amalek, Philistia, Tyre, and Asshur with them (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Ten nations sign a treaty to erase Israel's name, and the psalm reads it as a treaty against God.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, do not keep silence; do not hold your peace or be still, O God! For behold, your enemies make an uproar; those who hate you have raised their heads. They lay crafty plans against your people; they consult together against your treasured ones. They say, "Come, let us wipe them out as a nation; let the name of Israel be remembered no more!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
O God, do not keep silence; do not hold your peace or be still, O God!

Three ways of saying the same thing in one breath — do not be silent, do not hold your peace, do not be still. It is the prayer of someone who can hear the enemy clearly and cannot hear God at all. God's silence, while the noise of opposition rises, is one of the hardest things a believer is asked to endure, and the psalm does not dress it up. It simply asks him to speak.

For behold, your enemies make an uproar; those who hate you have raised their heads. They lay crafty plans against your people; they consult together against your treasured ones.

Watch the pronouns. Your enemies, those who hate you, your people, your treasured ones. The psalm refuses to describe this as a border dispute. Israel is God's treasure, stored away as precious, and a plot against her is a plot against the one who treasures her.

Make an uproar is the roar of a crowd, and raised their heads is the posture of defiance — chin up, no longer bowed. It is Psalm 2 again: Why do the nations rage ... and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his Anointed (Ps 2:1-2). The consulting and the crafty planning are the same, and so is the reason heaven is not alarmed by them.

They say, Come, let us wipe them out as a nation; let the name of Israel be remembered no more!

The goal is not conquest but erasure: that there should be no Israel left even to remember. It has been tried many times since, by empires ancient and modern, and it has never worked — because the survival of God's people does not depend on their strength but on his promise. Him who dishonors you I will curse, God had told Abraham (Gen 12:3).

verseByVerse.quote: For they conspire with one accord; against you they make a covenant— the tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagrites, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, Philistia with the inhabitants of Tyre; Asshur also has joined them; they are the strong arm of the children of Lot. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they conspire with one accord; against you they make a covenant

They make a covenant. Israel was the people bound to God by covenant, and the nations answer with a covenant of their own, signed against him. That is how the psalm reads every united front against God's people: it is a counter-treaty, and its real target is in heaven.

The tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagrites, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, Philistia with the inhabitants of Tyre; Asshur also has joined them; they are the strong arm of the children of Lot.

Count them: Edom, the Ishmaelites, Moab, the Hagrites, Gebal, Ammon, Amalek, Philistia, Tyre, Asshur. Ten peoples, and they come from every direction — desert tribes to the south and east, Philistia on the coast, Tyre and Gebal (Byblos) to the north, and Assyria backing the lot. Several of them were relatives: Edom was Esau's line, the Ishmaelites Abraham's other son's, and the children of Lot were Moab and Ammon (Gen 19:37-38). The family had gathered against the family.

No recorded battle matches the whole list. The coalition of Moab, Ammon and Edom that came against Jehoshaphat is a partial fit (2 Chr 20:1-2), and on that occasion a Levite of the sons of Asaph stood up and prophesied (2 Chr 20:14). That is suggestive, no more. The list may describe that crisis, or it may be a picture of the whole ring of hostility that surrounded Israel at one time or another. Either way, a believer who feels surrounded is not imagining the geography.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–18 — That They May Seek Your Name
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do to them as you did to Midian, as to Sisera and Jabin at the river Kishon (v. 9); make their nobles like Oreb and Zeeb and their princes like Zebah and Zalmunna, who wanted God's pastures (vv. 10-12). Make them like whirling dust and chaff, pursue them with fire and tempest (vv. 13-15). Fill their faces with shame, that they may seek your name, O LORD (v. 16) — that they may know that you alone, whose name is the LORD, are the Most High over all the earth (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The fiercest prayer in the psalm has a surprising goal: that the enemies should come looking for God.

verseByVerse.quote: Do to them as you did to Midian, as to Sisera and Jabin at the river Kishon, who were destroyed at En-dor, who became dung for the ground. Make their nobles like Oreb and Zeeb, all their princes like Zebah and Zalmunna, who said, "Let us take possession for ourselves of the pastures of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do to them as you did to Midian, as to Sisera and Jabin at the river Kishon, who were destroyed at En-dor, who became dung for the ground.

Against ten nations, the psalm reaches for two memories from the book of Judges — and both were victories that Israel had no business winning.

Jabin, king of Canaan, had 900 chariots of iron and oppressed Israel for twenty years (Judg 4:3). His commander Sisera's army was destroyed when the Kishon rose and swept them away (Judg 5:21) — the song says the stars themselves fought against him. Midian came like locusts in number, with camels that could not be counted (Judg 6:5), and God cut Gideon's army down to the 300 men who lapped before he would give the victory (Judg 7:7). Amalek was in that host too (Judg 7:12), and Amalek is on this psalm's list (v. 7): the same enemy, and the same God.

Make their nobles like Oreb and Zeeb, all their princes like Zebah and Zalmunna, who said, Let us take possession for ourselves of the pastures of God.

Oreb and Zeeb were the princes of Midian captured and killed at a rock and a winepress that still bore their names (Judg 7:25); Zebah and Zalmunna were the kings Gideon killed himself (Judg 8:21). What they wanted was the pastures of God. The land was never Israel's to lose or Midian's to take. It was God's grazing ground, and he had put his flock on it.

Who became dung for the ground is a grim detail, chosen on purpose. Four psalms earlier the complaint was that Israel's dead lay unburied around Jerusalem (79:2-3). Here the psalm remembers that same end falling on those who once came against Israel, and asks for the harm to come back on the heads that were raised (v. 2).

The point of the memory is that the size of the coalition does not settle the outcome. It never did.

verseByVerse.quote: O my God, make them like whirling dust, like chaff before the wind. As fire consumes the forest, as the flame sets the mountains ablaze, so may you pursue them with your tempest and terrify them with your hurricane!
verseByVerse.commentary:
O my God, make them like whirling dust, like chaff before the wind. As fire consumes the forest, as the flame sets the mountains ablaze, so may you pursue them with your tempest and terrify them with your hurricane!

The images grow in violence: whirling dust, chaff, a forest fire, a hillside in flames, a storm. The ESV notes that whirling dust may be rendered "like a tumbleweed" — the dried thistle-head that breaks off in the autumn wind and rolls away across the fields, weightless, with nothing to hold it.

That is the picture of a coalition that seemed invincible: ten nations, a treaty, a plan, and all of it blown away like a dead plant across a threshing floor. The psalm does not ask God to fight on Israel's side. It asks him to be the weather.

verseByVerse.quote: Fill their faces with shame, that they may seek your name, O LORD. Let them be put to shame and dismayed forever; let them perish in disgrace, that they may know that you alone, whose name is the LORD, are the Most High over all the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fill their faces with shame, that they may seek your name, O LORD.

And here is the turn that changes how the whole psalm should be read. After the fire and the hurricane, the purpose of the shame is stated: that they may seek your name. The humiliation is aimed at conversion. The psalmist wants his enemies beaten so thoroughly that they stop trusting their gods and their treaty and come looking for the LORD.

That is not a softening of the prayer; it is the prayer's real ambition. There is a shame that crushes and a shame that sends a person searching, and the psalm asks for the second.

Let them be put to shame and dismayed forever; let them perish in disgrace, that they may know that you alone, whose name is the LORD, are the Most High over all the earth.

Verse 17 is the other possibility: those who will not seek will perish. The psalm holds both outcomes open, and they end in the same place — that they may know. Whether the enemy comes seeking or goes down in disgrace, the name of the LORD will be known as the only Most High, over all the earth, including Edom, Tyre and Assyria.

Follow the word name through the psalm. The enemies wanted Israel's name to be remembered no more (v. 4). The psalmist prays that they may seek your name (v. 16), and ends with the God whose name is the LORD (v. 18). The plot was to erase a name; the answer is that a greater name is made known, and those who seek it are given a place under it.

A Christian prays this psalm with the cross in view, and so prays verse 16 hardest. One of the fiercest enemies of the first church was a man still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord (Acts 9:1) — and his face was filled with shame on the Damascus road until he sought the name he had been trying to erase. The ten nations of this psalm are, in the end, invited. The name of Israel was not wiped out. It was widened to include anyone from Edom to Tyre who seeks the LORD.

83.title: Do Not Keep Silence
83.overview: The last of Asaph's psalms asks God not to keep silence while his enemies make an uproar and plot against his treasured people: let the name of Israel be remembered no more! (vv. 1-4). They make a covenant against God himself — ten peoples on every side, from Edom and Moab to Philistia, Tyre and Asshur (vv. 5-8). The psalmist asks God to do to them what he did in the days of the Judges to Sisera and Jabin at the Kishon and to the Midianite princes Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah and Zalmunna, who wanted God's pastures (vv. 9-12); to scatter them like tumbleweed and chaff and pursue them with fire and storm (vv. 13-15). Fill their faces with shame, that they may seek your name, O LORD (v. 16), and let all know that the LORD alone is Most High over all the earth (vv. 17-18).
83.theology:
Opposition to God's people is read as opposition to God: your enemies against your treasured ones (vv. 2-3), and the alliance is a counter-covenant against him (v. 5). The aim of erasing Israel's name (v. 4) runs against God's promise to Abraham (Gen 12:3).

The appeal to Judges (vv. 9-12) makes the point that the size of a coalition has never settled the outcome; the land was the pastures of God.

The imprecations have a stated goal: shame that leads the enemies to seek the LORD's name (v. 16), or, failing that, their perishing (v. 17) — and in both cases the knowledge that the LORD alone is Most High over all the earth (v. 18). A Christian prays with the cross in view and presses hardest on v. 16.
83.examples:
Three ways of saying: speak.

A treaty signed against heaven.

Ten nations, every direction, and the relatives among them.

Nine hundred iron chariots and a river in flood.

A dead thistle-head rolling across the field.

Shame that crushes, and shame that sends a man searching.

The persecutor on the Damascus road, seeking the name.
