84.text: To the choirmaster: according to The Gittith. A Psalm of the Sons of Korah. 1How lovely is your dwelling place, O LORD of hosts!2My soul longs, yes, faints for the courts of the LORD; my heart and flesh sing for joy to the living God.3Even the sparrow finds a home, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, at your altars, O LORD of hosts, my King and my God.4Blessed are those who dwell in your house, ever singing your praise! Selah5Blessed are those whose strength is in you, in whose heart are the highways to Zion.6As they go through the Valley of Baca they make it a place of springs; the early rain also covers it with pools.7They go from strength to strength; each one appears before God in Zion.8O LORD God of hosts, hear my prayer; give ear, O God of Jacob! Selah9Behold our shield, O God; look on the face of your anointed!10For a day in your courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of wickedness.11For the LORD God is a sun and shield; the LORD bestows favor and honor. No good thing does he withhold from those who walk uprightly.12O LORD of hosts, blessed is the one who trusts in you!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Even the Sparrow Finds a Home
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How lovely is your dwelling place, O LORD of hosts! My soul longs, yes, faints for the courts of the LORD; my heart and flesh sing for joy to the living God (vv. 1-2). Even the sparrow finds a home, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, at your altars, O LORD of hosts, my King and my God (v. 3). Blessed are those who dwell in your house, ever singing your praise! (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: A worshipper who cannot be there envies the birds that nest in the temple walls.

verseByVerse.quote: How lovely is your dwelling place, O LORD of hosts! My soul longs, yes, faints for the courts of the LORD; my heart and flesh sing for joy to the living God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How lovely is your dwelling place, O LORD of hosts!

The superscription says this is a psalm of the Sons of Korah, and the name carries a story. Korah led a rebellion against Moses in the wilderness and the ground swallowed him — but the sons of Korah did not die (Num 26:11). Generations later their descendants served at the sanctuary as keepers of the thresholds of the tent (1 Chr 9:19). A family whose ancestor tried to seize the holy place spent its history guarding the door of it, and wrote this song about how lovely it is. That is grace, in a family tree.

Lovely is a word for what is loved. The psalm does not open with a description of the building's architecture. It opens with affection — the way a man speaks of his home when he is a long way from it.

My soul longs, yes, faints for the courts of the LORD; my heart and flesh sing for joy to the living God.

The longing is total: soul, heart and flesh. Faints: pining away, worn thin by wanting. And the whole person does not merely long; it sings for joy. Longing and joy are not opposites here. The ache for God is itself a kind of gladness, because the one longed for is real and alive.

That is the phrase that gives the psalm its depth: the living God. It was the same cry in Psalm 42, also from the sons of Korah: My soul thirsts for God, for the living God (42:2). The courts are lovely because of who lives in them. No one faints with longing for a building. The man is homesick for a person.

If you have never felt anything like this, the psalm is not a rebuke; it is an invitation to ask for it. And if you have felt it and lost it, the psalm is proof that the desire is meant to be there, and can be asked for again.

verseByVerse.quote: Even the sparrow finds a home, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, at your altars, O LORD of hosts, my King and my God. Blessed are those who dwell in your house, ever singing your praise! Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the sparrow finds a home, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, at your altars, O LORD of hosts, my King and my God.

The singer is somewhere else — and he is jealous of the birds. Sparrows and swallows nested in the eaves and the crevices of the temple walls, flying in and out over the altars, raising their chicks in the busiest holy place in the country. Nobody drove them away. The smallest and least valued creatures in Israel had a permanent address in God's house, and he did not.

Jesus pointed to sparrows too, sold cheaply in the market and not one forgotten by the Father (Matt 10:29-31). If God makes room at his altar for a sparrow's nest, the believer who feels too small or too far from God to be wanted in his house has misread the house.

And notice the title at the end: my King and my God. It is personal. The birds have a nest; he wants the King.

Blessed are those who dwell in your house, ever singing your praise!

The first of three beatitudes in the psalm. The people who live at the temple — priests and Levites, and the families of doorkeepers — are called happy, and the reason given is not their security or their income but their occupation: ever singing your praise. Luke describes a woman like that, the widow Anna, who did not depart from the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day (Luke 2:37). She was eighty-four, and she was one of the first people on earth to recognise the child Jesus.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Blessed are those whose strength is in you, in whose heart are the highways to Zion (v. 5). As they go through the Valley of Baca they make it a place of springs; the early rain also covers it with pools (v. 6). They go from strength to strength; each one appears before God in Zion (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Pilgrims on the road to God turn a dry valley into a spring and arrive stronger than they set out.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those whose strength is in you, in whose heart are the highways to Zion. As they go through the Valley of Baca they make it a place of springs; the early rain also covers it with pools. They go from strength to strength; each one appears before God in Zion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are those whose strength is in you, in whose heart are the highways to Zion.

The second beatitude is for the people who cannot live there but are on their way. Their strength is not in themselves. And they carry the road inside them — in whose heart are the highways. The ESV notes that the Hebrew does not actually say "to Zion"; it simply says the highways are in their heart. The pilgrim routes have been worn into their affections. Their hearts are shaped like the road to God.

That is a searching test. Everyone's heart has a well-worn road in it — the direction the mind drifts when it is not being directed. Where the road in your heart runs is where your treasure is (Matt 6:21).

As they go through the Valley of Baca they make it a place of springs; the early rain also covers it with pools.

No one knows exactly where the Valley of Baca was, and the name itself is uncertain. Either way it is the dry stretch of the journey, the valley every pilgrim had to cross.

And the astonishing thing is what the pilgrims do to it. They do not merely get through the valley; they make it a place of springs. People whose strength is in God leave the dry places they pass through wetter than they found them. Then God adds his part — the early rain also covers it with pools. The traveller digs; heaven fills.

Paul described that kind of life: as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich (2 Cor 6:10). Some of the most refreshing believers you will ever meet are walking through their own dry valley, and have turned it into a well other people drink from.

They go from strength to strength; each one appears before God in Zion.

A long walk normally goes from strength to weakness. The pilgrims go the other way. The nearer they get to God, the stronger they grow, and the journey ends with every one of them — each one, none lost on the road — standing before God. That is the Christian life described as a pilgrimage: strangers who desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one (Heb 11:16), and who will arrive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–12 — A Day in Your Courts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O LORD God of hosts, hear my prayer; give ear, O God of Jacob! (v. 8). Behold our shield, O God; look on the face of your anointed! (v. 9). For a day in your courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of wickedness (v. 10). For the LORD God is a sun and shield; the LORD bestows favor and honor. No good thing does he withhold from those who walk uprightly (v. 11). O LORD of hosts, blessed is the one who trusts in you! (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: A doorkeeper's family sings that the threshold of God's house is better than the best room anywhere else.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD God of hosts, hear my prayer; give ear, O God of Jacob! Selah Behold our shield, O God; look on the face of your anointed!
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD God of hosts, hear my prayer; give ear, O God of Jacob!

For the fourth time in twelve verses the psalm calls God the LORD of hosts (vv. 1, 3, 8, 12) — the commander of heaven's armies — and here pairs it with God of Jacob, the God of the patriarch who limped and schemed and was loved anyway. The sovereign of the universe and the God of one flawed man are the same God, and the pilgrim can ask both to listen.

Behold our shield, O God; look on the face of your anointed!

A prayer for the king. Your anointed is the king in Jerusalem, and in parallel our shield appears to be the king too — the one who protects the people. The worshippers ask God to look kindly on the face of the man who represents them.

It is a small verse with a large reach. The Anointed One — the Messiah, the Christ — is the one on whose face God looks for his people's sake. A believer's standing before God rests not on God looking at his own face, but on God looking at the face of Christ, and accepting all who are his. That is why the Christian comes into the courts of God with confidence.

verseByVerse.quote: For a day in your courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of wickedness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For a day in your courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of wickedness.

The arithmetic is deliberate: one day against a thousand, nearly three years of days. Twenty-four hours in God's presence outweighs a thousand days anywhere else, however those days are filled.

And then the job comparison, which carries more weight when you remember who wrote it. The sons of Korah were keepers of the thresholds (1 Chr 9:19). A doorkeeper stood at the entrance — not in the inner courts, not at the altar, not in the choir — at the edge of the holy place, where he could see in. The singer says he would rather have that position, the least of the temple posts, than live comfortably inside the tents of the wicked.

That is a verse for anyone who serves in an unnoticed corner of God's house — the person who sets up the chairs, runs the door, washes the cups, or simply sits at the back. The threshold of God's house is better than the best room in any other.

And it is a question for anyone weighing a comfortable life that requires living among the tents of wickedness against a smaller one at the edge of God's people. The psalm has already done the sums.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD God is a sun and shield; the LORD bestows favor and honor. No good thing does he withhold from those who walk uprightly. O LORD of hosts, blessed is the one who trusts in you!
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the LORD God is a sun and shield; the LORD bestows favor and honor. No good thing does he withhold from those who walk uprightly.

Two images, both of what God gives. A sun — light, warmth, life, the thing that makes growth possible. A shield — protection. God is the source of everything good and the defence against everything harmful. Nowhere else in the Psalms is God called a sun. Isaiah later promised that the LORD will be your everlasting light (Isa 60:19), and Malachi that the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings (Mal 4:2) — and the pilgrim in the dark valley needs exactly that.

No good thing does he withhold. This is a promise believers sometimes find hard, because they can name things they asked for and did not get. The promise is not that God gives everything we want, but that he withholds nothing that is truly good for those who walk with him. If he has held something back, the promise says that from where he sees, it was not good for you — or not yet.

And the proof that he means it is the gift he did not withhold: He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (Rom 8:32). A God who gave that is not a God who is being stingy with the rest.

O LORD of hosts, blessed is the one who trusts in you!

The third beatitude, and it is different from the first two. Verse 4 blessed those who live in the temple. Verse 5 blessed those on the road to it. Verse 12 blesses the one who trusts — with no mention of a location at all. The psalm that began with homesickness for a building ends with a blessing that can be had anywhere.

Which is how the psalm reaches the believer today. Jesus said the hour was coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem would people worship the Father, but in spirit and truth (John 4:21-23). Christians have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God (Heb 12:22), and in the city to come there is no temple, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (Rev 21:22). The dwelling place is lovely because he is in it, and the one who trusts him is already home.

84.title: How Lovely Is Your Dwelling Place
84.overview: A psalm of the sons of Korah, whose family kept the temple doors. The singer longs with soul, heart and flesh for the courts of the living God, and envies the sparrow and swallow that nest at God's altars (vv. 1-3). Three beatitudes follow the psalm's movement: blessed are those who dwell in God's house, ever praising him (v. 4); blessed are the pilgrims whose strength is in God and whose hearts hold the highways, who make the Valley of Baca a place of springs and go from strength to strength until each appears before God (vv. 5-7). He prays for the king, God's anointed (vv. 8-9). A day in your courts is better than a thousand elsewhere; better a doorkeeper in God's house than a dweller in the tents of wickedness (v. 10). The LORD is sun and shield, withholding no good thing from the upright, and blessed is the one who trusts in you! (vv. 11-12).
84.theology:
The longing is for a person, not a place: the living God (v. 2; 42:2). The family of Korah, spared when their ancestor perished (Num 26:11) and appointed keepers of the thresholds (1 Chr 9:19), sings that the threshold of God's house is better than any other dwelling (v. 10).

God makes room at his altars for the smallest creatures (v. 3). Pilgrims whose strength is in God transform the dry valley and grow stronger on the road (vv. 5-7), strangers seeking a better country (Heb 11:16).

The people's welfare is bound to God's regard for the face of his anointed (v. 9), fulfilled in Christ. God is sun and shield and withholds no good thing (v. 11), a promise sealed by the gift of his Son (Rom 8:32).

The final beatitude blesses trust without reference to place (v. 12): worship in spirit and truth (John 4:23), the heavenly Zion (Heb 12:22), the city whose temple is God and the Lamb (Rev 21:22).
84.examples:
A rebel's descendants guarding the door he tried to force.

Homesick for a person, not a building.

Jealous of the sparrows in the temple eaves.

A heart shaped like the road to God.

Leaving the dry valley wetter than you found it.

A long walk that ends stronger than it began.

The chair-stacker at the back of God's house.

A blessing with no address attached.

85.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of the Sons of Korah. 1LORD, you were favorable to your land; you restored the fortunes of Jacob.2You forgave the iniquity of your people; you covered all their sin. Selah3You withdrew all your wrath; you turned from your hot anger.4Restore us again, O God of our salvation, and put away your indignation toward us!5Will you be angry with us forever? Will you prolong your anger to all generations?6Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?7Show us your steadfast love, O LORD, and grant us your salvation.8Let me hear what God the LORD will speak, for he will speak peace to his people, to his saints; but let them not turn back to folly.9Surely his salvation is near to those who fear him, that glory may dwell in our land.10Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other.11Faithfulness springs up from the ground, and righteousness looks down from the sky.12Yes, the LORD will give what is good, and our land will yield its increase.13Righteousness will go before him and make his footsteps a way.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: LORD, you were favorable to your land; you restored the fortunes of Jacob. You forgave the iniquity of your people; you covered all their sin (vv. 1-2), and withdrew all his wrath (v. 3). Restore us again, O God of our salvation, and put away your indignation toward us! (v. 4). Will you be angry with us forever? (v. 5). Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you? (v. 6). Show us your steadfast love, O LORD, and grant us your salvation (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: A people who have already been brought back ask to be brought back again — which is how the life of grace actually feels.

verseByVerse.quote: LORD, you were favorable to your land; you restored the fortunes of Jacob. You forgave the iniquity of your people; you covered all their sin. Selah You withdrew all your wrath; you turned from your hot anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
LORD, you were favorable to your land; you restored the fortunes of Jacob. You forgave the iniquity of your people; you covered all their sin.

Every verb is past tense. God was favourable, restored, forgave, covered. The psalm opens with a memory of a great turning — very probably the return from exile, when the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia to send the captives home (Ezra 1:1), though the psalm does not name the occasion.

And look at what the psalm counts as the heart of that restoration. Not the journey home, not the land recovered, but forgiveness: you forgave the iniquity ... you covered all their sin. The exile had been the punishment for sin, so the return meant the sin had been dealt with. All their sin — the account was not reduced; it was covered completely.

You withdrew all your wrath; you turned from your hot anger.

The third statement completes the memory. The anger that had burned against them was pulled back, entirely. That is the believer's past, too: whatever else is uncertain, the wrath has been turned away, because the sin has been covered. The rest of the psalm is prayed from that ground.

verseByVerse.quote: Restore us again, O God of our salvation, and put away your indignation toward us! Will you be angry with us forever? Will you prolong your anger to all generations? Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you? Show us your steadfast love, O LORD, and grant us your salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Restore us again, O God of our salvation, and put away your indignation toward us!

And then, abruptly, a present-tense plea — restore us again. They had been restored. Now they need restoring. If the setting is the return from Babylon, the disappointment is easy to picture: the people came home to ruins, poor harvests and a half-built temple. Haggai described those years: You have sown much, and harvested little. You eat, but you never have enough (Hag 1:6).

That is a very familiar experience. A person is converted, forgiven, brought home to God — and some years later finds the joy thin and the harvest small, and needs to be restored again. The psalm does not treat that as a contradiction of the first restoration. It builds the second prayer on the first mercy: you did it then; do it again.

Will you be angry with us forever? Will you prolong your anger to all generations? Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?

Three questions, and the third is the one that matters. Revive us again — give us life again. Habakkuk prayed the same thing: in the midst of the years revive it ... in wrath remember mercy (Hab 3:2). And the purpose is stated: that your people may rejoice in you. Not in better harvests, though those would come. In God. Revival, in the biblical sense, is not excitement; it is a people made glad in God again.

Show us your steadfast love, O LORD, and grant us your salvation.

The request underneath all the others. Show us — let us see it again — the covenant love that was never actually withdrawn.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — Let Me Hear What God Will Speak
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Let me hear what God the LORD will speak, for he will speak peace to his people, to his saints; but let them not turn back to folly (v. 8). His salvation is near to those who fear him, that glory may dwell in our land (v. 9). Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other (v. 10). Faithfulness springs from the ground and righteousness looks down from the sky (v. 11); the land yields its increase, and righteousness goes before him (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm stops asking and listens, and hears four of God's attributes embrace — which happened at the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Let me hear what God the LORD will speak, for he will speak peace to his people, to his saints; but let them not turn back to folly. Surely his salvation is near to those who fear him, that glory may dwell in our land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let me hear what God the LORD will speak, for he will speak peace to his people, to his saints; but let them not turn back to folly.

Here the psalm does something prayer often forgets to do: it stops talking and listens. Let me hear what God the LORD will speak. After seven verses of asking, the singer waits for an answer, and he knows what kind of answer is coming — he will speak peace.

But there is a condition folded into the promise: let them not turn back to folly. The peace God speaks is not permission to return to whatever caused the exile in the first place. A restored person who goes straight back to the old folly has misheard the word of peace.

Surely his salvation is near to those who fear him, that glory may dwell in our land.

Near — not distant, not only future, but at hand for those who fear him. And the goal of salvation is that glory may dwell in our land: God's own glorious presence, which had left the temple before the exile, settling back among his people.

John chose the language of dwelling for the moment that prayer was answered beyond anything the returning exiles imagined: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory (John 1:14). The glory came back to the land in a person.

verseByVerse.quote: Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other. Faithfulness springs up from the ground, and righteousness looks down from the sky. Yes, the LORD will give what is good, and our land will yield its increase. Righteousness will go before him and make his footsteps a way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other.

This is the most beautiful verse in the psalm. Four of God's attributes are pictured as people who meet on a road and embrace.

Steadfast love and faithfulness are the pair God announced to Moses on the mountain — abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod 34:6): his loyal love, and his reliability. Those two sit easily together.

The harder pair is righteousness and peace. Righteousness demands that sin be judged; peace means the sinner is reconciled. How can both be satisfied at once? A just judge cannot simply make peace with the guilty. Isaiah had said the effect of righteousness will be peace (Isa 32:17), but no one could see how.

The cross is where they kissed. God put Christ forward as a propitiation so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Rom 3:26). Righteousness was fully satisfied, and so peace became possible: since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God (Rom 5:1). He himself is our peace (Eph 2:14).

Faithfulness springs up from the ground, and righteousness looks down from the sky.

Now the picture is of earth and heaven. Faithfulness grows up out of the soil like a plant; righteousness leans down from above like the sun. Isaiah used the same image: Shower, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down righteousness; let the earth open, that salvation and righteousness may bear fruit (Isa 45:8). Heaven and earth meet — which is what the angels announced over Bethlehem: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace (Luke 2:14).

Yes, the LORD will give what is good, and our land will yield its increase. Righteousness will go before him and make his footsteps a way.

The meagre harvests of the restoration years — sown much, harvested little — are answered: our land will yield its increase. And the last image is of God walking through his land with righteousness going ahead of him like a herald, marking out the path. His people can walk in his footsteps, because righteousness has made them a road. The psalm that began with a forgiven people needing to be restored again ends with a way to walk on.

85.title: Righteousness and Peace Kiss Each Other
85.overview: The sons of Korah remember a past restoration: God was favourable to his land, restored Jacob's fortunes, forgave and covered all his people's sin and withdrew his wrath (vv. 1-3). Yet they need restoring again: Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you? (vv. 4-7). The singer stops to listen: God will speak peace to his people — only let them not turn back to folly (v. 8). His salvation is near, that glory may dwell in the land (v. 9). Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other (v. 10); faithfulness springs from the ground and righteousness looks down from heaven, the land yields its increase, and righteousness goes before God to make his footsteps a way (vv. 11-13).
85.theology:
Past forgiveness is the ground of present prayer (vv. 1-4). A restored people can need restoring again, and revival is a people made glad in God (v. 6; Hab 3:2).

Prayer includes listening (v. 8), and God's word of peace carries a call not to return to folly.

The dwelling of glory in the land (v. 9) is fulfilled when the Word dwelt among us (John 1:14). Righteousness and peace, which seem to pull apart, meet at the cross, where God is just and the justifier (v. 10; Rom 3:26; Rom 5:1; Eph 2:14), and heaven and earth are joined (v. 11; Isa 45:8; Luke 2:14).
85.examples:
Everything forgiven, and all means all.

Home from exile to ruins and a thin harvest.

You did it then; do it again.

Revival: not excitement, but gladness in God.

After seven verses of asking, the singer listens.

Two attributes that seemed unable to meet, embracing at the cross.

Righteousness going ahead of God, marking out a road.

86.text: A Prayer of David. 1Incline your ear, O LORD, and answer me, for I am poor and needy.2Preserve my life, for I am godly; save your servant, who trusts in you—you are my God.3Be gracious to me, O Lord, for to you do I cry all the day.4Gladden the soul of your servant, for to you, O Lord, do I lift up my soul.5For you, O Lord, are good and forgiving, abounding in steadfast love to all who call upon you.6Give ear, O LORD, to my prayer; listen to my plea for grace.7In the day of my trouble I call upon you, for you answer me.8There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, nor are there any works like yours.9All the nations you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord, and shall glorify your name.10For you are great and do wondrous things; you alone are God.11Teach me your way, O LORD, that I may walk in your truth; unite my heart to fear your name.12I give thanks to you, O Lord my God, with my whole heart, and I will glorify your name forever.13For great is your steadfast love toward me; you have delivered my soul from the depths of Sheol.14O God, insolent men have risen up against me; a band of ruthless men seeks my life, and they do not set you before them.15But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.16Turn to me and be gracious to me; give your strength to your servant, and save the son of your maidservant.17Show me a sign of your favor, that those who hate me may see and be put to shame because you, LORD, have helped me and comforted me.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — For I Am Poor and Needy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Incline your ear, O LORD, and answer me, for I am poor and needy (v. 1). Preserve and save your servant, who trusts in you; be gracious, gladden his soul (vv. 2-4). For you, O Lord, are good and forgiving, abounding in steadfast love to all who call upon you (v. 5). In the day of my trouble I call upon you, for you answer me (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Every request comes with a reason, and the reasons are his need and God's character.

verseByVerse.quote: Incline your ear, O LORD, and answer me, for I am poor and needy. Preserve my life, for I am godly; save your servant, who trusts in you—you are my God. Be gracious to me, O Lord, for to you do I cry all the day. Gladden the soul of your servant, for to you, O Lord, do I lift up my soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Incline your ear, O LORD, and answer me, for I am poor and needy.

This is the only psalm in Book Three that bears David's name, and it is a prayer made almost entirely of borrowed phrases — lines that appear in other psalms and in the law — woven into one plea. That is not a weakness. When a man is in trouble he reaches for the words he already knows, and the psalm shows a mind so stocked with Scripture that its own prayers come out in Scripture's language.

The first reason he gives God for listening is his condition: poor and needy, the words of 40:17. It is the reason God responds to. Nobody gets God's ear by being impressive.

Preserve my life, for I am godly; save your servant, who trusts in you — you are my God.

For I am godly sounds like boasting until you read on. It is a claim to covenant loyalty, not to sinlessness. The very next clause says what the loyalty consists of: who trusts in you. His claim is not that he deserves saving but that he belongs to God and has put his weight on him.

Be gracious to me, O Lord, for to you do I cry all the day. Gladden the soul of your servant, for to you, O Lord, do I lift up my soul.

Count the word for through this psalm: in verses 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10 and 13. David does not simply ask; he argues. Every request is backed by a reason — because I am needy, because I trust you, because I cry to you all day, because I lift my soul to you. That is not manipulation. It is prayer that thinks, and a believer is invited to pray that way.

Gladden the soul is a request for joy, not merely rescue. He wants to be made glad again, and he knows where gladness comes from, because that is where he has lifted his soul.

verseByVerse.quote: For you, O Lord, are good and forgiving, abounding in steadfast love to all who call upon you. Give ear, O LORD, to my prayer; listen to my plea for grace. In the day of my trouble I call upon you, for you answer me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you, O Lord, are good and forgiving, abounding in steadfast love to all who call upon you.

Now the reasons move from David's condition to God's character — which is the stronger ground. Good and forgiving, abounding in steadfast love echoes what God proclaimed about himself to Moses, and the psalm will quote that proclamation in full at verse 15.

And the scope: to all who call upon you. There is no qualifying test beyond the calling. Paul says the same of Christ, who is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him (Rom 10:12). A person who wonders whether God's steadfast love extends to him has only to ask whether he has called.

Give ear, O LORD, to my prayer; listen to my plea for grace. In the day of my trouble I call upon you, for you answer me.

For you answer me — present tense, a settled expectation. He has not yet been answered this time; the trouble is still on. But his history with God has taught him that God is the kind who answers, and he calls on that basis.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — There Is None Like You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, nor are there any works like yours (v. 8). All the nations he made shall come and worship; you alone are God (vv. 9-10). Teach me your way, O LORD, that I may walk in your truth; unite my heart to fear your name (v. 11). He will give thanks with his whole heart, for God's steadfast love has delivered him from the depths of Sheol (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: In the middle of trouble a man asks, above all, for a heart that is no longer split.

verseByVerse.quote: There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, nor are there any works like yours. All the nations you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord, and shall glorify your name. For you are great and do wondrous things; you alone are God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, nor are there any works like yours.

In the middle of a personal crisis, David lifts his eyes to the whole world. It is a deliberate move. Trouble shrinks our horizon to the size of the problem, and the cure is to remember how big God is: there is no other god that compares, and no other works like his.

All the nations you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord, and shall glorify your name. For you are great and do wondrous things; you alone are God.

The logic is careful. God made the nations, so they belong to him, and one day they shall come. A poor and needy man in a corner of Israel prays with the whole world's future in view. John heard the song of the redeemed at the end of history saying exactly this: All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed (Rev 15:4).

You alone are God. That is the confession that makes a man's private trouble manageable. If God alone is God, then the insolent men of verse 14 are not.

verseByVerse.quote: Teach me your way, O LORD, that I may walk in your truth; unite my heart to fear your name. I give thanks to you, O Lord my God, with my whole heart, and I will glorify your name forever. For great is your steadfast love toward me; you have delivered my soul from the depths of Sheol.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teach me your way, O LORD, that I may walk in your truth; unite my heart to fear your name.

This is the centre of the psalm, and one of the great prayers of the Bible. With enemies after his life, David's deepest request is not for rescue but for teaching and for an undivided heart.

Unite my heart. He knows his heart is split — part of it fearing God, part of it fearing men; part trusting, part scheming; loyalties pulling in several directions. James calls that man a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways (Jas 1:8). And a divided heart cannot fear God properly, because fear of God is the whole heart bowed in one direction.

Only God can do this. It is a request, not a resolution. God later promised it as a gift of the new covenant: I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever (Jer 32:39). Anyone who has tried to love God with a heart that keeps going elsewhere can pray this verse every morning, and should.

I give thanks to you, O Lord my God, with my whole heart, and I will glorify your name forever. For great is your steadfast love toward me; you have delivered my soul from the depths of Sheol.

And here is the answer in the next line: with my whole heart. The united heart is a thankful one. The reason for thanks is a rescue from the depths of Sheol — whether a past deliverance or one so certain he speaks of it as done. Either way, the man who asked for a whole heart ends up using it to give thanks.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Insolent and ruthless men seek his life, and they do not set you before them (v. 14). But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (v. 15). Turn to me and be gracious to me; give your strength to your servant, and save the son of your maidservant (v. 16). He asks for a sign of favour that his enemies can see (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Against a gang who leave God out of the reckoning, David sets the name God proclaimed on Sinai.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, insolent men have risen up against me; a band of ruthless men seeks my life, and they do not set you before them. But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness. Turn to me and be gracious to me; give your strength to your servant, and save the son of your maidservant. Show me a sign of your favor, that those who hate me may see and be put to shame because you, LORD, have helped me and comforted me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O God, insolent men have risen up against me; a band of ruthless men seeks my life, and they do not set you before them.

The trouble is named at last: arrogant men, a gang, ruthless, after his life. And the diagnosis is exact: they do not set you before them. It is the reverse of Psalm 16, where David said, I have set the LORD always before me (16:8). The difference between the godly man and the ruthless one is not that one is stronger. It is what each keeps in front of his eyes. People who leave God out of their reckoning will do anything.

But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.

Against the gang who leave God out, David sets God's own name — almost word for word the proclamation from Sinai: The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod 34:6). He answers the threat with a creed. When men are ruthless, the believer's refuge is that God is not.

Turn to me and be gracious to me; give your strength to your servant, and save the son of your maidservant.

The son of your maidservant is a household term. A servant born to a servant in the house was not bought from outside; he belonged to the household from birth and had a claim on its master's protection. David says he was born into God's house. Psalm 116 uses the same words: I am your servant, the son of your maidservant (116:16).

Show me a sign of your favor, that those who hate me may see and be put to shame because you, LORD, have helped me and comforted me.

The last request is modest: a sign, something visible, enough that his enemies can see God is on his side. And the final words are the two things God does for the poor and needy man of verse 1 — helped me and comforted me. Help for the trouble outside; comfort for the soul inside. He asks for both, and the psalm speaks of both as already given.

86.title: Unite My Heart to Fear Your Name
86.overview: David, poor and needy, asks God to hear and preserve his servant who trusts in him, and to gladden his soul (vv. 1-4), because God is good, forgiving and abounding in steadfast love to all who call (vv. 5-7). There is none like God among the gods; all the nations he made will come and worship, you alone are God (vv. 8-10). Teach me your way, O LORD, that I may walk in your truth; unite my heart to fear your name (v. 11) — and he will give thanks with his whole heart for deliverance from the depths of Sheol (vv. 12-13). Insolent, ruthless men seek his life and do not set God before them (v. 14), but God is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (v. 15); he asks for strength, salvation and a sign of favour (vv. 16-17).
86.theology:
Prayer is argued with reasons: the petitioner's need and trust (vv. 1-4), and above all God's character (v. 5), open to all who call (Rom 10:12). Godly (v. 2) means covenant-loyal and trusting, not sinless.

Personal trouble is set within God's universal reign: the nations he made will worship him (vv. 8-10; Rev 15:4).

The deepest request is for an undivided heart (v. 11), which only God can give (Jer 32:39) and which issues in whole-hearted thanks (v. 12).

The ruthless are those who do not set God before them (v. 14; contrast 16:8). The answer to them is God's self-proclaimed name from Sinai (v. 15; Exod 34:6), and a servant born into God's household can claim his protection (v. 16).
86.examples:
A prayer made of borrowed Scripture.

Nobody gets God's ear by being impressive.

Eight reasons in seventeen verses.

Trouble shrinks the horizon; the nations widen it.

A heart pulled in several directions, asking to be made one.

What each man keeps in front of his eyes.

A creed set against a gang.

A servant born in the house.

87.text: A Psalm of the Sons of Korah. A Song. 1On the holy mount stands the city he founded;2the LORD loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwelling places of Jacob.3Glorious things of you are spoken, O city of God. Selah4Among those who know me I mention Rahab and Babylon; behold, Philistia and Tyre, with Cush — "This one was born there," they say.5And of Zion it shall be said, "This one and that one were born in her"; for the Most High himself will establish her.6The LORD records as he registers the peoples, "This one was born there." Selah7Singers and dancers alike say, "All my springs are in you."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the holy mount stands the city he founded; the LORD loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwelling places of Jacob (vv. 1-2). Glorious things of you are spoken, O city of God (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The city is glorious not for its walls but because God founded it and loves it.

verseByVerse.quote: On the holy mount stands the city he founded; the LORD loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwelling places of Jacob. Glorious things of you are spoken, O city of God. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the holy mount stands the city he founded; the LORD loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwelling places of Jacob.

The psalm opens abruptly, almost mid-thought, with the foundation of a city. Its founder is not named in the first line — just he — because in Israel there was only one person who could be meant. Zion was not chosen because it was strong or beautiful; it stands because God founded it.

And he loves it. The gates of Zion — where people came in to worship, where the city met — are loved more than every other town in Israel. God's love for a place is really his love for what happens there: it is where he chose to put his name and meet his people.

Glorious things of you are spoken, O city of God.

Then the singer turns and speaks to the city directly. Glorious things have been said about her — and the rest of the psalm tells us what the most glorious of them is. It is not the temple, the palace or the walls. It is the list of who lives there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–7 — This One Was Born There
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Among those who know me I mention Rahab and Babylon; behold, Philistia and Tyre, with Cush — each is said to have been born there (v. 4). And of Zion it shall be said, This one and that one were born in her; for the Most High himself will establish her (v. 5). The LORD records as he registers the peoples, This one was born there (v. 6). Singers and dancers alike say, All my springs are in you (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's worst enemies are enrolled as native citizens of the city of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Among those who know me I mention Rahab and Babylon; behold, Philistia and Tyre, with Cush — "This one was born there," they say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Among those who know me I mention Rahab and Babylon; behold, Philistia and Tyre, with Cush — This one was born there, they say.

Now God speaks, and he reads out a list of nations — and every one of them is a shock.

Rahab is a poetic name for Egypt (Isaiah calls Egypt Rahab who sits still, Isa 30:7) — the house of slavery, the first oppressor. Babylon is the empire that burned the temple and carried the people away. Philistia was the old enemy on the coast, Goliath's people. Tyre was the wealthy, proud trading city. And Cush, which the ESV notes is probably Nubia, lay at the far southern edge of the known world.

These are the nations God lists among those who know me. Knowing God is covenant language; it is what was said of Israel. And of each of them: This one was born there — born in Zion. Not a visitor, not a resident alien, not a tolerated guest. A native.

The prophets glimpsed the same thing. Isaiah heard God say, Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance (Isa 19:25). The enemies of God's people become God's people.

verseByVerse.quote: And of Zion it shall be said, "This one and that one were born in her"; for the Most High himself will establish her. The LORD records as he registers the peoples, "This one was born there." Selah Singers and dancers alike say, "All my springs are in you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And of Zion it shall be said, This one and that one were born in her; for the Most High himself will establish her.

This one and that one — person by person, individual by individual. Membership of the city of God is not granted to nations in the mass; each one is counted. And the city's security rests where it did in verse 1: the Most High himself will establish her.

Paul spoke of this city. The Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother (Gal 4:26). A Gentile Christian from Galatia or Rome or Ethiopia has a birthplace in the city of God. You are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God (Eph 2:19).

The LORD records as he registers the peoples, This one was born there.

The picture is a census. God himself keeps the register and writes each name in, with the entry: born in Zion. It is the register Jesus told his disciples to rejoice in: rejoice that your names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). Hebrews calls the church the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven (Heb 12:23).

That is the answer for anyone who feels like an outsider to God's people — from the wrong background, the wrong nation, with the wrong past. Citizenship of this city is not by ancestry but by God's registration, and his entry is born there. Jesus called it being born again (John 3:3). Luke tells of an Ethiopian official from that far south who had come to Jerusalem to worship (Acts 8:27) and went home with his name in the register.

Singers and dancers alike say, All my springs are in you.

The psalm ends in a festival. The newly enrolled citizens of every nation are singing and dancing together, and their song is short: All my springs are in you. Every source of life and refreshment they have, they find in the city of God — which is to say, in the God of the city. In a dry land, a spring is the reason a town exists. John saw the end of it: a multitude from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb (Rev 7:9). Egypt and Babylon among them.

87.title: Glorious Things of You Are Spoken
87.overview: The LORD founded his city on the holy mountain and loves the gates of Zion more than all Jacob's dwellings; glorious things are spoken of her (vv. 1-3). Then God names Rahab (Egypt) and Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Cush among those who know him, and says of each, This one was born there (v. 4). Of Zion it will be said, This one and that one were born in her, for the Most High will establish her (v. 5); the LORD records it as he registers the peoples (v. 6). Singers and dancers say, All my springs are in you (v. 7).
87.theology:
The city's glory lies in God's founding and love (vv. 1-3), and its most glorious feature is its citizenship.

Israel's oppressors and distant nations are enrolled as native-born citizens of Zion (v. 4), as Isaiah foresaw (Isa 19:24-25). Enrolment is individual (this one and that one, v. 5) and recorded by God himself (v. 6).

The New Testament identifies the city as the Jerusalem above, mother of believers (Gal 4:26), in which Gentiles are fellow citizens (Eph 2:19) with names written in heaven (Luke 10:20; Heb 12:23). Every source of life is found there (v. 7), and the end is a multitude from every nation (Rev 7:9).
87.examples:
A city that stands because God founded it.

Egypt and Babylon on the list of those who know God.

Not a visitor or a guest: a native.

Counted one by one: this one and that one.

God keeping the register himself.

An Ethiopian official with his name in the book.

A festival of former enemies singing about springs.

88.text: A Song. A Psalm of the Sons of Korah. To the choirmaster: according to Mahalath Leannoth. A Maskil of Heman the Ezrahite. 1O LORD, God of my salvation, I cry out day and night before you.2Let my prayer come before you; incline your ear to my cry!3For my soul is full of troubles, and my life draws near to Sheol.4I am counted among those who go down to the pit; I am a man who has no strength,5like one set loose among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, like those whom you remember no more, for they are cut off from your hand.6You have put me in the depths of the pit, in the regions dark and deep.7Your wrath lies heavy upon me, and you overwhelm me with all your waves. Selah8You have caused my companions to shun me; you have made me a horror to them. I am shut in so that I cannot escape;9my eye grows dim through sorrow. Every day I call upon you, O LORD; I spread out my hands to you.10Do you work wonders for the dead? Do the departed rise up to praise you? Selah11Is your steadfast love declared in the grave, or your faithfulness in Abaddon?12Are your wonders known in the darkness, or your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?13But I, O LORD, cry to you; in the morning my prayer comes before you.14O LORD, why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face from me?15Afflicted and close to death from my youth up, I suffer your terrors; I am helpless.16Your wrath has swept over me; your dreadful assaults destroy me.17They surround me like a flood all day long; they close in on me together.18You have caused my beloved and my friend to shun me; my companions have become darkness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — I Cry Out Day and Night
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O LORD, God of my salvation, I cry out day and night before you (v. 1). My soul is full of troubles, and my life draws near to Sheol (v. 3); he is counted among the dead, like those whom you remember no more (vv. 4-5). You have put me in the depths of the pit; your wrath lies heavy upon me (vv. 6-7). His companions shun him, he is shut in and his eye grows dim, and every day I call upon you, O LORD (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: A man near death keeps praying to the God he believes has put him there.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, God of my salvation, I cry out day and night before you. Let my prayer come before you; incline your ear to my cry!
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD, God of my salvation, I cry out day and night before you. Let my prayer come before you; incline your ear to my cry!

No psalm is darker than this one. Almost every other lament in the Psalter turns somewhere — to trust, to a vow of praise, to a remembered mercy. This one does not. It begins in trouble and ends in darkness, and nothing in between lifts.

Which makes the first line all the more important. O LORD, God of my salvation. It is the only statement of hope in the psalm, and it is spoken before a word of complaint. The man still calls God the God who saves him. He cannot see it, he does not feel it, and nothing that follows will confirm it — but he says it, and he says it first.

And he says it day and night. He has not stopped praying. That is itself the faith of this psalm: not a feeling of confidence, but a refusal to stop speaking to God. Heman was a name associated with wisdom (1 Kgs 4:31) and with the temple singers (1 Chr 6:33), and this is what a wise man's prayer sounds like when there is no light at all.

verseByVerse.quote: For my soul is full of troubles, and my life draws near to Sheol. I am counted among those who go down to the pit; I am a man who has no strength, like one set loose among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, like those whom you remember no more, for they are cut off from your hand. You have put me in the depths of the pit, in the regions dark and deep. Your wrath lies heavy upon me, and you overwhelm me with all your waves. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
For my soul is full of troubles, and my life draws near to Sheol. I am counted among those who go down to the pit; I am a man who has no strength,

Full — the soul has no room left. He is near death and people already treat him as good as dead: counted among those who go down to the pit. A man who has no strength is a man whom others have stopped expecting anything from. Anyone who has been seriously ill for a long time knows how it feels to be written off while still alive.

like one set loose among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, like those whom you remember no more, for they are cut off from your hand.

The fear goes deeper than death. It is being remembered no more by God, cut off from your hand. The Old Testament believer had only a dim view of what lay beyond the grave, and the horror here is not pain but abandonment — being set loose, like a discharged soldier, into a place God does not visit.

You have put me in the depths of the pit, in the regions dark and deep. Your wrath lies heavy upon me, and you overwhelm me with all your waves.

Notice who the subject of every verb is. You have put me there; your wrath, your waves. He does not blame chance, or enemies, or even himself. He says God did it. That is terrible, and it is also, strangely, a kind of faith — he refuses to believe his suffering is outside God's hand. Jonah, in the belly of the fish, used the same image: all your breakers and your waves passed over me (Jonah 2:3).

verseByVerse.quote: You have caused my companions to shun me; you have made me a horror to them. I am shut in so that I cannot escape; my eye grows dim through sorrow. Every day I call upon you, O LORD; I spread out my hands to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have caused my companions to shun me; you have made me a horror to them. I am shut in so that I cannot escape;

The illness — whatever it was — has isolated him. His friends avoid him. He has become a horror to them (the ESV notes "an abomination" as a possible rendering), perhaps because the disease made him unclean, perhaps simply because long suffering is unbearable to watch and people stay away. Job said the same: He has put my brothers far from me, and those who knew me are wholly estranged from me (Job 19:13). Shut in so that I cannot escape — confined, quarantined, trapped.

my eye grows dim through sorrow. Every day I call upon you, O LORD; I spread out my hands to you.

His eyes are failing from weeping. And again: every day I call upon you. He spreads out his hands, the posture of a beggar or a drowning man, empty and reaching. Nothing comes back. He does it the next day.

If you are praying like this — every day, for a long time, with no answer — this psalm is in the Bible for you. God has put into his own book the prayer of a man for whom nothing got better, and has called it a song.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–12 — Do the Departed Rise Up to Praise You?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do you work wonders for the dead? Do the departed rise up to praise you? (v. 10). Is your steadfast love declared in the grave, or your faithfulness in Abaddon? Are your wonders known in the darkness, or your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness? (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Six questions that argue with God: if I die, you lose a worshipper.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you work wonders for the dead? Do the departed rise up to praise you? Selah Is your steadfast love declared in the grave, or your faithfulness in Abaddon? Are your wonders known in the darkness, or your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you work wonders for the dead? Do the departed rise up to praise you?

Now he argues, with a string of six questions. The logic is simple: if I die, who gains? The dead do not sing in the temple. If God wants to be praised by this man, he had better keep him alive.

Is your steadfast love declared in the grave, or your faithfulness in Abaddon? Are your wonders known in the darkness, or your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?

Abaddon means destruction, and the land of forgetfulness is a haunting name for the grave — the place where the dead forget and are forgotten. The questions expect the answer no.

In Heman's day that was as far as the light reached. But the questions have since been answered in a way he could not have imagined. Do the departed rise up to praise you? — the answer given on the third day was yes. God did work a wonder for the dead. And now nothing, not even death, can separate a believer from God's steadfast love: neither death nor life ... nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord (Rom 8:38-39). The land of forgetfulness is not beyond God's memory after all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–18 — Why Do You Hide Your Face?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But I, O LORD, cry to you; in the morning my prayer comes before you (v. 13). O LORD, why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face from me? (v. 14). Afflicted from his youth, overwhelmed by God's terrors like a flood (vv. 15-17). You have caused my beloved and my friend to shun me; my companions have become darkness (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm ends without a resolution, and its last word is darkness.

verseByVerse.quote: But I, O LORD, cry to you; in the morning my prayer comes before you. O LORD, why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face from me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I, O LORD, cry to you; in the morning my prayer comes before you.

But I. After the questions that seem to leave no room for hope, he goes back to praying — in the morning, first thing, before anything else. Day and night (v. 1), every day (v. 9), in the morning (v. 13). The psalm has no answer from God in it, but it has a man who keeps turning up.

O LORD, why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face from me?

The worst of it is not the illness or the loneliness. It is God's hidden face. The man who has lost his friends could perhaps bear it if God's face were turned towards him. It is not.

Someone has prayed these words more completely than Heman. On the cross Jesus cried, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Matt 27:46). The Son experienced the hidden face of the Father fully, so that no one who belongs to him ever will — whatever it feels like in the dark.

verseByVerse.quote: Afflicted and close to death from my youth up, I suffer your terrors; I am helpless. Your wrath has swept over me; your dreadful assaults destroy me. They surround me like a flood all day long; they close in on me together. You have caused my beloved and my friend to shun me; my companions have become darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Afflicted and close to death from my youth up, I suffer your terrors; I am helpless.

From my youth up. This is not a crisis that arrived last month. It has been his whole life. Some people carry a sickness, a darkness of mind, or a sorrow from childhood that never lifts, and this verse is theirs. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew word rendered "helpless" is uncertain — which fits. There are states that do not have a clear word.

Your wrath has swept over me; your dreadful assaults destroy me. They surround me like a flood all day long; they close in on me together.

The flood again, rising from every side. It is the language of drowning — not one wave but water that closes over the head.

You have caused my beloved and my friend to shun me; my companions have become darkness.

And there it ends. The last word of the psalm is darkness. The ESV gives another rendering: "darkness has become my only companion". No resolution, no praise, no ray of light.

Do not rush past that. God's people have always needed a psalm that does not resolve, because life does not always resolve on schedule, and a believer in the long dark should not be made to feel his faith has failed because he cannot write the happy last verse. Heman couldn't either, and his prayer is Scripture.

But he is not alone in the dark. Jesus said, My soul is very sorrowful, even to death (Matt 26:38). He was a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief (Isa 53:3); at the cross all his acquaintances ... stood at a distance (Luke 23:49). He offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard (Heb 5:7). The God of Heman's salvation went down into this psalm himself, and came out the other side, and the darkness is not the last companion of anyone who is his.

88.title: My Companions Have Become Darkness
88.overview: Heman cries day and night to the God of his salvation (vv. 1-2). His soul is full of troubles; he is near death, counted among the dead, like those God remembers no more (vv. 3-5). God has put him in the pit, his wrath heavy and his waves overwhelming (vv. 6-7); his companions shun him and he is shut in, yet every day he spreads out his hands to God (vv. 8-9). Six questions: do the dead praise God, is his steadfast love declared in the grave, his wonders known in the land of forgetfulness? (vv. 10-12). Every morning he prays, and asks why God casts him off and hides his face (vv. 13-14). Afflicted from youth, overwhelmed by God's terrors like a flood (vv. 15-17), he ends: my companions have become darkness (v. 18).
88.theology:
Unlike almost every other lament, this psalm ends with no turn to trust or praise. Its faith lies in its first words, God of my salvation (v. 1), and in unbroken prayer — day and night, every day, every morning (vv. 1, 9, 13).

Suffering is attributed to God's own hand (vv. 6-8, 16-18), which is anguish and also a refusal to place it outside his control. The fear beneath death is being forgotten by God (v. 5).

The six questions (vv. 10-12) reflect the limited Old Testament light on the grave; they are answered by the resurrection and by the promise that nothing in death separates believers from God's love (Rom 8:38-39).

The hidden face (v. 14) was borne fully by Christ (Matt 27:46), the man of sorrows abandoned by his friends (Isa 53:3; Luke 23:49), who was heard (Heb 5:7). The Bible includes an unresolved prayer so that believers in lasting darkness are not told their faith has failed.
88.examples:
The only light in the psalm is its first line.

Written off while still alive.

Every verb has God as its subject.

Friends who stay away because suffering is hard to watch.

Hands spread out every day, and nothing comes back.

The land of forgetfulness — not beyond God's memory.

A sorrow carried from childhood.

The last word is darkness, and the psalm is still Scripture.

89.text: A Maskil of Ethan the Ezrahite. 1I will sing of the steadfast love of the LORD forever; with my mouth I will make known your faithfulness to all generations.2For I said, "Steadfast love will be built up forever; in the heavens you will establish your faithfulness."3You have said, "I have made a covenant with my chosen one; I have sworn to David my servant:4'I will establish your offspring forever, and build your throne for all generations.'" Selah5Let the heavens praise your wonders, O LORD, your faithfulness in the assembly of the holy ones!6For who in the skies can be compared to the LORD? Who among the heavenly beings is like the LORD,7a God greatly to be feared in the council of the holy ones, and awesome above all who are around him?8O LORD God of hosts, who is mighty as you are, O LORD, with your faithfulness all around you?9You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them.10You crushed Rahab like a carcass; you scattered your enemies with your mighty arm.11The heavens are yours; the earth also is yours; the world and all that is in it, you have founded them.12The north and the south, you have created them; Tabor and Hermon joyously praise your name.13You have a mighty arm; strong is your hand, high your right hand.14Righteousness and justice are the foundation of your throne; steadfast love and faithfulness go before you.15Blessed are the people who know the festal shout, who walk, O LORD, in the light of your face,16who exult in your name all the day and in your righteousness are exalted.17For you are the glory of their strength; by your favor our horn is exalted.18For our shield belongs to the LORD, our king to the Holy One of Israel.19Of old you spoke in a vision to your godly one, and said: "I have granted help to one who is mighty; I have exalted one chosen from the people.20I have found David, my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him,21so that my hand shall be established with him; my arm also shall strengthen him.22The enemy shall not outwit him; the wicked shall not humble him.23I will crush his foes before him and strike down those who hate him.24My faithfulness and my steadfast love shall be with him, and in my name shall his horn be exalted.25I will set his hand on the sea and his right hand on the rivers.26He shall cry to me, 'You are my Father, my God, and the Rock of my salvation.'27And I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth.28My steadfast love I will keep for him forever, and my covenant will stand firm for him.29I will establish his offspring forever and his throne as the days of the heavens.30If his children forsake my law and do not walk according to my rules,31if they violate my statutes and do not keep my commandments,32then I will punish their transgression with the rod and their iniquity with stripes,33but I will not remove from him my steadfast love or be false to my faithfulness.34I will not violate my covenant or alter the word that went forth from my lips.35Once for all I have sworn by my holiness; I will not lie to David.36His offspring shall endure forever, his throne as long as the sun before me.37Like the moon it shall be established forever, a faithful witness in the skies." Selah38But now you have cast off and rejected; you are full of wrath against your anointed.39You have renounced the covenant with your servant; you have defiled his crown in the dust.40You have breached all his walls; you have laid his strongholds in ruins.41All who pass by plunder him; he has become the scorn of his neighbors.42You have exalted the right hand of his foes; you have made all his enemies rejoice.43You have also turned back the edge of his sword, and you have not made him stand in battle.44You have made his splendor to cease and cast his throne to the ground.45You have cut short the days of his youth; you have covered him with shame. Selah46How long, O LORD? Will you hide yourself forever? How long will your wrath burn like fire?47Remember how short my time is! For what vanity you have created all the children of man!48What man can live and never see death? Who can deliver his soul from the power of Sheol? Selah49Lord, where is your steadfast love of old, which by your faithfulness you swore to David?50Remember, O Lord, how your servants are mocked, and how I bear in my heart the insults of all the many nations,51with which your enemies mock, O LORD, with which they mock the footsteps of your anointed.52Blessed be the LORD forever! Amen and Amen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — I Will Sing of the Steadfast Love of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I will sing of the steadfast love of the LORD forever; with my mouth I will make known your faithfulness to all generations (v. 1). God has sworn to David: I will establish your offspring forever (vv. 3-4). None in the heavens compares with him (vv. 5-8); he rules the raging sea and crushed Rahab (vv. 9-10); heaven and earth are his (vv. 11-13). Righteousness and justice are the foundation of your throne; steadfast love and faithfulness go before you (v. 14). Blessed are the people who walk in the light of his face, whose king belongs to the Holy One of Israel (vv. 15-18).
verseByVerse.theology: Before the crisis is named, Ethan builds the case: this is the God who made an oath, and nothing in heaven or sea can stop him keeping it.

verseByVerse.quote: I will sing of the steadfast love of the LORD forever; with my mouth I will make known your faithfulness to all generations. For I said, "Steadfast love will be built up forever; in the heavens you will establish your faithfulness." You have said, "I have made a covenant with my chosen one; I have sworn to David my servant: 'I will establish your offspring forever, and build your throne for all generations.'" Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will sing of the steadfast love of the LORD forever; with my mouth I will make known your faithfulness to all generations.

This psalm is by Ethan the Ezrahite — a man whose name was a byword for wisdom (1 Kgs 4:31) and who led the temple singers with Heman and Asaph (1 Chr 15:17, 19). It opens with joy, and it will end in something close to despair. The first verse is a promise to sing forever about two things: God's steadfast love and his faithfulness.

Hold on to those two words, because the whole psalm is an argument about them. Steadfast love comes six times and faithfulness eight. They are praised in the first half, promised in the middle, and questioned at the end: where is your steadfast love of old, which by your faithfulness you swore to David? (v. 49). Ethan is going to sing about God's faithfulness while looking at evidence that seems to contradict it. That is why the psalm is so valuable.

For I said, Steadfast love will be built up forever; in the heavens you will establish your faithfulness.

The picture is construction. God's steadfast love is being built up like a house, course by course, and his faithfulness is fixed in the heavens where nothing on earth can reach it.

You have said, I have made a covenant with my chosen one; I have sworn to David my servant: I will establish your offspring forever, and build your throne for all generations.

And here is the thing God built: a covenant with David. Through Nathan, God had promised David, I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever (2 Sam 7:13). The same verb — build — links God's love in verse 2 to David's throne in verse 4. The throne is how the love will be seen on earth. Keep that connection in mind; it is what makes the end of the psalm so painful.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the heavens praise your wonders, O LORD, your faithfulness in the assembly of the holy ones! For who in the skies can be compared to the LORD? Who among the heavenly beings is like the LORD, a God greatly to be feared in the council of the holy ones, and awesome above all who are around him? O LORD God of hosts, who is mighty as you are, O LORD, with your faithfulness all around you? You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them. You crushed Rahab like a carcass; you scattered your enemies with your mighty arm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the heavens praise your wonders, O LORD, your faithfulness in the assembly of the holy ones! For who in the skies can be compared to the LORD? Who among the heavenly beings is like the LORD,

Before Ethan says anything about the crisis, he builds up the size of the God who made the promise. The scene moves to heaven, where the holy ones are gathered — the ESV notes that heavenly beings is literally "the sons of God", or "the sons of might". Among all the powers of heaven, not one compares to the LORD.

a God greatly to be feared in the council of the holy ones, and awesome above all who are around him? O LORD God of hosts, who is mighty as you are, O LORD, with your faithfulness all around you?

Even the angels fear him. And the detail at the end is beautiful: God's faithfulness is all around you, like a robe or a retinue. He does not have faithfulness as one quality among others; it surrounds everything he is and does.

You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them. You crushed Rahab like a carcass; you scattered your enemies with your mighty arm.

To an ancient Israelite the sea was the image of chaos, and Rahab the monster of the deep — a name also used for Egypt. Job said, By his power he stilled the sea; by his understanding he shattered Rahab (Job 26:12). God rules the chaos; he has already crushed it.

The disciples saw this with their own eyes in a boat on Galilee, when Jesus rebuked the wind and said to the sea, Peace! Be still! (Mark 4:39). The God who stills the waves in verse 9 was asleep on a cushion in the stern.

verseByVerse.quote: The heavens are yours; the earth also is yours; the world and all that is in it, you have founded them. The north and the south, you have created them; Tabor and Hermon joyously praise your name. You have a mighty arm; strong is your hand, high your right hand. Righteousness and justice are the foundation of your throne; steadfast love and faithfulness go before you. Blessed are the people who know the festal shout, who walk, O LORD, in the light of your face, who exult in your name all the day and in your righteousness are exalted. For you are the glory of their strength; by your favor our horn is exalted. For our shield belongs to the LORD, our king to the Holy One of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heavens are yours; the earth also is yours; the world and all that is in it, you have founded them. The north and the south, you have created them; Tabor and Hermon joyously praise your name. You have a mighty arm; strong is your hand, high your right hand.

Everything belongs to him because he made it — heaven, earth, north, south. Tabor and Hermon are two of Israel's great mountains, the rounded hill in Galilee and the snow-capped peak in the far north, and they are pictured singing. The creation that God founded cannot be taken from him.

Righteousness and justice are the foundation of your throne; steadfast love and faithfulness go before you.

Here is the throne behind David's throne. It stands on righteousness and justice — its foundations do not shift. And the two great words of the psalm walk ahead of God like heralds in a royal procession: wherever he goes, steadfast love and faithfulness arrive first.

Blessed are the people who know the festal shout, who walk, O LORD, in the light of your face, who exult in your name all the day and in your righteousness are exalted.

Happy are those who know how to shout at the festival — who recognise the trumpet call and the cry of praise — and who live in the light of God's face. Their joy is not in themselves but in his name, and their standing is not their own righteousness but his.

For you are the glory of their strength; by your favor our horn is exalted. For our shield belongs to the LORD, our king to the Holy One of Israel.

The hymn ends on the king. Our shield — the king who protects the people — belongs to the LORD. That is the whole ground of the psalm's hope. The king in Jerusalem is not an independent ruler whose fortunes rise and fall on his own; he is God's property. So whatever happens to the king happens to something that belongs to the Holy One of Israel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–37 — I Will Not Lie to David
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I have found David, my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him (v. 20). God's hand will strengthen him and crush his foes (vv. 21-25). He shall cry to me, You are my Father; I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth (vv. 26-27). If his children forsake the law, I will punish their transgression with the rod, but I will not remove from him my steadfast love or be false to my faithfulness (vv. 30-33). Once for all I have sworn by my holiness; I will not lie to David (v. 35). His throne will last like the sun and the moon, a faithful witness in the skies (vv. 36-37).
verseByVerse.theology: God's promise to David is repeated at length, with its one condition — the rod — and its unconditional core: the love will not be withdrawn.

verseByVerse.quote: Of old you spoke in a vision to your godly one, and said: "I have granted help to one who is mighty; I have exalted one chosen from the people. I have found David, my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him, so that my hand shall be established with him; my arm also shall strengthen him. The enemy shall not outwit him; the wicked shall not humble him. I will crush his foes before him and strike down those who hate him. My faithfulness and my steadfast love shall be with him, and in my name shall his horn be exalted. I will set his hand on the sea and his right hand on the rivers. He shall cry to me, 'You are my Father, my God, and the Rock of my salvation.' And I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth. My steadfast love I will keep for him forever, and my covenant will stand firm for him. I will establish his offspring forever and his throne as the days of the heavens.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of old you spoke in a vision to your godly one, and said: I have granted help to one who is mighty; I have exalted one chosen from the people. I have found David, my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him,

Now Ethan repeats God's promise to David at length — almost as if reading it back to God. It came in a vision, to Nathan (the ESV notes some manuscripts read "godly ones"). And it begins with God's choosing: I have found David. Paul quoted the same testimony in the synagogue at Antioch: I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart (Acts 13:22). A shepherd boy chosen out of the people, anointed with God's own oil.

One chosen from the people is a pointed phrase. David did not come from a royal house; he was the youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem, out with the sheep when Samuel arrived. God's king is taken from among the people he will rule, not imposed on them from outside — and the last Son of David was born in the same small town, into a carpenter's household.

so that my hand shall be established with him; my arm also shall strengthen him. The enemy shall not outwit him; the wicked shall not humble him. I will crush his foes before him and strike down those who hate him. My faithfulness and my steadfast love shall be with him, and in my name shall his horn be exalted.

The same arm that scattered God's enemies (v. 10) will strengthen David. And the two great words are promised to him personally: my faithfulness and my steadfast love shall be with him.
