And the end of verse 24: in my name shall his horn be exalted. The horn is the strength of a wild ox, and verse 17 used it of the whole people. The king's strength is raised in my name — not in his army or his alliances. Whatever power David's line held, it held on God's name, which is why its loss later in the psalm is felt as God's own name being put to shame.

I will set his hand on the sea and his right hand on the rivers.

A remarkable line. In verse 9 it was God who ruled the raging of the sea. Now God puts the king's hand on the sea. The king is given a share in God's own rule over chaos — which no king of Israel ever exercised, and one Son of David did, on Galilee.

He shall cry to me, You are my Father, my God, and the Rock of my salvation. And I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth.

God promised David's line, I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son (2 Sam 7:14), and Hebrews applies those words to Christ (Heb 1:5). The firstborn is the heir with the highest rank, and the highest of the kings of the earth is a claim over every throne in the world. John opens Revelation with Jesus Christ, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of kings on earth (Rev 1:5).

My steadfast love I will keep for him forever, and my covenant will stand firm for him. I will establish his offspring forever and his throne as the days of the heavens.

Forever, and again forever (the ESV notes stand firm may be rendered "remain faithful"). The throne will last as long as the sky does.

verseByVerse.quote: If his children forsake my law and do not walk according to my rules, if they violate my statutes and do not keep my commandments, then I will punish their transgression with the rod and their iniquity with stripes, but I will not remove from him my steadfast love or be false to my faithfulness. I will not violate my covenant or alter the word that went forth from my lips. Once for all I have sworn by my holiness; I will not lie to David. His offspring shall endure forever, his throne as long as the sun before me. Like the moon it shall be established forever, a faithful witness in the skies." Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
If his children forsake my law and do not walk according to my rules, if they violate my statutes and do not keep my commandments, then I will punish their transgression with the rod and their iniquity with stripes,

Now the condition. God foresaw that David's sons would not all be faithful (the ESV notes rules may be "just decrees"). If they sin, they will be punished — the rod and stripes, the same words God used to Nathan: I will discipline him with the rod of men, with the stripes of the sons of men (2 Sam 7:14). Discipline is built into the covenant from the start. It is not a sign the covenant has failed; it is one of its terms. The Lord disciplines the one he loves (Heb 12:6).

but I will not remove from him my steadfast love or be false to my faithfulness. I will not violate my covenant or alter the word that went forth from my lips.

And here is the unconditional core. The rod may fall, but the love will not be removed. God had told Nathan, my steadfast love will not depart from him (2 Sam 7:15). Sin in David's line would bring punishment; it would not cancel the promise. God staked his own faithfulness on it.

Once for all I have sworn by my holiness; I will not lie to David. His offspring shall endure forever, his throne as long as the sun before me. Like the moon it shall be established forever, a faithful witness in the skies.

God swears by my holiness — there is nothing higher to swear by. I will not lie to David. Hebrews says God confirmed his promise with an oath so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement (Heb 6:18).

And the throne is compared to the sun and the moon. The moon is a faithful witness in the skies — every night it rises, and every night it testifies that God keeps his word. Revelation calls Jesus Christ the faithful witness (Rev 1:5) in the same breath as the firstborn. The two titles of this oracle meet in one person.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 38–52 — But Now You Have Cast Off
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But now you have cast off and rejected; you are full of wrath against your anointed. You have renounced the covenant with your servant; you have defiled his crown in the dust (vv. 38-39). Walls breached, sword blunted, throne cast down, youth cut short (vv. 40-45). How long, O LORD? Will you hide yourself forever? (v. 46). Lord, where is your steadfast love of old, which by your faithfulness you swore to David? (v. 49). His servants are mocked, and the footsteps of the anointed (vv. 50-51). Blessed be the LORD forever! Amen and Amen (v. 52).
verseByVerse.theology: The promise said forever. The facts say the crown is in the dust. Ethan holds God to his word, and the book closes with Amen.

verseByVerse.quote: But now you have cast off and rejected; you are full of wrath against your anointed. You have renounced the covenant with your servant; you have defiled his crown in the dust. You have breached all his walls; you have laid his strongholds in ruins. All who pass by plunder him; he has become the scorn of his neighbors. You have exalted the right hand of his foes; you have made all his enemies rejoice. You have also turned back the edge of his sword, and you have not made him stand in battle. You have made his splendor to cease and cast his throne to the ground. You have cut short the days of his youth; you have covered him with shame. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now you have cast off and rejected; you are full of wrath against your anointed. You have renounced the covenant with your servant; you have defiled his crown in the dust.

But now. Thirty-seven verses of praise and promise, and then everything turns. The accusation is breathtakingly direct: you have renounced the covenant. The word God said he would never violate (v. 34), Ethan says God has renounced. The crown that was to last as long as the sun is lying in the dirt.

What happened? The psalm does not say. The most likely setting is the collapse of David's line under Babylon. Lamentations mourns the breath of our nostrils, the LORD's anointed, was captured in their pits (Lam 4:20). Zedekiah's sons were killed before his eyes and then his eyes were put out (2 Kgs 25:7).

You have breached all his walls; you have laid his strongholds in ruins. All who pass by plunder him; he has become the scorn of his neighbors. You have exalted the right hand of his foes; you have made all his enemies rejoice.

Every promise of the oracle is reversed, one by one. God had said I will crush his foes (v. 23); now God has exalted the right hand of his foes. God had said the enemy shall not outwit him (v. 22); now all who pass by plunder him. Ethan is not complaining vaguely. He lays the promise beside the facts, line against line.

And the words themselves have been heard before in Book Three. You have breached all his walls ... All who pass by plunder him is what Psalm 80 asked about the vine: Why then have you broken down its walls, so that all who pass along the way pluck its fruit? (80:12). The scorn of his neighbors is Psalm 79's complaint, We have become a taunt to our neighbors (79:4). The king has suffered exactly what the city and the vine suffered. The anointed is not above his people's ruin; he goes down into it with them.

You have also turned back the edge of his sword, and you have not made him stand in battle. You have made his splendor to cease and cast his throne to the ground. You have cut short the days of his youth; you have covered him with shame.

The clauses of verses 43 and 44 read like answers to verses 21 to 25. The arm that was to strengthen him has turned back the edge of his sword; the foes that were to be crushed now stand while he cannot; the splendour God gave has been made to cease. Ethan is holding God to the text.

The days of his youth cut short: Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, reigned three months, and was taken to Babylon (2 Kgs 24:8, 12). A young king in chains, the throne on the ground. It looked like the end of God's promise.

verseByVerse.quote: How long, O LORD? Will you hide yourself forever? How long will your wrath burn like fire? Remember how short my time is! For what vanity you have created all the children of man! What man can live and never see death? Who can deliver his soul from the power of Sheol? Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
How long, O LORD? Will you hide yourself forever? How long will your wrath burn like fire?

Forever has been the psalm's word for God's promise. Now Ethan turns it around: will you hide yourself forever? The same word, used for the love and now used for the silence. He cannot make them fit, and he does not pretend to.

Remember how short my time is! For what vanity you have created all the children of man! What man can live and never see death? Who can deliver his soul from the power of Sheol?

And the argument becomes personal. God's promise is for all generations, but Ethan has one lifetime, and it is short. If the promise is going to be kept, he would like to see it. And behind that is a larger question: who can deliver his soul from the power of Sheol? No king, not even David's son, has escaped death. The throne that was supposed to last forever keeps passing to men who die.

For what vanity you have created all the children of man! If every life is short and ends in Sheol, and even the promised king is cut down young, what was the point of making human beings at all? It is a real question, and the Psalter answers it in the very next psalm, where Moses asks God to establish the work of our hands (90:17). Short lives are not vanity when God establishes what is done in them.

The question has only one answer that satisfies it. A Son of David who died and was raised, no more to return to corruption (Acts 13:34), is the only king whose throne can actually last as long as the sun.

verseByVerse.quote: Lord, where is your steadfast love of old, which by your faithfulness you swore to David? Remember, O Lord, how your servants are mocked, and how I bear in my heart the insults of all the many nations, with which your enemies mock, O LORD, with which they mock the footsteps of your anointed. Blessed be the LORD forever! Amen and Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, where is your steadfast love of old, which by your faithfulness you swore to David?

Here is the psalm's great question, and both of its great words are in it. Where is your steadfast love? Not "did it ever exist" — Ethan has spent the whole psalm insisting it did. But where is it now? The question is only possible for someone who believes the promise. An unbeliever looking at the ruins would conclude there was never a promise. Ethan concludes God owes him an explanation.

That is a form of faith, and a very robust one. Paul faced the same tension: Does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means! Let God be true though every one were a liar (Rom 3:3-4).

Remember, O Lord, how your servants are mocked, and how I bear in my heart the insults of all the many nations, with which your enemies mock, O LORD, with which they mock the footsteps of your anointed.

The last complaint is mockery (the ESV notes the Hebrew lacks the word "insults", though it is implied). The nations jeer at the fallen king — they mock the footsteps of your anointed, following him along the road and laughing at where he has ended up. When the true Anointed walked to his execution, those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads (Matt 27:39). This psalm was being fulfilled at that moment in a way no one watching understood.

Notice also I bear in my heart the insults of all the many nations. The one praying carries the nations' contempt inside himself, as though the insults aimed at God and his king had landed on him. Paul saw Christ in exactly that place: Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me (Rom 15:3). The true Anointed bore in his own heart, and in his body, the insults aimed at God.

Blessed be the LORD forever! Amen and Amen.

This line closes not only Psalm 89 but the whole of Book Three of the Psalter, as similar doxologies close Books One and Two (41:13; 72:19). It may have been added by those who arranged the collection. But look where they put it. Directly after where is your steadfast love?, with the throne in the dust and the anointed mocked, they wrote Blessed be the LORD forever — and added Amen twice.

That is the right response to a promise that seems broken: not to stop believing it, but to bless God with the question still open. The answer came. The angel told Mary that God would give her son the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:32-33). All the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory (2 Cor 1:20). Amen and Amen.

89.title: Where Is Your Steadfast Love of Old?
89.overview: Ethan promises to sing forever of God's steadfast love and faithfulness, and recalls God's oath to establish David's offspring and throne forever (vv. 1-4). No heavenly being compares with the LORD, who rules the sea, crushed Rahab, owns heaven and earth, and has a throne founded on justice, with steadfast love and faithfulness going before him; blessed are the people who walk in the light of his face, whose king belongs to the Holy One of Israel (vv. 5-18). God's promise to David is recited: anointed, strengthened, made the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth, his throne enduring like the sun and moon; if his sons sin, they will be disciplined with the rod, but God will not remove his steadfast love or lie to David (vv. 19-37). But now God has cast off his anointed, renounced the covenant, thrown the crown in the dust and cut short the king's youth (vv. 38-45). How long? Life is short and no one escapes Sheol (vv. 46-48). Lord, where is your steadfast love of old, which by your faithfulness you swore to David? — while the nations mock the footsteps of the anointed (vv. 49-51). Book Three closes: Blessed be the LORD forever! Amen and Amen (v. 52).
89.theology:
The psalm is an argument about steadfast love (six times) and faithfulness (eight times): praised (vv. 1-18), promised (vv. 19-37), and questioned (vv. 38-51).

The Davidic covenant (2 Sam 7:12-16) carries discipline as one of its terms (vv. 30-32; Heb 12:6) while the steadfast love at its core is unconditional and sworn by God's holiness (vv. 33-35; Heb 6:18).

The king is given a share in God's own rule over the sea (vv. 9, 25), called the firstborn and highest of kings (v. 27), and compared to the moon as a faithful witness (v. 37) — titles Revelation gives to Jesus Christ together (Rev 1:5).

Ethan lays the promise beside its apparent reversal line by line (vv. 38-45) and asks where the steadfast love has gone (v. 49) — a question possible only to faith (Rom 3:3-4). No king escapes Sheol (v. 48) until the Son of David is raised, never to see corruption (Acts 13:34), whose kingdom has no end (Luke 1:32-33). The doxology blesses God with the question still open (v. 52); in Christ every promise finds its Yes and Amen (2 Cor 1:20).
89.examples:
Six times steadfast love, eight times faithfulness — then the question.

Faithfulness worn like a robe.

The God who stills the sea, asleep in the stern.

The king's hand on the sea.

The rod written into the covenant from the start.

The moon: a faithful witness every night.

Promise laid beside the facts, line against line.

An eighteen-year-old king in chains.

Blessed be the LORD — with the question still open.

90.text: A Prayer of Moses, the man of God. 1Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations.2Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever you had formed the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting you are God.3You return man to dust and say, "Return, O children of man!"4For a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday when it is past, or as a watch in the night.5You sweep them away as with a flood; they are like a dream, like grass that is renewed in the morning:6in the morning it flourishes and is renewed; in the evening it fades and withers.7For we are brought to an end by your anger; by your wrath we are dismayed.8You have set our iniquities before you, our secret sins in the light of your presence.9For all our days pass away under your wrath; we bring our years to an end like a sigh.10The years of our life are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty; yet their span is but toil and trouble; they are soon gone, and we fly away.11Who considers the power of your anger, and your wrath according to the fear of you?12So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom.13Return, O LORD! How long? Have pity on your servants!14Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love, that we may rejoice and be glad all our days.15Make us glad for as many days as you have afflicted us, and for as many years as we have seen evil.16Let your work be shown to your servants, and your glorious power to their children.17Let the favor of the Lord our God be upon us, and establish the work of our hands upon us; yes, establish the work of our hands!

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations. Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever you had formed the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting you are God (vv. 1-2). You return man to dust (v. 3). For a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday when it is past, or as a watch in the night (v. 4). Men are swept away like a dream, like grass that flourishes in the morning and withers by evening (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The eternal God is his people's home, and the people themselves are grass.

verseByVerse.quote: Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations. Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever you had formed the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting you are God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations.

Book Four of the Psalms begins here, and the placement is deliberate. Book Three ended with David's crown in the dust and the question where is your steadfast love of old? (89:49). Book Four opens with a prayer from Moses — the only psalm that bears his name, the man of God, as Deuteronomy calls him (Deut 33:1). Before there was a king, before there was a temple, before there was a Jerusalem, Moses led a people with no land and no throne through the wilderness. When the throne has fallen, the Psalter takes us back to him.

And his first sentence is the answer to the loss of everything: you have been our dwelling place. Moses spent forty years in tents, and the people he led had no home. Their home was God. (The ESV notes some manuscripts read "our refuge".) A believer who has lost house, country, security or a way of life has not lost his dwelling place, because it was never those things.

Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever you had formed the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting you are God.

The mountains are the oldest things a person can see — and God was there before them. Brought forth is birth language, as though the mountains were born. He was there before the world was formed, and he will be there after. From everlasting to everlasting — not merely that he lasts a very long time, but that he has no beginning and no end.

John began his Gospel in the same place: In the beginning was the Word (John 1:1). And Jesus used the divine present tense of himself: before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58). The God who was before the mountains is the one who walked among the hills of Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: You return man to dust and say, "Return, O children of man!" For a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday when it is past, or as a watch in the night. You sweep them away as with a flood; they are like a dream, like grass that is renewed in the morning: in the morning it flourishes and is renewed; in the evening it fades and withers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You return man to dust and say, Return, O children of man!

From God's eternity, the psalm turns abruptly to man's frailty. You return man to dust — the sentence spoken in Eden: you are dust, and to dust you shall return (Gen 3:19). The ESV notes that children of man may be rendered "of Adam". Every death is Adam's sentence carried out again. God speaks one word — Return — and a generation goes back to the ground.

For a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday when it is past, or as a watch in the night.

The contrast is almost unbearable. For God, a thousand years is like yesterday — and yesterday, once it is past, seems short. Or like a watch in the night: a few hours that a sleeping man does not even notice. Peter used this verse to explain why Christ's return seems slow: with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day (2 Pet 3:8). God is not late. He simply does not measure time as we do.

You sweep them away as with a flood; they are like a dream, like grass that is renewed in the morning: in the morning it flourishes and is renewed; in the evening it fades and withers.

Three images of how quickly human lives go. A flash flood in a dry valley, sweeping everything away. A dream, vivid at night and gone by breakfast. And grass — in that climate, grass sprang up green after the morning dew and was scorched brown by the afternoon sun.

Isaiah heard the same message: All flesh is grass ... The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever (Isa 40:6, 8). That is the only thing that outlasts the grass.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Teach Us to Number Our Days
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For we are brought to an end by your anger; God has set our secret sins in the light of your presence (vv. 7-8). Our years end like a sigh (v. 9). The years of our life are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty; yet their span is but toil and trouble; they are soon gone, and we fly away (v. 10). Who considers the power of God's anger? (v. 11). So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Life is short because of sin, and the wise response is to learn to count.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are brought to an end by your anger; by your wrath we are dismayed. You have set our iniquities before you, our secret sins in the light of your presence. For all our days pass away under your wrath; we bring our years to an end like a sigh. The years of our life are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty; yet their span is but toil and trouble; they are soon gone, and we fly away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we are brought to an end by your anger; by your wrath we are dismayed. You have set our iniquities before you, our secret sins in the light of your presence.

Now Moses gives the reason life is so short, and it is not merely biology. We are brought to an end by your anger. Death is not natural; it is the judgment on sin. Moses had seen that more clearly than almost anyone — he watched God's anger consume a generation in the wilderness.

And the most searching line: our secret sins in the light of your presence. The sins no one else knows about are set out on the table in front of God, lit by the brightness of his face. No creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account (Heb 4:13). A person who has a secret sin should read this verse slowly.

For all our days pass away under your wrath; we bring our years to an end like a sigh.

Like a sigh — a breath let out, a small sound, and then nothing. That is how a whole life ends, looked at from outside.

The years of our life are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty; yet their span is but toil and trouble; they are soon gone, and we fly away.

This verse is often quoted, and there is something striking about who wrote it. Moses was 120 years old when he died (Deut 34:7). He was not describing his own lifespan. He was describing the generation he had led — every Israelite over twenty who left Egypt, except Caleb and Joshua, died in the wilderness (Num 14:30). God had said, your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness (Num 14:29), and for forty years Moses attended their funerals. He had watched hundreds of thousands of lives run out at seventy or eighty.

And even the extra years, by reason of strength (the ESV notes "pride" as another rendering), are toil and trouble. Then we fly away — like a bird off a branch.

verseByVerse.quote: Who considers the power of your anger, and your wrath according to the fear of you? So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who considers the power of your anger, and your wrath according to the fear of you?

Almost nobody. That is Moses' point. People know they will die, but very few think seriously about why — about the anger of God behind death, and how much he should be feared. We live as if life were long, sin were small and God were mild.

So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom.

Here is the practical centre of the psalm, and it is a request to be taught to count. Not years — days. A person who reaches seventy has lived roughly twenty-five thousand days; most people have fewer left than they imagine. Numbering them means knowing that they are limited, that each one is gone when it is spent, and that there will be a last one.

The purpose is a heart of wisdom. The fool in Jesus' parable planned for years and God said to him, Fool! This night your soul is required of you (Luke 12:20). James asks, What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes (Jas 4:14). Paul says, Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time (Eph 5:15-16).

Try this. What would you stop doing if you knew your days were numbered — and what would you start? They are. The wisdom Moses asks for is not morbid; it is the clarity of someone who has stopped pretending there is always tomorrow.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Satisfy Us in the Morning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Return, O LORD! How long? Have pity on your servants! (v. 13). Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love, that we may rejoice and be glad all our days (v. 14). Make us glad for as many days as we have been afflicted; show your work to your servants and your glory to their children (vv. 15-16). Let the favor of the Lord our God be upon us, and establish the work of our hands upon us; yes, establish the work of our hands! (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Moses asks that short lives be filled with God's love, and that the work done in them should last.

verseByVerse.quote: Return, O LORD! How long? Have pity on your servants! Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love, that we may rejoice and be glad all our days. Make us glad for as many days as you have afflicted us, and for as many years as we have seen evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Return, O LORD! How long? Have pity on your servants!

Now the prayer turns, and it uses God's own word. In verse 3 God said to man, Return — go back to dust. Here Moses says to God, Return, O LORD! — come back to us. You have sent us back to the ground; now turn back to your servants. It is bold, and it is the only hope a dying people has.

Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love, that we may rejoice and be glad all our days.

Remember the grass that flourished in the morning and withered by evening (v. 6). Now Moses asks for something else in the morning: God's steadfast love, which does not wither. The day will still end; the life will still be short. But a short life satisfied with God's love every morning is a glad life all our days. Jeremiah found it in the ruins of Jerusalem: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning (Lam 3:22-23).

This is the answer to the fear of a short life. Not a longer one, but a fuller one — filled, every morning, with something that lasts.

Make us glad for as many days as you have afflicted us, and for as many years as we have seen evil.

A daring request: joy measured to match the sorrow. Forty years in the wilderness — give us forty years of gladness. God will do more than that. For those who belong to him, the joy to come is not matched to the affliction but beyond all comparison: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more (Rev 21:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Let your work be shown to your servants, and your glorious power to their children. Let the favor of the Lord our God be upon us, and establish the work of our hands upon us; yes, establish the work of our hands!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let your work be shown to your servants, and your glorious power to their children.

Moses knew that his generation would not enter the land. So he prays for the next one: let us see your work, and let our children see your glory. A dying generation can still pray for its children, and should.

Let the favor of the Lord our God be upon us, and establish the work of our hands upon us; yes, establish the work of our hands!

The last request is for the favor of the Lord — the ESV notes it can be rendered "beauty" — to rest on them. And then, twice, establish the work of our hands. Make it last. Everything in the psalm has spoken of how quickly lives pass: dust, dreams, grass, a sigh. Moses does not ask that he himself should last. He asks that the work God gave him to do should.

That prayer is answered for believers. Their days are still few, and the grass still withers, but work done in the Lord is not lost with them: be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain (1 Cor 15:58). The eternal God, who was before the mountains, is the one who establishes the work of mortal hands. Numbering your days does not make them meaningless. It makes you ask him to make them count.

90.title: Teach Us to Number Our Days
90.overview: Moses, opening Book Four, confesses that the Lord has been his people's dwelling place in every generation, God from everlasting to everlasting, before the mountains (vv. 1-2). God returns man to dust; a thousand years are like yesterday to him, and human lives are swept away like a dream, like grass that flourishes in the morning and withers by evening (vv. 3-6). Life ends under God's anger, secret sins exposed in his presence; our years end like a sigh — seventy, or eighty, toil and trouble, and we fly away (vv. 7-11). So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom (v. 12). Return, O LORD! — satisfy us in the morning with steadfast love, make us glad for as many days as we were afflicted, show your work to us and your glory to our children, and establish the work of our hands (vv. 13-17).
90.theology:
After Book Three closed on the fallen throne (89:38-51), Book Four begins with Moses and a God who was Israel's home before any king (vv. 1-2). His eternity (John 1:1; 8:58) is set against human transience: dust (Gen 3:19), dream and grass (vv. 3-6; Isa 40:6-8; 2 Pet 3:8).

Death is the outworking of God's anger at sin, including secret sin exposed before him (vv. 7-9; Heb 4:13). Moses, who lived to 120 (Deut 34:7), watched a generation die in the wilderness (Num 14:29) and states the span of life at seventy or eighty (v. 10).

Wisdom begins with numbering our days (v. 12; Luke 12:20; Jas 4:14; Eph 5:15-16). God's steadfast love, new each morning, satisfies short lives (v. 14; Lam 3:22-23), and the joy to come outweighs affliction (v. 15; Rev 21:4). The eternal God establishes the work of mortal hands (v. 17; 1 Cor 15:58).
90.examples:
When the throne falls, the Psalter goes back to a man who lived in tents.

Home is a person, not a place.

Older than the mountains.

Grass green at dawn and brown by afternoon.

Secret sins on the table, in the light.

A man of 120 attending forty years of funerals.

About twenty-five thousand days at seventy.

God said return to man; Moses says it to God.

Establish the work of our hands — twice.

91.text: <sup>1</sup>He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty.<sup>2</sup>I will say to the LORD, "My refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust."<sup>3</sup>For he will deliver you from the snare of the fowler and from the deadly pestilence.<sup>4</sup>He will cover you with his pinions, and under his wings you will find refuge; his faithfulness is a shield and buckler.<sup>5</sup>You will not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow that flies by day,<sup>6</sup>nor the pestilence that stalks in darkness, nor the destruction that wastes at noonday.<sup>7</sup>A thousand may fall at your side, ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not come near you.<sup>8</sup>You will only look with your eyes and see the recompense of the wicked.<sup>9</sup>Because you have made the LORD your dwelling place— the Most High, who is my refuge —<sup>10</sup>no evil shall be allowed to befall you, no plague come near your tent.<sup>11</sup>For he will command his angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways.<sup>12</sup>On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.<sup>13</sup>You will tread on the lion and the adder; the young lion and the serpent you will trample underfoot.<sup>14</sup>"Because he holds fast to me in love, I will deliver him; I will protect him, because he knows my name.<sup>15</sup>When he calls to me, I will answer him; I will be with him in trouble; I will rescue him and honor him.<sup>16</sup>With long life I will satisfy him and show him my salvation."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Shelter of the Most High
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty (v. 1). I will say to the LORD, My refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust (v. 2). He delivers from the fowler's snare and the deadly pestilence; under his wings you will find refuge (vv. 3-4). You will not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow that flies by day (v. 5), nor plague in darkness or destruction at noon (v. 6). A thousand may fall at your side, ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not come near you (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Round the clock and against every danger, the one who lives with God lives under his wings.

verseByVerse.quote: He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty. I will say to the LORD, "My refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty.

The psalm has no title and no author's name. It simply begins with a place to live. Dwells and abide are words for staying, not visiting. The promise of this psalm is not for someone who runs to God in an emergency and leaves when the danger passes; it is for the one who lives there.

Shelter is a hiding place, and shadow is the shade a traveller finds from the sun — or the shadow of wings, as verse 4 will make clear. In that climate shade was not a luxury. Without it, people died.

I will say to the LORD, My refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust.

Count the names in two verses: the Most High, the Almighty, the LORD, my God. The highest, the all-powerful, the covenant name, and then the personal one. The psalm moves from God's greatness to God's nearness, and the last name is the one that makes the others useful. A fortress is only a refuge to the person who goes into it.

And the speaker says it out loud: I will say to the LORD (the ESV notes the Greek translation reads "He will say"). Faith here is not a private feeling; it is a confession made to God's face. There is strength in saying to God, in words, you are my refuge — especially on a day when it does not feel true.

verseByVerse.quote: For he will deliver you from the snare of the fowler and from the deadly pestilence. He will cover you with his pinions, and under his wings you will find refuge; his faithfulness is a shield and buckler.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he will deliver you from the snare of the fowler and from the deadly pestilence.

Now another voice speaks to the believer, promising what God will do. Two dangers: the snare of the fowler, the hidden trap set by someone who wants to catch you, and the deadly pestilence, the sickness no one sets but which kills anyway. One is malice, the other is simply the world as it is. God delivers from both.

He will cover you with his pinions, and under his wings you will find refuge; his faithfulness is a shield and buckler.

And then the most tender picture in the psalm: God as a bird covering its young. Moses sang of God like an eagle that stirs up its nest, that flutters over its young, spreading out its wings (Deut 32:11). Boaz blessed Ruth, a foreigner, as one who had come under whose wings you have come to take refuge (Ruth 2:12). And Jesus used the image of himself over Jerusalem: as a hen gathers her brood under her wings (Matt 23:37).

The picture is of warmth and closeness as much as protection. A chick under the wing does not see the danger; it sees feathers. And the wings are backed by armour: his faithfulness is a shield and buckler, the large shield that covers the whole body and the small one for close fighting. His keeping of his word is what stands between the believer and what is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: You will not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow that flies by day, nor the pestilence that stalks in darkness, nor the destruction that wastes at noonday. A thousand may fall at your side, ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not come near you. You will only look with your eyes and see the recompense of the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow that flies by day, nor the pestilence that stalks in darkness, nor the destruction that wastes at noonday.

The dangers go round the clock: night, day, darkness, noon. The terror that comes in the dark and the arrow in broad daylight; the disease that creeps unseen and the disaster that strikes in full view. There is no hour when the believer is outside the shelter.

Notice the promise is first about fear: you will not fear. The dangers are named as real. What changes is that they no longer own the person who lives under God's wings.

A thousand may fall at your side, ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not come near you. You will only look with your eyes and see the recompense of the wicked.

The picture is of a plague or a battle in which people fall all around. Israel had seen something like it on the night of the Passover, when God struck Egypt and will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses to strike you (Exod 12:23). The same night, the same land, and death passed over the houses under the blood.

This is where the psalm needs to be read honestly. Faithful believers have died in plagues and wars. Hebrews lists men and women of faith who were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were killed with the sword (Heb 11:37). The psalm is not promising that no Christian will ever catch an infection. It is promising that nothing reaches the one who dwells in God except by God's permission, and that nothing which reaches him can separate him from God's shelter. The destroyer does not get into the house.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — He Will Command His Angels
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because you have made the LORD your dwelling place, no evil or plague will come near your tent (vv. 9-10). For he will command his angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways. On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone (vv. 11-12). You will tread on the lion and the adder (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The verses the devil quoted to Jesus — and the way Jesus refused to use them.

verseByVerse.quote: Because you have made the LORD your dwelling place— the Most High, who is my refuge — no evil shall be allowed to befall you, no plague come near your tent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because you have made the LORD your dwelling place — the Most High, who is my refuge — no evil shall be allowed to befall you, no plague come near your tent.

The promise is repeated, and the condition is repeated with it: because you have made the LORD your dwelling place. The speaker breaks in with his own testimony — who is my refuge — as if he cannot hear the promise without saying amen to it. (The ESV notes the verse may be read differently: "For you, O LORD, are my refuge! You have made the Most High your dwelling place".)

No evil shall be allowed to befall you. The phrasing matters: allowed. Evil exists, and it wants to reach the believer. It is not permitted to. The question is always who is doing the permitting — and the answer is the one whose wings cover the tent.

verseByVerse.quote: For he will command his angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways. On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone. You will tread on the lion and the adder; the young lion and the serpent you will trample underfoot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he will command his angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways. On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.

These are the verses the devil quoted. He took Jesus to the pinnacle of the temple and said, If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, He will command his angels concerning you (Matt 4:6). It was an accurate quotation, used to push God's Son into testing God.

Jesus did not deny the promise. He answered with another Scripture: You shall not put the Lord your God to the test (Matt 4:7). The promise is for someone walking in all your ways — the ordinary path of obedience — not for someone who jumps off a building to see whether God will catch him. A believer who takes reckless risks and calls it faith has not trusted Psalm 91; he has done what the devil suggested.

The angels are real. They are ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation (Heb 1:14). Most of what they do, we will never see. The picture is almost playful: angels carrying a child over rough ground so he does not stub his toe.

You will tread on the lion and the adder; the young lion and the serpent you will trample underfoot.

The dangers now are wild animals — the lion that attacks openly and the snake that strikes from hiding. And the believer does not merely escape them; he walks over them. The serpent under the foot recalls the first promise of rescue in the Bible, that the woman's offspring shall bruise your head (Gen 3:15). Jesus gave his disciples authority to tread on serpents and scorpions (Luke 10:19); a viper hung from Paul's hand on Malta and he shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm (Acts 28:5); and the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet (Rom 16:20).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–16 — I Will Be with Him in Trouble
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because he holds fast to me in love, I will deliver him; I will protect him, because he knows my name (v. 14). When he calls to me, I will answer him; I will be with him in trouble; I will rescue him and honor him (v. 15). With long life I will satisfy him and show him my salvation (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: God himself speaks the last word: not a promise of no trouble, but of his presence in it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Because he holds fast to me in love, I will deliver him; I will protect him, because he knows my name. When he calls to me, I will answer him; I will be with him in trouble; I will rescue him and honor him. With long life I will satisfy him and show him my salvation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because he holds fast to me in love, I will deliver him; I will protect him, because he knows my name.

Now God himself speaks, and the voice changes from you to him. God is talking about the believer, the way a father talks about a child he loves.

Two reasons: he holds fast to me in love — the word means clinging, attached with desire — and he knows my name, knows who God is and has called on him. Neither is a work that earns anything. Both are descriptions of a person who belongs.

When he calls to me, I will answer him; I will be with him in trouble; I will rescue him and honor him. With long life I will satisfy him and show him my salvation.

Count what God says he will do: deliver, protect, answer, be with him, rescue, honour, satisfy, show. Eight promises in three verses, all in the first person.

And look carefully at the fourth: I will be with him in trouble. Not "I will keep him out of trouble". The psalm that seemed to promise that nothing bad would happen ends by admitting that trouble will come, and promising something better than its absence: God's presence inside it, and rescue out of it.

There is one person who fulfilled this psalm perfectly. Jesus dwelt in the shelter of the Most High more completely than anyone, refused to test God, trod on the serpent — and was not spared the cross. God did not keep him out of trouble. He was with him in it, and rescued him from death, and honoured him, and showed him his salvation on the third day. With long life I will satisfy him is finally true of a life that does not end, and it is true of everyone who is hidden in him. If you are in trouble now, the promise of this psalm is not broken. It is being kept in the way it said it would be: I will be with him in trouble.

91.title: Under His Wings
91.overview: The one who dwells in the shelter of the Most High abides in the shadow of the Almighty and says to the LORD, My refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust (vv. 1-2). God delivers from the fowler's snare and deadly pestilence, covering the believer with his wings, his faithfulness a shield (vv. 3-4); there is no need to fear terror by night or arrow by day, though thousands fall around (vv. 5-8). Because the LORD is his dwelling place, no evil will be allowed to befall him; God will command his angels to guard him in all his ways, and he will tread on lion and serpent (vv. 9-13). God speaks: because he holds fast to me in love and knows my name, I will deliver, protect, answer, be with him in trouble, rescue, honour, satisfy him with long life and show him my salvation (vv. 14-16).
91.theology:
The promises belong to those who dwell with God, not those who visit him (vv. 1, 9). God's names move from greatness to nearness (vv. 1-2), and his care is pictured as a bird's wings (v. 4; Deut 32:11; Ruth 2:12; Matt 23:37).

The psalm does not guarantee that believers never suffer (Heb 11:36-38); it promises that nothing is allowed to reach them outside God's permission or beyond his shelter (vv. 7, 10; Exod 12:23). The devil used vv. 11-12 to tempt Christ to test God, and Christ refused (Matt 4:6-7).

Treading on the serpent (v. 13) echoes Gen 3:15 and is fulfilled in Christ and shared with his people (Luke 10:19; Rom 16:20).

God's closing words include I will be with him in trouble (v. 15): presence in trouble, then rescue and honour. Christ was not spared the cross but was delivered from death, and the promise of satisfying life and salvation is kept in him (v. 16).
91.examples:
Living there, not visiting.

Four names, from greatness to nearness.

A chick under the wing sees feathers, not danger.

Night, day, darkness, noon — no hour outside the shelter.

The destroyer not allowed into the house.

The devil quoting accurately.

Jumping off the temple is not faith.

Eight promises, and the fourth is in trouble, not out of it.

92.text: A Psalm. A Song for the Sabbath. 1It is good to give thanks to the LORD, to sing praises to your name, O Most High;2to declare your steadfast love in the morning, and your faithfulness by night,3to the music of the lute and the harp, to the melody of the lyre.4For you, O LORD, have made me glad by your work; at the works of your hands I sing for joy.5How great are your works, O LORD! Your thoughts are very deep!6The stupid man cannot know; the fool cannot understand this:7that though the wicked sprout like grass and all evildoers flourish, they are doomed to destruction forever;8but you, O LORD, are on high forever.9For behold, your enemies, O LORD, for behold, your enemies shall perish; all evildoers shall be scattered.10But you have exalted my horn like that of the wild ox; you have poured over me fresh oil.11My eyes have seen the downfall of my enemies; my ears have heard the doom of my evil assailants.12The righteous flourish like the palm tree and grow like a cedar in Lebanon.13They are planted in the house of the LORD; they flourish in the courts of our God.14They still bear fruit in old age; they are ever full of sap and green,15to declare that the LORD is upright; he is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — It Is Good to Give Thanks
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: It is good to give thanks to the LORD, to sing praises to your name, O Most High; to declare your steadfast love in the morning, and your faithfulness by night (vv. 1-2), with lute, harp and lyre (v. 3). For you, O LORD, have made me glad by your work; at the works of your hands I sing for joy (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: A Sabbath song begins where the Sabbath began: with gladness in what God has made and done.

verseByVerse.quote: It is good to give thanks to the LORD, to sing praises to your name, O Most High; to declare your steadfast love in the morning, and your faithfulness by night, to the music of the lute and the harp, to the melody of the lyre. For you, O LORD, have made me glad by your work; at the works of your hands I sing for joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is good to give thanks to the LORD, to sing praises to your name, O Most High; to declare your steadfast love in the morning, and your faithfulness by night, to the music of the lute and the harp, to the melody of the lyre.

The title says this is a Song for the Sabbath, and it begins with a statement that sounds simple: it is good to give thanks. Good for God, who deserves it. Good for the one who does it, because thanks puts a person back in the right relation to everything. On the day of rest, when work stops, this is what fills the space.

And the thanks has a timetable. Steadfast love in the morning — start the day with the love that never fails, before the day has had a chance to argue. Faithfulness by night — end it by looking back and seeing that God kept his word through another day. The psalm before this one asked God to satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love (90:14). This one says what to do when he has.

Lute, harp and lyre: thanks is meant to be beautiful, not merely correct.

For you, O LORD, have made me glad by your work; at the works of your hands I sing for joy.

The Sabbath was God's own day of rest after the work of creation, and the psalm picks up that thread. The worshipper rests from his work and looks at God's — creation, providence, rescue — and finds himself glad. The Christian's rest goes further. There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God's rest has also rested from his works as God did from his (Heb 4:9-10). The deepest Sabbath is resting from trying to earn God's favour, and singing for joy at the work he has already done.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — But You, O LORD, Are on High Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How great are your works, O LORD! Your thoughts are very deep! (v. 5). The stupid man cannot understand that though the wicked sprout like grass and all evildoers flourish, they are doomed to destruction forever (vv. 6-7). But you, O LORD, are on high forever (v. 8). His enemies will perish, while the psalmist's horn is exalted and anointed with fresh oil (vv. 9-11).
verseByVerse.theology: At the exact centre of the psalm stands one line about God, and everything else is measured against it.

verseByVerse.quote: How great are your works, O LORD! Your thoughts are very deep! The stupid man cannot know; the fool cannot understand this: that though the wicked sprout like grass and all evildoers flourish, they are doomed to destruction forever; but you, O LORD, are on high forever. For behold, your enemies, O LORD, for behold, your enemies shall perish; all evildoers shall be scattered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How great are your works, O LORD! Your thoughts are very deep!

From gladness the psalm moves to wonder. God's works are great, and behind them are thoughts very deep — purposes too far down for us to see the bottom. That is especially true of the question the psalm is about to raise: why the wicked do so well.

The stupid man cannot know; the fool cannot understand this: that though the wicked sprout like grass and all evildoers flourish, they are doomed to destruction forever;

The stupid man is not unintelligent; he is brutish, living on the level of what he can see. And what he sees is that the wicked flourish. They do. The psalm does not deny it. But they sprout like grass — quick, green, everywhere, and gone. Psalm 90 had just described grass that flourishes in the morning and fades and withers by evening (90:6). The fool sees the morning. He cannot see the evening.

but you, O LORD, are on high forever.

This is verse 8 of fifteen. Seven verses stand before it and seven after, and it is the shortest line in the psalm. At the exact centre of a song about the wicked flourishing and the righteous growing old, there is one sentence about God: you ... are on high forever. Everything else is measured by that. The grass is temporary; the LORD is not. Any trouble looks different when you set it against the one fixed point in the universe.

For behold, your enemies, O LORD, for behold, your enemies shall perish; all evildoers shall be scattered.

Your enemies, twice, with a behold each time, as though the singer is pointing. They are God's enemies before they are his, and so their end is certain.

verseByVerse.quote: But you have exalted my horn like that of the wild ox; you have poured over me fresh oil. My eyes have seen the downfall of my enemies; my ears have heard the doom of my evil assailants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you have exalted my horn like that of the wild ox; you have poured over me fresh oil.

The singer turns to his own experience. The horn of the wild ox is raw strength held high; God has given him that. And fresh oil poured over the head was the sign of refreshment, honour and gladness — the oil a host poured on a welcome guest. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew in this line is uncertain, and the rendering follows the Syriac, but the sense of renewal is plain.

My eyes have seen the downfall of my enemies; my ears have heard the doom of my evil assailants.

He has lived long enough to see it. The grass that was so green has withered in front of him. That is one of the gifts of a long life with God: a person begins to see the evening of things he once only saw in the morning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–15 — Still Bearing Fruit in Old Age
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The righteous flourish like the palm tree and grow like a cedar in Lebanon. They are planted in the house of the LORD; they flourish in the courts of our God (vv. 12-13). They still bear fruit in old age; they are ever full of sap and green, to declare that the LORD is upright; he is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: The wicked spring up like grass; the righteous grow like trees that are still bearing fruit when they are old.

verseByVerse.quote: The righteous flourish like the palm tree and grow like a cedar in Lebanon. They are planted in the house of the LORD; they flourish in the courts of our God. They still bear fruit in old age; they are ever full of sap and green, to declare that the LORD is upright; he is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The righteous flourish like the palm tree and grow like a cedar in Lebanon.

The wicked flourish like grass (v. 7). The righteous flourish too — the same verb — but like trees. The date palm grows in the desert, sending its roots down to hidden water, and goes on bearing fruit year after year. The cedar of Lebanon is the image of height, strength and long life. Grass is quick and shallow; these are slow and deep.

Jeremiah drew the same contrast: the one who trusts in the LORD is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes, for its leaves remain green (Jer 17:8). And the whole Psalter began there: He is like a tree planted by streams of water (1:3).

They are planted in the house of the LORD; they flourish in the courts of our God.

The secret is the soil. These trees are planted — put there by someone else — in God's house. A believer does not flourish by effort alone but by where he has been rooted: in the worship, the word and the people of God, week after week, Sabbath after Sabbath.

They still bear fruit in old age; they are ever full of sap and green,

Here is a promise for the elderly, and it is a beautiful one. The world treats old age as decline. God promises fruit. The body weakens — our outer self is wasting away — but our inner self is being renewed day by day (2 Cor 4:16). Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is gained in a righteous life (Prov 16:31).

Think of the two old people in the temple when Mary and Joseph brought the baby: Simeon, righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel (Luke 2:25), and Anna, a widow in her eighties who did not depart from the temple (Luke 2:37). Planted in the house of the LORD, still full of sap, and the first to recognise the Christ. If you are old, your fruit-bearing years are not behind you.

to declare that the LORD is upright; he is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him.

And the purpose of the fruit is not the tree's glory. It is to declare that the LORD is upright. An old believer still green after decades of trouble is a living argument that God is faithful. He is my rock — said by someone who has leaned on him for a lifetime — and there is no unrighteousness in him. The long life that has seen the wicked flourish and fade ends its song not with a complaint but with a verdict: God has never once done wrong.

92.title: Planted in the House of the LORD
92.overview: A song for the Sabbath: it is good to give thanks to the Most High, declaring his steadfast love in the morning and his faithfulness at night, with lute, harp and lyre, glad at the works of his hands (vv. 1-4). His works are great and his thoughts deep; the stupid man cannot see that the wicked, though they sprout like grass, are doomed (vv. 5-7). But you, O LORD, are on high forever (v. 8). God's enemies will perish, while the singer's horn is exalted and he is anointed with fresh oil (vv. 9-11). The righteous flourish like the palm and the cedar, planted in the house of the LORD; they still bear fruit in old age, declaring that the LORD is upright, a rock with no unrighteousness in him (vv. 12-15).
92.theology:
Thanksgiving is good, and it frames the day: love in the morning, faithfulness at night (vv. 1-2). Sabbath rest is gladness in God's works (v. 4), fulfilled in resting from our works in Christ (Heb 4:9-10).

The prosperity of the wicked is real but grass-like (v. 7; 90:5-6). The centre verse of the psalm, you, O LORD, are on high forever (v. 8), is the fixed point by which all else is measured.

The righteous are trees planted in God's house (vv. 12-13; 1:3; Jer 17:7-8). Their fruitfulness in old age (v. 14; 2 Cor 4:16; Prov 16:31) exists to declare God's uprightness (v. 15).
92.examples:
Love at the start of the day, faithfulness at the end of it.

The deepest Sabbath: resting from earning.

The fool sees the morning grass and cannot see the evening.

Seven verses either side of one line about God.

Palm roots going down to hidden water.

Planted — by someone else — in God's house.

Simeon and Anna, old and still green.

A lifetime's verdict: no unrighteousness in him.

93.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD reigns; he is robed in majesty; the LORD is robed; he has put on strength as his belt. Yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved.<sup>2</sup>Your throne is established from of old; you are from everlasting.<sup>3</sup>The floods have lifted up, O LORD, the floods have lifted up their voice; the floods lift up their roaring.<sup>4</sup>Mightier than the thunders of many waters, mightier than the waves of the sea, the LORD on high is mighty!<sup>5</sup>Your decrees are very trustworthy; holiness befits your house, O LORD, forevermore.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD reigns; he is robed in majesty; the LORD is robed; he has put on strength as his belt. Yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved (v. 1). Your throne is established from of old; you are from everlasting (v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology: Five short verses begin with three words that settle everything else.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD reigns; he is robed in majesty; the LORD is robed; he has put on strength as his belt. Yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved. Your throne is established from of old; you are from everlasting.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD reigns; he is robed in majesty; the LORD is robed; he has put on strength as his belt.

Three words open the psalm and carry it: The LORD reigns. The same words open Psalms 97 and 99, and Psalm 96 tells Israel to say them among the nations (96:10). They are not a hope or a wish. They are a report.

And the King is described getting dressed. He is robed in majesty — the psalm says it twice, as if the singer cannot take his eyes off the robe — and he has put on strength as his belt, the belt a man tightened before work or battle. This is not a king dozing on a throne. He is dressed and ready.

Yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved.

Because he reigns, the world stands. The same sentence was sung when the ark came into Jerusalem: yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved (1 Chr 16:30). When everything in a person's life seems to be shifting, this is where the ground is. Not in the circumstances; in the reign.

Your throne is established from of old; you are from everlasting.

The throne did not begin at some point; it is from of old. And the King is from everlasting, the phrase Moses used three psalms earlier: from everlasting to everlasting you are God (90:2). He was not elected, did not inherit and will not be succeeded. Of the Son, Hebrews says, Your throne, O God, is forever and ever (Heb 1:8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–5 — Mightier Than the Waves of the Sea
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The floods have lifted up, O LORD, the floods have lifted up their voice; the floods lift up their roaring (v. 3). Mightier than the thunders of many waters, mightier than the waves of the sea, the LORD on high is mighty! (v. 4). Your decrees are very trustworthy; holiness befits your house, O LORD, forevermore (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The flood keeps rising, and the King above it does not move.

verseByVerse.quote: The floods have lifted up, O LORD, the floods have lifted up their voice; the floods lift up their roaring. Mightier than the thunders of many waters, mightier than the waves of the sea, the LORD on high is mighty!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The floods have lifted up, O LORD, the floods have lifted up their voice; the floods lift up their roaring.

Now the danger, and the poetry makes you hear it rising. The floods have lifted up — the floods have lifted up their voice — the floods lift up their roaring. Three times, each line longer and louder, like a tide coming in wave after wave.

To Israel the sea was the image of chaos, everything that threatens to swallow the ordered world. And the prophets used the same picture for hostile nations: Ah, the roar of nations; they roar like the roaring of mighty waters! (Isa 17:12). Whatever the floods are in a believer's life — hostile powers, overwhelming grief, a culture rising against God — they are loud, and they are rising.

Mightier than the thunders of many waters, mightier than the waves of the sea, the LORD on high is mighty!

And the answer is not that the flood is small. It is that the LORD is mightier. The psalm gives the waters their full volume — thunders of many waters — and then sets God above them: on high.

The disciples found this out in a boat. After Jesus stilled the storm, they were filled with great fear and said to one another, Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? (Mark 4:41). On another night he came to them, walking on the sea (Matt 14:25) — on top of the thing that terrified them.

And at the end John heard the roar of many waters again, but it had changed. It was the voice of a great multitude, like the roar of many waters, and it was crying, Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns (Rev 19:6). The noise that once threatened now sings Psalm 93. And in the new creation, the sea was no more (Rev 21:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Your decrees are very trustworthy; holiness befits your house, O LORD, forevermore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your decrees are very trustworthy; holiness befits your house, O LORD, forevermore.

The ending is unexpected. After the robes, the throne and the roaring sea, the psalm does not finish with a display of power. It finishes with God's word and God's holiness.

Your decrees are very trustworthy. The King who rules the flood also speaks, and what he says can be relied on completely. His power would be terrifying if his word were not trustworthy. Because it is, his power is the believer's safety.

Holiness befits your house. The fitting thing in the palace of such a King is holiness — the seraphim cry Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts (Isa 6:3) — and those who live in his house are called to share it: You shall be holy, for I am holy (1 Pet 1:16).

That is how to live when the floods are rising. Believe his decrees, and live as members of a holy house. The kingdom you belong to cannot be shaken (Heb 12:28), because the LORD reigns, and he will, forevermore.

93.title: The LORD Reigns
93.overview: The LORD reigns: robed in majesty and belted with strength, he has established the world so that it cannot be moved; his throne is from of old and he is from everlasting (vv. 1-2). The floods lift up their voice and their roaring, but mightier than the thunder of many waters and the waves of the sea is the LORD on high (vv. 3-4). His decrees are very trustworthy, and holiness befits his house forever (v. 5).
93.theology:
God's reign is stated as fact (v. 1; cf. 96:10; 97:1; 99:1). Because he reigns, the world is established (1 Chr 16:30), and his throne and being are without beginning (v. 2; 90:2; Heb 1:8).

The rising floods represent chaos and hostile nations (v. 3; Isa 17:12-13); God is mightier (v. 4), as Christ showed on the sea (Mark 4:41; Matt 14:25), and the roar of many waters becomes the praise of the redeemed (Rev 19:6) before the sea is no more (Rev 21:1).

The psalm closes on the trustworthiness of God's word and the holiness fitting his house (v. 5; Isa 6:3; 1 Pet 1:16), and on a kingdom that cannot be shaken (Heb 12:28).
93.examples:
Three words that are a report, not a wish.

A King dressed and belted, ready.

The ground is in the reign, not the circumstances.

A tide coming in, wave after wave, louder each time.

Walking on top of the thing that terrified them.

The roar of the waters turned into Hallelujah.

Power made safe by a trustworthy word.

94.text: <sup>1</sup>O LORD, God of vengeance, O God of vengeance, shine forth!<sup>2</sup>Rise up, O judge of the earth; repay to the proud what they deserve!<sup>3</sup>O LORD, how long shall the wicked, how long shall the wicked exult?<sup>4</sup>They pour out their arrogant words; all the evildoers boast.<sup>5</sup>They crush your people, O LORD, and afflict your heritage.<sup>6</sup>They kill the widow and the sojourner, and murder the fatherless;<sup>7</sup>and they say, "The LORD does not see; the God of Jacob does not perceive."<sup>8</sup>Understand, O dullest of the people! Fools, when will you be wise?<sup>9</sup>He who planted the ear, does he not hear? He who formed the eye, does he not see?<sup>10</sup>He who disciplines the nations, does he not rebuke? He who teaches man knowledge—<sup>11</sup>the LORD—knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath.<sup>12</sup>Blessed is the man whom you discipline, O LORD, and whom you teach out of your law,<sup>13</sup>to give him rest from days of trouble, until a pit is dug for the wicked.<sup>14</sup>For the LORD will not forsake his people; he will not abandon his heritage;<sup>15</sup>for justice will return to the righteous, and all the upright in heart will follow it.<sup>16</sup>Who rises up for me against the wicked? Who stands up for me against evildoers?<sup>17</sup>If the LORD had not been my help, my soul would soon have lived in the land of silence.<sup>18</sup>When I thought, "My foot slips," your steadfast love, O LORD, held me up.<sup>19</sup>When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul.<sup>20</sup>Can wicked rulers be allied with you, those who frame injustice by statute?<sup>21</sup>They band together against the life of the righteous and condemn the innocent to death.<sup>22</sup>But the LORD has become my stronghold, and my God the rock of my refuge.<sup>23</sup>He will bring back on them their iniquity and wipe them out for their wickedness; the LORD our God will wipe them out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — O God of Vengeance, Shine Forth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O LORD, God of vengeance, O God of vengeance, shine forth! Rise up, O judge of the earth; repay to the proud what they deserve! (vv. 1-2). O LORD, how long shall the wicked, how long shall the wicked exult? (v. 3). They crush God's people and kill the widow, the sojourner and the fatherless (vv. 4-6), and they say, The LORD does not see (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: A prayer for justice from people who have watched the powerful kill the powerless and assume no one is looking.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, God of vengeance, O God of vengeance, shine forth! Rise up, O judge of the earth; repay to the proud what they deserve! O LORD, how long shall the wicked, how long shall the wicked exult?
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD, God of vengeance, O God of vengeance, shine forth! Rise up, O judge of the earth; repay to the proud what they deserve!

The opening makes modern readers flinch: God of vengeance, twice. But the word does not mean spite. It means just retribution — the setting right of wrongs by the one who has the authority to do it. The psalm is not asking God to lose his temper. It is asking the judge of the earth to act like one.

And this is exactly where the New Testament sends believers who have been wronged. Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord (Rom 12:19). Praying Psalm 94 is not the opposite of forgiving your enemy. It is the thing that makes forgiveness possible, because the wrong has been handed to someone who will deal with it justly, and you no longer have to carry it.

Shine forth is a request for God to appear — to step out of hiddenness into the light where the wicked can see him.

O LORD, how long shall the wicked, how long shall the wicked exult?

How long, twice — the cry of the martyrs under the altar (Rev 6:10). Jesus answered the question in a parable: will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night? Will he delay long over them? (Luke 18:7). The answer is no. But he added a harder question: when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth? (Luke 18:8). The danger in the waiting is not that God will fail to act, but that we will stop praying.

verseByVerse.quote: They pour out their arrogant words; all the evildoers boast. They crush your people, O LORD, and afflict your heritage. They kill the widow and the sojourner, and murder the fatherless; and they say, "The LORD does not see; the God of Jacob does not perceive."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They pour out their arrogant words; all the evildoers boast. They crush your people, O LORD, and afflict your heritage.

The wicked here are not foreign invaders. They are powerful people inside the nation, and they talk a great deal. Arrogant words pour out of them like water from a broken jar. And what they crush is your people, your heritage — the psalm insists the victims belong to God.

They kill the widow and the sojourner, and murder the fatherless;

The three victims named are the three the law of Moses singled out for protection: the widow with no husband, the foreigner with no family, the orphan with no father. They had no one to defend them in court. So they were exactly the people a corrupt ruler could destroy without consequence — and exactly the people God had said he would defend.

and they say, The LORD does not see; the God of Jacob does not perceive.

Here is the root of it. These men do not deny that God exists; they are Israelites, and they use his names. They simply live as if he were not watching. That is practical atheism, and it is far more common than the theoretical kind. Anyone who does in private what he would never do if God were visibly in the room has, for that moment, said this verse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — He Who Planted the Ear
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He who planted the ear, does he not hear? He who formed the eye, does he not see? (v. 9). God knows the thoughts of man, that they are a breath (vv. 10-11). Blessed is the man whom you discipline, O LORD, and whom you teach out of your law (v. 12). For the LORD will not forsake his people, and justice will return to the righteous (vv. 13-15).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who made ears is not deaf, and the God who disciplines his people has not abandoned them.

verseByVerse.quote: Understand, O dullest of the people! Fools, when will you be wise? He who planted the ear, does he not hear? He who formed the eye, does he not see? He who disciplines the nations, does he not rebuke? He who teaches man knowledge— the LORD—knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Understand, O dullest of the people! Fools, when will you be wise?

Now the psalmist turns and speaks to the oppressors — and he calls them the dullest of the people. They think they are clever. They are the stupidest people in the country, because they have based their whole way of life on a mistake about God.

He who planted the ear, does he not hear? He who formed the eye, does he not see?

The argument is simple and devastating. The ear did not make itself. The eye did not design its own lens. Someone planted the ear and formed the eye — and is he supposed to be deaf and blind? The one who invented hearing hears everything. Every whispered cruelty, every private plan, has been heard by the designer of the ear that heard it.

He who disciplines the nations, does he not rebuke? He who teaches man knowledge — the LORD — knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath.

God disciplines whole nations; he will not overlook a few corrupt men. He teaches every human being whatever they know; does he not know what they think? And his verdict on human thinking is short: but a breath. The ESV notes that the Greek translation reads "they are futile", and Paul quotes it that way to puncture intellectual pride: The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile (1 Cor 3:20). The cleverest schemes of the powerful weigh about as much as an exhaled breath.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the man whom you discipline, O LORD, and whom you teach out of your law, to give him rest from days of trouble, until a pit is dug for the wicked. For the LORD will not forsake his people; he will not abandon his heritage; for justice will return to the righteous, and all the upright in heart will follow it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is the man whom you discipline, O LORD, and whom you teach out of your law, to give him rest from days of trouble, until a pit is dug for the wicked.

An astonishing turn. The same word — discipline — that God uses on the nations (v. 10) he also uses on his own people. And the person under that discipline is called blessed.

This is how a believer reads his own suffering while the wicked flourish. It is not punishment from an enemy; it is training from a Father who is teaching him out of your law. Hebrews says the same: God disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness, and though it seems painful rather than pleasant, later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness (Heb 12:10-11).

And the discipline has an end in view: rest from days of trouble. Meanwhile, somewhere, a pit is dug for the wicked — slowly, patiently, out of sight. The righteous man learns and rests; the wicked man walks confidently towards a hole he cannot see.

For the LORD will not forsake his people; he will not abandon his heritage; for justice will return to the righteous, and all the upright in heart will follow it.

Here is the certainty the whole psalm rests on. Whatever the powerful do to God's people, he will not forsake them. Paul leaned on that same assurance about Israel: God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew (Rom 11:2). And justice, which has gone missing from the courts, will return — like an exile coming home — and the upright will fall in behind it.

Notice the word that ties this verse to verse 5. There the wicked afflict your heritage. Here he will not abandon his heritage. The oppressors thought they were crushing a people with no owner. The word heritage says otherwise: this is God's inheritance, and an owner does not abandon his inheritance to vandals.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–23 — When I Thought, My Foot Slips
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Who rises up for me against the wicked? (v. 16). Without the LORD's help his soul would have gone to the land of silence (v. 17). When I thought, My foot slips, your steadfast love, O LORD, held me up. When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul (vv. 18-19). Wicked rulers frame injustice by statute (vv. 20-21), but the LORD has become my stronghold, and he will bring their iniquity back on them (vv. 22-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Against legalised injustice, a man finds that God's love caught him the moment he felt himself slip.

verseByVerse.quote: Who rises up for me against the wicked? Who stands up for me against evildoers? If the LORD had not been my help, my soul would soon have lived in the land of silence. When I thought, "My foot slips," your steadfast love, O LORD, held me up. When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who rises up for me against the wicked? Who stands up for me against evildoers?
