The psalm becomes intensely personal. He looks around for a defender — a judge, a friend, anyone who will stand up for him — and there is no one. That is one of the loneliest experiences there is: to be wronged by powerful people and to find that nobody will speak up.

The question also echoes the opening. In verse 2 he prayed, Rise up, O judge of the earth. Now he asks, Who rises up for me? The answer to the second question is the answer to the first prayer: nobody on earth rose up for him, and the Judge of the earth did.

If the LORD had not been my help, my soul would soon have lived in the land of silence.

The land of silence is the grave. He was that close. And the only reason he is still alive to write this is that someone did stand up for him after all.

When I thought, My foot slips, your steadfast love, O LORD, held me up.

This is one of the most comforting verses in the Psalter, so read it slowly. The moment is precise: when I thought, My foot slips. Not after he fell. At the instant he felt his footing go — on the scree, on the edge — God's steadfast love caught him. The love was there before the fall could happen.

Many believers know that moment. The diagnosis, the phone call, the sudden sense that faith itself is giving way under your feet. The psalm does not say he never slipped. It says that the love of God was quicker than the fall.

When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul.

The cares of my heart are the anxious thoughts that multiply at night, crowding and tangling. Against their many, God sets his consolations — plural, one for each. Paul knew the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction (2 Cor 1:3-4). The comfort does not remove every care. It cheers the soul in the middle of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Can wicked rulers be allied with you, those who frame injustice by statute? They band together against the life of the righteous and condemn the innocent to death. But the LORD has become my stronghold, and my God the rock of my refuge. He will bring back on them their iniquity and wipe them out for their wickedness; the LORD our God will wipe them out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can wicked rulers be allied with you, those who frame injustice by statute?

Now the psalm names the worst kind of wickedness: injustice written into law. These rulers do not break the law to oppress people; they frame (the ESV notes "fashion") injustice by statute. Their cruelty is legal. And the question is whether a government like that can claim God as its ally. The answer is obviously no, however religious its language.

They band together against the life of the righteous and condemn the innocent to death.

The ESV notes the Hebrew literally says they condemn innocent blood. A court, following procedure, sentences an innocent man to die. It happened many times in Israel, and it happened once in Jerusalem in a way that changed the world, when a council and a governor lawfully condemned the only wholly innocent man who ever lived.

But the LORD has become my stronghold, and my God the rock of my refuge. He will bring back on them their iniquity and wipe them out for their wickedness; the LORD our God will wipe them out.

But the LORD. Against a legal system turned into a weapon, he has a stronghold that no statute can reach. And the psalm ends where it began, with the God of vengeance: their own iniquity will be brought back on their heads. The psalmist does not do it. He has handed it over, and he has found in the meantime that the God who will judge them is also the God who caught him when he slipped.

And listen to the last pronouns. Verse 22 is personal: my stronghold, my God. Verse 23 ends with the LORD our God. The man who stood alone, with no one to rise up for him, finishes the psalm among a people. What God did for one sufferer becomes the confidence of the whole congregation that sings his prayer.

94.title: Your Consolations Cheer My Soul
94.overview: The psalmist calls on the God of vengeance, the judge of the earth, to shine forth and repay the proud (vv. 1-2). How long will the wicked exult? They boast, crush God's people, kill the widow, the sojourner and the fatherless, and say the LORD does not see (vv. 3-7). He rebukes them as fools: the one who planted the ear hears, the one who formed the eye sees, and he knows that human thoughts are a breath (vv. 8-11). Blessed is the one God disciplines and teaches, given rest until a pit is dug for the wicked; the LORD will not forsake his people, and justice will return (vv. 12-15). No one rose up for him, but the LORD helped him: When I thought, My foot slips, your steadfast love, O LORD, held me up. When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul (vv. 16-19). Wicked rulers frame injustice by statute and condemn the innocent, but the LORD is his stronghold and will bring their iniquity back on them (vv. 20-23).
94.theology:
Vengeance belongs to God as the just judge of the earth (vv. 1-2); handing it to him is the ground of not avenging ourselves (Rom 12:19). The prayer how long (v. 3) is answered by the promise that God will give justice to his elect (Luke 18:7-8).

Oppression of the defenceless flows from practical atheism, the assumption that God does not see (vv. 6-7). The Creator of ear and eye hears and sees, and knows human thoughts to be futile (vv. 9-11; 1 Cor 3:20).

God's discipline of his people is a blessing and a training (v. 12; Heb 12:10-11), and he will not forsake them (v. 14; Rom 11:2). His steadfast love catches the believer as the foot begins to slip, and his consolations meet the multitude of anxious cares (vv. 18-19; 2 Cor 1:3-4). Injustice framed by law cannot claim God as its ally (v. 20).
94.examples:
Vengeance handed over, so it no longer has to be carried.

Widow, foreigner, orphan: the people with no one to speak in court.

Believing in God and living as if he were not looking.

The inventor of the ear is not deaf.

A pit being dug, slowly, out of sight.

Caught at the instant the footing went.

One consolation for each anxious thought.

Cruelty made legal.

95.text: <sup>1</sup>Oh come, let us sing to the LORD; let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation!<sup>2</sup>Let us come into his presence with thanksgiving; let us make a joyful noise to him with songs of praise!<sup>3</sup>For the LORD is a great God, and a great King above all gods.<sup>4</sup>In his hand are the depths of the earth; the heights of the mountains are his also.<sup>5</sup>The sea is his, for he made it, and his hands formed the dry land.<sup>6</sup>Oh come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the LORD, our Maker!<sup>7</sup>For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand. Today, if you hear his voice,<sup>8</sup>do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah, as on the day at Massah in the wilderness,<sup>9</sup>when your fathers put me to the test and put me to the proof, though they had seen my work.<sup>10</sup>For forty years I loathed that generation and said, "They are a people who go astray in their heart, and they have not known my ways."<sup>11</sup>Therefore I swore in my wrath, "They shall not enter my rest."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Oh Come, Let Us Sing to the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Oh come, let us sing to the LORD; let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation! (v. 1). Let us come into his presence with thanksgiving (v. 2). For the LORD is a great God, and a great King above all gods (v. 3): the depths of the earth, the heights of the mountains, the sea and the dry land are his, for he made them (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: A call to loud, glad worship of the King who owns everything from the ocean floor to the mountain tops.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh come, let us sing to the LORD; let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation! Let us come into his presence with thanksgiving; let us make a joyful noise to him with songs of praise!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh come, let us sing to the LORD; let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation!

For many centuries this psalm has opened the church's morning worship, and it begins as an invitation — Oh come — spoken by one worshipper to the rest. It is not a solitary prayer. It is a congregation calling itself together.

And the call is to make a joyful noise. That is a shout, the kind of sound a crowd makes when its king rides in. Worship in this psalm is not muted. People who have been saved are allowed to be loud about it.

Notice the title they shout to: the rock of our salvation. Hold on to that phrase, because the psalm will come back to it. At Massah and Meribah (v. 8) the fathers stood in front of a rock in the wilderness, quarrelling with God, and water came out of it (Exod 17:6-7). Paul says the Rock was Christ (1 Cor 10:4). Every generation of God's people sings to the same Rock their fathers complained at.

Let us come into his presence with thanksgiving; let us make a joyful noise to him with songs of praise!

The way in is thanksgiving. Nobody enters God's presence by complaint, entitlement or indifference — only by remembering what he has done and saying thank you for it.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD is a great God, and a great King above all gods. In his hand are the depths of the earth; the heights of the mountains are his also. The sea is his, for he made it, and his hands formed the dry land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the LORD is a great God, and a great King above all gods.

Now the reasons, and they begin with size. The nations around Israel had many gods: gods of the sea, of the mountains, of the underworld, of the harvest. The LORD is a great King above all of them. Whatever else people worship — then or now — sits below him.

In his hand are the depths of the earth; the heights of the mountains are his also. The sea is his, for he made it, and his hands formed the dry land.

The psalm surveys the world from bottom to top — the deepest places, the highest peaks — and from wet to dry — the sea, the land. Every territory that pagan gods were thought to rule belongs to him, and the reason is simple: he made it. Ownership comes from making.

The picture is of hands. The depths are in his hand; his hands formed the land, as a potter shapes clay. The same hands will appear in verse 7, holding sheep.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–7 — Let Us Kneel Before the LORD, Our Maker
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Oh come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the LORD, our Maker! (v. 6). For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand. Today, if you hear his voice (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The shouting gives way to kneeling, and then, in the middle of a sentence, God begins to speak.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the LORD, our Maker! For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand. Today, if you hear his voice,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the LORD, our Maker!

The invitation comes again — Oh come — but the posture has changed. In verse 1 they were shouting. Now they are going down: bow down, kneel. The great King who owns the mountains is not only to be cheered but knelt to. Joy and reverence belong together, and a church that has only one of them has lost something.

And the reason is personal: the LORD, our Maker. Not only the maker of the sea — the maker of us. The day will come when at the name of Jesus every knee should bow (Phil 2:10). The psalm invites us to kneel willingly now.

For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand.

From King and Maker, the psalm comes to Shepherd. The sheep of his hand is a tender phrase — the hands that formed the dry land now lead, lift and carry the flock. The God of verse 3 is enormous; the God of verse 7 is close enough to touch.

Today, if you hear his voice,

And then, in the middle of the verse, everything changes. The singing stops. A different voice begins, and it is God's. The psalm has spent seven verses inviting people to come near and praise; now it warns them about what can happen to worshippers who come near and do not listen.

Today is the key word. Not someday, not when life is less busy — today, while the voice is speaking. The sheep of his hand are the ones who hear the Shepherd's voice. The question is whether they will.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–11 — They Shall Not Enter My Rest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah, as on the day at Massah in the wilderness, when your fathers put me to the test and put me to the proof, though they had seen my work (vv. 8-9). For forty years I loathed that generation, a people who went astray in heart and did not know God's ways (v. 10). Therefore I swore in my wrath, They shall not enter my rest (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The worship song ends with a warning from God about a generation that sang and saw and still would not listen.

verseByVerse.quote: do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah, as on the day at Massah in the wilderness, when your fathers put me to the test and put me to the proof, though they had seen my work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah, as on the day at Massah in the wilderness,

The warning points back to a specific day. Shortly after the Red Sea, Israel ran out of water and turned on Moses, and the place was named Massah (testing) and Meribah (quarrelling), because they tested the LORD by saying, Is the LORD among us or not? (Exod 17:7).

A hard heart does not begin as open rebellion. It begins with that question — is God really here? — asked in a moment of need, and answered with a complaint rather than with trust. And it hardens a little more each time.

when your fathers put me to the test and put me to the proof, though they had seen my work.

Though they had seen my work. That is the frightening part. These were not people who lacked evidence. They had watched the plagues, walked through the sea and eaten manna. They had seen more of God's work than almost anyone in history, and they still demanded that he prove himself again.

Experience of God does not protect a heart from hardening. A person can sit in worship every week, sing every song and have a long memory of answered prayers, and still be hardening. Here is a test to run. When something goes wrong this week, what will your first question be? Whether God is with you, or what he is doing?

verseByVerse.quote: For forty years I loathed that generation and said, "They are a people who go astray in their heart, and they have not known my ways." Therefore I swore in my wrath, "They shall not enter my rest."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For forty years I loathed that generation and said, They are a people who go astray in their heart, and they have not known my ways.

Forty years. Not one bad day but a lifetime pattern. God had told Moses that these people had put me to the test these ten times and have not obeyed my voice (Num 14:22). And the diagnosis is in the heart: they go astray in their heart. Their feet followed the cloud through the wilderness; their hearts wandered somewhere else. They walked with God for forty years and have not known my ways.

Loathed is a strong word, and the psalm means it to be. God is not indifferent to a people who take his gifts and refuse his voice.

Therefore I swore in my wrath, They shall not enter my rest.

And the psalm stops. It does not return to praise. A worship song that began Oh come, let us sing ends with a door being shut: They shall not enter my rest. The rest was the land of promise, and a whole generation died outside it.

Hebrews takes this psalm and preaches it to Christians at length (Heb 3:7-4:11). It quotes the Greek translation, so the wording differs a little — I was provoked with that generation — but the point is the same. And it draws out what the word Today means for us: exhort one another every day, as long as it is called today, that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin (Heb 3:13).

The door that shut on the wilderness generation is still open. God spoke this psalm, Hebrews says, saying through David, long afterwards (Heb 4:7), which means the rest was never only Canaan. There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God (Heb 4:9), and we who have believed enter that rest (Heb 4:3). The rest is Christ himself, and every time this psalm is read it is still today. If you hear his voice in it, the one thing to do is not to harden your heart, but to come.

95.title: Today, If You Hear His Voice
95.overview: An invitation to worship: come, sing, shout for joy to the rock of our salvation, and enter his presence with thanksgiving (vv. 1-2), for the LORD is a great King above all gods, owner of the depths, the heights, the sea and the land, which he made (vv. 3-5). Come, bow down and kneel before the LORD our Maker, for we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand (vv. 6-7). Then God speaks: Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah and Massah, where the fathers tested him though they had seen his work (vv. 7-9). For forty years he loathed that generation, who went astray in heart, and swore in his wrath, They shall not enter my rest (vv. 10-11).
95.theology:
Worship is both joyful noise to the Rock of salvation (vv. 1-2) and kneeling before the Maker (v. 6), grounded in God's ownership of all creation (vv. 3-5) and his shepherding of his people (v. 7).

Worship must include hearing God's voice, and the psalm turns mid-verse from praise to warning (v. 7). A heart hardens through testing God despite having seen his work (vv. 8-9; Exod 17:7), and wandering of heart can coexist with outward following (v. 10; Num 14:22).

The psalm ends on exclusion from God's rest (v. 11). Hebrews applies it to Christians: today remains open (Heb 3:13; 4:7), a Sabbath rest remains (Heb 4:9), and those who believe enter it (Heb 4:3).
95.examples:
A congregation calling itself together.

Singing to the Rock the fathers quarrelled at.

Ownership comes from making.

From shouting to kneeling in five verses.

The hands that formed the land, holding sheep.

The song stops mid-sentence and God speaks.

They had seen more than almost anyone, and still hardened.

A worship song that ends with a shut door — still open today.

96.text: <sup>1</sup>Oh sing to the LORD a new song; sing to the LORD, all the earth!<sup>2</sup>Sing to the LORD, bless his name; tell of his salvation from day to day.<sup>3</sup>Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples!<sup>4</sup>For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; he is to be feared above all gods.<sup>5</sup>For all the gods of the peoples are worthless idols, but the LORD made the heavens.<sup>6</sup>Splendor and majesty are before him; strength and beauty are in his sanctuary.<sup>7</sup>Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the peoples, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength!<sup>8</sup>Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name; bring an offering, and come into his courts!<sup>9</sup>Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth!<sup>10</sup>Say among the nations, "The LORD reigns! Yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved; he will judge the peoples with equity."<sup>11</sup>Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice; let the sea roar, and all that fills it;<sup>12</sup>let the field exult, and everything in it! Then shall all the trees of the forest sing for joy<sup>13</sup>before the LORD, for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world in righteousness, and the peoples in his faithfulness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Declare His Glory Among the Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Oh sing to the LORD a new song; sing to the LORD, all the earth! (v. 1). Tell of his salvation from day to day. Declare his glory among the nations (vv. 2-3). For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; all the gods of the peoples are worthless idols, but the LORD made the heavens (vv. 4-5). Splendour, majesty, strength and beauty surround him (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel is told to sing to the whole world about a God who made the heavens while the other gods are nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh sing to the LORD a new song; sing to the LORD, all the earth! Sing to the LORD, bless his name; tell of his salvation from day to day. Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh sing to the LORD a new song; sing to the LORD, all the earth! Sing to the LORD, bless his name; tell of his salvation from day to day.

Three times, sing to the LORD. And the choir is enormous: all the earth. This is not a song for Israel alone. It is Israel inviting every nation to join in.

A new song is the kind of song people sing when God has done something new — a fresh rescue that the old songs cannot quite contain. Most of this psalm appears again in 1 Chronicles 16 (vv. 23-33), in the thanks sung before the ark. And the greatest new song of all is sung in heaven to the Lamb: Worthy are you ... for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (Rev 5:9). The all the earth of this psalm is finally a choir of the redeemed from every nation.

Tell of his salvation from day to day — not an occasional report but a daily one. The news of what God has done does not go stale, and it is meant to be passed on every day.

Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples!

This is a missionary verse, written centuries before the Great Commission. God's people are not to keep his glory to themselves. The marvelous works he has done for them are news that belongs to all the peoples, and a church that is content to sing only to itself has not yet sung this psalm.

verseByVerse.quote: For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; he is to be feared above all gods. For all the gods of the peoples are worthless idols, but the LORD made the heavens. Splendor and majesty are before him; strength and beauty are in his sanctuary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; he is to be feared above all gods.

Why should the nations listen? Because of who he is. He is great, and his praise should match his size: greatly. And he is to be feared above all gods — whatever the nations currently worship, he is higher and more to be reckoned with.

For all the gods of the peoples are worthless idols, but the LORD made the heavens.

Here is the crucial move. Having said the LORD is above all gods, the psalm immediately clarifies: the other gods are worthless idols — nothings, empty. The Hebrew word for idols sounds like the word for gods, a scornful pun: godlets, nobodies. Paul says the same: an idol has no real existence (1 Cor 8:4).

And the proof is the sky. But the LORD made the heavens. The idols were made by men; the LORD made the heavens those men were standing under. Every modern substitute for God — money, career, pleasure, the self — is equally a thing that was made, and cannot bear the weight of worship.

Splendor and majesty are before him; strength and beauty are in his sanctuary.

Four qualities attend him like courtiers: splendor, majesty, strength, beauty. Strength without beauty would be merely frightening; beauty without strength would be fragile. In God they are together, and they fill his sanctuary.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–9 — Ascribe to the LORD, O Families of the Peoples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the peoples, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength! Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name; bring an offering, and come into his courts! (vv. 7-8). Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth! (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The nations are invited into the courts of Israel's God with offerings in their hands.

verseByVerse.quote: Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the peoples, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength! Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name; bring an offering, and come into his courts! Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the peoples, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength! Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name;

Ascribe, three times. To ascribe is to give credit — to acknowledge publicly what is true. In Psalm 29 the same threefold call went to the heavenly beings: Ascribe to the LORD, O heavenly beings (29:1). Here it goes to the families of the peoples — every clan and nation on earth. What the angels do in heaven, the nations are summoned to do on earth.

The glory due his name — not glory added to him, but glory owed. Worship is not a favour we do God. It is paying a debt.

bring an offering, and come into his courts!

This is remarkable. The courts of the temple were Israel's. But the psalm invites the nations to come into his courts with an offering in their hands — a picture of the day when the dividing wall would come down. John saw an angel with an eternal gospel to proclaim ... to every nation and tribe and language and people, calling, Fear God and give him glory ... and worship him who made heaven and earth (Rev 14:6-7).

Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth!

The splendor of holiness (the ESV notes "in holy attire" as another rendering) — dressed for a holy occasion. And the invitation holds joy and trembling together. The nations are welcome, and they are to come trembling, because the God they approach is holy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–13 — For He Comes to Judge the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Say among the nations, The LORD reigns! — the world is established, and he will judge the peoples with equity (v. 10). Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice; let the sea roar; let the fields exult and the trees sing (vv. 11-12) before the LORD, for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world in righteousness, and the peoples in his faithfulness (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole creation sings because the Judge is coming — and his coming is the best news the world could hear.

verseByVerse.quote: Say among the nations, "The LORD reigns! Yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved; he will judge the peoples with equity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Say among the nations, The LORD reigns! Yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved; he will judge the peoples with equity.

Here is the message the nations are to hear, and it is three words long: The LORD reigns — the same words that opened Psalm 93. This is what evangelism is at its root: not first an offer of improvement, but an announcement of who is King.

And the announcement has two consequences. The world is established — because he reigns, the creation holds together. And he will judge the peoples with equity — fairly, evenly, without favourites. For the oppressed of the earth, that is the best news there is.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice; let the sea roar, and all that fills it; let the field exult, and everything in it! Then shall all the trees of the forest sing for joy before the LORD, for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world in righteousness, and the peoples in his faithfulness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice; let the sea roar, and all that fills it; let the field exult, and everything in it! Then shall all the trees of the forest sing for joy

Now the invitation widens beyond people. The heavens, the earth, the sea and every creature in it, the fields, the forests — the whole creation is told to celebrate. The sea that roared in Psalm 93 as a threat now roars for joy. The trees sing.

Isaiah heard the same music: the mountains and the hills before you shall break forth into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands (Isa 55:12). And Paul explains why creation would be glad: it was subjected to futility, and waits with eager longing to be set free from its bondage to corruption (Rom 8:19-21). The creation has been groaning under the curse. It will sing when it is set free.

before the LORD, for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world in righteousness, and the peoples in his faithfulness.

And the reason for all the joy: he comes, for he comes — twice, as though the singer can already hear him approaching. He comes to judge the earth.

That is the surprise of this psalm. Judgment is the cause of celebration. We tend to hear "judgment" as only bad news. But for a world full of injustice, a world where the widow is crushed and the innocent condemned (94:6, 21), the coming of a righteous Judge is the moment everything is finally set right. The trees sing because the Judge is on his way.

Paul told the philosophers of Athens who that Judge is: God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31). The same words — judge the world in righteousness — and now a name attached. For everyone who belongs to him, his coming is not a terror but the day the whole creation has been singing towards. For he comes.

96.title: Sing to the LORD a New Song
96.overview: All the earth is called to sing a new song to the LORD, to bless his name, tell of his salvation daily and declare his glory among the nations (vv. 1-3). He is great and to be feared above all gods, for the gods of the peoples are worthless idols, but the LORD made the heavens; splendour, majesty, strength and beauty surround him (vv. 4-6). The families of the peoples are to ascribe to him glory and strength, bring offerings into his courts and worship in the splendour of holiness (vv. 7-9). Say among the nations, The LORD reigns! — he will judge the peoples with equity (v. 10). Heavens, earth, sea, fields and trees rejoice before the LORD, for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth, in righteousness and faithfulness (vv. 11-13).
96.theology:
The psalm is missionary: Israel is to declare God's glory among all nations (vv. 1-3), a new song finally sung by the redeemed of every nation (Rev 5:9).

The LORD is the Creator; the gods of the nations are nothings (v. 5; 1 Cor 8:4). The nations are summoned to ascribe glory to him and come into his courts (vv. 7-9), as heavenly beings are in 29:1 and as the eternal gospel proclaims (Rev 14:6-7).

The core announcement is The LORD reigns (v. 10). Creation rejoices at the coming of the Judge (vv. 11-13), because his judgment sets the world right (Rom 8:19-21), and the Judge is the man God has appointed and raised from the dead (Acts 17:31).
96.examples:
A new song for a new rescue.

Glory news that goes out every day.

Gods and godlets: the pun on the idols.

The proof is the sky.

Glory owed, not glory added.

Gentiles invited into the courts with offerings.

The roaring sea turned to singing.

The trees sing because the Judge is coming.

97.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD reigns, let the earth rejoice; let the many coastlands be glad!<sup>2</sup>Clouds and thick darkness are all around him; righteousness and justice are the foundation of his throne.<sup>3</sup>Fire goes before him and burns up his adversaries all around.<sup>4</sup>His lightnings light up the world; the earth sees and trembles.<sup>5</sup>The mountains melt like wax before the LORD, before the Lord of all the earth.<sup>6</sup>The heavens proclaim his righteousness, and all the peoples see his glory.<sup>7</sup>All worshipers of images are put to shame, who make their boast in worthless idols; worship him, all you gods!<sup>8</sup>Zion hears and is glad, and the daughters of Judah rejoice, because of your judgments, O LORD.<sup>9</sup>For you, O LORD, are most high over all the earth; you are exalted far above all gods.<sup>10</sup>O you who love the LORD, hate evil! He preserves the lives of his saints; he delivers them from the hand of the wicked.<sup>11</sup>Light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart.<sup>12</sup>Rejoice in the LORD, O you righteous, and give thanks to his holy name!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Clouds and Thick Darkness Are All Around Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD reigns, let the earth rejoice; let the many coastlands be glad! (v. 1). Clouds and thick darkness are all around him; righteousness and justice are the foundation of his throne (v. 2). Fire goes before him, his lightnings light up the world, the mountains melt like wax before the LORD (vv. 3-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The King appears as he did at Sinai — cloud, fire, lightning — and his throne stands on justice.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD reigns, let the earth rejoice; let the many coastlands be glad! Clouds and thick darkness are all around him; righteousness and justice are the foundation of his throne.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD reigns, let the earth rejoice; let the many coastlands be glad!

The same three words that opened Psalm 93 open this one, but here they lead straight to joy. The coastlands are the islands and far shores of the Mediterranean — the edges of the known world. God's reign is good news as far away as anyone lives.

Clouds and thick darkness are all around him; righteousness and justice are the foundation of his throne.

The picture is Sinai. When God came down on the mountain there were thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud on the mountain, and the LORD had descended on it in fire (Exod 19:16, 18). The King who reigns is surrounded by darkness — he cannot be seen, examined or managed.

And yet, inside the cloud, the throne stands on righteousness and justice — almost the words of 89:14. That is the comfort in this verse for anyone who cannot understand what God is doing. His ways are often wrapped in cloud. His throne is never built on anything but justice. We may not see what he is doing; we can know what he is.

verseByVerse.quote: Fire goes before him and burns up his adversaries all around. His lightnings light up the world; the earth sees and trembles. The mountains melt like wax before the LORD, before the Lord of all the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fire goes before him and burns up his adversaries all around. His lightnings light up the world; the earth sees and trembles.

Now the storm breaks. Fire goes ahead of the King like an advance guard, and it consumes whatever stands against him. Lightning flashes across the whole world, and for an instant everything is lit — every hidden thing exposed. The earth sees and trembles.

The mountains melt like wax before the LORD, before the Lord of all the earth.

Mountains are the image of permanence, the things that do not move. Before this King they soften and run like candle wax near a flame. John saw the end of it: From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them (Rev 20:11).

And the title matters: the Lord of all the earth. Not the god of one hill or one nation. Everything people rely on as solid — institutions, wealth, the ground itself — is wax before him. Only he is not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — Worship Him, All You Gods
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The heavens proclaim his righteousness, and all the peoples see his glory (v. 6). All worshipers of images are put to shame, who make their boast in worthless idols; worship him, all you gods! (v. 7). Zion hears and is glad (v. 8), for you, O LORD, are most high over all the earth (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: When God appears, the idols are exposed as nothing and everything that was worshipped bows.

verseByVerse.quote: The heavens proclaim his righteousness, and all the peoples see his glory. All worshipers of images are put to shame, who make their boast in worthless idols; worship him, all you gods!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heavens proclaim his righteousness, and all the peoples see his glory.

The sky itself becomes a herald, announcing that God is righteous, and all the peoples see it. When God comes, his glory will not be a private experience for a few. Everyone will see.

All worshipers of images are put to shame, who make their boast in worthless idols; worship him, all you gods!

And in that light the idols are exposed. Isaiah said the same: They are turned back and utterly put to shame, who trust in carved idols (Isa 42:17). The shame is not merely that the idol fails to help. It is that the worshipper boasted in it — staked his pride on something that turns out to be nothing.

Then a command addressed past the idol-worshippers to whatever powers they thought stood behind their idols: worship him, all you gods! Every rival power in heaven or earth is told to bow. Hebrews uses similar words, from the Greek Old Testament, of the Son when he enters the world: Let all God's angels worship him (Heb 1:6). The one to whom all powers bow is the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: Zion hears and is glad, and the daughters of Judah rejoice, because of your judgments, O LORD. For you, O LORD, are most high over all the earth; you are exalted far above all gods.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zion hears and is glad, and the daughters of Judah rejoice, because of your judgments, O LORD.

Almost the same words appear in Psalm 48 (48:11). The daughters of Judah are the towns and villages of the country around Jerusalem. The judgments that terrify the idol-worshippers make God's people glad — because God's judgments are the rescue of those who belong to him.

For you, O LORD, are most high over all the earth; you are exalted far above all gods.

The psalm turns to speak to God directly. Not just high — most high. Not just above the gods — far above. The distance between the LORD and anything else that is worshipped is not a small margin. It is infinite.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–12 — O You Who Love the LORD, Hate Evil
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O you who love the LORD, hate evil! He preserves the lives of his saints; he delivers them from the hand of the wicked (v. 10). Light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart (v. 11). Rejoice in the LORD, O you righteous, and give thanks to his holy name! (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Loving the King means hating what he hates, and the reward is light scattered like seed.

verseByVerse.quote: O you who love the LORD, hate evil! He preserves the lives of his saints; he delivers them from the hand of the wicked. Light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart. Rejoice in the LORD, O you righteous, and give thanks to his holy name!
verseByVerse.commentary:
O you who love the LORD, hate evil! He preserves the lives of his saints; he delivers them from the hand of the wicked.

Now the psalm turns to those who love God, and gives them one command: hate evil. Love of God is not a warm feeling that sits comfortably alongside sin. If you love a person, you hate what destroys him and what he hates. Paul put it just as bluntly: Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good (Rom 12:9).

Here is a searching test. What evil do you find merely regrettable, or even entertaining, that God hates? Loving the LORD will slowly teach you to hate it too.

And the promise attached is protection: he preserves the lives of his saints. Those who side with God against evil will find evil siding against them — and God siding with them.

Light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart.

A beautiful image. Light is sown, like seed scattered along a furrow. You cannot see much at sowing time; the harvest comes later. The righteous may walk in shadow now, but light has been planted along their path, and it will come up. (The ESV notes that some ancient witnesses read "Light dawns" — the same promise from another angle.)

Malachi promised that for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings (Mal 4:2). And John tells us what the light is: God is light, and in him is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5). The God who is surrounded by cloud (v. 2) sows light for his people.

Rejoice in the LORD, O you righteous, and give thanks to his holy name!

The psalm began with the whole earth told to rejoice, and it ends with the righteous rejoicing. The fire, the lightning, the melting mountains are all real — and for those who love him, the right response to the King who comes in fire is gladness and thanks.

97.title: Light Is Sown for the Righteous
97.overview: The LORD reigns: let the earth and the far coastlands rejoice (v. 1). Cloud and thick darkness surround him, and his throne stands on righteousness and justice (v. 2); fire goes before him, lightning lights the world, and mountains melt like wax before the Lord of all the earth (vv. 3-5). The heavens proclaim his righteousness and all peoples see his glory; idol-worshippers are put to shame, and all gods are told to worship him (vv. 6-7). Zion rejoices at his judgments, for he is most high over all the earth (vv. 8-9). O you who love the LORD, hate evil! — he preserves his saints; light is sown for the righteous and joy for the upright; rejoice and give thanks to his holy name (vv. 10-12).
97.theology:
God's reign is hidden in cloud yet founded on justice (v. 2; 89:14), revealed as at Sinai (Exod 19:16-18) in fire before which all that seems permanent melts (vv. 3-5; Rev 20:11).

His appearing exposes idolatry as shameful boasting in nothing (v. 7; Isa 42:17); all powers are summoned to worship him, words Hebrews applies to the Son (Heb 1:6).

Love of God entails hatred of evil (v. 10; Rom 12:9). God preserves his saints, and light is sown for the righteous (v. 11), the rising of the sun of righteousness (Mal 4:2) from the God who is light (1 John 1:5).
97.examples:
Good news as far as the farthest coastline.

We may not see what he is doing; we can know what he is.

Mountains running like candle wax.

The shame of boasting in nothing.

Every rival power told to bow.

Loving a person means hating what destroys him.

Light planted in a furrow, waiting to come up.

98.text: A Psalm. 1Oh sing to the LORD a new song, for he has done marvelous things! His right hand and his holy arm have worked salvation for him.2The LORD has made known his salvation; he has revealed his righteousness in the sight of the nations.3He has remembered his steadfast love and faithfulness to the house of Israel. All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.4Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth; break forth into joyous song and sing praises!5Sing praises to the LORD with the lyre, with the lyre and the sound of melody!6With trumpets and the sound of the horn make a joyful noise before the King, the LORD!7Let the sea roar, and all that fills it; the world and those who dwell in it!8Let the rivers clap their hands; let the hills sing for joy together9before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, and the peoples with equity.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — He Has Done Marvelous Things
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Oh sing to the LORD a new song, for he has done marvelous things! His right hand and his holy arm have worked salvation for him (v. 1). He has made his salvation known and revealed his righteousness to the nations (v. 2). He has remembered his steadfast love and faithfulness to the house of Israel. All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: God has saved his people with his own arm, and the whole world has watched.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh sing to the LORD a new song, for he has done marvelous things! His right hand and his holy arm have worked salvation for him. The LORD has made known his salvation; he has revealed his righteousness in the sight of the nations. He has remembered his steadfast love and faithfulness to the house of Israel. All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh sing to the LORD a new song, for he has done marvelous things! His right hand and his holy arm have worked salvation for him.

Psalm 96 began the same way — a new song — and gave as its reason who God is. This psalm gives a different reason: what God has done. Everything in verses 1 to 3 is past tense. Something has happened, and it needs a new song.

And the salvation was done single-handed: his right hand and his holy arm have worked salvation for him. No army helped. No one contributed. Isaiah saw God look for someone to intervene and find no one, then his own arm brought him salvation (Isa 59:16). That is the shape of every true rescue in Scripture, and above all of the cross, where God did alone what no one else could do.

The LORD has made known his salvation; he has revealed his righteousness in the sight of the nations.

The rescue was not done in a corner. It was made known, revealed, done in the sight of the nations. God's salvation of his people is also a display of his righteousness to the world — proof that he keeps his word.

He has remembered his steadfast love and faithfulness to the house of Israel. All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.

He remembered — not that he had forgotten, but that he acted on his promises. When Mary sang about the child she was carrying, she used this language: He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy (Luke 1:54). And old Simeon, holding the baby in the temple, said, my eyes have seen your salvation that you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:30-32).

Isaiah had promised that all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God (Isa 52:10). The psalm sings it as already done — have seen. Faith sings future promises in the past tense, because God's word is as good as his deed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–6 — Before the King, the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth; break forth into joyous song and sing praises! (v. 4). Lyre and melody (v. 5); With trumpets and the sound of the horn make a joyful noise before the King, the LORD! (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole earth is handed instruments and told to play for its King.

verseByVerse.quote: Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth; break forth into joyous song and sing praises! Sing praises to the LORD with the lyre, with the lyre and the sound of melody! With trumpets and the sound of the horn make a joyful noise before the King, the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth; break forth into joyous song and sing praises!

Now the whole earth is summoned. Break forth: something bursting out that cannot be held in. The response to God's salvation is not quiet appreciation.

Sing praises to the LORD with the lyre, with the lyre and the sound of melody! With trumpets and the sound of the horn make a joyful noise before the King, the LORD!

Strings, then brass. The lyre gives melody; the trumpets and the ram's horn give volume — the sounds of a coronation. And the one being crowned is named at the end: the King, the LORD. Everything in this psalm is played in front of him.

That is the thing to remember in any church arguing about music. The question is not the instrument. It is whether the noise is being made before the King.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–9 — Let the Rivers Clap Their Hands
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Let the sea roar, and all that fills it; the world and those who dwell in it! (v. 7). Let the rivers clap their hands; let the hills sing for joy together before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, and the peoples with equity (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Sea, rivers and hills join the song, because the Judge is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the sea roar, and all that fills it; the world and those who dwell in it! Let the rivers clap their hands; let the hills sing for joy together before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, and the peoples with equity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the sea roar, and all that fills it; the world and those who dwell in it! Let the rivers clap their hands; let the hills sing for joy together

These verses repeat the ending of Psalm 96 with deliberate changes. There the fields and trees sang; here the rivers clap their hands and the hills sing for joy together. The whole landscape is applauding. A well-known Christmas carol, "Joy to the World", is based on this psalm — and it is right to sing it at Christmas, because the King the psalm expects is the one who came.

before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, and the peoples with equity.

Psalm 96 said for he comes, for he comes; this psalm says it once. Psalm 96 said he will judge the peoples in his faithfulness; this one says with equity — fairly, evenly, with the same standard for every nation.

And again the surprising thing is that the creation is glad about judgment. A world that has seen God's salvation (v. 3) is not afraid of his coming to judge. John heard the redeemed singing that song by the sea of glass: Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations! (Rev 15:3). The one who worked salvation with his own arm is the one who comes to judge — which is why those he saved can clap along with the rivers.

98.title: His Holy Arm Has Worked Salvation
98.overview: Sing a new song, for the LORD has done marvellous things: his right hand and holy arm have worked salvation (v. 1). He has made his salvation known and revealed his righteousness to the nations, remembering his steadfast love and faithfulness to Israel, and all the ends of the earth have seen it (vv. 2-3). All the earth is to break into song with lyre, trumpet and horn before the King, the LORD (vv. 4-6). Let the sea roar, the rivers clap their hands and the hills sing together before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth, with righteousness and equity (vv. 7-9).
98.theology:
Salvation is God's own work, done by his arm alone (v. 1; Isa 59:16), publicly revealed to the nations (v. 2), and rooted in his remembering of covenant love to Israel (v. 3) — language taken up by Mary and Simeon at Christ's birth (Luke 1:54-55; 2:30-32).

The promise that the ends of the earth shall see (Isa 52:10) is sung as done (v. 3).

Worship is noise made before the King (v. 6). Creation joins in at the coming of the Judge, whose judgment is righteous and even-handed (vv. 7-9), the song of the redeemed (Rev 15:3-4).
98.examples:
A new song because something has happened.

A rescue done single-handed.

Simeon with the baby: my eyes have seen your salvation.

A promise sung in the past tense.

Strings, then brass: coronation music.

Rivers applauding.

A Christmas carol that is really this psalm.

99.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD reigns; let the peoples tremble! He sits enthroned upon the cherubim; let the earth quake!<sup>2</sup>The LORD is great in Zion; he is exalted over all the peoples.<sup>3</sup>Let them praise your great and awesome name! Holy is he!<sup>4</sup>The King in his might loves justice. You have established equity; you have executed justice and righteousness in Jacob.<sup>5</sup>Exalt the LORD our God; worship at his footstool! Holy is he!<sup>6</sup>Moses and Aaron were among his priests, Samuel also was among those who called upon his name. They called to the LORD, and he answered them.<sup>7</sup>In the pillar of the cloud he spoke to them; they kept his testimonies and the statute that he gave them.<sup>8</sup>O LORD our God, you answered them; you were a forgiving God to them, but an avenger of their wrongdoings.<sup>9</sup>Exalt the LORD our God, and worship at his holy mountain; for the LORD our God is holy!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The King in His Might Loves Justice
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD reigns; let the peoples tremble! He sits enthroned upon the cherubim; let the earth quake! (v. 1). He is great in Zion and exalted over all peoples; Let them praise your great and awesome name! Holy is he! (vv. 2-3). The King in his might loves justice (v. 4). Exalt the LORD our God; worship at his footstool! Holy is he! (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The King enthroned above the mercy seat is holy, and his holiness shows itself as justice.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD reigns; let the peoples tremble! He sits enthroned upon the cherubim; let the earth quake! The LORD is great in Zion; he is exalted over all the peoples. Let them praise your great and awesome name! Holy is he!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD reigns; let the peoples tremble! He sits enthroned upon the cherubim; let the earth quake!

Psalm 97 opened The LORD reigns, let the earth rejoice. This one opens The LORD reigns; let the peoples tremble! Both are right. The reign of God is joy and it is terror, depending on where you stand — and a believer who has only ever felt one of them has not yet seen the King clearly.

Enthroned upon the cherubim takes us to the ark in the Most Holy Place. The two gold cherubim spread their wings over the lid, and God said, from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim ... I will speak with you (Exod 25:22). The throne of the King of the universe on earth was the mercy seat — the place where the blood of atonement was sprinkled. His throne and his mercy are in the same place.

The LORD is great in Zion; he is exalted over all the peoples. Let them praise your great and awesome name! Holy is he!

And here is the first refrain: Holy is he! Listen for it. It comes three times in this psalm (vv. 3, 5, 9), the way the seraphim cried three times, Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts (Isa 6:3). Holiness means God is utterly other — set apart from everything created, and from everything sinful. It is the attribute the seraphim chose to cry three times over.

verseByVerse.quote: The King in his might loves justice. You have established equity; you have executed justice and righteousness in Jacob. Exalt the LORD our God; worship at his footstool! Holy is he!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The King in his might loves justice. You have established equity; you have executed justice and righteousness in Jacob.

What does holiness look like when it acts? Justice. The King in his might loves justice (the ESV notes another reading: "The might of the King loves justice"). His strength is not raw power; it is power in love with what is right. Human kings with great might have usually loved something else.

And he has not only loved justice in theory. He has established it and executed it, in Jacob — in the actual history of his people.

Exalt the LORD our God; worship at his footstool! Holy is he!

His footstool is the place on earth where the King of heaven, so to speak, rests his feet — the ark and the temple. The picture is humbling in both directions. God is so great that the holiest place on earth is only where his feet rest. And God is so gracious that he rests them among his people. The right response is to go down on your face at the foot of the throne. And the second refrain sounds: Holy is he!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — A Forgiving God, but an Avenger
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses and Aaron were among his priests, Samuel also was among those who called upon his name. They called to the LORD, and he answered them (v. 6). He spoke to them in the pillar of cloud (v. 7). O LORD our God, you answered them; you were a forgiving God to them, but an avenger of their wrongdoings (v. 8). Exalt the LORD our God, and worship at his holy mountain; for the LORD our God is holy! (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The greatest intercessors in Israel's history were heard and forgiven — and still disciplined, because God is holy.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses and Aaron were among his priests, Samuel also was among those who called upon his name. They called to the LORD, and he answered them. In the pillar of the cloud he spoke to them; they kept his testimonies and the statute that he gave them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses and Aaron were among his priests, Samuel also was among those who called upon his name. They called to the LORD, and he answered them.

Now the psalm turns to history and names three men. What they have in common is prayer — they called upon his name, and he answered. Each was a great intercessor.

After the golden calf, Moses went back up the mountain and prayed, if you will forgive their sin — but if not, please blot me out of your book (Exod 32:32). When the Philistines threatened, Samuel cried out to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answered him (1 Sam 7:9). Centuries later God named Moses and Samuel as the greatest pleaders Israel had ever known (Jer 15:1).

The holy God is not remote from prayer. His holiness does not make him deaf. Men who called to him were answered.

In the pillar of the cloud he spoke to them; they kept his testimonies and the statute that he gave them.

And he spoke back. When Moses entered the tent, the pillar of cloud would descend and stand at the entrance of the tent, and the LORD would speak with Moses (Exod 33:9). Prayer was a conversation. And the result was obedience: they kept his testimonies.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD our God, you answered them; you were a forgiving God to them, but an avenger of their wrongdoings. Exalt the LORD our God, and worship at his holy mountain; for the LORD our God is holy!
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD our God, you answered them; you were a forgiving God to them, but an avenger of their wrongdoings.

Here is the line that makes this psalm unforgettable. God was a forgiving God to these men — and at the same time an avenger of their wrongdoings. Both, to the same people.

Think of Moses and Aaron at Meribah. They struck the rock in anger, and God said, Because you did not believe in me, to uphold me as holy in the eyes of the people of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land (Num 20:12). They were not cast off. Moses remained God's friend and servant to the end of his life. But he died on the wrong side of the Jordan. Forgiven, and disciplined.

This is what holiness means for believers. Forgiveness does not always remove consequences. A holy God can forgive a sin completely and still let its fruit be felt, not as punishment to pay the debt, but as discipline to make his people holy. Our God is a consuming fire (Heb 12:29) — and he is the God who forgives. Any view of God that keeps only one of those has lost the God of this psalm.

Exalt the LORD our God, and worship at his holy mountain; for the LORD our God is holy!

The third refrain, and it is the longest: for the LORD our God is holy! The first two said Holy is he; the last says he is holy and he is ours — our God. That is the wonder the psalm ends on. The holy one, enthroned above the mercy seat, whom Moses and Samuel could only approach as intercessors, belongs to his people. And the believer now has a greater intercessor than Moses or Samuel, who always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Heb 7:25).

99.title: Holy Is He
99.overview: The LORD reigns; let the peoples tremble! He is enthroned upon the cherubim, great in Zion and exalted over all peoples: Holy is he! (vv. 1-3). The King in his might loves justice and has established equity in Jacob; worship at his footstool: Holy is he! (vv. 4-5). Moses, Aaron and Samuel called on his name and he answered them, speaking from the pillar of cloud, and they kept his statutes (vv. 6-7). He was a forgiving God to them, yet an avenger of their wrongdoings (v. 8). Exalt the LORD our God, and worship at his holy mountain; for the LORD our God is holy! (v. 9).
99.theology:
God's reign calls for trembling as well as joy (v. 1; cf. 97:1). His throne on earth is above the mercy seat (Exod 25:22). Holiness is proclaimed three times (vv. 3, 5, 9; Isa 6:3), and it shows itself in love of justice (v. 4).

The holy God hears prayer: Moses, Aaron and Samuel called and were answered (vv. 6-7; Exod 32:30-32; 1 Sam 7:9; Jer 15:1).

He forgives and also disciplines the forgiven (v. 8; Num 20:12; Heb 12:29). The final refrain joins holiness to belonging — the LORD our God is holy (v. 9) — and Christ is the greater intercessor (Heb 7:25).
99.examples:
Rejoice (97:1) and tremble (99:1): both.

The throne and the mercy seat in the same place.

Holy, holy, holy — three refrains.

Might in love with what is right.

The holiest place on earth: where his feet rest.

Moses: blot me out of your book.

Forgiven, and still died on the wrong side of the Jordan.

Holy — and ours.

100.text: A Psalm for giving thanks. 1Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth!2Serve the LORD with gladness! Come into his presence with singing!3Know that the LORD, he is God! It is he who made us, and we are his; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.4Enter his gates with thanksgiving, and his courts with praise! Give thanks to him; bless his name!5For the LORD is good; his steadfast love endures forever, and his faithfulness to all generations.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Know That the LORD, He Is God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth! Serve the LORD with gladness! Come into his presence with singing! (vv. 1-2). Know that the LORD, he is God! It is he who made us, and we are his; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole earth is called to glad worship, and the reason is simple: he made us, and we belong to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth! Serve the LORD with gladness! Come into his presence with singing!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth!

The title calls this a Psalm for giving thanks, and it is one of the best known in the Bible — five verses that many believers learned by heart as children. It comes after several psalms that celebrate the LORD as King, and it gathers them into a single invitation.

Count the commands in these five verses: make a joyful noise, serve, come, know, enter, give thanks, bless. Seven. And the first is addressed to all the earth. This is Israel's worship, but the invitation has no border.

Serve the LORD with gladness! Come into his presence with singing!

Serve is a servant's word — the work of a slave for a master, or a priest in the temple. And the psalm joins it to gladness. That combination is the whole Christian life in two words. Service without gladness turns into drudgery and resentment. Gladness without service turns into self-indulgence. The psalm will not let them be separated.

Here is a test for any Monday. Is the work you do for God — at home, in church, at your job — done with gladness? If it has become grim duty, the problem may not be the work. It may be that you have forgotten verse 3.

Come into his presence with singing — the way a crowd arrives at a festival, not the way a defendant enters a court.

verseByVerse.quote: Know that the LORD, he is God! It is he who made us, and we are his; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Know that the LORD, he is God!

In the middle of all the noise and singing, a command to know. Worship is not only feeling; it rests on something known. The LORD — the covenant God of Israel, not a vague divine presence — he is God. There is no other. Everything glad in the psalm depends on that being true.

It is he who made us, and we are his;

Two facts, and they are the ground of everything. He made us. And therefore we are his. We did not make ourselves, and we do not own ourselves.

The ESV notes another way of reading the Hebrew: "It is he who made us, and not we ourselves." The two readings differ by one small word, and both are true. We did not make ourselves — which cuts off every kind of pride. And we are his — which is the deepest comfort there is. Paul says believers are God's twice over: we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus (Eph 2:10). He made us once in creation, and again in Christ.

we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.

And the one who made us is not a distant manufacturer. He is a shepherd, and we are the sheep of his pasture — the phrase Psalm 95 used (95:7). Sheep are not impressive animals. They wander, they panic, they cannot defend themselves. Their whole safety is the shepherd.

Isaiah saw the shepherd who will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom (Isa 40:11). And Jesus said, I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me (John 10:14); My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:27-28). Peter wrote to believers, you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls (1 Pet 2:25).

That is why service can be glad. You serve a Shepherd who owns you, and nothing can take you out of his hand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–5 — For the LORD Is Good
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Enter his gates with thanksgiving, and his courts with praise! Give thanks to him; bless his name! (v. 4). For the LORD is good; his steadfast love endures forever, and his faithfulness to all generations (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The way into God's house is thanks, and the reason for thanks will never run out.

verseByVerse.quote: Enter his gates with thanksgiving, and his courts with praise! Give thanks to him; bless his name!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Enter his gates with thanksgiving, and his courts with praise! Give thanks to him; bless his name!

The picture is a procession approaching the temple: first through the outer gates, then into the courts. And the entry fee at each stage is the same: thanks, and praise. No one walks into God's presence on the strength of their achievements. They come in thanking him.

That matters, because ingratitude is where human ruin began. Paul traces the whole downward slide of mankind to this: although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him (Rom 1:21). The opposite of that slide is this verse. A thankful heart is a heart turned back towards God.

For Christians the temple gates have become a person. Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name (Heb 13:15). Thanks is now the sacrifice we bring, and it is meant to be continual: give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you (1 Thess 5:18).

Try it at the door of the next service you attend, or the next time you begin to pray. Before asking anything, name three things God has done for you this week. That is how the psalm says to go in.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD is good; his steadfast love endures forever, and his faithfulness to all generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the LORD is good; his steadfast love endures forever, and his faithfulness to all generations.

And the final reason. Verse 3 said whose we are; verse 5 says what he is like. Three statements, each larger than the last.

The LORD is good. Not merely that he does good things, but that goodness is what he is. Everything he does flows out of it.

His steadfast love endures forever. His covenant love never runs out and never expires. The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning (Lam 3:22-23).

And his faithfulness to all generations. The pair — steadfast love and faithfulness — is the name God proclaimed to Moses (Exod 34:6). And to all generations means that the God who kept faith with the Israelites who first sang this psalm is keeping faith with you, and will keep it with your children and grandchildren.

That is why the whole earth should make a joyful noise. Not because life is easy, but because the God we serve is good, his love has no end, and his faithfulness will outlast every generation that sings about it.

100.title: Enter His Gates with Thanksgiving
100.overview: A psalm for giving thanks. All the earth is called to make a joyful noise to the LORD, to serve him with gladness and come before him singing (vv. 1-2). Know that the LORD, he is God! He made us, and we are his — his people and the sheep of his pasture (v. 3). So enter his gates with thanksgiving and his courts with praise, giving thanks and blessing his name (v. 4), for the LORD is good; his steadfast love endures forever, and his faithfulness to all generations (v. 5).
100.theology:
Seven commands to worship rest on two grounds: God's ownership of us as Creator and Shepherd (v. 3) and his goodness, love and faithfulness (v. 5).

Service and gladness belong together (v. 2). Worship rests on knowledge that the LORD alone is God (v. 3). We did not make ourselves and we belong to him (see the ESV note at v. 3), twice over in Christ (Eph 2:10), and we are sheep kept by the Good Shepherd (John 10:14, 27-28; 1 Pet 2:25).

Thanksgiving is the way into God's presence (v. 4), the reversal of humanity's first ingratitude (Rom 1:21), and the continual sacrifice offered through Christ (Heb 13:15; 1 Thess 5:18). God's steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod 34:6) endure to every generation (v. 5).
100.examples:
Seven commands and two reasons.

Service without gladness is drudgery; gladness without service is self-indulgence.

Arriving like a festival crowd, not a defendant.

We did not make ourselves, and we are not our own.

Sheep: their whole safety is the shepherd.

The entry fee at the gate is thanks.

Three things God did this week, before asking for anything.

Faithful to the first singers, and to your grandchildren.

101.text: A Psalm of David. 1I will sing of steadfast love and justice; to you, O LORD, I will make music.2I will ponder the way that is blameless. Oh when will you come to me? I will walk with integrity of heart within my house;3I will not set before my eyes anything that is worthless. I hate the work of those who fall away; it shall not cling to me.4A perverse heart shall be far from me; I will know nothing of evil.5Whoever slanders his neighbor secretly I will destroy. Whoever has a haughty look and an arrogant heart I will not endure.6I will look with favor on the faithful in the land, that they may dwell with me; he who walks in the way that is blameless shall minister to me.7No one who practices deceit shall dwell in my house; no one who utters lies shall continue before my eyes.8Morning by morning I will destroy all the wicked in the land, cutting off all the evildoers from the city of the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — I Will Ponder the Way That Is Blameless
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I will sing of steadfast love and justice; to you, O LORD, I will make music (v. 1). I will ponder the way that is blameless. Oh when will you come to me? I will walk with integrity of heart within my house (v. 2). I will not set before my eyes anything that is worthless (v. 3); a perverse heart shall be far from him (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: A king makes promises about his own heart, his home and his eyes — and in the middle cries out for God to come.

verseByVerse.quote: I will sing of steadfast love and justice; to you, O LORD, I will make music. I will ponder the way that is blameless. Oh when will you come to me? I will walk with integrity of heart within my house;
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will sing of steadfast love and justice; to you, O LORD, I will make music.

This is a king's vow, and the words I will come ten times in eight verses. David is setting out how he intends to rule. And he begins not with policy but with worship: he will sing.

The two things he sings about are the two things a ruler most needs: steadfast love and justice. Love without justice becomes favouritism; justice without love becomes cruelty. God holds both perfectly, and a king who has sung about them will try to rule by both.

I will ponder the way that is blameless. Oh when will you come to me? I will walk with integrity of heart within my house;

He will ponder the blameless way — think about it, study it. Integrity does not happen by accident; it is thought through.

And then, right in the middle of the resolutions, a cry: Oh when will you come to me? It interrupts the list. David knows that a string of good intentions is not enough. Unless God comes to him, all the I wills in the psalm will collapse. That is the most honest line in the psalm, and the one to pray first.

I will walk with integrity of heart within my house. Before he says anything about the kingdom, he speaks about his home. It is possible to have a spotless public reputation and a private life at home that no one sees. David resolves that the man inside the house will be the same man as the king in the gate. A leader's integrity is tested first where there is no audience: with his wife, his children, his servants, behind the door.

verseByVerse.quote: I will not set before my eyes anything that is worthless. I hate the work of those who fall away; it shall not cling to me. A perverse heart shall be far from me; I will know nothing of evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will not set before my eyes anything that is worthless.

The eyes are the gateway, and he guards them. Anything that is worthless — anything vile, useless or corrupting — will not be set before his eyes, placed there to be looked at. He cannot prevent every sight from reaching him. He can decide what he sits and looks at.

For a generation that carries a screen everywhere, this is one of the most practical verses in the Psalter. What do you set before your eyes, deliberately, in the evening? David wrote this vow, and later, from the roof of his palace one evening, he looked at a woman bathing and did not look away (2 Sam 11:2). The vow was right. He broke it, and it cost a man's life and a child's.

I hate the work of those who fall away; it shall not cling to me.

Sin clings. It sticks to a person like mud. The work of those who fall away from God is not merely something to disapprove of at a distance; it is something that will attach itself to you if you handle it.

A perverse heart shall be far from me; I will know nothing of evil.

Know nothing of evil means to have no intimate acquaintance with it — not to become familiar, not to get comfortable. There are things it is better not to be an expert in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — No One Who Practices Deceit Shall Dwell in My House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The secret slanderer and the arrogant he will not tolerate (v. 5). I will look with favor on the faithful in the land, that they may dwell with me (v. 6). No one who practices deceit shall dwell in my house (v. 7). Morning by morning I will destroy all the wicked in the land, cutting off all the evildoers from the city of the LORD (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The king chooses his company and guards his court, so that the city of God is clean.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever slanders his neighbor secretly I will destroy. Whoever has a haughty look and an arrogant heart I will not endure. I will look with favor on the faithful in the land, that they may dwell with me; he who walks in the way that is blameless shall minister to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever slanders his neighbor secretly I will destroy. Whoever has a haughty look and an arrogant heart I will not endure.

Now the king turns to his court, and he names two kinds of person he will not have near him. The first is the secret slanderer — the man who whispers against others in private, poisoning the king's mind. Every court has them, and so does every office, family and church. The second is the proud man with the haughty look — the one who looks down on everyone else.

These are not the most spectacular sins. They are the ones that quietly rot a community from the inside, and a wise leader deals with them early.

I will look with favor on the faithful in the land, that they may dwell with me; he who walks in the way that is blameless shall minister to me.

And instead he will look for the faithful — not the impressive, the flattering or the useful, but the trustworthy — and bring them close. His servants will be people who walk blamelessly.

Every person has a court of some kind: the friends they listen to, the voices they let near. The psalm asks who is in yours. The company a person chooses shapes the person he becomes.

verseByVerse.quote: No one who practices deceit shall dwell in my house; no one who utters lies shall continue before my eyes. Morning by morning I will destroy all the wicked in the land, cutting off all the evildoers from the city of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one who practices deceit shall dwell in my house; no one who utters lies shall continue before my eyes.

Deceit and lies are banished from the house and from the king's presence. A ruler surrounded by liars can never know the truth about his own kingdom.

Morning by morning I will destroy all the wicked in the land, cutting off all the evildoers from the city of the LORD.

Kings in Israel heard cases in the morning, and the picture is of a king who does justice every day, not occasionally. A king who sits on the throne of judgment winnows all evil with his eyes (Prov 20:8). And the reason is the name of the city: it is the city of the LORD. Evil does not belong there.

No king of Israel kept this psalm. David wrote it and failed it — the eyes, the house, the lies, the murder. Every one of his sons failed it too. The vow stood unfulfilled until a King came who could say every line of it and mean it: whose heart had integrity inside his house, who set nothing worthless before his eyes, in whose mouth no deceit was found.

That King now asks the same of those who follow him. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt 5:8). Leaders in his church are to be above reproach (1 Tim 3:2). No Christian can keep this psalm by resolution alone. But everyone can begin where David did — with the cry in verse 2: Oh when will you come to me? — and find that the King who kept it perfectly has come.

101.title: Integrity of Heart Within My House
101.overview: David vows how he will rule. He will sing of steadfast love and justice and ponder the blameless way — Oh when will you come to me? — walking with integrity in his own house (vv. 1-2). He will set nothing worthless before his eyes, hate the work of those who fall away and keep a perverse heart far from him (vv. 3-4). He will not tolerate the secret slanderer or the arrogant, but will bring the faithful near to serve him (vv. 5-6). No deceiver will dwell in his house, and every morning he will cut off the wicked from the city of the LORD (vv. 7-8).
101.theology:
Rule must be shaped by steadfast love and justice (v. 1). Integrity begins at home, out of public view (v. 2), and depends on God coming to help — the cry in the middle of the vow.

The guarding of the eyes (v. 3) and the refusal of intimacy with evil (v. 4) are the private roots of public righteousness. A ruler shapes his realm by the company he keeps — excluding slanderers, the proud and liars, and favouring the faithful (vv. 5-7) — and does justice daily (v. 8; Prov 20:8).
