David failed the vow (2 Sam 11); it is fulfilled in Christ the King, and its standard remains for his people and their leaders (Matt 5:8; 1 Tim 3:2).
101.examples:
Ten I wills — and one cry for help in the middle.

The same man behind the front door as in the gate.

What you set before your eyes in the evening.

Sin that clings like mud.

Some things it is better not to be an expert in.

The whisperer in the court.

Who is in your court?

A vow no king kept, until one did.

102.text: A Prayer of one afflicted, when he is faint and pours out his complaint before the LORD. 1Hear my prayer, O LORD; let my cry come to you!2Do not hide your face from me in the day of my distress! Incline your ear to me; answer me speedily in the day when I call!3For my days pass away like smoke, and my bones burn like a furnace.4My heart is struck down like grass and has withered; I forget to eat my bread.5Because of my loud groaning my bones cling to my flesh.6I am like a desert owl of the wilderness, like an owl of the waste places;7I lie awake; I am like a lonely sparrow on the housetop.8All the day my enemies taunt me; those who deride me use my name for a curse.9For I eat ashes like bread and mingle tears with my drink,10because of your indignation and anger; for you have taken me up and thrown me down.11My days are like an evening shadow; I wither away like grass.12But you, O LORD, are enthroned forever; you are remembered throughout all generations.13You will arise and have pity on Zion; it is the time to favor her; the appointed time has come.14For your servants hold her stones dear and have pity on her dust.15Nations will fear the name of the LORD, and all the kings of the earth will fear your glory.16For the LORD builds up Zion; he appears in his glory;17he regards the prayer of the destitute and does not despise their prayer.18Let this be recorded for a generation to come, so that a people yet to be created may praise the LORD:19that he looked down from his holy height; from heaven the LORD looked at the earth,20to hear the groans of the prisoners, to set free those who were doomed to die,21that they may declare in Zion the name of the LORD, and in Jerusalem his praise,22when peoples gather together, and kingdoms, to worship the LORD.23He has broken my strength in midcourse; he has shortened my days.24"O my God," I say, "take me not away in the midst of my days— you whose years endure throughout all generations!"25Of old you laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands.26They will perish, but you will remain; they will all wear out like a garment. You will change them like a robe, and they will pass away,27but you are the same, and your years have no end.28The children of your servants shall dwell secure; their offspring shall be established before you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — My Days Pass Away Like Smoke
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hear my prayer, O LORD; let my cry come to you! (v. 1). For my days pass away like smoke, and my bones burn like a furnace (v. 3). His heart withers like grass; he forgets to eat; he is like a desert owl and a lonely sparrow on the housetop (vv. 4-7). Enemies taunt him; he eats ashes like bread because of your indignation and anger (vv. 8-10). My days are like an evening shadow; I wither away like grass (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: A man with no name, sleepless and wasting, pours out everything to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear my prayer, O LORD; let my cry come to you! Do not hide your face from me in the day of my distress! Incline your ear to me; answer me speedily in the day when I call!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear my prayer, O LORD; let my cry come to you! Do not hide your face from me in the day of my distress! Incline your ear to me; answer me speedily in the day when I call!

The title of this psalm does not name an author. It names a condition: A Prayer of one afflicted, when he is faint and pours out his complaint before the LORD. That makes it a prayer for anyone. If you are afflicted and faint, this psalm has your name on it.

And the title gives permission for what follows. It calls the prayer a complaint, poured out. God has put in his book a psalm whose purpose is to let a suffering person empty everything out in front of him, without tidying it first.

The first requests are for God's face, ear and speed: do not hide, lean down, answer quickly. When you are faint, you have no strength for long prayers or patience for delay.

verseByVerse.quote: For my days pass away like smoke, and my bones burn like a furnace. My heart is struck down like grass and has withered; I forget to eat my bread. Because of my loud groaning my bones cling to my flesh. I am like a desert owl of the wilderness, like an owl of the waste places; I lie awake; I am like a lonely sparrow on the housetop.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For my days pass away like smoke, and my bones burn like a furnace. My heart is struck down like grass and has withered; I forget to eat my bread.

Now the complaint, in a flood of images. His days vanish like smoke — visible for a moment, then gone. His bones burn like a furnace — fever, or the burning ache of long illness or grief. His heart withers like cut grass.

And a small, true detail: I forget to eat my bread. Anyone who has been through deep grief or depression recognises it. Food loses its point. Meals are missed without noticing.

Because of my loud groaning my bones cling to my flesh.

He has wasted away until he is skin and bone.

I am like a desert owl of the wilderness, like an owl of the waste places; I lie awake; I am like a lonely sparrow on the housetop.

The birds are pictures of loneliness. The ESV notes that the exact species are uncertain, but the point is not: a bird that lives in ruins and deserts, calling in the dark; a single sparrow on a roof, alone, awake, when every other bird has gone to roost. I lie awake. The sleepless nights of the sufferer are in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: All the day my enemies taunt me; those who deride me use my name for a curse. For I eat ashes like bread and mingle tears with my drink, because of your indignation and anger; for you have taken me up and thrown me down. My days are like an evening shadow; I wither away like grass.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the day my enemies taunt me; those who deride me use my name for a curse.

His suffering has made him a byword. People use his name as an example of misfortune — "may you end up like him".

For I eat ashes like bread and mingle tears with my drink, because of your indignation and anger; for you have taken me up and thrown me down.

Ashes are the sign of mourning, and he says he eats them; tears fall into his cup as he drinks. And then the hardest line: because of your indignation and anger. He believes God's hand is in it. You have taken me up and thrown me down — like someone lifted high and dashed to the ground. The height he once had makes the fall worse.

My days are like an evening shadow; I wither away like grass.

An evening shadow grows longer and fainter as the sun goes down, until it disappears into the dark. That is how he feels his life is ending: stretched thin, and fading.

Notice that the complaint is framed by grass. It began with my heart is struck down like grass and has withered (v. 4), and it ends with I wither away like grass (v. 11). Everything between is the long afternoon of a plant in the sun. That is what makes the next verse land so hard.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–22 — But You, O LORD, Are Enthroned Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But you, O LORD, are enthroned forever (v. 12). God will arise and have pity on Zion, whose stones his servants love; nations will fear his name (vv. 13-17). Let this be recorded for a generation to come, so that a people yet to be created may praise the LORD (v. 18): he looked down to hear the groans of the prisoners and set free those doomed to die, that his praise may be declared in Zion when the peoples gather (vv. 19-22).
verseByVerse.theology: From his own ruin the sufferer looks up to the eternal King, and writes for readers not yet born.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, O LORD, are enthroned forever; you are remembered throughout all generations. You will arise and have pity on Zion; it is the time to favor her; the appointed time has come. For your servants hold her stones dear and have pity on her dust. Nations will fear the name of the LORD, and all the kings of the earth will fear your glory. For the LORD builds up Zion; he appears in his glory; he regards the prayer of the destitute and does not despise their prayer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you, O LORD, are enthroned forever; you are remembered throughout all generations.

And here the psalm turns. Nothing about his condition has changed, but he looks away from his shadow to God's throne. His days are smoke; God is enthroned forever. He is forgotten and cursed; God is remembered throughout all generations. Psalm 92 put the same sentence at its centre: but you, O LORD, are on high forever (92:8).

That is the way out of the pit of self-absorption that suffering digs. Not denial — he has told the truth about his pain — but a second look, upwards.

You will arise and have pity on Zion; it is the time to favor her; the appointed time has come. For your servants hold her stones dear and have pity on her dust.

His personal ruin is tied to Zion's. The city lies in ruins, and God's servants love even its rubble — her stones, her dust. Exiles who had lost everything still loved the broken place where God had put his name. And he is sure that the appointed time has come for God to act.

Nations will fear the name of the LORD, and all the kings of the earth will fear your glory. For the LORD builds up Zion; he appears in his glory; he regards the prayer of the destitute and does not despise their prayer.

The rebuilding of Zion will be a world event. And the heart of it is in the last line: he regards the prayer of the destitute. The God whose glory makes kings afraid is the God who listens to the prayer of people with nothing, and does not despise it. The afflicted man of the title has just described himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Let this be recorded for a generation to come, so that a people yet to be created may praise the LORD: that he looked down from his holy height; from heaven the LORD looked at the earth, to hear the groans of the prisoners, to set free those who were doomed to die, that they may declare in Zion the name of the LORD, and in Jerusalem his praise, when peoples gather together, and kingdoms, to worship the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He appears in his glory is placed right beside the LORD builds up Zion. God's glory is not only seen in thunder on a mountain. It is seen in the patient rebuilding of what was ruined — which is the work he is still doing in every broken life and every broken church that is his.

Let this be recorded for a generation to come, so that a people yet to be created may praise the LORD:

This is an extraordinary verse. The sufferer asks that his experience be recorded — written down — for people not yet born, so that they will praise God. He is thinking of readers far in the future.

You are one of them. A people yet to be created includes every believer who has ever opened this psalm. A man in affliction, whose name we do not know, prayed that God would use his suffering for someone else's praise, and God did it. No affliction handed to God is wasted.

that he looked down from his holy height; from heaven the LORD looked at the earth, to hear the groans of the prisoners, to set free those who were doomed to die,

Here is what is to be recorded: God looked down. The words groans of the prisoners and doomed to die are the words of Psalm 79 (79:11), where they were a desperate request. Here they are recorded as something God did. The prayer of one psalm is the praise of another.

that they may declare in Zion the name of the LORD, and in Jerusalem his praise, when peoples gather together, and kingdoms, to worship the LORD.

And the end of rescue is worship — not just Israel, but peoples and kingdoms gathering together. The set-free prisoners join the nations in praise.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He has broken my strength in midcourse; he has shortened my days (v. 23). He pleads not to be taken in the midst of his days (v. 24). Of old you laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands. They will perish, but you will remain (vv. 25-26); but you are the same, and your years have no end (v. 27). His servants' children will dwell secure (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: A man whose life is being cut short takes refuge in the one whose years never end — words Hebrews says are spoken to the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: He has broken my strength in midcourse; he has shortened my days. "O my God," I say, "take me not away in the midst of my days— you whose years endure throughout all generations!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has broken my strength in midcourse; he has shortened my days.

The psalm returns to the man. The vision of Zion has not removed his own suffering. His strength is broken in midcourse — halfway through the journey. He is not old. His life is being cut off in the middle.

O my God, I say, take me not away in the midst of my days — you whose years endure throughout all generations!

His plea sets two lengths of time against each other: the midst of my days, and God's years that endure throughout all generations. You have endless years; don't take my few.

There was one man whose strength was broken in midcourse more starkly than this — cut off in his early thirties, in the middle of his days. And the next verses, astonishingly, the New Testament says are spoken to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Of old you laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands. They will perish, but you will remain; they will all wear out like a garment. You will change them like a robe, and they will pass away, but you are the same, and your years have no end. The children of your servants shall dwell secure; their offspring shall be established before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of old you laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands. They will perish, but you will remain; they will all wear out like a garment. You will change them like a robe, and they will pass away,

The heavens and the earth feel permanent. They are not. God made them, and they will wear out like a garment — like an old coat that thins and frays — and God will change them as a man changes clothes. The universe is his wardrobe.

but you are the same, and your years have no end.

Everything wears out except him. You are the same.

Now the astonishing thing. The letter to the Hebrews quotes these three verses — You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the work of your hands; they will perish, but you remain — and says they are addressed to the Son (Heb 1:8, 10-12). The God to whom the afflicted man prays, whose years have no end, is the Son of God.

Put that beside verse 23. The Son, whose years have no end, took on a human life and let his strength be broken in midcourse. The eternal one was cut off in the midst of his days. He knows this psalm from the inside, both halves of it — the sufferer's and the eternal King's. And because he is the same, and his years have no end, those who belong to him have a future too.

Hebrews ends with the same confidence: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever (Heb 13:8). The one this psalm calls the same is not a changeless idea but a changeless person, and the believer who is wearing out like the old coat of verse 26 is held by him.

The children of your servants shall dwell secure; their offspring shall be established before you.

The psalm ends not with the man's own recovery — we are never told whether he got better — but with the security of the next generation. His days may be short. God's are not, and God's people will go on. the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now (Rom 8:22), and when it is changed like a robe, the children of God's servants will still be standing before him.

102.title: Your Years Have No End
102.overview: A prayer for anyone afflicted and faint. He begs God not to hide his face (vv. 1-2). His days vanish like smoke, his bones burn, he forgets to eat, he is like a lonely owl or a sparrow awake on a rooftop, taunted by enemies, eating ashes and drinking tears under God's anger, fading like an evening shadow (vv. 3-11). But you, O LORD, are enthroned forever (v. 12): God will have pity on Zion, whose stones his servants love, and nations will fear him, for he regards the prayer of the destitute (vv. 13-17). This is to be recorded for a people yet to be created: the LORD looked down to free prisoners doomed to die, so that peoples and kingdoms may worship him (vv. 18-22). His strength is broken in midcourse; he pleads not to be taken in the midst of his days (vv. 23-24). The heavens will wear out like a garment, but you are the same, and your years have no end, and the children of his servants will dwell secure (vv. 25-28).
102.theology:
The title makes the psalm available to every sufferer and legitimises poured-out complaint (title; vv. 1-11). The turn comes by looking from one's own fading days to God's eternal throne (v. 12; cf. 92:8).

The God whose glory makes kings tremble regards the prayer of the destitute (v. 17). Suffering handed to God can be recorded for the praise of later generations (v. 18), and the plea of 79:11 becomes the praise of vv. 19-20.

Creation is impermanent; God alone is the same (vv. 25-27). Hebrews addresses these verses to the Son (Heb 1:10-12), so the eternal one whose years have no end is the one who was cut off in the midst of his days. God's servants' children are secure in him (v. 28; Rom 8:22).
102.examples:
A psalm with a condition for its author's name.

Forgetting to eat.

A single sparrow awake on the roof.

A shadow stretching thin at evening.

Exiles who love the rubble.

Written for readers not yet born — you.

The universe wearing out like an old coat.

The eternal one cut off in midcourse.

103.text: Of David. 1Bless the LORD, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name!2Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits,3who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases,4who redeems your life from the pit, who crowns you with steadfast love and mercy,5who satisfies you with good so that your youth is renewed like the eagle's.6The LORD works righteousness and justice for all who are oppressed.7He made known his ways to Moses, his acts to the people of Israel.8The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love.9He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever.10He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities.11For as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is his steadfast love toward those who fear him;12as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us.13As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him.14For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust.15As for man, his days are like grass; he flourishes like a flower of the field;16for the wind passes over it, and it is gone, and its place knows it no more.17But the steadfast love of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him, and his righteousness to children's children,18to those who keep his covenant and remember to do his commandments.19The LORD has established his throne in the heavens, and his kingdom rules over all.20Bless the LORD, O you his angels, you mighty ones who do his word, obeying the voice of his word!21Bless the LORD, all his hosts, his ministers, who do his will!22Bless the LORD, all his works, in all places of his dominion. Bless the LORD, O my soul!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Bless the LORD, O My Soul
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bless the LORD, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name! Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits (vv. 1-2), who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from the pit, who crowns you with steadfast love and mercy, who satisfies you with good so that your youth is renewed like the eagle's (vv. 3-5).
verseByVerse.theology: David preaches to his own soul, and the first benefit on the list is forgiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: Bless the LORD, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name! Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bless the LORD, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name!

David is talking to himself. Not to God first, not to the congregation, but to his own soul: Bless the LORD, O my soul. There are times when the soul does not feel like praising, and the right thing to do is not to wait for the feeling but to address the soul and give it orders.

And the order is total: all that is within me. Mind, affections, memory, will. Worship with part of yourself while the rest wanders is not what he means. The whole person bends towards his holy name.

Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits,

The command is repeated, and its enemy is named: forgetting. The soul does not usually stop praising because it has decided God is not good. It stops because it has forgotten what he has done. Ingratitude is mostly a failure of memory.

So the cure is to remember, specifically. All his benefits — not a vague sense of blessing, but a list. Try it: before you go to sleep tonight, name what God has done for you, one thing at a time. That is what David is about to do.

verseByVerse.quote: who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from the pit, who crowns you with steadfast love and mercy, who satisfies you with good so that your youth is renewed like the eagle's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases,

Five benefits follow, and the order matters. The first is forgiveness. Before health, before rescue, before anything else, the greatest thing God does for a person is forgive all his iniquity. A man with perfect health and unforgiven sin is in a far worse position than a sick man who is forgiven.

Who heals all your diseases is a true promise, and it must be read honestly. God does heal, and every recovery is his gift. But believers still get ill and die. The promise is not that every disease is cured in this life; it is that the God who forgives all iniquity will finally heal every disease, when death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore (Rev 21:4). Forgiveness comes first because it is the root; healing follows because it is the fruit.

who redeems your life from the pit, who crowns you with steadfast love and mercy, who satisfies you with good so that your youth is renewed like the eagle's.

Three more. He redeems — buys back — your life from the pit of death. He crowns you: the one pulled out of the pit is not merely rescued but honoured, and the crown is made of steadfast love and mercy. And he satisfies you with good, until your strength comes back like an eagle's. Isaiah promised the same: they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles (Isa 40:31).

Count them back: forgiven, healed, redeemed, crowned, satisfied. From the pit to a crown to a full table. That is the story of every believer's life, told in five verbs.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — As Far as the East Is from the West
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD works justice for the oppressed and made known his ways to Moses (vv. 6-7): The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love (v. 8). He does not deal with us according to our sins (v. 10). For as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is his steadfast love toward those who fear him; as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us (vv. 11-12). As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD does, for he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: God's love is measured by the height of the sky, and our sins are removed as far as east from west.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD works righteousness and justice for all who are oppressed. He made known his ways to Moses, his acts to the people of Israel. The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD works righteousness and justice for all who are oppressed. He made known his ways to Moses, his acts to the people of Israel.

Now the psalm moves from what God has done for one soul to what God is like. He is on the side of the oppressed — all of them. And he has not left people guessing about his character: he made known his ways to Moses.

The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love.

This is what he showed Moses. After the golden calf, God passed before Moses and proclaimed his own name: The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod 34:6). David quotes it almost exactly. It is the Old Testament's most repeated description of God — and it was first spoken to a people who had just broken the covenant. God revealed his mercy at the moment his people least deserved it.

And notice a small difference in verse 7. To Moses God made known his ways; to the people of Israel, his acts. The people saw what God did — the plagues, the sea, the manna. Moses was shown why, and what kind of God does such things. It is possible to see God's acts all your life and never ask to know his ways. Moses asked, and was answered with verse 8.

verseByVerse.quote: He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever. He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever.

God does rebuke. He does grow angry at sin. But he does not always chide, and he does not keep his anger forever. A believer under God's discipline can know that it has an end.

He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities.

Here is the most astonishing sentence in the psalm. If God dealt with us according to our sins, no one would survive. He does not.

But how can a just God do that? Not by pretending the sins do not matter. The New Testament gives the answer David could only glimpse: God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom 5:8). God does not deal with us according to our sins, because he dealt with his Son according to them. The repayment we deserved was not cancelled; it was paid.

verseByVerse.quote: For as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is his steadfast love toward those who fear him; as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is his steadfast love toward those who fear him;

How big is God's love? Look up. It is as high as the sky is above the ground. David had no telescope, but he knew the sky had no measurable top, and that is the point: his steadfast love cannot be measured.

as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us.

And how far away are our sins? Walk east. However far you go, you never arrive at the west — they never meet. That is the distance God puts between a forgiven person and his sins. He does not put them on a shelf where they can be taken down again.

The prophets reach for the same picture: You will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea (Mic 7:19); you have cast all my sins behind your back (Isa 38:17). And the new covenant promise: I will remember their sins no more (Heb 8:12). If you are in Christ and your conscience keeps digging up a sin you have confessed, this verse is your answer. God has moved it further away than your memory can travel.

verseByVerse.quote: As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him. For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him.

Now the image becomes a family. A good father's compassion for his children is not earned by them; it comes from being their father. Jesus told of a son who came home in disgrace, and while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him (Luke 15:20). That is the compassion of this verse.

For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust.

And the reason for his compassion is that he knows exactly what we are made of. Our frame — the ESV notes it can be read "how we are formed" — is dust, as Moses said (90:3). God does not expect dust to behave like steel. He remembers our weakness, our limits, how quickly we tire and fail.

That is a verse for anyone exhausted by their own weakness, or afraid that God is disappointed in how little they can manage. He is not surprised. He made the dust, and he remembers it with compassion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–22 — His Kingdom Rules over All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As for man, his days are like grass; the wind passes and it is gone (vv. 15-16). But the steadfast love of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him, and his righteousness to children's children (vv. 17-18). The LORD has established his throne in the heavens, and his kingdom rules over all (v. 19). Angels, hosts and all his works are called to bless him — Bless the LORD, O my soul! (vv. 20-22).
verseByVerse.theology: Short human lives rest on everlasting love, and the whole universe is summoned into one man's song.

verseByVerse.quote: As for man, his days are like grass; he flourishes like a flower of the field; for the wind passes over it, and it is gone, and its place knows it no more. But the steadfast love of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him, and his righteousness to children's children, to those who keep his covenant and remember to do his commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for man, his days are like grass; he flourishes like a flower of the field; for the wind passes over it, and it is gone, and its place knows it no more.

From dust to grass. A human life flourishes like a wildflower — bright, and brief. A hot wind passes over it and it is gone. Its place knows it no more: the patch of ground where it grew does not remember it. Within a generation or two, most of us will be forgotten even by the places we lived.

But the steadfast love of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him, and his righteousness to children's children, to those who keep his covenant and remember to do his commandments.

But. Against the brevity of grass stands a love that is from everlasting to everlasting — it had no beginning and will have no end. The flower fades; the love that rests on it does not. And it outlasts the individual, reaching children's children.

Notice the word remember again. God remembers that we are dust (v. 14); his people are to remember to do his commandments (v. 18); and David began by telling his soul not to forget (v. 2). The psalm is about remembering in both directions.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD has established his throne in the heavens, and his kingdom rules over all. Bless the LORD, O you his angels, you mighty ones who do his word, obeying the voice of his word! Bless the LORD, all his hosts, his ministers, who do his will! Bless the LORD, all his works, in all places of his dominion. Bless the LORD, O my soul!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD has established his throne in the heavens, and his kingdom rules over all.

The love that forgives, heals and remembers our frame belongs to the King of everything. His kingdom rules over all. There is nothing outside it.

Bless the LORD, O you his angels, you mighty ones who do his word, obeying the voice of his word! Bless the LORD, all his hosts, his ministers, who do his will! Bless the LORD, all his works, in all places of his dominion.

And now the circle of praise widens. The psalm began with one soul. Now it summons the angels, the mighty ones who do his word; then all the hosts of heaven; then all his works, in all places of his dominion — every star, sea and creature. The whole universe is called into the song.

And look at how the angels bless him: they are mighty ones who do his word, obeying the voice of his word, ministers, who do his will. The highest praise in heaven is not only singing; it is obedience. That is why Jesus taught his disciples to pray that God's will be done on earth as it is in heaven. A life that does what God says is a psalm.

Bless the LORD, O my soul!

And then, having gathered the entire creation, the psalm comes back to where it began: O my soul. The last voice in the universal choir is David's own. It is as though he says: the angels are singing, the stars are singing — and I will not be the one voice missing. The next psalm opens with the same words (104:1), and moves from redemption to creation.

If your soul is silent today, this psalm tells you what to do. Talk to it. Remind it of the list — forgiven, healed, redeemed, crowned, satisfied — and of a love as high as the heavens, and a Father who remembers you are dust. Bless the LORD, O my soul.

103.title: Forget Not All His Benefits
103.overview: David commands his soul to bless the LORD and not forget his benefits: he forgives all iniquity, heals all diseases, redeems from the pit, crowns with steadfast love and mercy, and satisfies with good (vv. 1-5). The LORD works justice for the oppressed and made known his ways to Moses — merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love (vv. 6-8). He will not always chide and does not deal with us according to our sins (vv. 9-10); his love is as high as the heavens, and he removes our transgressions as far as the east is from the west (vv. 11-12). Like a father he has compassion, knowing we are dust (vv. 13-14). Man's days are like grass, but the LORD's steadfast love is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him (vv. 15-18). His kingdom rules over all; angels, hosts and all his works are called to bless him — Bless the LORD, O my soul! (vv. 19-22).
103.theology:
Praise is commanded of one's own soul and hindered chiefly by forgetfulness (vv. 1-2). God's benefits begin with forgiveness, the root from which healing and final restoration grow (vv. 3-5; Rev 21:4).

God's character is revealed as he declared it to Moses (v. 8; Exod 34:6). He does not deal with us according to our sins (v. 10) because Christ died for sinners (Rom 5:8). Forgiveness removes sin immeasurably far (vv. 11-12; Mic 7:19; Isa 38:17; Heb 8:12).

God's compassion is a father's (v. 13; Luke 15:20), grounded in his knowledge of our frailty (v. 14). Everlasting love rests on brief human lives and reaches their descendants (vv. 15-18). God reigns over all, and all creation is summoned to bless him, ending with the individual soul (vv. 19-22).
103.examples:
Giving your own soul orders.

Ingratitude is mostly forgetting.

Forgiven, healed, redeemed, crowned, satisfied.

Mercy revealed right after the golden calf.

Walk east forever and you never reach the west.

The father running down the road.

God does not expect dust to behave like steel.

The angels are singing — and I will not be the voice missing.

104.text: <sup>1</sup>Bless the LORD, O my soul! O LORD my God, you are very great! You are clothed with splendor and majesty,<sup>2</sup>covering yourself with light as with a garment, stretching out the heavens like a tent.<sup>3</sup>He lays the beams of his chambers on the waters; verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Clothed with Splendor and Majesty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bless the LORD, O my soul! O LORD my God, you are very great! You are clothed with splendor and majesty, covering yourself with light as with a garment, stretching out the heavens like a tent (vv. 1-2). He rides on the clouds and the wind (vv. 3-4). He set the earth on its foundations (v. 5); at his rebuke the waters fled to their appointed place, and he set them a boundary (vv. 6-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The Creator dresses in light, pitches the sky like a tent, and tells the sea where to stop.

verseByVerse.quote: Bless the LORD, O my soul! O LORD my God, you are very great! You are clothed with splendor and majesty, covering yourself with light as with a garment, stretching out the heavens like a tent. He lays the beams of his chambers on the waters; he makes the clouds his chariot; he rides on the wings of the wind; he makes his messengers winds, his ministers a flaming fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bless the LORD, O my soul! O LORD my God, you are very great! You are clothed with splendor and majesty,

The previous psalm began and ended with Bless the LORD, O my soul, and it praised God for redemption — forgiveness, healing, compassion. This one begins and ends with the same words (vv. 1, 35) and praises him for creation. The two belong together: the God who forgives our sins is the God who made the world.

covering yourself with light as with a garment, stretching out the heavens like a tent.

The picture is of God dressing. He puts on light like a coat — the first thing created in Genesis, and here it is his clothing. Then he stretches out the sky as easily as a bedouin pitches a tent. The vastness of space is, to him, a canopy put up in an afternoon.

He lays the beams of his chambers on the waters; he makes the clouds his chariot; he rides on the wings of the wind; he makes his messengers winds, his ministers a flaming fire.

His house is built above the waters of the sky; the clouds are his chariot; the wind carries him. The forces of nature that people have always feared or worshipped are his vehicles and servants. Hebrews applies verse 4 to the angels: He makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flame of fire (Heb 1:7) — and then contrasts them with the Son, who is not a servant of creation but its Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: He set the earth on its foundations, so that it should never be moved. You covered it with the deep as with a garment; the waters stood above the mountains. At your rebuke they fled; at the sound of your thunder they took to flight. The mountains rose, the valleys sank down to the place that you appointed for them. You set a boundary that they may not pass, so that they might not again cover the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He set the earth on its foundations, so that it should never be moved.

The ground under your feet is stable because God set it. Every morning the earth is still there, and that is not an accident.

Psalm 93 said the same: the world is established; it shall never be moved (93:1). The ground stays put because the King reigns. Earthquakes are real, and verse 32 will mention the earth trembling, but they happen inside his rule, not outside it.

You covered it with the deep as with a garment; the waters stood above the mountains. At your rebuke they fled; at the sound of your thunder they took to flight.

In the beginning the earth was wrapped in water — darkness was over the face of the deep (Gen 1:2) — the waters higher than the mountains. And God rebuked them, and they ran. The image is almost comic: the ocean, fleeing like a scolded animal at the sound of God's voice.

The mountains rose, the valleys sank down to the place that you appointed for them. You set a boundary that they may not pass, so that they might not again cover the earth.

Mountains rise, valleys sink, and every one goes to the place that you appointed. And the sea is given a line it cannot cross. Anyone who has stood on a beach and watched the tide stop at its mark has seen this verse. The chaos is on a leash, and the leash is God's word.

So that they might not again cover the earth recalls the flood, and God's promise afterwards that the waters would never again destroy the earth (cf. Gen 9:11). Every shoreline is a line he drew and a promise he is keeping.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–23 — Wine to Gladden the Heart of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: You make springs gush forth in the valleys, watering beasts and birds (vv. 10-13). You cause the grass to grow for the livestock and plants for man to cultivate — bread, and wine to gladden the heart of man, oil to make his face shine (vv. 14-15). Trees, storks, wild goats and rock badgers each have their place (vv. 16-18). The moon marks the seasons; lions seek their food from God by night; man goes out to his work and to his labor until the evening (vv. 19-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Every creature has its home and its food, and God gives people not only enough but gladness.

verseByVerse.quote: You make springs gush forth in the valleys; they flow between the hills; they give drink to every beast of the field; the wild donkeys quench their thirst. Beside them the birds of the heavens dwell; they sing among the branches. From your lofty abode you water the mountains; the earth is satisfied with the fruit of your work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You make springs gush forth in the valleys; they flow between the hills; they give drink to every beast of the field; the wild donkeys quench their thirst.

The waters that were rebuked are now put to work. The same water that once covered the mountains now runs in springs through the valleys, and every animal drinks — even the wild donkeys, creatures of the desert that no one feeds. God does.

Beside them the birds of the heavens dwell; they sing among the branches.

Where there is water, there are trees; where there are trees, there are birds; and the birds sing. God did not only make a world that works. He made one with music in it.

From your lofty abode you water the mountains; the earth is satisfied with the fruit of your work.

Rain falls from God's house onto the hills, and the earth is satisfied — full, content, like a guest who has eaten well.

verseByVerse.quote: You cause the grass to grow for the livestock and plants for man to cultivate, that he may bring forth food from the earth and wine to gladden the heart of man, oil to make his face shine and bread to strengthen man's heart. The trees of the LORD are watered abundantly, the cedars of Lebanon that he planted. In them the birds build their nests; the stork has her home in the fir trees. The high mountains are for the wild goats; the rocks are a refuge for the rock badgers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You cause the grass to grow for the livestock and plants for man to cultivate, that he may bring forth food from the earth and wine to gladden the heart of man, oil to make his face shine and bread to strengthen man's heart.

Grass for cattle, crops for people — and man is given a part to play: plants for man to cultivate. God grows, and man farms. And then the list of what comes out of the earth goes beyond survival. Bread to strengthen — that is necessity. But also wine to gladden the heart and oil to make his face shine. Gladness. Beauty. God did not make a world that merely keeps us alive. He made one that makes us glad.

Paul told a pagan crowd in Lystra that God did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness (Acts 14:17). Every good meal is a sermon from the Creator. The Christian who receives God's gifts with thanks is not less spiritual than the one who refuses them.

The trees of the LORD are watered abundantly, the cedars of Lebanon that he planted. In them the birds build their nests; the stork has her home in the fir trees. The high mountains are for the wild goats; the rocks are a refuge for the rock badgers.

The great cedars are the trees of the LORD — he planted them. And every creature has an address: the stork in the fir, the wild goat on the peaks, the small rock badger hiding in the cliffs. Nothing in God's world is homeless by design.

verseByVerse.quote: He made the moon to mark the seasons; the sun knows its time for setting. You make darkness, and it is night, when all the beasts of the forest creep about. The young lions roar for their prey, seeking their food from God. When the sun rises, they steal away and lie down in their dens. Man goes out to his work and to his labor until the evening.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He made the moon to mark the seasons; the sun knows its time for setting.

The moon marks the seasons — the ESV notes it may mean "the appointed times", the calendar of Israel's feasts, as in Genesis 1:14. And the sun knows when to set, as though it were an obedient servant.

You make darkness, and it is night, when all the beasts of the forest creep about. The young lions roar for their prey, seeking their food from God.

Even the night is God's making, and the predators that hunt in it are, the psalm says, seeking their food from God. The lion's roar is, in its way, a prayer. The whole food chain, including its fierceness, is under his provision.

When the sun rises, they steal away and lie down in their dens. Man goes out to his work and to his labor until the evening.

And then a beautifully ordinary verse. The lions go to bed; people go to work. Shift change. The night belongs to the beasts, the day to human labour, and both are part of God's order. Your commute, your shift, your ordinary day's work until the evening is in this psalm, among the wonders of creation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–35 — When You Send Forth Your Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O LORD, how manifold are your works! In wisdom have you made them all (v. 24). The sea teems with life, and Leviathan plays in it (vv. 25-26). These all look to you, to give them their food in due season; when you send forth your Spirit, they are created, and you renew the face of the ground (vv. 27-30). May the LORD rejoice in his works (v. 31). I will sing to the LORD as long as I live (v. 33) — let sinners be consumed; Bless the LORD, O my soul! Praise the LORD! (vv. 34-35).
verseByVerse.theology: Every living thing depends moment by moment on God's open hand and his breath, and the singer resolves to praise him for life.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, how manifold are your works! In wisdom have you made them all; the earth is full of your creatures. Here is the sea, great and wide, which teems with creatures innumerable, living things both small and great. There go the ships, and Leviathan, which you formed to play in it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD, how manifold are your works! In wisdom have you made them all; the earth is full of your creatures.

The singer stops listing and simply exclaims. Manifold — countless, varied, overflowing. And all of it was made in wisdom: nothing is random or wasted. Paul says all things were created through him and for him — the Son — and in him all things hold together (Col 1:16-17).

Here is the sea, great and wide, which teems with creatures innumerable, living things both small and great. There go the ships, and Leviathan, which you formed to play in it.

Now the sea — no longer a threat but a teeming aquarium, creatures innumerable, from plankton to whales. Ships go by. And Leviathan, the great sea monster, the symbol of terror elsewhere in the Bible, is here God's creature, formed to play in it. The ESV notes it may mean "to play with" — the monster as God's pet. What terrifies sailors is, to God, something that frolics in a bath he made.

verseByVerse.quote: These all look to you, to give them their food in due season. When you give it to them, they gather it up; when you open your hand, they are filled with good things. When you hide your face, they are dismayed; when you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust. When you send forth your Spirit, they are created, and you renew the face of the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These all look to you, to give them their food in due season. When you give it to them, they gather it up; when you open your hand, they are filled with good things.

Every creature in the psalm — donkeys, birds, goats, lions, Leviathan, people — looks to God. They do not know it, but they are waiting at his hand. And when he opens it, they are filled. Jesus pointed at the same birds: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? (Matt 6:26).

When you hide your face, they are dismayed; when you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust.

And their life depends on him moment by moment. If he turns his face away, they panic. If he takes their breath, they die. No creature, including the strongest human being, is self-sustaining. The Son upholds the universe by the word of his power (Heb 1:3), and if he stopped, everything would fall back into dust.

Return to their dust is the sentence from Eden — to dust you shall return (Gen 3:19). Death is not merely a biological event in this psalm. It is God withdrawing the breath he lent.

When you send forth your Spirit, they are created, and you renew the face of the ground.

But he does not stop. He sends out his Spirit — the ESV notes the word can mean "breath", and in Hebrew it is the same word — and new life appears. Every spring is a small new creation. The same Spirit who was hovering over the face of the waters at the beginning (Gen 1:2) is still breathing life into the world, and will one day renew it entirely.

verseByVerse.quote: May the glory of the LORD endure forever; may the LORD rejoice in his works, who looks on the earth and it trembles, who touches the mountains and they smoke! I will sing to the LORD as long as I live; I will sing praise to my God while I have being. May my meditation be pleasing to him, for I rejoice in the LORD. Let sinners be consumed from the earth, and let the wicked be no more! Bless the LORD, O my soul! Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
May the glory of the LORD endure forever; may the LORD rejoice in his works, who looks on the earth and it trembles, who touches the mountains and they smoke!

May the LORD rejoice in his works. The psalm wishes God joy in what he has made — as he did at the beginning, when God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good (Gen 1:31). And yet this same gentle Creator only has to glance at the earth to make it shake, and touch a mountain to make it smoke.

That is Sinai again, where the whole mountain trembled greatly and was wrapped in smoke (Exod 19:18). The God who waters the wild donkeys is the God who shook the mountain. His gentleness is never weakness.

I will sing to the LORD as long as I live; I will sing praise to my God while I have being. May my meditation be pleasing to him, for I rejoice in the LORD.

After surveying the whole creation, the singer makes a lifelong vow: as long as I live. The breath God gives (v. 29) will be spent praising him. And he hopes his meditation — this long, careful look at the world — will please God. Looking thoughtfully at creation, and seeing God in it, is itself a form of worship.

The prayer echoes the end of Psalm 19, which also moved from the heavens to the heart: Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight (19:14).

Let sinners be consumed from the earth, and let the wicked be no more!

This line can seem jarring at the end of such a gentle psalm. But it is exactly right. In all this beauty there is one thing that does not belong: sin, and those who persist in it. It is the one blot on the good world. The creation itself has been groaning together under it (Rom 8:22). A person who loves the world God made will long for the day when nothing spoils it.

Bless the LORD, O my soul! Praise the LORD!

And the psalm ends where it began, with one more line added: Praise the LORD! — in Hebrew, Hallelujah — the first time the Psalter says it. The soul that has looked carefully at the springs, the storks, the lions going to bed and the workman going out has only one thing left to say. Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things (Rev 4:11).

104.title: How Manifold Are Your Works
104.overview: Bless the LORD, who is clothed in splendour and light, stretches out the heavens like a tent, rides on the clouds and wind, and makes winds and fire his servants (vv. 1-4). He founded the earth, rebuked the waters that covered it and set them a boundary (vv. 5-9). He makes springs for the beasts and birds, waters the mountains, grows grass for livestock and crops for man — bread, and wine and oil for gladness — and gives every creature its home (vv. 10-18). Moon and sun keep their times; lions seek food from God by night; man works by day (vv. 19-23). How manifold are his works, made in wisdom: the teeming sea, the ships, Leviathan at play (vv. 24-26). All creatures look to him for food; when he hides his face they are dismayed, when he takes their breath they die, when he sends his Spirit they are created (vv. 27-30). May God rejoice in his works; the singer will praise him all his life; let sinners be no more. Bless the LORD, O my soul! Praise the LORD! (vv. 31-35).
104.theology:
Creation (Ps 104) is paired with redemption (Ps 103) under the same call to bless the LORD. God is utterly above nature, using its forces as his clothing, vehicles and servants (vv. 1-4; Heb 1:7).

He orders and restrains chaos (vv. 5-9), provides for every creature, and gives humanity not only sustenance but gladness (vv. 14-15; Acts 14:17). Work, day and night, predator and prey all have their place in his order (vv. 19-23).

All things were made in wisdom (v. 24; Col 1:16-17) and depend moment by moment on God's provision and Spirit for life (vv. 27-30; Gen 1:2; Heb 1:3; Matt 6:26). God delights in his works (v. 31; Gen 1:31), and sin is the one thing that does not belong in them (v. 35; Rom 8:22).
104.examples:
Light worn like a coat.

The ocean running away like a scolded animal.

Wild donkeys no one feeds — God does.

Wine and oil: a world made for gladness, not just survival.

The lion's roar as a prayer for dinner.

Lions go to bed; people go to work.

Leviathan: God's pet in a bath he made.

Every spring, a small new creation.

Praise the LORD!

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Oh give thanks to the LORD; call upon his name; make known his deeds among the peoples! (v. 1). Sing, glory in his name, seek him (vv. 2-4); Remember the wondrous works that he has done (v. 5). He remembers his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations (v. 8) — the covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob to give them Canaan (vv. 9-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel is told to remember, because God remembers — and the history that follows is all his doing.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh give thanks to the LORD; call upon his name; make known his deeds among the peoples! Sing to him, sing praises to him; tell of all his wondrous works! Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice! Seek the LORD and his strength; seek his presence continually! Remember the wondrous works that he has done, his miracles, and the judgments he uttered, O offspring of Abraham, his servant, children of Jacob, his chosen ones!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh give thanks to the LORD; call upon his name; make known his deeds among the peoples! Sing to him, sing praises to him; tell of all his wondrous works!

Three psalms in the Psalter tell Israel's history at length, and each tells it for a different reason. Psalm 78 told it as a warning to the children. Psalm 106, which follows this one, tells it as a confession of sin. Psalm 105 tells it as praise. The same events, and in this psalm every one of them is a reason to give thanks.

The first fifteen verses were sung when the ark came to Jerusalem (1 Chr 16:8-22), and they begin with a pile of commands: give thanks, call, make known, sing, tell. And the audience is wider than Israel: among the peoples. God's history with his people is news for the nations.

Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice! Seek the LORD and his strength; seek his presence continually!

Seek, three times. The psalm is about God seeking and keeping his people, and their response is to seek him back — continually, not in emergencies only.

Remember the wondrous works that he has done, his miracles, and the judgments he uttered, O offspring of Abraham, his servant, children of Jacob, his chosen ones!

And the key verb of the psalm: remember. Faith that forgets what God has done withers. The whole psalm is an exercise in remembering on purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: He is the LORD our God; his judgments are in all the earth. He remembers his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations, the covenant that he made with Abraham, his sworn promise to Isaac, which he confirmed to Jacob as a statute, to Israel as an everlasting covenant, saying, "To you I will give the land of Canaan as your portion for an inheritance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is the LORD our God; his judgments are in all the earth. He remembers his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations,

Israel is told to remember (v. 5) because God remembers (v. 8). That is the ground of the whole history. His memory is not a vague recollection; it is covenant faithfulness, and it runs for a thousand generations — a way of saying forever.

the covenant that he made with Abraham, his sworn promise to Isaac, which he confirmed to Jacob as a statute, to Israel as an everlasting covenant, saying, To you I will give the land of Canaan as your portion for an inheritance.

One promise, made to three generations in turn — Abraham, Isaac, Jacob — and never withdrawn. When the rest of this history is told, every event is God keeping that one sworn word. A believer's life is the same: not a string of random events, but one promise being kept through many chapters.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–25 — He Had Sent a Man Ahead of Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the patriarchs were few and wandering, God let no one harm them: Touch not my anointed ones (vv. 12-15). He summoned a famine, but he had sent a man ahead of them, Joseph, who was sold as a slave (vv. 16-17); fettered and tested by God's word until he was set free and made ruler (vv. 18-22). Israel came to Egypt, multiplied, and God turned the Egyptians' hearts to hate them (vv. 23-25).
verseByVerse.theology: Behind famine, slavery and a prison cell, God had already placed the man who would save his people.

verseByVerse.quote: When they were few in number, of little account, and sojourners in it, wandering from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people, he allowed no one to oppress them; he rebuked kings on their account, saying, "Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they were few in number, of little account, and sojourners in it, wandering from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people,

The family that received the promise was tiny, unimportant and homeless — a handful of tent-dwellers moving between kingdoms. Nothing about them looked like the founders of a nation.

he allowed no one to oppress them; he rebuked kings on their account, saying, Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm!

But they were protected. God rebuked Pharaoh and Abimelech when they took the patriarchs' wives, and he calls these vulnerable wanderers my anointed ones and my prophets. The weakness of God's people is never the measure of their safety. Kings who touch them answer to God.

verseByVerse.quote: When he summoned a famine on the land and broke all supply of bread, he had sent a man ahead of them, Joseph, who was sold as a slave. His feet were hurt with fetters; his neck was put in a collar of iron; until what he had said came to pass, the word of the LORD tested him. The king sent and released him; the ruler of the peoples set him free; he made him lord of his house and ruler of all his possessions, to bind his princes at his pleasure and to teach his elders wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he summoned a famine on the land and broke all supply of bread,

The famine did not simply happen. God summoned it, like a servant, and broke the supply of bread — the ESV notes the Hebrew is staff, the staff of bread that people lean on.

he had sent a man ahead of them, Joseph, who was sold as a slave.

And here is one of the most comforting sentences in the history. Before the famine came, God had sent a man ahead. From Joseph's side it looked like betrayal — his brothers sold him. Stephen told it the same way: the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him (Acts 7:9). The worst thing that ever happened to Joseph was God sending him ahead to save his family.

His feet were hurt with fetters; his neck was put in a collar of iron; until what he had said came to pass, the word of the LORD tested him.

Genesis does not mention the fetters and the iron collar; the psalm fills in how prison felt (Gen 39:20). And the real test was not the iron. It was the word of the LORD — the dreams God had given him, which seemed ridiculous from a cell. He held on to a promise that looked false for years. Many believers are in that cell now.

The king sent and released him; the ruler of the peoples set him free; he made him lord of his house and ruler of all his possessions, to bind his princes at his pleasure and to teach his elders wisdom.

From the collar to the palace: Pharaoh said, You shall be over my house (Gen 41:40). (The ESV notes the ancient translations read instruct his princes rather than bind them.) The slave became the teacher of Egypt's rulers. Joseph's story is the pattern of the one who was sold, bound, and raised to rule in order to save the people who had rejected him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Israel came to Egypt; Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham. And the LORD made his people very fruitful and made them stronger than their foes. He turned their hearts to hate his people, to deal craftily with his servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Israel came to Egypt; Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham. And the LORD made his people very fruitful and made them stronger than their foes. He turned their hearts to hate his people, to deal craftily with his servants.

A startling verse: God turned their hearts to hate his people. The psalm does not flinch from saying that even Egypt's hostility was within God's control. Not that God made the Egyptians sin against their will, but that their hatred served his purpose — it drove Israel to cry out, and set the stage for the exodus. God rules even the enemies of his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–45 — He Brought His People Out with Joy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He sent Moses, his servant, and Aaron, whom he had chosen (v. 26). Darkness, blood, frogs, flies, gnats, hail, locusts, and the death of the firstborn (vv. 27-36). He brought Israel out with silver and gold, spread a cloud and fire, gave quail, bread from heaven and water from the rock (vv. 37-41). For he remembered his holy promise, and Abraham, his servant. So he brought his people out with joy (vv. 42-43), and gave them the land that they might keep his statutes and observe his laws. Praise the LORD! (vv. 44-45).
verseByVerse.theology: The exodus told without a single failure of Israel's — because this telling is about God's faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: He sent Moses, his servant, and Aaron, whom he had chosen. They performed his signs among them and miracles in the land of Ham. He sent darkness, and made the land dark; they did not rebel against his words. He turned their waters into blood and caused their fish to die. Their land swarmed with frogs, even in the chambers of their kings. He spoke, and there came swarms of flies, and gnats throughout their country. He gave them hail for rain, and fiery lightning bolts through their land. He struck down their vines and fig trees, and shattered the trees of their country. He spoke, and the locusts came, young locusts without number, which devoured all the vegetation in their land and ate up the fruit of their ground. He struck down all the firstborn in their land, the firstfruits of all their strength.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He sent Moses, his servant, and Aaron, whom he had chosen. They performed his signs among them and miracles in the land of Ham.

As he sent Joseph ahead, he sent Moses. The history is a history of God sending the right servant at the right time.

He sent darkness, and made the land dark; they did not rebel against his words.

Then the plagues, and the psalm tells them its own way. Exodus lists ten; the psalm names eight. It leaves out the disease on the livestock and the boils. And it begins with darkness, which in Exodus came ninth — perhaps because darkness was a direct strike at Egypt's sun-god, and sums up what all the plagues were. They did not rebel against his words probably means Moses and Aaron obeyed (the ESV notes some ancient translations omit the not).

He turned their waters into blood and caused their fish to die. Their land swarmed with frogs, even in the chambers of their kings. He spoke, and there came swarms of flies, and gnats throughout their country.

Blood, frogs, then flies and gnats — Exodus has the gnats before the flies. The detail even in the chambers of their kings makes the point: no palace wall kept God out.

He gave them hail for rain, and fiery lightning bolts through their land. He struck down their vines and fig trees, and shattered the trees of their country. He spoke, and the locusts came, young locusts without number, which devoured all the vegetation in their land and ate up the fruit of their ground.

Twice, he spoke. The plagues were not natural disasters that God used; they came at his word. And then the last: He struck down all the firstborn in their land, the firstfruits of all their strength.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he brought out Israel with silver and gold, and there was none among his tribes who stumbled. Egypt was glad when they departed, for dread of them had fallen upon it. He spread a cloud for a covering, and fire to give light by night. They asked, and he brought quail, and gave them bread from heaven in abundance. He opened the rock, and water gushed out; it flowed through the desert like a river.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he brought out Israel with silver and gold, and there was none among his tribes who stumbled. Egypt was glad when they departed, for dread of them had fallen upon it.

God had told Abraham centuries before that his descendants would come out with great possessions (Gen 15:14), and they did: Thus they plundered the Egyptians (Exod 12:36). Slaves walked out with their masters' gold, and no one stumbled.

And Egypt was glad when they departed. The empire that had refused for so long to let them go was relieved to see the back of them. When God is finished with a people's oppressors, the oppressors are glad to be rid of the oppressed.

He spread a cloud for a covering, and fire to give light by night. They asked, and he brought quail, and gave them bread from heaven in abundance. He opened the rock, and water gushed out; it flowed through the desert like a river.

Now notice what is missing. Psalm 78 told these same events — the quail, the water from the rock — and told them as stories of rebellion. Psalm 106 will do the same. Here there is not a word about grumbling. They asked, and God gave. Even the cloud is described differently: in Exodus it led the way; here it is a covering, a canopy spread over a people in the desert sun. That is not because the psalmist has forgotten the sins. It is because this psalm is telling one strand of the history — what God did — and letting it shine on its own. There is a time to confess our failures, and a time to look only at God's faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: For he remembered his holy promise, and Abraham, his servant. So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing. And he gave them the lands of the nations, and they took possession of the fruit of the peoples' toil, that they might keep his statutes and observe his laws. Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he remembered his holy promise, and Abraham, his servant. So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing.

The reason for everything is stated one last time: he remembered his holy promise. The psalm opened with God remembering his covenant (v. 8) and it closes the same way. Between those two verses lie famine, slavery, prison, plagues and the desert — and all of it was God keeping one promise to one man. And the result was not grim survival but joy and singing.

And he gave them the lands of the nations, and they took possession of the fruit of the peoples' toil, that they might keep his statutes and observe his laws. Praise the LORD!

And the purpose, in the last verse: that they might keep his statutes. God did not save Israel because they kept his law; he saved them so that they would. Grace comes first, and obedience is its goal. The Christian life has exactly that order. We are not rescued because we obey; we are rescued in order to obey, as free people in a land we did not earn.

And the history ends not with a moral but with a shout: Praise the LORD! When you look back over your own life and can see only one strand — God remembering his promise — that is the right thing to say.

105.title: He Remembers His Covenant Forever
105.overview: A call to give thanks, sing, seek the LORD and remember his works, addressed to Abraham's offspring (vv. 1-6), because God remembers his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob to give them Canaan (vv. 7-11). He protected the few wandering patriarchs (vv. 12-15), sent Joseph ahead into slavery and prison until God's word raised him to rule Egypt (vv. 16-22), and multiplied Israel in Egypt (vv. 23-25). He sent Moses and Aaron and struck Egypt with plagues (vv. 26-36), brought Israel out with silver and gold, and provided cloud, fire, quail, bread and water (vv. 37-41). He remembered his promise to Abraham, brought his people out with joy and gave them the land, that they might keep his statutes and observe his laws. Praise the LORD! (vv. 42-45).
105.theology:
This is Israel's history told entirely as praise, in contrast to the warning of Psalm 78 and the confession of Psalm 106. God remembers his covenant (vv. 8, 42), so his people must remember his works (v. 5).

God protects the weak bearers of his promise (vv. 12-15), rules famine and even the hostility of enemies (vv. 16, 25), and sends deliverers ahead of need (vv. 17, 26). Joseph was tested by God's word before its fulfilment (v. 19; Acts 7:9-10).

The plagues came at God's word (vv. 28-36). The promise of Gen 15:14 was kept at the exodus (v. 37). Grace precedes obedience, which is its goal (v. 45).
105.examples:
One history, three tellings: warning, praise, confession.

Israel remembers because God remembers.

A handful of tent-dwellers kings could not touch.

Sold by his brothers — sent by God.

Tested by a promise that looked false from a cell.

Frogs in the king's bedroom.

Slaves walking out with their masters' gold.

Saved in order to obey, not because we obeyed.
