verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Praise the LORD! Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever! (v. 1). Who can utter the mighty deeds of the LORD (v. 2)? Blessed are they who observe justice (v. 3). Remember me, O LORD, when you show favor to your people; help me when you save them (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Before confessing the nation's sins, the psalmist asks to be included in God's mercy to his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD! Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever! Who can utter the mighty deeds of the LORD, or declare all his praise? Blessed are they who observe justice, who do righteousness at all times! Remember me, O LORD, when you show favor to your people; help me when you save them, that I may look upon the prosperity of your chosen ones, that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation, that I may glory with your inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Praise the LORD! Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever! Who can utter the mighty deeds of the LORD, or declare all his praise?

This psalm tells the same history as Psalm 105, and tells it completely differently. Psalm 105 told only what God did. Psalm 106 tells what Israel did — and it is a long record of sin. Yet it opens, like 105, with praise. That is the key to reading it. Confession of sin is not the opposite of praise. A people who can tell the whole truth about their failures and still say his steadfast love endures forever have understood grace.

Blessed are they who observe justice, who do righteousness at all times!

At all times. The rest of the psalm shows that Israel did not. The blessing is stated first so that the failure can be measured against it.

Remember me, O LORD, when you show favor to your people; help me when you save them, that I may look upon the prosperity of your chosen ones, that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation, that I may glory with your inheritance.

Before the confession, a personal plea: remember me. When God shows favour to his people, do not leave me out. (The ESV notes it may read "with the favor you show to your people".) The singer does not want private blessing apart from the community; he wants to rejoice with God's people. It is the prayer of the thief on the cross — remember me — offered by a man about to confess that he deserves nothing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–33 — They Forgot God, Their Savior
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Both we and our fathers have sinned (v. 6). At the Red Sea they rebelled, yet he saved them for his name's sake (vv. 7-12). They craved, envied Moses and Aaron, and exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox that eats grass (vv. 13-20); Moses stood in the breach (vv. 21-23). They despised the land, joined the Baal of Peor until Phinehas intervened, and angered God at Meribah (vv. 24-33).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's wilderness history, told as a list of sins — and a list of rescues God kept making anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: Both we and our fathers have sinned; we have committed iniquity; we have done wickedness. Our fathers, when they were in Egypt, did not consider your wondrous works; they did not remember the abundance of your steadfast love, but rebelled by the sea, at the Red Sea. Yet he saved them for his name's sake, that he might make known his mighty power. He rebuked the Red Sea, and it became dry, and he led them through the deep as through a desert. So he saved them from the hand of the foe and redeemed them from the power of the enemy. And the waters covered their adversaries; not one of them was left. Then they believed his words; they sang his praise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Both we and our fathers have sinned; we have committed iniquity; we have done wickedness.

Here is the heading of the whole history. Three words for sin, and the crucial word we. The singer does not stand outside Israel's past and judge it. Both we and our fathers. The sins of the wilderness generation are the same sins his own generation commits. Honest confession never says "they" when it means "we".

Our fathers, when they were in Egypt, did not consider your wondrous works; they did not remember the abundance of your steadfast love, but rebelled by the sea, at the Red Sea.

The rebellion started immediately. They had just watched ten plagues, and at the edge of the sea they panicked and complained. The root is named: they did not consider and did not remember. Sin in this psalm begins as forgetting.

Yet he saved them for his name's sake, that he might make known his mighty power. He rebuked the Red Sea, and it became dry ... So he saved them from the hand of the foe and redeemed them from the power of the enemy.

Yet. Rebellion, and yet rescue. And the reason is not their repentance; it is for his name's sake. God saved people who were complaining at him while he saved them.

Then they believed his words; they sang his praise.

After the rescue — faith and song. The song of Moses on the far shore. For a moment, everything was right.

verseByVerse.quote: But they soon forgot his works; they did not wait for his counsel. But they had a wanton craving in the wilderness, and put God to the test in the desert; he gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them. When men in the camp were jealous of Moses and Aaron, the holy one of the LORD, the earth opened and swallowed up Dathan, and covered the company of Abiram. Fire also broke out in their company; the flame burned up the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they soon forgot his works; they did not wait for his counsel. But they had a wanton craving in the wilderness, and put God to the test in the desert;

Soon. The singing lasted a few days. Then they forgot again, and would not wait for God's timing. Faith that sings on the shore and complains three days later is very familiar.

he gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them.

One of the most sobering sentences in the Bible. They demanded meat, and God gave them exactly what they asked — and with it, a wasting sickness; the Hebrew is leanness in the soul. There is a kind of answered prayer that is judgment: God lets people have what they insist on, and it empties them.

When men in the camp were jealous of Moses and Aaron, the holy one of the LORD, the earth opened and swallowed up Dathan, and covered the company of Abiram. Fire also broke out in their company; the flame burned up the wicked.

Next, envy of God's appointed leaders. Dathan and Abiram rebelled against Moses, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up (Num 16:32). Jealousy of those God has placed over his people is not a small sin in this list.

verseByVerse.quote: They made a calf in Horeb and worshiped a metal image. They exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox that eats grass. They forgot God, their Savior, who had done great things in Egypt, wondrous works in the land of Ham, and awesome deeds by the Red Sea. Therefore he said he would destroy them— had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They made a calf in Horeb and worshiped a metal image. They exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox that eats grass.

At the very mountain where God had spoken, they made a calf. And the psalm's verdict is withering: they exchanged the glory of God — the ESV notes the Hebrew is their glory, the glory that was theirs because God was theirs — for the image of an ox that eats grass. The living God, for a statue of a farm animal. Paul described the whole human race doing the same: they exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images (Rom 1:23). Every idol is a bad trade.

They forgot God, their Savior, who had done great things in Egypt, wondrous works in the land of Ham, and awesome deeds by the Red Sea.

Forgetting again — the same root as verse 7.

Therefore he said he would destroy them — had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them.

God said to Moses, let me alone, that my wrath may burn hot against them and I may consume them. But Moses implored the LORD his God (Exod 32:10-11). He stood in the breach — the gap in a broken city wall where the enemy pours in — and put himself between God's wrath and the people. The nation survived because one man stood in the gap. That is a picture of a greater Mediator who did more than plead: he took the wrath himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they despised the pleasant land, having no faith in his promise. They murmured in their tents, and did not obey the voice of the LORD. Therefore he raised his hand and swore to them that he would make them fall in the wilderness, and would make their offspring fall among the nations, scattering them among the lands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they despised the pleasant land, having no faith in his promise. They murmured in their tents, and did not obey the voice of the LORD.

At the border of Canaan, after the spies' report, they despised the pleasant land. The gift God had been promising for centuries, and they did not want it. The reason: having no faith in his promise. Unbelief does not only doubt God's power; it despises his gifts. And it grumbles privately — in their tents.

Therefore he raised his hand and swore to them that he would make them fall in the wilderness, and would make their offspring fall among the nations, scattering them among the lands.

The wilderness generation died outside the land. And the psalm reaches forward to the exile — scattering them among the lands — as though the refusal at the border contained the seed of the later catastrophe.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they yoked themselves to the Baal of Peor, and ate sacrifices offered to the dead; they provoked the LORD to anger with their deeds, and a plague broke out among them. Then Phinehas stood up and intervened, and the plague was stayed. And that was counted to him as righteousness from generation to generation forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they yoked themselves to the Baal of Peor, and ate sacrifices offered to the dead; they provoked the LORD to anger with their deeds, and a plague broke out among them.

At Peor, on the edge of the promised land, Israelite men joined Moabite women in the worship of Baal. They yoked themselves — bound themselves like oxen in a team — to a false god.

Then Phinehas stood up and intervened, and the plague was stayed. And that was counted to him as righteousness from generation to generation forever.

Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, killed an Israelite man and a Midianite woman in the act, and the plague stopped. And the psalm says it was counted to him as righteousness — the exact phrase used of Abraham: he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness (Gen 15:6), which Paul uses to explain justification by faith (Rom 4:3).

Does this mean Phinehas was justified by a deed rather than by faith? No. Abraham's faith was reckoned to him as the righteousness that put him right with God. Phinehas's act was reckoned as righteous — recognised by God as true covenant faithfulness — because, as God said, he was jealous with my jealousy (Num 25:11). His zeal was the fruit of a faith that took God's honour seriously when everyone around him did not. One text is about how a sinner is accepted; the other is about God publicly honouring what a believer did.

verseByVerse.quote: They angered him at the waters of Meribah, and it went ill with Moses on their account, for they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They angered him at the waters of Meribah, and it went ill with Moses on their account, for they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips.

Even Moses fell. The people provoked him until he spoke rashly and struck the rock, and he was barred from the land (see 99:8). (The ESV notes the phrase may mean "they rebelled against God's Spirit".) The man who stood in the breach for them in verse 23 was worn down by them in verse 33. Leaders are not immune, and a people's constant complaining can make even a faithful man sin.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 34–48 — Nevertheless, He Looked upon Their Distress
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the land they mixed with the nations, served their idols and sacrificed their sons and their daughters to the demons (vv. 34-39). God handed them to their enemies; Many times he delivered them (vv. 40-43). Nevertheless, he looked upon their distress, when he heard their cry, and remembered his covenant (vv. 44-46). Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from among the nations (v. 47). Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting! (v. 48).
verseByVerse.theology: Centuries of unfaithfulness end in exile — and in a prayer to be gathered home by the God who never stopped remembering.

verseByVerse.quote: They did not destroy the peoples, as the LORD commanded them, but they mixed with the nations and learned to do as they did. They served their idols, which became a snare to them. They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to the demons; they poured out innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the idols of Canaan, and the land was polluted with blood. Thus they became unclean by their acts, and played the whore in their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They did not destroy the peoples, as the LORD commanded them, but they mixed with the nations and learned to do as they did. They served their idols, which became a snare to them.

In the land, the pattern continued. The decline is gradual: they did not obey, then they mixed, then they learned, then they served. No one wakes up an idolater. They arrive there by mixing and learning, one small accommodation at a time.

They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to the demons; they poured out innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the idols of Canaan, and the land was polluted with blood.

And this is where it ends: child sacrifice. The idols of Canaan demanded children, and Israel gave them. The psalm calls the idols demons, and Paul said the same of pagan worship: what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God (1 Cor 10:20). Idolatry is never harmless. It always ends by consuming what is most precious.

Thus they became unclean by their acts, and played the whore in their deeds.

The language of adultery. Israel was God's bride, and went after other lovers.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the anger of the LORD was kindled against his people, and he abhorred his heritage; he gave them into the hand of the nations, so that those who hated them ruled over them. Their enemies oppressed them, and they were brought into subjection under their power. Many times he delivered them, but they were rebellious in their purposes and were brought low through their iniquity. Nevertheless, he looked upon their distress, when he heard their cry. For their sake he remembered his covenant, and relented according to the abundance of his steadfast love. He caused them to be pitied by all those who held them captive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the anger of the LORD was kindled against his people, and he abhorred his heritage; he gave them into the hand of the nations, so that those who hated them ruled over them. Their enemies oppressed them, and they were brought into subjection under their power.

This is the book of Judges in four lines. God handed them over; enemies ruled them.

Many times he delivered them, but they were rebellious in their purposes and were brought low through their iniquity.

Many times. The cycle repeated: rescue, rebellion, oppression, rescue. Whenever the judge died, they turned back and were more corrupt than their fathers (Judg 2:19).

Nevertheless, he looked upon their distress, when he heard their cry. For their sake he remembered his covenant, and relented according to the abundance of his steadfast love. He caused them to be pitied by all those who held them captive.

Nevertheless — the most important word in the psalm. After forty verses of sin, nevertheless. He looked; he heard; he remembered his covenant — the same thing Psalm 105 said he did (105:8, 42). Both psalms end in the same place: God's memory is better than his people's. Even their captors were made to pity them.

That is the gospel in the Old Testament. Not that the people improved, but that God's steadfast love was more abundant than their sin.

verseByVerse.quote: Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from among the nations, that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise. Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting! And let all the people say, "Amen!" Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from among the nations, that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise.

The confession ends in exile — scattered among the nations, just as verse 27 warned. And the prayer is simple: gather us. Bring us home, so that we can thank you. The very next psalm, which opens Book Five, begins with God's people gathered in from the lands, from the east and from the west (107:3). The prayer at the end of one book is answered at the start of the next.

Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting! And let all the people say, Amen! Praise the LORD!

This closes Book Four of the Psalms. When it was sung before the ark, all the people said, Amen! and praised the LORD (1 Chr 16:36).

Paul wrote that Israel's wilderness history happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction (1 Cor 10:11). This psalm is the church's mirror. Every sin in it — forgetting, craving, envy, idolatry, unbelief, compromise — is a Christian temptation. And every yet and nevertheless in it is a Christian hope. Honest confession, ending in Amen.

106.title: Both We and Our Fathers Have Sinned
106.overview: Praise the LORD, whose steadfast love endures forever; blessed are those who do righteousness; remember me when you favour your people (vv. 1-5). Both we and our fathers have sinned (v. 6). Israel rebelled at the Red Sea, yet God saved them for his name's sake, and they sang (vv. 7-12); they soon forgot, craved and tested God, who gave what they asked with a wasting disease (vv. 13-15); they envied Moses and Aaron, and Dathan and Abiram were swallowed (vv. 16-18); they made a calf, exchanging God's glory for an ox, and Moses stood in the breach (vv. 19-23); they despised the land (vv. 24-27); they joined the Baal of Peor until Phinehas intervened (vv. 28-31); they provoked Moses at Meribah (vv. 32-33). In the land they mixed with the nations and sacrificed their children to idols (vv. 34-39). God gave them to their enemies, delivering them many times; nevertheless he heard their cry and remembered his covenant (vv. 40-46). Save us ... and gather us from among the nations; blessed be the LORD forever (vv. 47-48).
106.theology:
Israel's history is told as confession, and the confessor includes himself: both we and our fathers (v. 6). Sin begins in forgetting God's works (vv. 7, 13, 21), and God can judge by granting what is craved (v. 15).

Idolatry exchanges God's glory for a creature (v. 20; Rom 1:23), ends in destroying what is most precious (vv. 37-38; 1 Cor 10:20), and grows by gradual accommodation (vv. 34-36). A mediator standing in the breach averts wrath (v. 23; Exod 32:10-11).

Phinehas's zeal was reckoned as righteousness (v. 31), not a rival to justification by faith (Gen 15:6; Rom 4:3) but God's recognition of covenant faithfulness (Num 25:11).

God's steadfast love outlasts repeated rebellion: nevertheless he remembered his covenant (vv. 44-45). The history was written for the church's instruction (1 Cor 10:11).
106.examples:
Confession that says we, not they.

Singing on the shore, complaining three days later.

An answered prayer that emptied them.

The glory of God traded for a statue of a farm animal.

One man standing in the gap in the wall.

No one wakes up an idolater.

Forty verses of sin — nevertheless.

A prayer at the end of one book answered at the start of the next.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Gathered In from the Lands
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever! (v. 1). Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom he has redeemed from trouble and gathered in from the lands, from the east and from the west, from the north and from the south (vv. 2-3).
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer at the end of Book Four — gather us — is answered in the first lines of Book Five.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever! Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom he has redeemed from trouble and gathered in from the lands, from the east and from the west, from the north and from the south.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever!

Book Five of the Psalms begins with the same words that opened Psalm 106. But the situation has changed. Psalm 106 ended in exile, with a prayer: gather us from among the nations (106:47).

Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom he has redeemed from trouble and gathered in from the lands, from the east and from the west, from the north and from the south.

And here is the answer. God's people have been gathered in from the lands — from every point of the compass. The prayer at the end of one book of the Psalter is answered in the first sentence of the next. (The ESV notes from trouble may be read "from the hand of the foe".)

And the command to the redeemed is short: say so. If God has rescued you, do not keep it quiet. Paul describes the gathering in its fullest form: you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Eph 2:13). John saw the final gathering, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages (Rev 7:9). The redeemed from east, west, north and south are still being gathered, and they are still told to say so.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–32 — Then They Cried to the LORD in Their Trouble
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some wandered in the desert, hungry and thirsty (vv. 4-9); some sat in darkness, prisoners in irons, for they had rebelled (vv. 10-16); some were fools, sick to the gates of death (vv. 17-22); some went to sea and were caught in the storm (vv. 23-27). Each time, Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress: he led, broke bonds, sent out his word and healed them, and made the storm be still (vv. 6, 13, 19-20, 28-29). Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love (vv. 8, 15, 21, 31).
verseByVerse.theology: Four kinds of trouble, one cry, one rescuer — and the same thanks each time.

verseByVerse.quote: Some wandered in desert wastes, finding no way to a city to dwell in; hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them. Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress. He led them by a straight way till they reached a city to dwell in. Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love, for his wondrous works to the children of man! For he satisfies the longing soul, and the hungry soul he fills with good things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some wandered in desert wastes, finding no way to a city to dwell in; hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them.

Now the psalm tells four stories, and they all have the same shape: a trouble, a cry, a rescue, a call to thanks, and a reason. The first is the lost. People wandering in the desert, unable to find a town, fainting from hunger and thirst.

It is a picture of the person without direction or home — lost not through wickedness in this case, just lost. Many people today recognise this one: wandering from one thing to the next, never arriving anywhere, spiritually starving.

Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress. He led them by a straight way till they reached a city to dwell in.

The first refrain. They cried, and he delivered. And the rescue fits the trouble exactly: lost people are given a straight way and a city to dwell in.

Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love, for his wondrous works to the children of man! For he satisfies the longing soul, and the hungry soul he fills with good things.

The second refrain — thanks — and the reason: he satisfies the longing soul. Every restless heart is looking for this.

verseByVerse.quote: Some sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, prisoners in affliction and in irons, for they had rebelled against the words of God, and spurned the counsel of the Most High. So he bowed their hearts down with hard labor; they fell down, with none to help. Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress. He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and burst their bonds apart. Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love, for his wondrous works to the children of man! For he shatters the doors of bronze and cuts in two the bars of iron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, prisoners in affliction and in irons, for they had rebelled against the words of God, and spurned the counsel of the Most High.

The second story is the prisoners. And these are in chains because of their own choices: they had rebelled. The psalm is honest. Some trouble is simply suffering. Some is the consequence of rebellion.

So he bowed their hearts down with hard labor; they fell down, with none to help.

God himself brought them low, until there was no one to help. Sometimes God lets a person reach the end of every other resource so that the cry of verse 13 becomes possible.

Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress. He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and burst their bonds apart.

Even rebels who are in chains through their own fault can cry — and be heard. That is grace. Zechariah sang of the dawn from on high coming to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death (Luke 1:79), and Jesus announced that he had come to proclaim liberty to the captives (Luke 4:18). When an angel came for Peter in prison, the chains fell off his hands (Acts 12:7).

Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love, for his wondrous works to the children of man! For he shatters the doors of bronze and cuts in two the bars of iron.

No prison built by sin is stronger than the God who breaks doors of bronze. Whatever habit, addiction or guilt has you in irons, this verse is written over the door.

verseByVerse.quote: Some were fools through their sinful ways, and because of their iniquities suffered affliction; they loathed any kind of food, and they drew near to the gates of death. Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress. He sent out his word and healed them, and delivered them from their destruction. Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love, for his wondrous works to the children of man! And let them offer sacrifices of thanksgiving, and tell of his deeds in songs of joy!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some were fools through their sinful ways, and because of their iniquities suffered affliction; they loathed any kind of food, and they drew near to the gates of death.

The third story: the sick. And again, this sickness is linked to their sinful ways. They are called fools — not unintelligent, but morally foolish. Their sin has made them ill, until they cannot eat and are at the gates of death. Not every illness is caused by sin, as Jesus made clear; but some self-destruction is.

Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress. He sent out his word and healed them, and delivered them from their destruction.

He sent out his word and healed them. God's word is pictured as a messenger sent on an errand of healing. A Roman centurion understood that: say the word, and let my servant be healed (Luke 7:7). And the Word that God finally sent out became flesh.

Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love, for his wondrous works to the children of man! And let them offer sacrifices of thanksgiving, and tell of his deeds in songs of joy!

The healed are to offer thanksgiving and tell the story. Recovery that is not followed by gratitude has missed the point.

verseByVerse.quote: Some went down to the sea in ships, doing business on the great waters; they saw the deeds of the LORD, his wondrous works in the deep. For he commanded and raised the stormy wind, which lifted up the waves of the sea. They mounted up to heaven; they went down to the depths; their courage melted away in their evil plight; they reeled and staggered like drunken men and were at their wits' end. Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress. He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed. Then they were glad that the waters were quiet, and he brought them to their desired haven. Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love, for his wondrous works to the children of man! Let them extol him in the congregation of the people, and praise him in the assembly of the elders.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some went down to the sea in ships, doing business on the great waters; they saw the deeds of the LORD, his wondrous works in the deep.

The fourth story is the longest: sailors. Israel was not a seafaring nation, and to them the sea was terrifying. These are merchants going about their ordinary business — and at sea they saw the deeds of the LORD.

For he commanded and raised the stormy wind, which lifted up the waves of the sea. They mounted up to heaven; they went down to the depths; their courage melted away in their evil plight; they reeled and staggered like drunken men and were at their wits' end.

The storm is God's: he commanded. And the description is vivid: the ship climbing to the sky, dropping into the troughs, men staggering like drunks. At their wits' end — the ESV notes the Hebrew is "all their wisdom was swallowed up". All their seamanship, all their skill, gone under. Some troubles are beyond every human competence.

Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress. He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed. Then they were glad that the waters were quiet, and he brought them to their desired haven.

And here the psalm walks into the Gospels. Terrified disciples in a boat cried out, and Jesus rebuked the wind and said to the sea, Peace! Be still! (Mark 4:39) — and there was a great calm (Matt 8:26). They asked, Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? (Mark 4:41). Anyone who knew Psalm 107 knew the answer. Only the LORD makes the storm be still.

He brought them to their desired haven. The ESV notes the Hebrew simply says "they" were glad and "he" brought "them". The rescue does not end mid-ocean with the waves calm. It ends in harbour, where they wanted to be. God does not merely stop the storm; he finishes the voyage.

Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love, for his wondrous works to the children of man! Let them extol him in the congregation of the people, and praise him in the assembly of the elders.

Four stories, and the two refrains come four times each (vv. 6, 13, 19, 28; vv. 8, 15, 21, 31). Lost, imprisoned, sick, storm-tossed — very different troubles, some innocent and some self-inflicted — and in every case the same thing happens: they cried to the LORD. Whatever your trouble is, the psalm has only one instruction for you before the rescue. Cry to him.

And notice where the sailors' thanks is to be given: in the congregation of the people and in the assembly of the elders. They were rescued alone on the sea. They are to give thanks in public. A private rescue owes a public song.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 33–43 — Consider the Steadfast Love of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He turns rivers into a desert and a desert into pools of water (vv. 33-35), settles the hungry and blesses their fields (vv. 36-38), pours contempt on princes but he raises up the needy out of affliction (vv. 39-41). The upright see it and are glad (v. 42). Whoever is wise, let him attend to these things; let them consider the steadfast love of the LORD (v. 43).
verseByVerse.theology: God overturns the fortunes of the proud and the poor, and the wise are told to watch it happen.

verseByVerse.quote: He turns rivers into a desert, springs of water into thirsty ground, a fruitful land into a salty waste, because of the evil of its inhabitants. He turns a desert into pools of water, a parched land into springs of water. And there he lets the hungry dwell, and they establish a city to live in; they sow fields and plant vineyards and get a fruitful yield. By his blessing they multiply greatly, and he does not let their livestock diminish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He turns rivers into a desert, springs of water into thirsty ground, a fruitful land into a salty waste, because of the evil of its inhabitants.

Now the psalm widens from four stories to a general truth about how God rules. He can dry up rivers and turn farmland to salt — because of the evil of its inhabitants. Prosperity is not guaranteed to the wicked.

He turns a desert into pools of water, a parched land into springs of water. And there he lets the hungry dwell, and they establish a city to live in; they sow fields and plant vineyards and get a fruitful yield. By his blessing they multiply greatly, and he does not let their livestock diminish.

And the reverse: deserts become pools, and the hungry — the wanderers of verse 5 — are settled there, build a city and plant vineyards. God reverses fortunes in both directions.

verseByVerse.quote: When they are diminished and brought low through oppression, evil, and sorrow, he pours contempt on princes and makes them wander in trackless wastes; but he raises up the needy out of affliction and makes their families like flocks. The upright see it and are glad, and all wickedness shuts its mouth. Whoever is wise, let him attend to these things; let them consider the steadfast love of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they are diminished and brought low through oppression, evil, and sorrow, he pours contempt on princes and makes them wander in trackless wastes; but he raises up the needy out of affliction and makes their families like flocks.

The reversals continue. Princes who oppressed are made to wander in the trackless wastes — becoming the lost people of the first story. And the needy are lifted up. It is the same overturning Mary sang about: the mighty brought down, the humble exalted.

He pours contempt on princes are the words of Job (Job 12:21), who saw the same God humble rulers. The powerful who crushed the weak become the wanderers they once despised.

The upright see it and are glad, and all wickedness shuts its mouth.

When God acts like this, the righteous rejoice, and the wicked have nothing left to say.

Whoever is wise, let him attend to these things; let them consider the steadfast love of the LORD.

The psalm ends like wisdom literature. Whoever is wise — pay attention. Consider these stories. Watch how God rescues the lost, the imprisoned, the sick and the storm-tossed; how he humbles princes and raises the poor. The wise person is not the one who has never been in trouble. It is the one who has learned, from trouble, to see the steadfast love of the LORD — and to say so.

107.title: Let the Redeemed of the LORD Say So
107.overview: Opening Book Five, the redeemed whom God has gathered from east, west, north and south are told to give thanks and say so (vv. 1-3). Four stories follow, each with the refrains Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress and Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love: wanderers in the desert led to a city (vv. 4-9); rebels imprisoned in darkness whose bonds he burst (vv. 10-16); fools sick to death whom he healed by sending his word (vv. 17-22); sailors in a storm he stilled (vv. 23-32). God turns rivers to desert and desert to pools, settles the hungry, humbles princes and raises the needy (vv. 33-42). Whoever is wise, let him attend to these things; let them consider the steadfast love of the LORD (v. 43).
107.theology:
Book Five opens with the gathering prayed for at the close of Book Four (v. 3; 106:47), fulfilled in the bringing near of those far off (Eph 2:13) from every nation (Rev 7:9). The redeemed must testify (v. 2).

Trouble may be innocent or self-inflicted (vv. 11, 17); in every case the cry to the LORD is heard. God leads the lost, frees captives (Luke 1:79; 4:18), heals by his word (v. 20; Luke 7:7) and stills the storm (v. 29), which Christ did in person (Mark 4:39-41).

God overturns fortunes, humbling the proud and raising the needy (vv. 33-42). Wisdom is attending to his steadfast love in these works (v. 43).
107.examples:
A prayer at the end of one book answered in the first line of the next.

Redeemed? Say so.

Wandering from one thing to the next, never arriving.

Chains that were their own fault — and still broken.

A word sent on an errand of healing.

All their wisdom swallowed by the sea.

Who then is this? Anyone who knew Psalm 107 knew.

The wise have learned from trouble to see steadfast love.

108.text: A Song. A Psalm of David. 1My heart is steadfast, O God! I will sing and make melody with all my being!2Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awake the dawn!3I will give thanks to you, O LORD, among the peoples; I will sing praises to you among the nations.4For your steadfast love is great above the heavens; your faithfulness reaches to the clouds.5Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth!6That your beloved ones may be delivered, give salvation by your right hand and answer me!7God has promised in his holiness: "With exultation I will divide up Shechem and portion out the Valley of Succoth.8Gilead is mine; Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is my helmet, Judah my scepter.9Moab is my washbasin; upon Edom I cast my shoe; over Philistia I shout in triumph."10Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom?11Have you not rejected us, O God? You do not go out, O God, with our armies.12Oh grant us help against the foe, for vain is the salvation of man!13With God we shall do valiantly; it is he who will tread down our foes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — I Will Awake the Dawn
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: My heart is steadfast, O God! I will sing and make melody with all my being! (v. 1). Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awake the dawn! (v. 2). He will give thanks among the nations, for your steadfast love is great above the heavens; your faithfulness reaches to the clouds (vv. 3-4). Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth! (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The closing praise of Psalm 57, sung again without the cave that came before it.

verseByVerse.quote: My heart is steadfast, O God! I will sing and make melody with all my being! Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awake the dawn! I will give thanks to you, O LORD, among the peoples; I will sing praises to you among the nations. For your steadfast love is great above the heavens; your faithfulness reaches to the clouds. Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth!
verseByVerse.commentary:
My heart is steadfast, O God! I will sing and make melody with all my being!

This psalm is made of two older psalms. Verses 1 to 5 are the end of Psalm 57, the song David wrote when he fled from Saul, in the cave (57, title). Verses 6 to 13 are the second half of Psalm 60, written after a defeat. Both of those psalms are expounded fully in their place. What makes Psalm 108 interesting is what has been left out, and what has been changed.

What has been left out is both laments. Psalm 57 began in the cave: my soul is in the midst of lions. Psalm 60 began with O God, you have rejected us, broken our defenses. Psalm 108 starts where those psalms ended — at the praise, at the promise. Someone took David's old songs, set the distress aside, and kept the confidence that grew out of it.

That is a thing believers do. A hymn written in grief is sung years later at a celebration. The faith that was forged in the cave becomes the song of people who were never in it.

And the small changes point the same way. Psalm 57 said, My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast! and then Awake, my glory! Here the repetition is gone, and my glory has moved into the first line as with all my being (the ESV notes the Hebrew is "with my glory"). The whole self is engaged from the start.

Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awake the dawn! I will give thanks to you, O LORD, among the peoples; I will sing praises to you among the nations.

He will not wait for morning to praise; he will wake the dawn with his music. And the praise goes out to the nations.

For your steadfast love is great above the heavens; your faithfulness reaches to the clouds. Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth!

Psalm 57 said God's steadfast love is great to the heavens. Psalm 108 says above the heavens. The later singer, looking back, finds that the love was even larger than David had said in the cave.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — Vain Is the Salvation of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: That your beloved ones may be delivered, give salvation by your right hand and answer me! (v. 6). God has promised in his holiness to portion out the land and rule the nations (vv. 7-9). Who will lead me to Edom? Have you not rejected us, O God? (vv. 10-11). Oh grant us help against the foe, for vain is the salvation of man! With God we shall do valiantly; it is he who will tread down our foes (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: The promise and hope of Psalm 60, sung again without its opening defeat — but with its hard question kept.

verseByVerse.quote: That your beloved ones may be delivered, give salvation by your right hand and answer me! God has promised in his holiness: "With exultation I will divide up Shechem and portion out the Valley of Succoth. Gilead is mine; Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is my helmet, Judah my scepter. Moab is my washbasin; upon Edom I cast my shoe; over Philistia I shout in triumph."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That your beloved ones may be delivered, give salvation by your right hand and answer me!

Now the psalm switches to Psalm 60. And one word has changed: Psalm 60 said answer us; Psalm 108 says answer me. The communal prayer becomes personal. What was once a nation's plea is taken up by an individual as his own.

God has promised in his holiness: With exultation I will divide up Shechem and portion out the Valley of Succoth. Gilead is mine; Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is my helmet, Judah my scepter. Moab is my washbasin; upon Edom I cast my shoe; over Philistia I shout in triumph.

Psalm 60 introduced this oracle with God has spoken; here it is God has promised. A spoken word has become a promise held on to. The content is God's claim to the whole land and to the surrounding nations: Israel's tribes are his armour and sceptre; Moab is the basin he washes his feet in; Edom is where he throws his shoe, claiming it as his property.

verseByVerse.quote: Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom? Have you not rejected us, O God? You do not go out, O God, with our armies. Oh grant us help against the foe, for vain is the salvation of man! With God we shall do valiantly; it is he who will tread down our foes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom? Have you not rejected us, O God? You do not go out, O God, with our armies.

And here is the striking thing. The lament was removed from the beginning of both psalms — but this question was kept. Have you not rejected us, O God? Even a psalm built from confident material does not pretend that God's people never feel abandoned. The promise of verses 7 to 9 and the question of verse 11 stand side by side. That is honest faith: holding God's word in one hand and an unanswered question in the other.

Oh grant us help against the foe, for vain is the salvation of man! With God we shall do valiantly; it is he who will tread down our foes.

And the answer to the question is not a strategy but a confession. Vain is the salvation of man — human help is empty. With God, and only with him, we shall do valiantly. Not that they will sit still; they will fight, and fight bravely. But it is he who will tread down our foes.

Psalm 108 is a lesson in how Scripture feeds later faith. Old songs of distress become new songs of confidence, the love of God turns out to be above the heavens and not merely up to them, and the victory still belongs entirely to God. The believer who sings these words now sings them in the light of a greater victory, won by the Son of David, who treads down every enemy.

108.title: My Heart Is Steadfast, O God
108.overview: Psalm 108 joins the closing praise of Psalm 57 (vv. 1-5) to the oracle and prayer of Psalm 60 (vv. 6-13), leaving out the laments with which both began. With a steadfast heart David will wake the dawn with music and praise God among the nations, for his steadfast love is great above the heavens (vv. 1-5). He asks for salvation for God's beloved ones; God has promised to portion out the land and rule the nations (vv. 6-9). Who will lead him to Edom — has God rejected them (vv. 10-11)? Human help is vain; With God we shall do valiantly; it is he who will tread down our foes (vv. 12-13).
108.theology:
Earlier Scripture is reused for new occasions: faith forged in distress (57, 60) becomes the confident song of later worshippers. See the full expositions at Psalms 57 and 60.

The changes heighten the praise (above the heavens, v. 4), personalise the prayer (answer me, v. 6) and turn God's spoken word into a promise (v. 7).

The retained question (v. 11) shows that confident faith still admits the experience of seeming rejection. Human salvation is vain; victory is God's (vv. 12-13).
108.examples:
Two old psalms joined, with the laments set aside.

A hymn written in grief, sung years later at a celebration.

The love was above the heavens, not just up to them.

Answer us becomes answer me.

God's word in one hand, an unanswered question in the other.

Fight bravely — and know who treads down the foe.

109.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1Be not silent, O God of my praise!2For wicked and deceitful mouths are opened against me, speaking against me with lying tongues.3They encircle me with words of hate, and attack me without cause.4In return for my love they accuse me, but I give myself to prayer.5So they reward me evil for good, and hatred for my love.6Appoint a wicked man against him; let an accuser stand at his right hand.7When he is tried, let him come forth guilty; let his prayer be counted as sin!8May his days be few; may another take his office!9May his children be fatherless and his wife a widow!10May his children wander about and beg, seeking food far from the ruins they inhabit!11May the creditor seize all that he has; may strangers plunder the fruits of his toil!12Let there be none to extend kindness to him, nor any to pity his fatherless children!13May his posterity be cut off; may his name be blotted out in the second generation!14May the iniquity of his fathers be remembered before the LORD, and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out!15Let them be before the LORD continually, that he may cut off the memory of them from the earth!16For he did not remember to show kindness, but pursued the poor and needy and the brokenhearted, to put them to death.17He loved to curse; let curses come upon him! He did not delight in blessing; may it be far from him!18He clothed himself with cursing as his coat; may it soak into his body like water, like oil into his bones!19May it be like a garment that he wraps around him, like a belt that he puts on every day!20May this be the reward of my accusers from the LORD, of those who speak evil against my life!21But you, O GOD my Lord, deal on my behalf for your name's sake; because your steadfast love is good, deliver me!22For I am poor and needy, and my heart is stricken within me.23I am gone like a shadow at evening; I am shaken off like a locust.24My knees are weak through fasting; my body has become gaunt, with no fat.25I am an object of scorn to my accusers; when they see me, they wag their heads.26Help me, O LORD my God! Save me according to your steadfast love!27Let them know that this is your hand; you, O LORD, have done it!28Let them curse, but you will bless! They arise and are put to shame, but your servant will be glad!29May my accusers be clothed with dishonor; may they be wrapped in their own shame as in a cloak!30With my mouth I will give great thanks to the LORD; I will praise him in the midst of the throng.31For he stands at the right hand of the needy one, to save him from those who condemn his soul to death.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — In Return for My Love They Accuse Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Be not silent, O God of my praise! (v. 1). Lying mouths are opened against him; they encircle me with words of hate, and attack me without cause (vv. 2-3). In return for my love they accuse me, but I give myself to prayer. So they reward me evil for good, and hatred for my love (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: A man repaid with hatred for his love answers not with a counter-attack but with prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not silent, O God of my praise! For wicked and deceitful mouths are opened against me, speaking against me with lying tongues. They encircle me with words of hate, and attack me without cause. In return for my love they accuse me, but I give myself to prayer. So they reward me evil for good, and hatred for my love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be not silent, O God of my praise! For wicked and deceitful mouths are opened against me, speaking against me with lying tongues.

The psalm opens with a man surrounded by talk. Mouths, tongues, words — the attack is verbal, and it is false. Against all the noise he asks one thing: that God not be silent. He calls God the God of my praise — the one he has always praised — even while everyone else is speaking against him.

They encircle me with words of hate, and attack me without cause. In return for my love they accuse me, but I give myself to prayer.

Without cause, and worse: in return for my love. He had loved these people. The pain of betrayal by those you have been kind to is its own kind of wound.

And his response is one of the most beautiful lines in the Psalter. The ESV has but I give myself to prayer; the ESV notes the Hebrew is simply "but I am prayer". They are accusation; he is prayer. That is the only answer a believer has to slander that does not turn him into a slanderer.

So they reward me evil for good, and hatred for my love.

Jesus quoted a similar psalm about his betrayer: He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me (John 13:18). The pattern of love repaid with hatred reaches its lowest point in the upper room.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–20 — May Another Take His Office
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Appoint a wicked man against him; let an accuser stand at his right hand (v. 6). Let him be condemned, may his days be few; may another take his office! (vv. 7-8). May his family be destitute and his name blotted out (vv. 9-15), for he did not remember to show kindness, but pursued the poor and needy (v. 16). He loved to curse; let curses come upon him! (vv. 17-19). May this be the reward of my accusers from the LORD (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The fiercest curses in the Psalter — spoken against a man who loved cursing and hunted the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: Appoint a wicked man against him; let an accuser stand at his right hand. When he is tried, let him come forth guilty; let his prayer be counted as sin! May his days be few; may another take his office! May his children be fatherless and his wife a widow! May his children wander about and beg, seeking food far from the ruins they inhabit!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Appoint a wicked man against him; let an accuser stand at his right hand. When he is tried, let him come forth guilty; let his prayer be counted as sin!

Now come the curses, and they are among the most shocking words in the Bible. Before reading them, notice a change in the grammar. In verses 2 to 5 the enemies are they, plural. In verses 6 to 19 the target is him, singular. In verse 20 it is plural again: my accusers.

Careful readers have understood this in two ways. Some take verses 6 to 19 as David's prayer against the leader of his enemies — one man who stands behind the rest. Others take them as David quoting what his enemies are saying about him: these are the curses they are hurling at me, and verse 20 answers, let this come back on them instead. The ESV's wording reads the first way, and it is the more common reading. On either reading, the curses are handed to God, not carried out by the man praying.

The legal picture is a trial. An accuser — the Hebrew word is satan — stands at the defendant's right hand, the place of the prosecutor. Hold that detail; the psalm will return to the right hand at the end.

And the most frightening line of all: let his prayer be counted as sin. In verse 4 David said, in effect, I am prayer. Here the enemy's prayer is itself asked to count against him. Prayer offered by a man who hunts the poor and has no intention of turning is not neutral; it is hypocrisy, and God is not fooled by it.

May his days be few; may another take his office!

When the apostles gathered after Judas's death, Peter quoted this verse: Let another take his office (Acts 1:20), and they chose Matthias. The man who repaid Jesus' love with betrayal is the man on whom this curse finally fell.

May his children be fatherless and his wife a widow! May his children wander about and beg, seeking food far from the ruins they inhabit!

The curse spreads to his family. These words are hard to read, and they should be. They are the language of a man who has been utterly wronged, praying in the categories of his time, where a man's house rose and fell with him.

verseByVerse.quote: May the creditor seize all that he has; may strangers plunder the fruits of his toil! Let there be none to extend kindness to him, nor any to pity his fatherless children! May his posterity be cut off; may his name be blotted out in the second generation! May the iniquity of his fathers be remembered before the LORD, and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out! Let them be before the LORD continually, that he may cut off the memory of them from the earth!
verseByVerse.commentary:
May the creditor seize all that he has; may strangers plunder the fruits of his toil! Let there be none to extend kindness to him, nor any to pity his fatherless children!

Ruin, and no pity. The prayer is that the man who showed no kindness (v. 16) receive none.

May his posterity be cut off; may his name be blotted out in the second generation! May the iniquity of his fathers be remembered before the LORD, and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out! Let them be before the LORD continually, that he may cut off the memory of them from the earth!

The deepest curse is to be forgotten: no descendants, no name, no memory. And the sins are to stay before the LORD continually. It is the exact opposite of what God does for the forgiven, whose transgressions he removes as far as east from west (103:12). This man is asked to receive what the unrepentant will receive.

How should a Christian pray words like these? Not by carrying them out, and not by praying them against a personal enemy. The New Testament says, Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them (Rom 12:14). But these words still teach something true: that God takes wrongs seriously, that the unrepentant enemies of his people face real judgment, and that the right place to put your rage at injustice is in God's hands.

verseByVerse.quote: For he did not remember to show kindness, but pursued the poor and needy and the brokenhearted, to put them to death. He loved to curse; let curses come upon him! He did not delight in blessing; may it be far from him! He clothed himself with cursing as his coat; may it soak into his body like water, like oil into his bones! May it be like a garment that he wraps around him, like a belt that he puts on every day! May this be the reward of my accusers from the LORD, of those who speak evil against my life!
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he did not remember to show kindness, but pursued the poor and needy and the brokenhearted, to put them to death.

Here is the reason for the curses, and it matters. This is not a private quarrel. The man pursued the poor and needy and the brokenhearted, to put them to death. He is a predator of the weak. The psalm's anger is the anger of justice on behalf of victims.

He loved to curse; let curses come upon him! He did not delight in blessing; may it be far from him! He clothed himself with cursing as his coat; may it soak into his body like water, like oil into his bones! May it be like a garment that he wraps around him, like a belt that he puts on every day!

And the principle: what a man loves, he gets. He loved to curse, so let curses come; he did not delight in blessing, so let blessing stay away. (The ESV notes these lines follow a small change of vowels; the Hebrew as pointed reads as statements — curses have come, blessing is far.) Cursing was his clothing, his daily belt. The judgment is not arbitrary; it is his own chosen garment, soaked in.

May this be the reward of my accusers from the LORD, of those who speak evil against my life!

From the LORD. Whatever the reading of the curses, the reward is left to God to give.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–31 — He Stands at the Right Hand of the Needy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But you, O GOD my Lord, deal on my behalf for your name's sake (v. 21). For I am poor and needy, gone like a shadow, gaunt, scorned — when they see me, they wag their heads (vv. 22-25). Help me, O LORD my God! (v. 26). Let them curse, but you will bless! (v. 28). For he stands at the right hand of the needy one, to save him from those who condemn his soul to death (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: The accuser stood at the wicked man's right hand; God stands at the right hand of the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, O GOD my Lord, deal on my behalf for your name's sake; because your steadfast love is good, deliver me! For I am poor and needy, and my heart is stricken within me. I am gone like a shadow at evening; I am shaken off like a locust. My knees are weak through fasting; my body has become gaunt, with no fat. I am an object of scorn to my accusers; when they see me, they wag their heads.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you, O GOD my Lord, deal on my behalf for your name's sake; because your steadfast love is good, deliver me!

But you. The psalm turns from the enemy to God. And the grounds are God's name and God's steadfast love, not David's deserving.

The name he uses is unusual: O GOD my Lord. The ESV prints the first word in capitals because it stands for the covenant name of God, joined here to my Lord, the word for a master. The one he appeals to is both the God who bound himself by covenant and the Master he serves. A servant under attack has a right to call on his master.

For I am poor and needy, and my heart is stricken within me. I am gone like a shadow at evening; I am shaken off like a locust. My knees are weak through fasting; my body has become gaunt, with no fat.

The man who prayed those fierce curses is himself fragile: a fading evening shadow, a locust shaken off a sleeve, weak-kneed and thin from fasting. He has been praying and fasting under the attack. His strength is gone. He is the poor and needy — the same people the wicked man hunted (v. 16).

I am an object of scorn to my accusers; when they see me, they wag their heads.

At the cross, those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads (Matt 27:39). The one who was truly poor and needy, repaid with hatred for his love, heard the head-wagging too.

verseByVerse.quote: Help me, O LORD my God! Save me according to your steadfast love! Let them know that this is your hand; you, O LORD, have done it! Let them curse, but you will bless! They arise and are put to shame, but your servant will be glad! May my accusers be clothed with dishonor; may they be wrapped in their own shame as in a cloak! With my mouth I will give great thanks to the LORD; I will praise him in the midst of the throng. For he stands at the right hand of the needy one, to save him from those who condemn his soul to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Help me, O LORD my God! Save me according to your steadfast love! Let them know that this is your hand; you, O LORD, have done it!

He wants the rescue to be unmistakably God's, so that his enemies will know who acted.

Let them curse, but you will bless! They arise and are put to shame, but your servant will be glad!

Here is the heart of the psalm, and the key to reading the curses. Let them curse, but you will bless. The enemies' words have no final power. If God blesses, their cursing is empty noise.

And this is the freedom the New Testament gives a believer who is slandered. Jesus, cursed and mocked, prayed, Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34). When he was reviled, he did not revile in return ... but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Pet 2:23). A Christian can let people curse, because God blesses.

May my accusers be clothed with dishonor; may they be wrapped in their own shame as in a cloak! With my mouth I will give great thanks to the LORD; I will praise him in the midst of the throng.

The one who wore cursing as a coat (v. 18) is wrapped in shame as a cloak; the one who was cursed opens his mouth in public thanks.

For he stands at the right hand of the needy one, to save him from those who condemn his soul to death.

And here is the last line, and the reversal of the whole psalm. In verse 6, an accuser stood at his right hand — the place of the prosecutor. Now God stands at the right hand of the needy one — the place of the defender. The poor man in the dock looks to his right, and the advocate standing there is God.

That is the comfort for anyone who is falsely accused. There may be an accuser at the enemy's side. There is a Defender at yours.

109.title: Let Them Curse, but You Will Bless
109.overview: David asks God not to be silent while lying mouths surround him; in return for his love they accuse him, and he gives himself to prayer (vv. 1-5). Then come curses on a single enemy: an accuser at his right hand, a guilty verdict, few days and another in his office, a destitute family, a name blotted out, his sins before the LORD continually (vv. 6-15) — because he pursued the poor and brokenhearted to death, loved cursing and clothed himself with it (vv. 16-19); May this be the reward of my accusers from the LORD (v. 20). David, poor, needy, gaunt and scorned, asks God to act for his name's sake (vv. 21-26). Let them curse, but you will bless! (v. 28). He will praise God publicly, for he stands at the right hand of the needy one (vv. 29-31).
109.theology:
Answering slander with prayer — I am prayer (v. 4) — is the believer's alternative to retaliation.

The curses (vv. 6-19) are read either as David's prayer against the chief accuser or as the enemies' curses quoted and turned back (v. 20). Either way they are handed to God, and they are grounded in the enemy's pursuit of the poor (v. 16). Peter applied v. 8 to Judas (Acts 1:20). Christians are to bless persecutors (Rom 12:14), following Christ who forgave and entrusted himself to the just Judge (Luke 23:34; 1 Pet 2:23).

What a man loves he receives (vv. 17-18). God's blessing makes curses empty (v. 28). The accuser at the wicked man's right hand (v. 6) is answered by God at the right hand of the needy (v. 31).
109.examples:
Surrounded by talk.

They are accusation; he is prayer.

A curse that fell on Judas.

Anger on behalf of the hunted poor.

Cursing worn as a coat, soaked in.

A locust shaken off a sleeve.

Let them curse — God blesses.

The Defender standing at the right hand of the accused.

110.text: A Psalm of David. 1The LORD says to my Lord: "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool."2The LORD sends forth from Zion your mighty scepter. Rule in the midst of your enemies!3Your people will offer themselves freely on the day of your power, in holy garments; from the womb of the morning, the dew of your youth will be yours.4The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind, "You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek."5The Lord is at your right hand; he will shatter kings on the day of his wrath.6He will execute judgment among the nations, filling them with corpses; he will shatter chiefs over the wide earth.7He will drink from the brook by the way; therefore he will lift up his head.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The LORD Says to My Lord
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD says to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool (v. 1). The LORD sends forth from Zion your mighty scepter. Rule in the midst of your enemies! (v. 2). Your people will offer themselves freely on the day of your power, in holy garments (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: David hears God speak to a King greater than David — seated beside God, reigning while his enemies remain.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD says to my Lord: "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD says to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool.

This short psalm is quoted or echoed in the New Testament more often than almost any other passage of the Old Testament, and this first verse is the reason. Read the opening words slowly. The LORD — the covenant name of God — says to my Lord. David is overhearing God speak to someone David calls my Lord. But who is a king's lord? In Israel, David was the king. No one on earth was his lord.

Jesus put exactly that question to the religious teachers in the temple. What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he? They said, the son of David. Then how is it that David calls him Lord? If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son? And no one was able to answer him a word (Matt 22:42-46). The answer they could not give is that the Messiah would be both David's son and David's Lord — human, and more than human.

Sit at my right hand. The right hand of a king was the place of highest honour and delegated power. And sit is the posture of a finished work. When Peter preached at Pentecost he said that David did not ascend into the heavens, but quoted this verse, and concluded, God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified (Acts 2:34-36). Hebrews explains why he sits: when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God (Heb 10:12). Priests in the temple never sat; their work was never done. This one sat down.

Until I make your enemies your footstool. The seat is not the end. There is an until. The King is enthroned now, and his enemies are not yet all under his feet. That is the age we live in. For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet (1 Cor 15:25), and he is waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool (Heb 10:13). At his trial Jesus told the high priest, you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power (Mark 14:62). The prisoner in the dock was quoting this verse about himself.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD sends forth from Zion your mighty scepter. Rule in the midst of your enemies! Your people will offer themselves freely on the day of your power, in holy garments; from the womb of the morning, the dew of your youth will be yours.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD sends forth from Zion your mighty scepter. Rule in the midst of your enemies!

The King's rule goes out from Zion, and it is exercised in the midst of your enemies. He does not wait until every enemy has gone before he begins to reign. He reigns now, surrounded by opposition. That is exactly how the church experiences Christ's kingship: he is Lord, and the world is still hostile, and both are true at once. God seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all rule and authority (Eph 1:20-21), while the church on earth still suffers.

Your people will offer themselves freely on the day of your power, in holy garments; from the womb of the morning, the dew of your youth will be yours.

The King's army is made of volunteers: your people will offer themselves freely. No one is conscripted into this kingdom. And they come in holy garments, dressed not in armour but like priests.

The rest of the verse is one of the hardest lines in the Psalms to translate, and the ESV is honest about it: it notes that on the day of your power may mean "on the day you lead your forces", that some manuscripts read "on the holy mountains", and that the meaning of the Hebrew in the last line is uncertain. The picture of the womb of the morning and the dew of your youth seems to be of fresh strength appearing like dew at dawn — a young army, or the King's own unfading vigour. It is wise not to build much on a line the translators themselves hold loosely.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind, You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek (v. 4). The Lord is at your right hand; he will shatter kings on the day of his wrath (v. 5), judging among the nations (v. 6). He will drink from the brook by the way; therefore he will lift up his head (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The King is also a Priest by God's oath — something no king of Israel could be — and he will judge the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind, "You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind, You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.

And now the most astonishing sentence in the psalm. God does not merely speak; he swears, and will not change his mind. And what he swears is that the King is also a priest.

In Israel, that was impossible. Kings came from Judah; priests came from Levi. The two offices were strictly separate, and when a king tried to act as a priest he was struck with leprosy. Yet God swears that this King is a priest — not of Aaron's order, but after the order of Melchizedek.

Melchizedek appears once in Genesis, and briefly. After Abraham's victory, Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. He was priest of God Most High. He blessed Abraham, and Abraham gave him a tenth of everything (Gen 14:18-20). A king and a priest in one person, in Salem — Jerusalem — centuries before Levi was born.

The letter to the Hebrews builds much of its argument on this verse. Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest, but was appointed by God, who said, You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek (Heb 5:5-6). And the oath matters: the Levitical priests were not appointed with an oath, but this one was made a priest with an oath by the one who said to him: The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind, You are a priest forever (Heb 7:21).

Here is why it matters for you. A king rules you; a priest represents you before God. Jesus is both. The one who sits on the throne is the one who offered the sacrifice for your sins and now intercedes for you. His priesthood is forever — it will never be handed to a successor who does not know you. And it rests on God's oath, which he will not change.

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord is at your right hand; he will shatter kings on the day of his wrath. He will execute judgment among the nations, filling them with corpses; he will shatter chiefs over the wide earth. He will drink from the brook by the way; therefore he will lift up his head.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord is at your right hand; he will shatter kings on the day of his wrath.

The picture shifts. In verse 1 the King sat at God's right hand; now the Lord is at your right hand, fighting beside him. And there is a day of his wrath coming, when kings who have set themselves against him will be shattered. The seated King will not sit forever while his enemies rage.

He will execute judgment among the nations, filling them with corpses; he will shatter chiefs over the wide earth.

The language is the language of a battlefield, and it is meant to be terrible. The ESV notes that chiefs may be read "the head". The same King who offers himself as priest will one day judge the nations. The gospel invitation is urgent because the day of wrath is real. There is time now, while he sits, to come to him as priest before he rises as judge.

He will drink from the brook by the way; therefore he will lift up his head.

The psalm ends with a quiet, strange image. The warrior-King, in the middle of the campaign, stops to drink from the brook by the way — refreshed on the march — and then will lift up his head, the posture of victory.

A Christian reading this after the Gospels cannot help seeing the pattern of the whole life of Christ in it: the King who stooped low, who walked the dusty road and drank from the brooks by the way like any traveller, who bowed his head in death — and who was lifted up, raised and seated at the right hand of God. The psalm begins with him sitting down and ends with his head lifted high. Everything between is his reign, and the church lives in the middle of verse 1, waiting for the until.

110.title: Sit at My Right Hand
110.overview: David hears the LORD say to David's Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool (v. 1). The LORD extends his scepter from Zion: Rule in the midst of your enemies! (v. 2). His people will offer themselves freely in holy garments on the day of his power (v. 3). The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind: You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek (v. 4). The Lord at his right hand will shatter kings, judge the nations and crush rulers over the wide earth (vv. 5-6); he will drink from the brook by the way and lift up his head (v. 7).
110.theology:
David calls the King my Lord (v. 1): the Messiah is David's son and David's Lord (Matt 22:41-46). He is seated at God's right hand, his sacrificial work finished (Acts 2:34-36; Heb 10:12), reigning until all enemies are subdued (1 Cor 15:25; Heb 10:13), exalted above all powers (Eph 1:20-22) while ruling amid enemies (v. 2).

His people are willing volunteers dressed as priests (v. 3); the details of v. 3 are uncertain in Hebrew and should be held loosely.

By an unchangeable oath he is a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek (v. 4; Gen 14:18-20), uniting kingship and priesthood as no Israelite could (Heb 5:5-6; 7:17, 21). The seated King will rise as Judge on the day of wrath (vv. 5-6), and his path runs from humiliation to exaltation (v. 7).
110.examples:
A question no one in the temple could answer.

Priests never sat down; this one did.

Living inside the word until.

Ruling in the middle of enemies.

An army of volunteers dressed as priests.

King and priest in one person, by oath.

A priest who will never hand you over to a successor.

A drink by the roadside, and the head lifted up.

111.text: <sup>1</sup>Praise the LORD! I will give thanks to the LORD with my whole heart, in the company of the upright, in the congregation.<sup>2</sup>Great are the works of the LORD, studied by all who delight in them.<sup>3</sup>Full of splendor and majesty is his work, and his righteousness endures forever.<sup>4</sup>He has caused his wondrous works to be remembered; the LORD is gracious and merciful.<sup>5</sup>He provides food for those who fear him; he remembers his covenant forever.<sup>6</sup>He has shown his people the power of his works, in giving them the inheritance of the nations.<sup>7</sup>The works of his hands are faithful and just; all his precepts are trustworthy;<sup>8</sup>they are established forever and ever, to be performed with faithfulness and uprightness.<sup>9</sup>He sent redemption to his people; he has commanded his covenant forever. Holy and awesome is his name!<sup>10</sup>The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom; all those who practice it have a good understanding. His praise endures forever!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Studied by All Who Delight in Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Praise the LORD! I will give thanks to the LORD with my whole heart, in the company of the upright, in the congregation (v. 1). Great are the works of the LORD, studied by all who delight in them (v. 2). His work is full of splendour, and his righteousness endures forever (v. 3). He has made his wonders memorable; the LORD is gracious and merciful (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: An alphabet of praise: God's works are great enough to study for a lifetime.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD! I will give thanks to the LORD with my whole heart, in the company of the upright, in the congregation. Great are the works of the LORD, studied by all who delight in them. Full of splendor and majesty is his work, and his righteousness endures forever. He has caused his wondrous works to be remembered; the LORD is gracious and merciful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Praise the LORD! I will give thanks to the LORD with my whole heart, in the company of the upright, in the congregation.

This psalm and the next are twins. Both begin Praise the LORD! Both are acrostics — as the ESV notes, each line in Hebrew begins with the next letter of the alphabet, twenty-two lines packed into ten verses. And they are designed as a pair: Psalm 111 describes God, and Psalm 112 describes the person who fears God, using many of the same words. Read together, they show a believer growing to resemble the God he worships.

An alphabet psalm is a way of saying: here is praise from A to Z. Nothing left out, everything in order.

And the praise is given with my whole heart and in the congregation — wholehearted and public. Private devotion and gathered worship belong together.

Great are the works of the LORD, studied by all who delight in them.

God's works are not only to be admired; they are to be studied — searched out, investigated, pondered. And the people who study them are all who delight in them. This verse is a charter for every believer who has ever looked through a microscope or a telescope, read history, or traced the providence of God in a single life. Study is a form of delight, and delight drives study.

Full of splendor and majesty is his work, and his righteousness endures forever. He has caused his wondrous works to be remembered; the LORD is gracious and merciful.

His righteousness endures forever — hold that phrase; Psalm 112 will say the same thing about a human being (112:3). And God has caused his wondrous works to be remembered: he built memorials into Israel's life — the Passover, the feasts, the stones by the Jordan — so that no generation would forget.
