The Lord's Supper does the same for Christians. And the character behind the works: gracious and merciful — words Psalm 112 will also use of the upright man (112:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–10 — Holy and Awesome Is His Name
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He provides food for those who fear him; he remembers his covenant forever (v. 5). He gave his people the inheritance of the nations (v. 6). The works of his hands are faithful and just; all his precepts are trustworthy (vv. 7-8). He sent redemption to his people; he has commanded his covenant forever. Holy and awesome is his name! (v. 9). The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who feeds and redeems his people is holy, and the first lesson of wisdom is to fear him.

verseByVerse.quote: He provides food for those who fear him; he remembers his covenant forever. He has shown his people the power of his works, in giving them the inheritance of the nations. The works of his hands are faithful and just; all his precepts are trustworthy; they are established forever and ever, to be performed with faithfulness and uprightness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He provides food for those who fear him; he remembers his covenant forever.

Food, first — the manna and the quail in the wilderness, and every daily meal since. God's greatness does not make him distant from ordinary needs. And the reason he keeps providing is that he remembers his covenant forever.

He has shown his people the power of his works, in giving them the inheritance of the nations.

The gift of the land was a demonstration of power — a people of slaves given the territory of nations stronger than they were.

The works of his hands are faithful and just; all his precepts are trustworthy; they are established forever and ever, to be performed with faithfulness and uprightness.

Notice how the psalm moves from God's works to God's precepts without a break. What God does and what God commands come from the same character: both are faithful, just, trustworthy. A person who trusts God's works but resents his commands has not understood that they are one. And the precepts are established — a word Psalm 112 will use of the believer's heart (the ESV notes it at 112:8, with a pointer back to this verse).

verseByVerse.quote: He sent redemption to his people; he has commanded his covenant forever. Holy and awesome is his name! The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom; all those who practice it have a good understanding. His praise endures forever!
verseByVerse.commentary:
He sent redemption to his people; he has commanded his covenant forever. Holy and awesome is his name!

The deepest work of all: he sent redemption. In Israel's history, that was the exodus and the return from exile. In its fullest sense, it is the redemption God sent in his Son.

And the response: Holy and awesome is his name! Mary, carrying that redemption in her womb, sang words that echo this line: for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name (Luke 1:49). The God who redeems is not made casual by his kindness. He remains holy and awesome, and redemption makes his name more fearsome, not less.

The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom; all those who practice it have a good understanding. His praise endures forever!

And so the psalm arrives at its conclusion, which is also the motto of the whole of the Bible's wisdom literature: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (cf. Prov 9:10). After studying God's great works, his grace, his faithfulness and his holiness, the wise response is fear — not terror that runs away, but reverent awe that bows down and obeys.

The beginning means both the starting point and the first principle. You cannot be wise about anything — money, marriage, work, death — while ignoring the God who made it. And wisdom is not only knowing: all those who practice it have a good understanding. The next psalm begins exactly where this one ends: Blessed is the man who fears the LORD (112:1).

111.title: The Fear of the LORD Is the Beginning of Wisdom
111.overview: An acrostic of praise. The psalmist will thank the LORD wholeheartedly in the congregation (v. 1). God's works are great, studied by all who delight in them, full of splendour; his righteousness endures forever; he has made his wonders memorable and is gracious and merciful (vv. 2-4). He provides food for those who fear him, remembers his covenant, and gave his people the nations' inheritance (vv. 5-6). His works are faithful and just and his precepts trustworthy and established forever (vv. 7-8). He sent redemption and commanded his covenant forever; holy and awesome is his name (v. 9). The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and his praise endures forever (v. 10).
111.theology:
Psalm 111 describes God; its twin, Psalm 112, describes the God-fearer in the same words (righteousness enduring, gracious and merciful, delight, established), showing worshippers conformed to the God they worship.

God's works invite delighted study (v. 2) and are made memorable by his design (v. 4). His works and his precepts share one character — faithful, just, trustworthy (vv. 7-8).

Redemption magnifies rather than diminishes his holiness (v. 9; Luke 1:49). The fear of the LORD is the starting point and first principle of wisdom, shown in practice (v. 10; Prov 9:10).
111.examples:
Praise from A to Z.

Twin psalms: God, and the person who fears him.

A charter for everyone with a microscope or a telescope.

Memorials built into the calendar.

Works and commands from the same character.

Kindness that does not make God casual.

You cannot be wise about money while ignoring the God who made it.

112.text: <sup>1</sup>Praise the LORD! Blessed is the man who fears the LORD, who greatly delights in his commandments!<sup>2</sup>His offspring will be mighty in the land; the generation of the upright will be blessed.<sup>3</sup>Wealth and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever.<sup>4</sup>Light dawns in the darkness for the upright; he is gracious, merciful, and righteous.<sup>5</sup>It is well with the man who deals generously and lends; who conducts his affairs with justice.<sup>6</sup>For the righteous will never be moved; he will be remembered forever.<sup>7</sup>He is not afraid of bad news; his heart is firm, trusting in the LORD.<sup>8</sup>His heart is steady; he will not be afraid, until he looks in triumph on his adversaries.<sup>9</sup>He has distributed freely; he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever; his horn is exalted in honor.<sup>10</sup>The wicked man sees it and is angry; he gnashes his teeth and melts away; the desire of the wicked will perish!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Blessed Is the Man Who Fears the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Praise the LORD! Blessed is the man who fears the LORD, who greatly delights in his commandments! (v. 1). His offspring and household are blessed, and his righteousness endures forever (vv. 2-3). Light dawns in the darkness for the upright; he is gracious, merciful, and righteous (v. 4). He deals generously and justly (v. 5), for the righteous will never be moved; he will be remembered forever (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Psalm 111 described God; Psalm 112 describes the person who fears him — and he has begun to look like God.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD! Blessed is the man who fears the LORD, who greatly delights in his commandments! His offspring will be mighty in the land; the generation of the upright will be blessed. Wealth and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Praise the LORD! Blessed is the man who fears the LORD, who greatly delights in his commandments!

Psalm 111 ended, The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. Psalm 112 begins by describing the man who has made that beginning. It is the twin psalm — another acrostic, as the ESV notes, another Praise the LORD! — and it uses the language of 111 deliberately. What was said of God there is said of the God-fearer here.

The first description links two things we might keep apart: he fears the LORD and he greatly delights in his commandments. Fear and delight together. It is the same man as the first psalm, whose delight is in the law of the LORD (1:2). Reverence for God does not make his commands a burden; it makes them a joy.

His offspring will be mighty in the land; the generation of the upright will be blessed. Wealth and riches are in his house,

Here the psalm describes the blessing that generally follows a godly life: strong children, a prosperous household. This must be read as the wisdom books read — as the normal pattern of God's world, not a guarantee for every individual. Job feared God and lost everything. Psalm 73 wrestled with the wicked prospering. The psalm is not a promise that believers will be rich; it is a picture of the goodness that tends to grow around a righteous life.

and his righteousness endures forever.

And here is the first echo. Psalm 111:3 said of God, his righteousness endures forever. Now the same words are used of a man. The righteousness of the God-fearer is a reflection of God's own, and because it is rooted in God it lasts. Wealth passes; this does not.

verseByVerse.quote: Light dawns in the darkness for the upright; he is gracious, merciful, and righteous. It is well with the man who deals generously and lends; who conducts his affairs with justice. For the righteous will never be moved; he will be remembered forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Light dawns in the darkness for the upright; he is gracious, merciful, and righteous.

The upright man is not spared darkness. But in the darkness, light dawns — the same promise as Psalm 97, where light is sown for the righteous and some ancient witnesses read "Light dawns" (97:11).

And the second echo: gracious, merciful. Psalm 111:4 said, the LORD is gracious and merciful. The man who fears God becomes gracious and merciful himself. This is the whole point of the twin psalms. We become like what we worship. A person who spends his life delighting in a gracious God will slowly become gracious.

It is well with the man who deals generously and lends; who conducts his affairs with justice.

The grace shows up in his finances. He deals generously and lends — not grasping, not exploiting. And his business is conducted with justice. Godliness is not only what happens in the congregation; it is visible in how a man handles money and contracts.

For the righteous will never be moved; he will be remembered forever.

Stable, and remembered. The memory of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot (Prov 10:7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He is not afraid of bad news; his heart is firm, trusting in the LORD. His heart is steady; he will not be afraid (vv. 7-8). He has distributed freely; he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever (v. 9). The wicked man sees it and is angry, and his desire perishes (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: A heart fixed on God does not panic at the phone call, and an open hand gives to the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: He is not afraid of bad news; his heart is firm, trusting in the LORD. His heart is steady; he will not be afraid, until he looks in triumph on his adversaries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is not afraid of bad news; his heart is firm, trusting in the LORD.

This is one of the most practical verses in the Psalter. He is not afraid of bad news. Not that bad news never comes — the verse assumes it will. The phone rings late at night; the letter from the hospital arrives; the manager asks to see you. The God-fearer is not immune to any of it. But he is not ruled by the dread of it.

Why? His heart is firm, trusting in the LORD. His heart is fixed on something that bad news cannot touch. Isaiah said the same: You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you (Isa 26:3). Fear of bad news is really fear that something will happen outside God's hand. The heart that trusts God knows nothing can.

Here is a test to run on yourself. What is the news you most dread? Put it into this verse: he is not afraid of that, his heart is firm, trusting in the LORD. The fear will not vanish in a moment. But the verse shows where the firmness comes from.

His heart is steady; he will not be afraid, until he looks in triumph on his adversaries.

Steady — the ESV notes it may be read "established", and points back to 111:8, where God's precepts are established forever. The man's heart is steady because it rests on what God has established. And the fearlessness lasts until — until he sees the outcome. Perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18).

verseByVerse.quote: He has distributed freely; he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever; his horn is exalted in honor. The wicked man sees it and is angry; he gnashes his teeth and melts away; the desire of the wicked will perish!
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has distributed freely; he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever; his horn is exalted in honor.

His generosity is not occasional. He distributed freely and given to the poor. And for the second time, his righteousness endures forever (vv. 3, 9).

Paul quoted this verse when he urged the Corinthians to give generously to the poor believers in Jerusalem: As it is written, He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever (2 Cor 9:9). Christian giving is not a tax; it is what the God-fearing heart does, and it lasts longer than the money that was given.

The wicked man sees it and is angry; he gnashes his teeth and melts away; the desire of the wicked will perish!

The psalm ends with a contrast, as Psalm 1 did. The wicked man watches the righteous man's steady, generous life and is enraged by it. He grinds his teeth — and melts away. His desires, which he pursued so hard, perish. The righteous man's righteousness endures forever; the wicked man's desire does not survive him.

Put the two psalms side by side one last time. Psalm 111: God's righteousness endures forever, he is gracious and merciful, his precepts are established. Psalm 112: the God-fearer's righteousness endures forever, he is gracious and merciful, his heart is established. That is what the fear of the LORD does to a person. It makes him like God.

112.title: He Is Not Afraid of Bad News
112.overview: Blessed is the man who fears the LORD and delights in his commandments: his children are mighty, his house prospers, and his righteousness endures forever (vv. 1-3). Light dawns for him in darkness; he is gracious, merciful and righteous, lends generously and deals justly (vv. 4-5). He will never be moved and will be remembered (v. 6). He is not afraid of bad news; his heart is firm, trusting in the LORD; his heart is steady until he sees his adversaries defeated (vv. 7-8). He gives freely to the poor, his righteousness endures, and he is honoured (v. 9). The wicked see it, grind their teeth and melt away (v. 10).
112.theology:
Psalm 112 answers 111: the God-fearer is described in the terms used of God — righteousness enduring forever (vv. 3, 9; 111:3), gracious and merciful (v. 4; 111:4), established (v. 8; 111:8). Worshippers are conformed to the God they fear.

Fear of God and delight in his commands belong together (v. 1; 1:2). Material blessing is the general pattern, not a guarantee (vv. 2-3). Godliness is visible in generosity and justice with money (vv. 5, 9), a pattern Paul applies to Christian giving (2 Cor 9:9).

A heart fixed on God is not ruled by fear of bad news (vv. 7-8; Isa 26:3; 1 John 4:18). The desires of the wicked perish (v. 10).
112.examples:
Fear and delight in the same heart.

A pattern, not a guarantee.

We become like what we worship.

Godliness visible in contracts and loans.

The late-night phone call.

Gifts distributed freely.

Psalm 111 and 112 side by side: the fear of the LORD makes a person like God.

113.text: <sup>1</sup>Praise the LORD! Praise, O servants of the LORD, praise the name of the LORD!<sup>2</sup>Blessed be the name of the LORD from this time forth and forevermore!<sup>3</sup>From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the LORD is to be praised!<sup>4</sup>The LORD is high above all nations, and his glory above the heavens!<sup>5</sup>Who is like the LORD our God, who is seated on high,<sup>6</sup>who looks far down on the heavens and the earth?<sup>7</sup>He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap,<sup>8</sup>to make them sit with princes, with the princes of his people.<sup>9</sup>He gives the barren woman a home, making her the joyous mother of children. Praise the LORD!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — From the Rising of the Sun to Its Setting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Praise the LORD! Praise, O servants of the LORD, praise the name of the LORD! (v. 1). Blessed be the name of the LORD from this time forth and forevermore! (v. 2). From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the LORD is to be praised! (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: Praise for the name of the LORD in every time and every place.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD! Praise, O servants of the LORD, praise the name of the LORD! Blessed be the name of the LORD from this time forth and forevermore! From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the LORD is to be praised!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Praise the LORD! Praise, O servants of the LORD, praise the name of the LORD!

This psalm opens a group of six (113-118) that in later Jewish practice were sung at the great festivals, and especially at Passover. They are the songs of a people who remembered being brought out of Egypt. It begins with praise three times over, and it calls the singers servants of the LORD — the ones who once served Pharaoh now serve and praise the LORD.

Blessed be the name of the LORD from this time forth and forevermore! From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the LORD is to be praised!

Three times in three verses: the name of the LORD. His name is his revealed character, and it is to be blessed in every direction. Verse 2 stretches it through time: from this time forth and forevermore. Verse 3 stretches it across space: from the rising of the sun to its setting — east to west, the whole width of the world. There is no hour and no place where praise of the LORD is out of place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — He Raises the Poor from the Dust
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD is high above all nations (v. 4). Who is like the LORD our God, who is seated on high, who looks far down on the heavens and the earth? (vv. 5-6). He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap, to make them sit with princes (vv. 7-8). He gives the barren woman a home, making her the joyous mother of children. Praise the LORD! (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The God so high that he stoops to see the sky stoops further still, to the rubbish heap, to lift the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is high above all nations, and his glory above the heavens! Who is like the LORD our God, who is seated on high, who looks far down on the heavens and the earth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is high above all nations, and his glory above the heavens!

Now the reason. God is high — above every nation and every empire, including the one Israel came out of. And his glory is above the heavens. The sky is not his ceiling; it is beneath his feet.

Who is like the LORD our God, who is seated on high, who looks far down on the heavens and the earth?

Read the last line carefully. God is so high that he looks far down — not only on the earth, but on the heavens. To see the stars, he has to stoop. That is how far above his creation he is. Who is like him? No one.

And yet the verb is looks down. The God who is too high for the heavens to reach does not stay aloof. He bends. This is the beginning of the most wonderful truth in the Bible, and it goes further than the psalmist could see: the Son, though he was in the form of God, emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, and humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Phil 2:6-8). God did not only look down. He came down.

verseByVerse.quote: He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap, to make them sit with princes, with the princes of his people. He gives the barren woman a home, making her the joyous mother of children. Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap, to make them sit with princes, with the princes of his people.

And here is where he looks. Not at the palaces, but at the dust and the ash heap — the town rubbish dump outside the walls, where the destitute and diseased sat and begged. The God who stoops to see the heavens stoops lower still, to the refuse pile, and picks up the poor.

And he does not merely feed them and leave them there. He seats them with princes. From the dump to the royal table.

These words are almost exactly the words of Hannah, the mother of Samuel, when God answered her prayer: He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap to make them sit with princes and inherit a seat of honor (1 Sam 2:8). And Mary sang the same reversal when she carried the Christ: he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; he has filled the hungry with good things (Luke 1:52-53). That is the gospel. God finds people on the rubbish heap of their sin and shame, and seats them at the King's table.

He gives the barren woman a home, making her the joyous mother of children. Praise the LORD!

And the psalm ends with the most personal reversal of all. In Israel a woman without children often lived with shame and insecurity. The Bible is full of them — Sarah, Rachel, Hannah, Elizabeth — and God gave each of them a child.

This verse needs to be handled tenderly. It describes the kind of thing God does; it is not a promise that every woman who longs for a child will have one, and many faithful women do not. But it tells every woman who carries that sorrow that God sees the one society overlooks, and that his heart is to give her a home — a place, belonging, joy. In Christ, no one in God's household is without family. The God who stoops to the ash heap has not stopped stooping. Praise the LORD!

113.title: Who Is Like the LORD Our God?
113.overview: The servants of the LORD are called to praise his name now and forever, from sunrise to sunset (vv. 1-3), for he is high above the nations and his glory above the heavens (v. 4). Who is like the LORD our God, enthroned so high that he looks down even on the heavens (vv. 5-6)? He raises the poor from the dust and the needy from the ash heap to sit with princes, and gives the barren woman a home as a joyful mother (vv. 7-9).
113.theology:
The name of the LORD is to be praised in all times and places (vv. 1-3). God is incomparably exalted, above the heavens themselves (vv. 4-6), yet he stoops — a pattern fulfilled when the Son humbled himself to the cross (Phil 2:6-8).

God's exaltation is shown in his care for the lowest: he raises the poor and seats them with princes (vv. 7-8), as Hannah and Mary sang (1 Sam 2:8; Luke 1:52-53). He gives the barren a home (v. 9) — a pattern of his compassion, not a promise to every individual.
113.examples:
The former slaves of Pharaoh, now servants of the LORD.

No hour and no place where praise is out of place.

A God who must stoop to see the stars.

He did not only look down; he came down.

From the town rubbish dump to the royal table.

Hannah's song, sung again.

The woman society overlooks, seen by God.

114.text: <sup>1</sup>When Israel went out from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of strange language,<sup>2</sup>Judah became his sanctuary, Israel his dominion.<sup>3</sup>The sea looked and fled; Jordan turned back.<sup>4</sup>The mountains skipped like rams, the hills like lambs.<sup>5</sup>What ails you, O sea, that you flee? O Jordan, that you turn back?<sup>6</sup>O mountains, that you skip like rams? O hills, like lambs?<sup>7</sup>Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob,<sup>8</sup>who turns the rock into a pool of water, the flint into a spring of water.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — When Israel Went Out from Egypt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Israel went out from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of strange language, Judah became his sanctuary, Israel his dominion (vv. 1-2). The sea looked and fled; Jordan turned back. The mountains skipped like rams, the hills like lambs (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: The exodus told as a poem in which the sea runs away and the mountains dance.

verseByVerse.quote: When Israel went out from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of strange language, Judah became his sanctuary, Israel his dominion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Israel went out from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of strange language,

This is the shortest and liveliest retelling of the exodus in the Psalms. It begins with a detail an Israelite would feel: Egypt was a people of strange language. Four hundred years in a land where the masters spoke a tongue that was not theirs. Coming out was coming home to being understood.

Judah became his sanctuary, Israel his dominion.

Notice what God's sanctuary is. Not a tent, not a temple — there was neither yet. Judah became his sanctuary. The people themselves were the place where God dwelt, and Israel was the territory he ruled. Before God lived in a building, he lived among a people. That is still where he lives: the church is not a building but a people in whom God is present.

And the word his is interesting. The psalm has not yet said whose sanctuary. It will not name him until verse 7.

verseByVerse.quote: The sea looked and fled; Jordan turned back. The mountains skipped like rams, the hills like lambs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sea looked and fled; Jordan turned back.

Forty years compressed into one line. At the start of the journey, the Red Sea: the LORD drove the sea back by a strong east wind all night and made the sea dry land (Exod 14:21). At the end, the Jordan: the waters coming down from above stood and rose up in a heap very far away (Josh 3:16). The first and last obstacles, both water, both got out of the way.

And the poet makes the sea a person. It looked — and fled. It saw something, and ran.

The mountains skipped like rams, the hills like lambs.

At Sinai the whole mountain trembled greatly (Exod 19:18). The psalm turns the earthquake into something almost comic: great mountains leaping like rams, little hills bouncing like lambs. The solid earth behaves like a flock of startled sheep.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — At the Presence of the God of Jacob
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What ails you, O sea, that you flee? O Jordan, that you turn back? O mountains, that you skip like rams? (vv. 5-6). Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob, who turns the rock into a pool of water, the flint into a spring of water (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: The poet asks creation what frightened it, and the answer is a name held back until the end.

verseByVerse.quote: What ails you, O sea, that you flee? O Jordan, that you turn back? O mountains, that you skip like rams? O hills, like lambs?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What ails you, O sea, that you flee? O Jordan, that you turn back? O mountains, that you skip like rams? O hills, like lambs?

Now the poet teases creation. He speaks to the sea, the river and the mountains as if they were frightened animals: what's the matter with you? Why are you running? Why are you jumping?

It is a wonderful way to hold the answer back. The questions build suspense. What could make an ocean run away and a mountain range jump?

verseByVerse.quote: Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob, who turns the rock into a pool of water, the flint into a spring of water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob,

And here is the answer, and here, for the first time in the psalm, is God's name. Through six verses he has been only his. Now: the Lord, the God of Jacob. It was his presence that the sea saw. Nothing else could do that.

And the poet turns the question into a command to the whole earth: Tremble. If the sea ran and the mountains jumped at his presence, everything should tremble. So should we. The presence of God is not a mild spiritual atmosphere. It is the thing oceans run from.

who turns the rock into a pool of water, the flint into a spring of water.

And yet the psalm ends not with terror but with a gift. The same presence that makes the sea flee makes a rock flow. In the desert God told Moses, you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it (Exod 17:6) — and not a trickle: a pool, a spring, out of flint, the hardest stone there is.

Paul says the people drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ (1 Cor 10:4). The God whose presence terrifies the sea is the God who became the Rock that was struck so that his people could drink. Tremble at his presence — and come to him thirsty.

114.title: The Sea Looked and Fled
114.overview: When Israel left Egypt, Judah became God's sanctuary and Israel his dominion (vv. 1-2). The sea saw and fled, the Jordan turned back, the mountains skipped like rams and the hills like lambs (vv. 3-4). What ails you, sea, river, mountains (vv. 5-6)? Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob, who turns rock into pools and flint into springs (vv. 7-8).
114.theology:
God's sanctuary was first a people, not a building (v. 2). The exodus and the crossing of the Jordan frame the whole journey as the retreat of creation before God's presence (v. 3; Exod 14:21; Josh 3:16), as does the quaking of Sinai (v. 4; Exod 19:18).

The divine name is withheld until v. 7, where the answer to creation's fear is the presence of the God of Jacob. That same presence brings water from the rock (v. 8; Exod 17:6), which Paul identifies with Christ (1 Cor 10:4).
114.examples:
Coming home to a language you understand.

A sanctuary made of people.

Forty years in one line: two waters, both out of the way.

Mountains like startled sheep.

What's the matter with you, sea?

A name held back for six verses.

Tremble at his presence — and come to him thirsty.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Those Who Make Them Become Like Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to your name give glory (v. 1). Why should the nations say, Where is their God? (v. 2). Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases (v. 3). Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands, with mouths, eyes, ears, noses, hands and feet that do nothing (vv. 4-7). Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Against the taunt of the nations, a God who acts — and idols that cannot, and turn their worshippers into themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to your name give glory, for the sake of your steadfast love and your faithfulness! Why should the nations say, "Where is their God?" Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to your name give glory, for the sake of your steadfast love and your faithfulness!

The psalm opens with a refusal, said twice for emphasis: not to us. Whatever God has done for his people, the credit is not theirs. It belongs to his name, and the reasons are his steadfast love and faithfulness, not their merit.

This is a searching prayer for anyone who has seen God bless their work — a growing church, a successful ministry, a family that turned out well. The temptation to take a little of the glory is very strong. Not to us, O LORD, not to us.

Why should the nations say, Where is their God?

The taunt of Psalm 42 and Psalm 79 again (42:3; 79:10). The nations can see their gods — statues in temples. Israel's God cannot be seen. So where is he?

Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases.

The answer is magnificent in its simplicity. Where is he? In the heavens — above everything, not in a shrine. And he does all that he pleases. He is not a statue waiting to be carried; he acts, freely and sovereignly. The invisibility of God is not a weakness. It is a sign that he is too great to be made into an object.

verseByVerse.quote: Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see. They have ears, but do not hear; noses, but do not smell. They have hands, but do not feel; feet, but do not walk; and they do not make a sound in their throat. Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands.

Now the contrast. The nations' gods are expensive — silver and gold — and man-made — the work of human hands. That second point is fatal. Something you make cannot be greater than you.

They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see. They have ears, but do not hear; noses, but do not smell. They have hands, but do not feel; feet, but do not walk; and they do not make a sound in their throat.

The psalm walks round the statue and inspects it, part by part: mouth, eyes, ears, nose, hands, feet, throat. Seven features, all carved beautifully, and not one of them works. The idol has a mouth and is silent; eyes and is blind. Our God does all that he pleases (v. 3); their god cannot do anything at all. Isaiah mocked the man who burns half a log to cook his dinner and carves the other half into a god, then prays to it and says, Deliver me, for you are my god! (Isa 44:17).

Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them.

And here is the devastating conclusion. Worshippers become like what they worship. People who bow to things that cannot see, hear or speak become spiritually blind, deaf and dumb themselves. The historian of Kings said the same of Israel: They went after false idols and became false (2 Kgs 17:15).

This is as true of modern idols as ancient ones. Worship money and you become hard and cold like it. Worship pleasure and you become shallow. Worship yourself and you shrink to your own size. The good news of the twin psalms 111 and 112 is the reverse: worship the living God and you become gracious and merciful like him. Little children, keep yourselves from idols (1 John 5:21).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–18 — He Is Their Help and Their Shield
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O Israel, trust in the LORD! He is their help and their shield — and so for the house of Aaron and all who fear him (vv. 9-11). The LORD has remembered us; he will bless us, both the small and the great (vv. 12-13). May he give increase (vv. 14-15). The heavens are the LORD's heavens, but the earth he has given to the children of man (v. 16). But we will bless the LORD from this time forth and forevermore (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: Three groups called to trust, three times the same answer, and a blessing for small and great alike.

verseByVerse.quote: O Israel, trust in the LORD! He is their help and their shield. O house of Aaron, trust in the LORD! He is their help and their shield. You who fear the LORD, trust in the LORD! He is their help and their shield.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O Israel, trust in the LORD! He is their help and their shield. O house of Aaron, trust in the LORD! He is their help and their shield. You who fear the LORD, trust in the LORD! He is their help and their shield.

Three groups, and three times the same call and the same answer. Israel — the whole nation (the ESV notes many manuscripts read "O house of Israel"). The house of Aaron — the priests. And you who fear the LORD — possibly all the faithful together, or perhaps foreigners who had come to worship Israel's God.

The refrain is the point: He is their help and their shield. Help for what they cannot do; shield against what would harm them. The idol has hands that cannot move (v. 7); the LORD's hand helps. The idol cannot see danger; the LORD is a shield against it. Whatever group you belong to in the church — ordinary member, leader, newcomer — the call is the same and so is the promise.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD has remembered us; he will bless us; he will bless the house of Israel; he will bless the house of Aaron; he will bless those who fear the LORD, both the small and the great. May the LORD give you increase, you and your children! May you be blessed by the LORD, who made heaven and earth!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD has remembered us; he will bless us; he will bless the house of Israel; he will bless the house of Aaron; he will bless those who fear the LORD, both the small and the great.

The idols forget nothing because they know nothing. The LORD has remembered us. And bless comes four times in two verses, to the same three groups — and then to both the small and the great. John heard that phrase at the end of history, when God rewards those who fear your name, both small and great (Rev 11:18). No one is too insignificant to be blessed, and no one is too important to need it.

May the LORD give you increase, you and your children! May you be blessed by the LORD, who made heaven and earth!

The blessing reaches the next generation, and it comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth — not from a god made by human hands, but from the Maker of everything.

verseByVerse.quote: The heavens are the LORD's heavens, but the earth he has given to the children of man. The dead do not praise the LORD, nor do any who go down into silence. But we will bless the LORD from this time forth and forevermore. Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heavens are the LORD's heavens, but the earth he has given to the children of man.

A short statement of the order of things. Heaven belongs to God. The earth he has entrusted to humanity — as a gift to be cared for under him, not as territory where he is absent. The idol-worshippers had it backwards: they tried to bring gods down to earth in silver and gold, instead of looking up to the God of heaven and serving him on the earth he gave them.

The dead do not praise the LORD, nor do any who go down into silence. But we will bless the LORD from this time forth and forevermore. Praise the LORD!

The dead are silent — Heman asked, Do the departed rise up to praise you? (88:10). Their praise on earth has ended. So the living must praise while they have breath. But we will bless the LORD — and then the phrase from Psalm 113: from this time forth and forevermore (113:2). Not only for this lifetime. The people who trust the living God will praise him forever, when every idol has been melted down and every voice that trusted in one has fallen silent.

Notice the word silence. The idols were silent: they do not make a sound in their throat (v. 7). The dead go down into silence (v. 17). Those who trust in idols end in the same silence as the idols they trusted. The people of the living God are the ones who break it: But we will bless the LORD.

115.title: Not to Us, O LORD
115.overview: Not to us, but to God's name be the glory, for his steadfast love and faithfulness (v. 1). Why should the nations ask where Israel's God is? He is in the heavens and does whatever he pleases (vv. 2-3). Their idols are silver and gold, made by human hands, with mouths, eyes, ears, noses, hands, feet and throats that do nothing; those who make and trust them become like them (vv. 4-8). Israel, the house of Aaron and all who fear the LORD are called to trust him, their help and shield (vv. 9-11). The LORD has remembered his people and will bless small and great and their children (vv. 12-15). The heavens are his, the earth given to humanity; the dead do not praise him, but we will bless the LORD from this time forth and forevermore (vv. 16-18).
115.theology:
Glory belongs to God's name, not to his people (v. 1). God's invisibility is not absence: he is in the heavens and sovereign (v. 3).

Idols are man-made and powerless (vv. 4-7), and worshippers become like what they worship (v. 8; 2 Kgs 17:15; Isa 44:17) — the reverse of the God-fearer who grows like God (111-112). Christians must keep themselves from idols (1 John 5:21).

All groups among God's people are called to trust him as help and shield (vv. 9-11), and he blesses small and great (v. 13; Rev 11:18). The living are to praise God now and forever (vv. 17-18).
115.examples:
Not to us, not to us — when God has blessed your work.

Invisible because too great to be an object.

Something you make cannot be greater than you.

Seven carved features, none of them working.

Worship money and become hard like it.

A shield where the idol cannot even see.

Too small to be blessed? Too great to need it? Neither.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — I Love the LORD, Because He Has Heard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I love the LORD, because he has heard my voice and my pleas for mercy. Because he inclined his ear to me, therefore I will call on him as long as I live (vv. 1-2). The snares of death encompassed me (v. 3). Then I called on the name of the LORD: O LORD, I pray, deliver my soul! (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: A man who nearly died begins with the simplest confession in the Psalter: I love the LORD, because he heard me.

verseByVerse.quote: I love the LORD, because he has heard my voice and my pleas for mercy. Because he inclined his ear to me, therefore I will call on him as long as I live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I love the LORD, because he has heard my voice and my pleas for mercy.

Few psalms open so simply. I love the LORD. And the reason is equally simple: because he has heard my voice. Not a theory about God, but an experience of him. The man cried, and God listened.

This is how love for God usually grows. It is not first commanded into existence; it is drawn out by being cared for. John would later write that we love because he first loved us. A person who struggles to feel love for God might begin by remembering, specifically, the times God has heard them.

Because he inclined his ear to me, therefore I will call on him as long as I live.

He inclined his ear — bent down to listen, the way a parent crouches to hear a small child. And the response is lifelong: as long as I live. One answered prayer has made him a praying man for the rest of his days.

verseByVerse.quote: The snares of death encompassed me; the pangs of Sheol laid hold on me; I suffered distress and anguish. Then I called on the name of the LORD: "O LORD, I pray, deliver my soul!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The snares of death encompassed me; the pangs of Sheol laid hold on me; I suffered distress and anguish.

Now he tells what happened. Death had him in a trap. The pangs of Sheol — the grave reaching up and gripping him. It may have been illness, or danger, or something else; the psalm does not say. It says it was nearly the end.

Then I called on the name of the LORD: O LORD, I pray, deliver my soul!

And the prayer he prayed at the worst moment of his life was seven words long. O LORD, I pray, deliver my soul! No eloquence, no theology — a cry. Anyone who has been in real extremity knows that the prayers that matter most are often the shortest. God heard that one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — Return, O My Soul, to Your Rest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gracious is the LORD, and righteous; our God is merciful (v. 5). When I was brought low, he saved me (v. 6). Return, O my soul, to your rest; for the LORD has dealt bountifully with you (v. 7). He was delivered from death, tears and stumbling, to walk before the LORD in the land of the living (vv. 8-9). I believed, even when I spoke (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: After the crisis, a man tells his own soul to come home and rest.

verseByVerse.quote: Gracious is the LORD, and righteous; our God is merciful. The LORD preserves the simple; when I was brought low, he saved me. Return, O my soul, to your rest; for the LORD has dealt bountifully with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gracious is the LORD, and righteous; our God is merciful.

Having been rescued, he describes the one who rescued him: gracious, righteous, merciful. Righteous in the middle — God's mercy never compromises his justice.

The LORD preserves the simple; when I was brought low, he saved me.

The simple are the unsophisticated, the people without resources, clever plans or influence. They are the ones God guards. The man puts himself in that group: when I was brought low, he saved me. You do not have to be spiritually impressive to be kept by God.

Return, O my soul, to your rest; for the LORD has dealt bountifully with you.

A beautiful moment. He speaks to his own soul, the way Psalm 42 did, but here the tone is gentle: Return, O my soul, to your rest. The soul has been out in the storm — frightened, running, anxious. The danger is over. Come home. Settle down. The LORD has dealt bountifully with you.

Some believers stay anxious long after God has rescued them, as if the soul has not heard the news. This verse is for them. Tell your soul what God has done, and tell it to rest.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling; I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling; I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living.

Three rescues: his soul from death, his eyes from tears, his feet from stumbling. Life, joy and steadiness, all restored. And the result is a walk: I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living. Given back his life, he will live it in God's sight.

verseByVerse.quote: I believed, even when I spoke: "I am greatly afflicted"; I said in my alarm, "All mankind are liars."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I believed, even when I spoke: I am greatly afflicted; I said in my alarm, All mankind are liars.

This is a difficult verse to translate, and the ESV notes other possibilities: "I believed, indeed", or, following the Greek translation, "I believed, therefore". The ESV's sense is that he kept believing even while he was saying how terribly he suffered. Faith and honest complaint lived together.

Paul quoted the Greek form when he described his own suffering ministry: Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written, I believed, and so I spoke, we also believe, and so we also speak (2 Cor 4:13). Faith speaks. It speaks about affliction honestly, and it speaks the gospel boldly, both at once.

All mankind are liars — said in my alarm. He admits it was a panicked thing to say. In the crisis every human support seemed to fail him. It was not a considered doctrine; it was the kind of thing a frightened man says. The psalm keeps it in, and keeps the confession that it was said in alarm.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — I Will Lift Up the Cup of Salvation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What shall I render to the LORD for all his benefits to me? I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD (vv. 12-13), and pay his vows publicly (v. 14). Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints (v. 15). O LORD, I am your servant ... You have loosed my bonds (v. 16). He will offer the sacrifice of thanksgiving in the courts of the LORD's house (vv. 17-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The only way to repay God is to take more from him — and to thank him in front of everyone.

verseByVerse.quote: What shall I render to the LORD for all his benefits to me? I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD, I will pay my vows to the LORD in the presence of all his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What shall I render to the LORD for all his benefits to me?

Now the grateful man asks what he can give back. What shall I render? It is the right question — and it has a surprising answer.

I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD,

He cannot repay God. Nothing he could offer would match what he has received. So what does he do? He will lift up the cup of salvation — he takes more. He raises the cup of thanksgiving at the feast and drinks from what God gives. And he calls on God's name again. The only way to repay grace is to receive more of it, gladly, and publicly.

If these psalms were sung at Passover, then on the night he was betrayed Jesus lifted a cup and said, This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me (1 Cor 11:25) — and then when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives (Matt 26:30). Every time a Christian lifts the cup at the Lord's Supper, this verse is being fulfilled: not paying God back, but receiving the cup of salvation.

I will pay my vows to the LORD in the presence of all his people,

In his distress he had made promises to God. Now he will keep them, and do it in the presence of all his people. The line is so important to him that he says it again word for word in verse 18.

verseByVerse.quote: Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.

This verse has comforted countless grieving believers, and it needs to be understood rightly. Precious means costly, weighty, of great value. The death of one of God's people is not a small thing to him. He does not shrug at it. He does not allow it carelessly. He watches it closely, and it matters to him greatly.

In the context, the man is thanking God for not letting him die — because God values the lives of his saints too highly to let them go cheaply. And when a believer does die, the verse still holds: that death was seen, weighed and precious in God's sight. No Christian dies unnoticed or unvalued.

And the one who makes that true is the Son, who partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery (Heb 2:14-15). If you are grieving someone who died in Christ, their death was precious to God — and for them, it was not the end.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, I am your servant; I am your servant, the son of your maidservant. You have loosed my bonds. I will offer to you the sacrifice of thanksgiving and call on the name of the LORD. I will pay my vows to the LORD in the presence of all his people, in the courts of the house of the LORD, in your midst, O Jerusalem. Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD, I am your servant; I am your servant, the son of your maidservant. You have loosed my bonds.

He says it twice: I am your servant. And then the phrase from Psalm 86, the son of your maidservant (86:16) — a servant born in the household, belonging from birth.

And the paradox: You have loosed my bonds. God freed him — and the freed man's response is to declare himself God's servant. The chains of death are off, and he binds himself willingly to the one who removed them. That is Christian freedom: not freedom from God, but freedom to serve him.

I will offer to you the sacrifice of thanksgiving and call on the name of the LORD. I will pay my vows to the LORD in the presence of all his people, in the courts of the house of the LORD, in your midst, O Jerusalem. Praise the LORD!

The psalm ends in public. Not privately grateful, but at the temple, in the crowd, in the city, offering thanks where everyone can see. A rescue that God performed in secret, at the edge of the grave, becomes a song sung in the presence of all his people. Praise the LORD!

116.title: What Shall I Render to the LORD?
116.overview: I love the LORD, because he has heard my voice; therefore the psalmist will call on him all his life (vv. 1-2). Caught in the snares of death, he prayed, O LORD, I pray, deliver my soul! (vv. 3-4). The LORD is gracious, righteous and merciful and preserves the simple; he tells his soul to return to its rest (vv. 5-7). Delivered from death, tears and stumbling, he will walk before the LORD among the living (vv. 8-9). He kept believing while he spoke of his affliction, though in alarm he called all men liars (vv. 10-11). What shall I render to the LORD? He will lift the cup of salvation, call on God and pay his vows publicly (vv. 12-14). Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints (v. 15). God's freed servant will offer thanksgiving in the courts of the LORD's house in Jerusalem (vv. 16-19).
116.theology:
Love for God grows from experienced answers to prayer (vv. 1-2). God preserves the simple and brought low (v. 6), and the soul is to be told to rest in what he has done (v. 7).

Faith and honest lament coexist (vv. 10-11); Paul's ministry takes up v. 10 (2 Cor 4:13). The only repayment of grace is receiving the cup of salvation and public thanks (vv. 12-14), fulfilled in the Lord's Supper (1 Cor 11:25; Matt 26:30).

The death of God's people is costly and weighty in his sight (v. 15), and Christ has broken death's power (Heb 2:14-15). Freed from bonds, the believer becomes God's willing servant (v. 16).
116.examples:
Love drawn out by being heard.

A seven-word prayer at the edge of the grave.

Come home, soul; the danger is over.

A panicked sentence, kept in and owned.

Repaying God by taking the cup.

No Christian dies unnoticed.

Freed from chains to become a willing servant.

A secret rescue becomes a public song.

117.text: <sup>1</sup>Praise the LORD, all nations! Extol him, all peoples!<sup>2</sup>For great is his steadfast love toward us, and the faithfulness of the LORD endures forever. Praise the LORD!

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Praise the LORD, all nations! Extol him, all peoples! (v. 1). For great is his steadfast love toward us, and the faithfulness of the LORD endures forever. Praise the LORD! (v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology: The shortest psalm has the widest reach: every nation called to praise, because of what God did for one.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD, all nations! Extol him, all peoples!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Praise the LORD, all nations! Extol him, all peoples!

This is the shortest psalm in the Psalter and the shortest chapter in the Bible — two verses. And it has the widest horizon of almost any psalm. It speaks to all nations and all peoples. Not Israel only. Every tribe, every language, every people on the face of the earth.

That was a startling thing for an Israelite to sing. The nations were the peoples who worshipped idols, who had enslaved and invaded Israel. And this psalm, sung in the temple, calls them to praise Israel's God.

Paul saw exactly what that meant. When he wanted to show the church in Rome — Jews and Gentiles struggling to accept one another — that God had always intended the Gentiles to be among his worshippers, he quoted this verse: Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him (Rom 15:11). The gospel going to the nations was not a change of plan. It was in the Psalms all along.

So this tiny psalm is a missionary charter. If you have ever wondered whether the gospel is really for every people group — the unreached tribe, the hostile nation, the neighbour from a culture you find strange — here is the answer in one line. God wants to be praised by all of them. That is why the church sends missionaries, and why it prays for the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: For great is his steadfast love toward us, and the faithfulness of the LORD endures forever. Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
For great is his steadfast love toward us, and the faithfulness of the LORD endures forever. Praise the LORD!

And here is the reason the nations should praise, and it is surprising. It is not a general statement about God's love for everyone. It is his steadfast love toward us — toward Israel. The nations are to praise God because of what he has done for one particular people.

That is exactly how the gospel works. God did not reveal himself in a vague, general way to humanity. He chose Abraham, rescued Israel from Egypt, made promises to David, and finally sent his Son as a Jew from Nazareth. His love toward that one people is the good news that goes to every other people. The nations praise God by looking at what he did for Israel, and in Christ they are brought in to share it.

Great is his steadfast love: not merely large, but stronger than the unfaithfulness it meets. It overcomes the unfaithfulness of the people it is set on.

And the faithfulness of the LORD endures forever. The two great words again — steadfast love and faithfulness — the name God proclaimed to Moses, abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod 34:6). His love is powerful; his faithfulness is permanent. What he has promised, he will do, forever.

Two verses, and the whole of redemption is in them: a God whose love prevails, whose faithfulness never ends, and who wants every nation on earth to know it. Praise the LORD!

117.title: Praise the LORD, All Nations
117.overview: All nations and all peoples are called to praise and extol the LORD (v. 1), for his steadfast love toward his people is great and his faithfulness endures forever (v. 2).
117.theology:
The shortest psalm summons every nation to worship Israel's God (v. 1), a text Paul uses to show the Gentiles' inclusion was always God's purpose (Rom 15:11).

The ground of universal praise is God's particular love toward his people (v. 2): his great steadfast love and enduring faithfulness (Exod 34:6), which reach the nations in Christ.
117.examples:
The shortest chapter, the widest horizon.

Israel's enemies invited to praise Israel's God.

The gospel for the nations was never a change of plan.

Praise for what God did for someone else.

Love stronger than the unfaithfulness it meets.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — His Steadfast Love Endures Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever! (v. 1). Let Israel say, let the house of Aaron say, let those who fear the LORD say, His steadfast love endures forever (vv. 2-4).
verseByVerse.theology: A festival procession begins with a call-and-response that every group of worshippers joins.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever! Let Israel say, "His steadfast love endures forever." Let the house of Aaron say, "His steadfast love endures forever." Let those who fear the LORD say, "His steadfast love endures forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever!

This is the last of the six psalms (113-118) that were sung at the great festivals, and it is the psalm the New Testament quotes most among them. If, as is very likely, these were the hymn Jesus and his disciples sang before they went out to the Mount of Olives (Matt 26:30), then this was the last song Jesus sang before his arrest — a song about a rejected stone.

The psalm is built like a procession. It begins outside, with a call to give thanks, and it will end at the gates of the temple and the altar.

Let Israel say, His steadfast love endures forever. Let the house of Aaron say, His steadfast love endures forever. Let those who fear the LORD say, His steadfast love endures forever.

A leader calls, and the crowd answers. The three groups are the same as in Psalm 115: the nation, the priests, and all who fear the LORD (115:9-11). And the response is the same line each time. Count it through the psalm: his steadfast love endures forever five times, and the last verse of the psalm is the first verse again (v. 29). Everything in between — distress, battle, rejection, rescue — is framed by that one sentence.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–18 — The LORD Is My Strength and My Song
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Out of my distress I called on the LORD; the LORD answered me and set me free (v. 5). The LORD is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me? (v. 6). Better to take refuge in the LORD than in princes (vv. 8-9). The nations surrounded him like bees; in the name of the LORD I cut them off! (vv. 10-12). The LORD is my strength and my song; he has become my salvation (v. 14). I shall not die, but I shall live, and recount the deeds of the LORD (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: A king surrounded and pushed to the point of falling sings the song Israel sang on the far side of the Red Sea.

verseByVerse.quote: Out of my distress I called on the LORD; the LORD answered me and set me free. The LORD is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me? The LORD is on my side as my helper; I shall look in triumph on those who hate me. It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man. It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in princes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of my distress I called on the LORD; the LORD answered me and set me free.

Now a single voice. The speaker seems to be a king or leader who has come through a terrible crisis. Out of my distress God set me free.

The LORD is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me? The LORD is on my side as my helper; I shall look in triumph on those who hate me.

This is one of the great fear-destroying verses of the Bible. What can man do to me? Men can do a great deal — the psalm will describe it. But nothing they do can undo the fact that the LORD is on my side. Hebrews gave these words to Christians facing loss and persecution: So we can confidently say, The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me? (Heb 13:6).

It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man. It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in princes.

Twice, and the second time more pointed: not just man, but princes — the powerful, the well-connected, the people who seem able to fix things. A king saying this about princes means it. He has seen how little they can do.

verseByVerse.quote: All nations surrounded me; in the name of the LORD I cut them off! They surrounded me, surrounded me on every side; in the name of the LORD I cut them off! They surrounded me like bees; they went out like a fire among thorns; in the name of the LORD I cut them off! I was pushed hard, so that I was falling, but the LORD helped me. The LORD is my strength and my song; he has become my salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All nations surrounded me; in the name of the LORD I cut them off! They surrounded me, surrounded me on every side; in the name of the LORD I cut them off! They surrounded me like bees; they went out like a fire among thorns; in the name of the LORD I cut them off!

The attack is total: all nations, on every side, swarming like bees. Three times he says he was surrounded, and three times the same answer: in the name of the LORD I cut them off. And the swarm that seemed so terrifying went out like a fire among thorns — thorn bushes blaze up fast and fierce, and burn out in minutes.

I was pushed hard, so that I was falling, but the LORD helped me.

The ESV notes the Hebrew speaks to the enemy directly: "You pushed me hard". He was actually going down. This is not a man who never stumbled; it is a man who was falling when God caught him.

The LORD is my strength and my song; he has become my salvation.

And here he quotes the oldest song of rescue Israel had. On the far shore of the Red Sea, Moses and Israel sang, The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation (Exod 15:2), and Isaiah promised the same song would be sung again (Isa 12:2). The king's rescue is a new exodus. God is not only his strength in the fight; he is his song afterwards. The one who saves becomes the subject of the singing.

verseByVerse.quote: Glad songs of salvation are in the tents of the righteous: "The right hand of the LORD does valiantly, the right hand of the LORD exalts, the right hand of the LORD does valiantly!" I shall not die, but I shall live, and recount the deeds of the LORD. The LORD has disciplined me severely, but he has not given me over to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Glad songs of salvation are in the tents of the righteous: The right hand of the LORD does valiantly, the right hand of the LORD exalts, the right hand of the LORD does valiantly!

The celebration spreads through the camp. And the song is about God's right hand — three times, like the three I cut them off of verses 10 to 12. The victory was not the king's right hand. It was God's.

I shall not die, but I shall live, and recount the deeds of the LORD.

He had been sure he was going to die. Now he declares that he will live — and the purpose of his life is to recount the deeds of the LORD. A rescued life is a testimony.

The LORD has disciplined me severely, but he has not given me over to death.

And a remarkable admission: the crisis was also God's discipline. Severely. He does not pretend the suffering was mild, and he does not pretend it was outside God's hand. But there is a limit God set: he has not given me over to death. A believer under God's hard discipline can hold on to that line. The discipline is real, and so is its boundary.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–29 — Blessed Is He Who Comes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Open to me the gates of righteousness (v. 19). The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This is the LORD's doing; it is marvelous in our eyes. This is the day that the LORD has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it (vv. 22-24). Save us, we pray, O LORD! (v. 25). Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD! (v. 26). Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever! (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: The procession reaches the temple gate, the rejected stone is set at the head of the corner, and the crowd shouts the words that greeted Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Open to me the gates of righteousness, that I may enter through them and give thanks to the LORD. This is the gate of the LORD; the righteous shall enter through it. I thank you that you have answered me and have become my salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Open to me the gates of righteousness, that I may enter through them and give thanks to the LORD.

The procession reaches the temple. The king stands outside and asks for the gates to be opened, so that he can go in and give thanks.

This is the gate of the LORD; the righteous shall enter through it.

A voice from inside — perhaps the gatekeepers — answers: this is the LORD's gate, and it is for the righteous. Who can go in? Jesus answered that question about himself: I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved (John 10:9). The gate of righteousness is a person, and those who enter through him are counted righteous.

I thank you that you have answered me and have become my salvation.

Inside, he says it to God directly: you have become my salvation — the words of verse 14 again, now as thanks.

verseByVerse.quote: The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This is the LORD's doing; it is marvelous in our eyes. This is the day that the LORD has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.

And now the most important verse in the psalm. The picture is of builders examining stones for a building, rejecting one as unfit — and that very stone becoming the cornerstone, or as the ESV notes, literally "the head of the corner", the stone that holds two walls together and bears the weight.

In the psalm the stone is the king, despised by the nations and the powerful, pushed until he was falling — and raised by God to the place of honour. But the New Testament sees the verse fulfilled completely in one person. After telling the parable of the tenants who killed the owner's son, Jesus said to the religious leaders, Have you never read in the Scriptures: The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes? (Matt 21:42). He was telling them they were the builders, and he was the stone.

Weeks later Peter stood before the same council and said it to their faces: Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead; This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone (Acts 4:10-11). The church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone (Eph 2:20). And the same stone divides people: the honor is for you who believe, but for those who do not believe, The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (1 Pet 2:7).

This is the LORD's doing; it is marvelous in our eyes. This is the day that the LORD has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.

This is the day is often quoted as a cheerful verse for any morning, and every day is indeed God's gift. But in the psalm it means a particular day: the day the rejected stone was made the cornerstone. For Christians, that day has a name. It is the day God raised the one the builders crucified. Every Sunday the church gathers on that day, and the right response is exactly what the psalm says: rejoice and be glad in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Save us, we pray, O LORD! O LORD, we pray, give us success! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD! We bless you from the house of the LORD. The LORD is God, and he has made his light to shine upon us. Bind the festal sacrifice with cords, up to the horns of the altar!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Save us, we pray, O LORD! O LORD, we pray, give us success!

Save us, we pray is one word in Hebrew, and it came into the Gospels untranslated: Hosanna.

Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD! We bless you from the house of the LORD.

And here the psalm walks straight into Palm Sunday. When Jesus rode into Jerusalem, the crowds that went before him and that followed him were shouting, Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest! (Matt 21:9). The festival crowd was singing Psalm 118 — and applying it to him.

Days later the same city rejected him. Jesus had already said what that meant: you will not see me until you say, Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! (Luke 13:35). The line that welcomed him on the road will one day be said again, by everyone, when he comes the second time.

The LORD is God, and he has made his light to shine upon us. Bind the festal sacrifice with cords, up to the horns of the altar!

His light to shine upon us — the priestly blessing, the LORD make his face to shine upon you (Num 6:25). And the procession ends at the altar, where the festival sacrifice is tied to the horns. The rejected stone, the one who comes in the LORD's name, the altar and the sacrifice — within a week of hearing this psalm on the road into Jerusalem, Jesus was all of them.

verseByVerse.quote: You are my God, and I will give thanks to you; you are my God; I will extol you. Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever!
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are my God, and I will give thanks to you; you are my God; I will extol you.

Twice, you are my God. After the crowd, the gates and the altar, the psalm narrows to one worshipper and his God.

Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever!

And the psalm ends with its first line. Surrounded, pushed, falling, disciplined, rejected — and at the end of all of it, the same confession as at the start. His steadfast love endures forever. If Jesus sang these words on the way to Gethsemane, he sang them knowing what the next day held. The steadfast love of God was not disproved by the cross. It was displayed there, and vindicated three days later, on the day the LORD made.

118.title: The Stone the Builders Rejected
118.overview: Give thanks to the LORD, for his steadfast love endures forever — let Israel, the priests and all who fear him say so (vv. 1-4). Out of distress the psalmist called and God set him free; the LORD is on his side, so what can man do? It is better to trust the LORD than princes (vv. 5-9). Surrounded by nations like bees, he cut them off in the LORD's name; pushed to falling, he was helped. The LORD is my strength and my song (vv. 10-14). The LORD's right hand does valiantly; he will live and recount God's deeds, disciplined but not given over to death (vv. 15-18). At the gates of righteousness he gives thanks (vv. 19-21). The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this is the LORD's doing and the day the LORD has made (vv. 22-24). Save us, we pray; Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD!; bind the sacrifice to the altar (vv. 25-27). You are my God; his steadfast love endures forever (vv. 28-29).
118.theology:
God's steadfast love frames every experience (vv. 1-4, 29). Because the LORD is on his side, the believer need not fear what man can do (v. 6; Heb 13:6); trust in princes is folly (vv. 8-9).

Rescue is a new exodus, sung in the words of Exod 15:2 (v. 14). God's discipline may be severe but is limited (v. 18). The gate of righteousness is fulfilled in Christ, the door (vv. 19-20; John 10:9).

The rejected stone made cornerstone (v. 22) is Christ, rejected by the builders and raised by God (Matt 21:42; Acts 4:10-11; Eph 2:20; 1 Pet 2:7); the day that the LORD has made is the day of that vindication (v. 24). The Hosanna and the blessing on the one who comes (vv. 25-26) greeted Jesus (Matt 21:9) and will be said at his return (Luke 13:35).
118.examples:
The last song before Gethsemane.

Five times, the same confession, at start and finish.

What can man do to me?

A swarm of bees, burned out like thorns.

Falling — and caught.

The song of the Red Sea sung again.

Builders who threw away the cornerstone.

This is the day: the day the stone was raised.

Hosanna on the road into Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Aleph: Blessed Are Those Whose Way Is Blameless
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Blessed are those whose way is blameless, who walk in the law of the LORD! (v. 1). Oh that my ways may be steadfast in keeping your statutes! (v. 5). I will keep your statutes; do not utterly forsake me! (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm opens with a blessing on obedience, and its first prayer admits how far the singer is from it.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those whose way is blameless, who walk in the law of the LORD! Blessed are those who keep his testimonies, who seek him with their whole heart, who also do no wrong, but walk in his ways! You have commanded your precepts to be kept diligently. Oh that my ways may be steadfast in keeping your statutes! Then I shall not be put to shame, having my eyes fixed on all your commandments. I will praise you with an upright heart, when I learn your righteous rules. I will keep your statutes; do not utterly forsake me!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are those whose way is blameless, who walk in the law of the LORD! Blessed are those who keep his testimonies, who seek him with their whole heart, who also do no wrong, but walk in his ways!

This is the longest psalm, and the longest chapter in the Bible: 176 verses in twenty-two stanzas. The ESV notes that it is an acrostic. Each stanza takes one letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and every one of its eight verses begins with that letter. It is a love song to the word of God written from A to Z, with every letter given its turn.

Almost every verse speaks of God's word, and the psalm uses a cluster of words for it: law, testimonies, precepts, statutes, commandments, rules (the ESV notes the sense is "just decrees"), word, promise. They are not a legal code for specialists. They are everything God has said, looked at from different sides.

It opens where the whole Psalter opened: Blessed (1:1). And notice that the law is not a set of rules held at arm's length. Those who keep it seek him with their whole heart. The commands lead to a person.

You have commanded your precepts to be kept diligently. Oh that my ways may be steadfast in keeping your statutes! Then I shall not be put to shame, having my eyes fixed on all your commandments.

And straight away the tone turns personal and honest. God commands diligence. The singer's response is a sigh: Oh that my ways may be steadfast. He is not boasting that he keeps the law. He wishes he did.

I will praise you with an upright heart, when I learn your righteous rules. I will keep your statutes; do not utterly forsake me!

The first stanza ends with a resolution and a plea in the same breath. I will keep — and do not utterly forsake me. This is the voice of the whole psalm: a man who loves God's word, knows he fails it, and holds on to God to keep him. Anyone who reads Psalm 119 as the boast of a self-righteous man has not listened to it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–16 — Beth: I Have Stored Up Your Word in My Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to your word (v. 9). I have stored up your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you (v. 11). I will delight in your statutes; I will not forget your word (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: The defence of a young life against sin is Scripture kept in the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to your word. With my whole heart I seek you; let me not wander from your commandments! I have stored up your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you. Blessed are you, O LORD; teach me your statutes! With my lips I declare all the rules of your mouth. In the way of your testimonies I delight as much as in all riches. I will meditate on your precepts and fix my eyes on your ways. I will delight in your statutes; I will not forget your word.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to your word.

A question every parent asks, and every honest young person. The pressures on a young life are strong, the temptations constant, and the answer is not a set of rules invented for the occasion. It is guarding the way according to your word — the way a watchman guards a road.

With my whole heart I seek you; let me not wander from your commandments! I have stored up your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.

Stored up is the word for treasure hidden away for safe keeping. Scripture read once and forgotten cannot help in the moment of temptation; Scripture stored in the heart is there when it is needed. That is the case for memorising the Bible. Jesus met the devil in the wilderness with Scripture he already knew, answering, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God (Matt 4:4). Paul says, Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly (Col 3:16), and Jesus told his disciples, Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you (John 15:3).

Blessed are you, O LORD; teach me your statutes! With my lips I declare all the rules of your mouth. In the way of your testimonies I delight as much as in all riches.

The young man blesses God and asks to be taught. He speaks the word aloud. And he enjoys it as much as in all riches — the pleasure a person takes in money, he takes in God's ways.
