I will meditate on your precepts and fix my eyes on your ways. I will delight in your statutes; I will not forget your word.

Meditate, fix, delight, not forget. Four habits of a young life kept pure. None of them is spectacular. All of them are daily.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (v. 18). I am a sojourner on the earth; hide not your commandments from me! (v. 19). Even though princes sit plotting against me, your servant will meditate on your statutes. Your testimonies are my delight; they are my counselors (vv. 23-24).
verseByVerse.theology: A stranger on earth asks for eyes to see the wonders already in front of him.

verseByVerse.quote: Deal bountifully with your servant, that I may live and keep your word. Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law. I am a sojourner on the earth; hide not your commandments from me! My soul is consumed with longing for your rules at all times. You rebuke the insolent, accursed ones, who wander from your commandments. Take away from me scorn and contempt, for I have kept your testimonies. Even though princes sit plotting against me, your servant will meditate on your statutes. Your testimonies are my delight; they are my counselors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Deal bountifully with your servant, that I may live and keep your word. Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law.

This is one of the most important prayers a Bible reader can pray. Open my eyes. The wonders are already in the text; the problem is the reader's blindness. Knowledge, study and intelligence are not enough to see them. God has to open the eyes. After his resurrection Jesus did exactly that for his disciples: he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45). Pray this verse before you open your Bible.

I am a sojourner on the earth; hide not your commandments from me! My soul is consumed with longing for your rules at all times.

A sojourner is a foreigner passing through, without citizenship or property. In a strange country, the one thing a traveller cannot do without is a guide. So: hide not your commandments from me. And his hunger for God's word is not occasional; it consumes him at all times.

You rebuke the insolent, accursed ones, who wander from your commandments. Take away from me scorn and contempt, for I have kept your testimonies. Even though princes sit plotting against me, your servant will meditate on your statutes.

Now the opposition appears, and it will run through the whole psalm: the insolent, the proud, and here princes — powerful men sitting in council, plotting against him. His response is not to plot back. Your servant will meditate on your statutes. While they discuss him, he thinks about God's word.

Your testimonies are my delight; they are my counselors.

The princes have their council. He has his: God's testimonies. When powerful people are deciding your fate, it matters very much whose counsel you are listening to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–32 — Daleth: My Soul Clings to the Dust
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: My soul clings to the dust; give me life according to your word! (v. 25). My soul melts away for sorrow; strengthen me according to your word! (v. 28). I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart! (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: From lying in the dust to running — and the difference is God's word and an enlarged heart.

verseByVerse.quote: My soul clings to the dust; give me life according to your word! When I told of my ways, you answered me; teach me your statutes! Make me understand the way of your precepts, and I will meditate on your wondrous works. My soul melts away for sorrow; strengthen me according to your word! Put false ways far from me and graciously teach me your law! I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me. I cling to your testimonies, O LORD; let me not be put to shame! I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart!
verseByVerse.commentary:
My soul clings to the dust; give me life according to your word!

The fourth stanza begins face down. My soul clings to the dust — flattened, as low as a person can go, the posture of mourning or defeat. And the prayer is for life, according to your word. The word is not only information; it gives life. Man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD (Deut 8:3).

When I told of my ways, you answered me; teach me your statutes! Make me understand the way of your precepts, and I will meditate on your wondrous works.

He had confessed his ways honestly to God — and God answered. Honest confession opens the way to being taught.

My soul melts away for sorrow; strengthen me according to your word! Put false ways far from me and graciously teach me your law!

His soul melts — drips away like wax — with grief. Not only is he in the dust; he is dissolving. And again the remedy is God's word, which strengthens. Notice graciously teach me your law. The law is received as grace.

I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me. I cling to your testimonies, O LORD; let me not be put to shame! I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart!

His soul clung to the dust in verse 25; now I cling to your testimonies. The same verb. He has transferred his grip from the dust to the word. And the stanza that began lying down ends running: I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart. The ESV notes another rendering: "for you set my heart free". Obedience does not come from a cramped, anxious heart. It comes from a heart God has made large and free.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Teach me, O LORD, the way of your statutes; and I will keep it to the end (v. 33). Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to selfish gain! Turn my eyes from looking at worthless things (vv. 36-37). In your righteousness give me life! (v. 40).
verseByVerse.theology: A stanza made almost entirely of requests: teach, lead, incline, turn, give life.

verseByVerse.quote: Teach me, O LORD, the way of your statutes; and I will keep it to the end. Give me understanding, that I may keep your law and observe it with my whole heart. Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I delight in it. Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to selfish gain! Turn my eyes from looking at worthless things; and give me life in your ways. Confirm to your servant your promise, that you may be feared. Turn away the reproach that I dread, for your rules are good. Behold, I long for your precepts; in your righteousness give me life!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teach me, O LORD, the way of your statutes; and I will keep it to the end. Give me understanding, that I may keep your law and observe it with my whole heart. Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I delight in it.

Almost every verse in this stanza is a request: teach me, give me understanding, lead me, incline my heart, turn my eyes, confirm, turn away, give me life. The singer knows he cannot keep God's word by willpower. He needs God to do something to him first.

I will keep it to the end — the ESV notes it may be read "keep it as my reward". Either way, obedience is not a burden to be endured until release. It is a path walked all the way, and a reward in itself.

Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to selfish gain! Turn my eyes from looking at worthless things; and give me life in your ways.

Two of the most searching prayers in the psalm. The heart leans naturally toward selfish gain — money, advantage, getting ahead. Only God can tilt it the other way. And the eyes are drawn to worthless things — empty, useless, corrupting. David vowed, I will not set before my eyes anything that is worthless (101:3). Here the same resolve becomes a prayer, because the man knows he cannot keep it alone. For anyone who struggles with what they look at, this is a verse to pray before picking up a phone.

Confirm to your servant your promise, that you may be feared. Turn away the reproach that I dread, for your rules are good. Behold, I long for your precepts; in your righteousness give me life!

Your rules are good. He does not merely submit to God's commands; he calls them good. And the last request of the stanza is the same as the first of the previous one: give me life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–48 — Waw: I Shall Walk in a Wide Place
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Let your steadfast love come to me, O LORD (v. 41), then shall I have an answer for him who taunts me (v. 42). I shall walk in a wide place, for I have sought your precepts (v. 45). I will also speak of your testimonies before kings (v. 46), for I find my delight in your commandments, which I love (v. 47).
verseByVerse.theology: God's commands, far from confining, set a man walking in open country and speaking before kings.

verseByVerse.quote: Let your steadfast love come to me, O LORD, your salvation according to your promise; then shall I have an answer for him who taunts me, for I trust in your word. And take not the word of truth utterly out of my mouth, for my hope is in your rules. I will keep your law continually, forever and ever, and I shall walk in a wide place, for I have sought your precepts. I will also speak of your testimonies before kings and shall not be put to shame, for I find my delight in your commandments, which I love. I will lift up my hands toward your commandments, which I love, and I will meditate on your statutes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let your steadfast love come to me, O LORD, your salvation according to your promise; then shall I have an answer for him who taunts me, for I trust in your word.

The stanza begins with God's steadfast love and salvation. Everything the singer does with the word flows from being loved and saved first. And the result is an answer for the man who mocks him. The word of God is the sword of the Spirit (Eph 6:17), and the believer who trusts it is not left without a reply.

And take not the word of truth utterly out of my mouth, for my hope is in your rules. I will keep your law continually, forever and ever, and I shall walk in a wide place, for I have sought your precepts.

Here is a verse that turns a common assumption upside down. People think of God's commands as a fence, narrowing life. The psalm says the opposite: I shall walk in a wide place, for I have sought your precepts. Open country. Room to move. James calls it the perfect law, the law of liberty (Jas 1:25). Sin promises freedom and delivers a cell; God's word looks like limits and turns out to be open ground.

I will also speak of your testimonies before kings and shall not be put to shame, for I find my delight in your commandments, which I love. I will lift up my hands toward your commandments, which I love, and I will meditate on your statutes.

The man who walks in a wide place is not intimidated in high places: before kings. And the stanza ends with love, said twice: which I love. He lifts his hands toward the commandments, the gesture of prayer and worship. This is not legalism. It is love for God expressed as love for what God has said. Jesus put it simply: If you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 49–56 — Zayin: Your Statutes Have Been My Songs
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Remember your word to your servant, in which you have made me hope (v. 49). This is my comfort in my affliction, that your promise gives me life (v. 50). Your statutes have been my songs in the house of my sojourning. I remember your name in the night, O LORD (vv. 54-55).
verseByVerse.theology: In affliction and far from home, God's promises become the songs a traveller sings at night.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember your word to your servant, in which you have made me hope. This is my comfort in my affliction, that your promise gives me life. The insolent utterly deride me, but I do not turn away from your law. When I think of your rules from of old, I take comfort, O LORD. Hot indignation seizes me because of the wicked, who forsake your law. Your statutes have been my songs in the house of my sojourning. I remember your name in the night, O LORD, and keep your law. This blessing has fallen to me, that I have kept your precepts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember your word to your servant, in which you have made me hope. This is my comfort in my affliction, that your promise gives me life.

He asks God to remember — not because God forgets, but because he wants to hold God to his promise. God's word created his hope in the first place: in which you have made me hope. And in suffering, the promise is his comfort. It does not remove the affliction. It gives me life in the middle of it.

That is the experience of countless believers in hospital beds and at gravesides. A single promise, remembered in the dark, keeps a person alive inside.

The insolent utterly deride me, but I do not turn away from your law. When I think of your rules from of old, I take comfort, O LORD. Hot indignation seizes me because of the wicked, who forsake your law.

Mockery does not move him. Remembering what God said long ago comforts him. And the wicked who abandon God's law make him burn with anger — not personal irritation, but grief at God being dishonoured.

Your statutes have been my songs in the house of my sojourning. I remember your name in the night, O LORD, and keep your law.

A lovely picture. The house of my sojourning is wherever a traveller stops for the night — a temporary lodging, far from home. And there, God's statutes become songs. The commandments are not recited like a legal code; they are sung, the way a homesick traveller sings the songs of home. And at night, when fear is strongest, he remembers your name.

This blessing has fallen to me, that I have kept your precepts.

Keeping God's word is not a burden laid on him. It is a blessing that has come to him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 57–64 — Heth: The LORD Is My Portion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD is my portion; I promise to keep your words (v. 57). I hasten and do not delay to keep your commandments (v. 60). At midnight I rise to praise you (v. 62). I am a companion of all who fear you; the earth, O LORD, is full of your steadfast love (vv. 63-64).
verseByVerse.theology: A man whose inheritance is God himself obeys without delay and sings at midnight.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is my portion; I promise to keep your words. I entreat your favor with all my heart; be gracious to me according to your promise. When I think on my ways, I turn my feet to your testimonies; I hasten and do not delay to keep your commandments. Though the cords of the wicked ensnare me, I do not forget your law. At midnight I rise to praise you, because of your righteous rules. I am a companion of all who fear you, of those who keep your precepts. The earth, O LORD, is full of your steadfast love; teach me your statutes!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is my portion; I promise to keep your words. I entreat your favor with all my heart; be gracious to me according to your promise.

The LORD is my portion — the language of Psalm 16 (16:5). Other people inherit land; his inheritance is God himself. And a man whose whole portion is God wants to keep God's words. He asks for favour with all my heart, and he asks it on the basis of God's promise, not his own record.

When I think on my ways, I turn my feet to your testimonies; I hasten and do not delay to keep your commandments.

Here is repentance in two verses. He thinks about the way he is going — takes stock honestly — and turns his feet. Then he acts at once: I hasten and do not delay. Delayed obedience is usually disobedience wearing a disguise. When you see what God's word requires, the time to do it is now.

Though the cords of the wicked ensnare me, I do not forget your law. At midnight I rise to praise you, because of your righteous rules.

Tied up by the wicked, he does not forget God's law. And at midnight he gets up to praise. Paul and Silas did exactly that in a prison in Philippi, singing hymns about midnight with their feet in the stocks.

I am a companion of all who fear you, of those who keep your precepts. The earth, O LORD, is full of your steadfast love; teach me your statutes!

The love of God's word draws a person into friendship with others who love it: a companion of all who fear you. And the stanza ends by looking up and out: the earth ... is full of your steadfast love. The man surrounded by the cords of the wicked sees a world full of God's love, and asks, again, to be taught.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 65–72 — Teth: It Is Good for Me That I Was Afflicted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: You have dealt well with your servant, O LORD (v. 65). Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I keep your word (v. 67). You are good and do good (v. 68). It is good for me that I was afflicted, that I might learn your statutes (v. 71); the law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver pieces (v. 72).
verseByVerse.theology: Looking back, a man calls his suffering good, because it brought him home to God's word.

verseByVerse.quote: You have dealt well with your servant, O LORD, according to your word. Teach me good judgment and knowledge, for I believe in your commandments. Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I keep your word. You are good and do good; teach me your statutes. The insolent smear me with lies, but with my whole heart I keep your precepts; their heart is unfeeling like fat, but I delight in your law. It is good for me that I was afflicted, that I might learn your statutes. The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver pieces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have dealt well with your servant, O LORD, according to your word. Teach me good judgment and knowledge, for I believe in your commandments.

The ninth stanza is a look back over suffering, and it begins with a verdict: You have dealt well with your servant. Everything that follows must be read in the light of that sentence.

Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I keep your word. You are good and do good; teach me your statutes.

Here is an honest confession. Before I was afflicted I went astray. Prosperity had made him careless. Things went well, and he drifted. Then trouble came, and it brought him back. But now I keep your word.

And in the middle of that confession, a statement about God that holds everything together: You are good and do good. God did not stop being good when the affliction came. The affliction was one of the good things he did.

The insolent smear me with lies, but with my whole heart I keep your precepts; their heart is unfeeling like fat, but I delight in your law.

The proud have hearts unfeeling like fat — insulated, gross, unable to feel anything. Comfort without God does that to a heart. Affliction with God does the opposite.

It is good for me that I was afflicted, that I might learn your statutes. The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver pieces.

This is one of the hardest and most precious sentences in Scripture. It is good for me that I was afflicted. No one says that during the affliction. It is the verdict of a man looking back from the other side, who can see what the pain taught him. Hebrews says the same: discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it (Heb 12:11).

If you are in the middle of affliction now, do not force yourself to say this verse yet. But hold on to the possibility that one day you will. And notice what he gained: God's law, better to me than thousands of gold and silver pieces. He lost comfort and found treasure.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 73–80 — Yodh: In Faithfulness You Have Afflicted Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Your hands have made and fashioned me; give me understanding (v. 73). I know, O LORD, that your rules are righteous, and that in faithfulness you have afflicted me (v. 75). Let your steadfast love comfort me (v. 76). May my heart be blameless in your statutes (v. 80).
verseByVerse.theology: The hands that made him are the hands that afflict him — and both are faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: Your hands have made and fashioned me; give me understanding that I may learn your commandments. Those who fear you shall see me and rejoice, because I have hoped in your word. I know, O LORD, that your rules are righteous, and that in faithfulness you have afflicted me. Let your steadfast love comfort me according to your promise to your servant. Let your mercy come to me, that I may live; for your law is my delight. Let the insolent be put to shame, because they have wronged me with falsehood; as for me, I will meditate on your precepts. Let those who fear you turn to me, that they may know your testimonies. May my heart be blameless in your statutes, that I may not be put to shame!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your hands have made and fashioned me; give me understanding that I may learn your commandments.

An argument from creation. God made him with his own hands; surely the Maker will teach the thing he made how to live. A craftsman does not build a delicate instrument and refuse to explain how it works.

Those who fear you shall see me and rejoice, because I have hoped in your word. I know, O LORD, that your rules are righteous, and that in faithfulness you have afflicted me.

In faithfulness you have afflicted me. The hands that fashioned him (v. 73) are the hands that have afflicted him — and he calls it faithfulness. Not cruelty, not carelessness, not a lapse. God afflicted him because God was being faithful to him, faithful to his purpose of making him holy. That is a conclusion only faith can reach, and it is a firm place to stand.

And his steadiness under trouble will encourage others: those who fear you shall see me and rejoice. A believer who holds on to God's word through suffering becomes a gift to the church.

Let your steadfast love comfort me according to your promise to your servant. Let your mercy come to me, that I may live; for your law is my delight.

But knowing the affliction is faithful does not make it painless. He still needs comfort, and he asks for it — from steadfast love and mercy. Faith that accepts God's hard providence is not faith that stops asking for tenderness.

Let the insolent be put to shame, because they have wronged me with falsehood; as for me, I will meditate on your precepts. Let those who fear you turn to me, that they may know your testimonies. May my heart be blameless in your statutes, that I may not be put to shame!

He wants to be a help to other believers — let those who fear you turn to me — and he wants his own heart to be blameless. The man who has suffered well becomes someone others come to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 81–88 — Kaph: Like a Wineskin in the Smoke
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: My soul longs for your salvation (v. 81). When will you comfort me? (v. 82). For I have become like a wineskin in the smoke, yet I have not forgotten your statutes (v. 83). How long must your servant endure? (v. 84). They have almost made an end of me on earth, but I have not forsaken your precepts (v. 87).
verseByVerse.theology: The lowest point of the psalm: shrivelled, persecuted, almost finished, and still holding on.

verseByVerse.quote: My soul longs for your salvation; I hope in your word. My eyes long for your promise; I ask, "When will you comfort me?" For I have become like a wineskin in the smoke, yet I have not forgotten your statutes. How long must your servant endure? When will you judge those who persecute me? The insolent have dug pitfalls for me; they do not live according to your law. All your commandments are sure; they persecute me with falsehood; help me! They have almost made an end of me on earth, but I have not forsaken your precepts. In your steadfast love give me life, that I may keep the testimonies of your mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My soul longs for your salvation; I hope in your word. My eyes long for your promise; I ask, When will you comfort me?

This stanza is the darkest in the psalm. His soul longs — the word means to faint, to waste away with waiting. His eyes are strained from looking for God's promise to come true. When will you comfort me? Faith asks when, not whether. But it does ask.

For I have become like a wineskin in the smoke, yet I have not forgotten your statutes.

A striking image. A leather wineskin hung near the fire in a house with no chimney would slowly dry out, blacken, shrivel and crack. That is how he feels: dried up, useless, smoke-stained, ready to split. Yet I have not forgotten your statutes. The container is ruined; the contents are kept.

How long must your servant endure? When will you judge those who persecute me?

The ESV notes the Hebrew is literally "How many are the days of your servant?" — how long do I have left? He wonders whether he will live long enough to see God act.

The insolent have dug pitfalls for me; they do not live according to your law. All your commandments are sure; they persecute me with falsehood; help me! They have almost made an end of me on earth, but I have not forsaken your precepts.

Traps dug in his path. Lies. And then: they have almost made an end of me. Almost. And the shortest prayer in the psalm, two words: help me! Against their lies, all your commandments are sure.

In your steadfast love give me life, that I may keep the testimonies of your mouth.

The stanza that began fainting ends asking for life — not so that he can escape, but so that he can keep God's word. Even at the bottom, his desire is to obey.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 89–96 — Lamedh: Forever, O LORD, Your Word Is Fixed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Forever, O LORD, your word is firmly fixed in the heavens (v. 89). If your law had not been my delight, I would have perished in my affliction (v. 92). I am yours; save me (v. 94). I have seen a limit to all perfection, but your commandment is exceedingly broad (v. 96).
verseByVerse.theology: At the centre of the psalm, the word that does not change holds up the man who nearly perished.

verseByVerse.quote: Forever, O LORD, your word is firmly fixed in the heavens. Your faithfulness endures to all generations; you have established the earth, and it stands fast. By your appointment they stand this day, for all things are your servants. If your law had not been my delight, I would have perished in my affliction. I will never forget your precepts, for by them you have given me life. I am yours; save me, for I have sought your precepts. The wicked lie in wait to destroy me, but I consider your testimonies. I have seen a limit to all perfection, but your commandment is exceedingly broad.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forever, O LORD, your word is firmly fixed in the heavens. Your faithfulness endures to all generations; you have established the earth, and it stands fast.

After the darkest stanza, the psalm lifts its eyes. And the turn is sudden and complete: Forever, O LORD, your word is firmly fixed in the heavens. On earth he was a shrivelled wineskin. In heaven the word stands like a fixed star. His life is nearly over; God's word is forever. The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever (Isa 40:8). Jesus said he had not come to abolish the law and the prophets but to fulfill them (Matt 5:17).

By your appointment they stand this day, for all things are your servants.

Heaven and earth keep standing because God appointed them to. All things are your servants — the sun, the sea, the seasons, and the troubles too. Nothing in creation is outside his service.

If your law had not been my delight, I would have perished in my affliction. I will never forget your precepts, for by them you have given me life.

Here is his testimony in one sentence. The thing that kept him alive through the affliction of the last stanza was his delight in God's law. Not his strength, not his circumstances. Anyone who has come through a long darkness with their faith intact can usually point to the passage that held them.

I am yours; save me, for I have sought your precepts. The wicked lie in wait to destroy me, but I consider your testimonies.

I am yours; save me. That is the whole ground of his appeal. Not "I have earned it", but "I belong to you". An owner saves his own.

I have seen a limit to all perfection, but your commandment is exceedingly broad.

He has looked at every human achievement, every perfect-seeming thing, and found where it ends. Everything has an edge. But God's word has none: exceedingly broad, wider than any life can exhaust. You can read it for eighty years and never reach the boundary.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 97–104 — Mem: Oh How I Love Your Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Oh how I love your law! It is my meditation all the day (v. 97). It makes him wiser than enemies, teachers and the aged (vv. 98-100). How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth! (v. 103). Through your precepts I get understanding (v. 104).
verseByVerse.theology: Love for God's law, tasted like honey, makes an ordinary believer wise.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh how I love your law! It is my meditation all the day. Your commandment makes me wiser than my enemies, for it is ever with me. I have more understanding than all my teachers, for your testimonies are my meditation. I understand more than the aged, for I keep your precepts. I hold back my feet from every evil way, in order to keep your word. I do not turn aside from your rules, for you have taught me. How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth! Through your precepts I get understanding; therefore I hate every false way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh how I love your law! It is my meditation all the day.

The most famous verse in the psalm, and it is an exclamation of love. Not "how I respect your law" or "how I obey your law", but how I love it. And love shows itself in attention: my meditation all the day. God told Joshua, you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it (Josh 1:8). What we love, we think about.

Your commandment makes me wiser than my enemies, for it is ever with me. I have more understanding than all my teachers, for your testimonies are my meditation. I understand more than the aged, for I keep your precepts.

Wiser than enemies, than teachers, than the aged (the ESV notes "the elders"). This is not arrogance. He is not claiming to be clever. He is saying where wisdom comes from. A person who meditates on God's word will understand life better than a brilliant person who does not, because Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness (2 Tim 3:16). And notice the last reason: for I keep your precepts. Wisdom grows by obeying, not only by reading.

I hold back my feet from every evil way, in order to keep your word. I do not turn aside from your rules, for you have taught me.

For you have taught me — the teacher is God himself.

How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth! Through your precepts I get understanding; therefore I hate every false way.

God's words are not medicine to be swallowed; they are honey to be tasted. Jeremiah said, Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart (Jer 15:16). If the Bible tastes dry to you, pray verse 18 again — open my eyes — and keep eating. Taste grows with feeding.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 105–112 — Nun: A Lamp to My Feet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path (v. 105). I am severely afflicted; give me life, O LORD, according to your word! (v. 107). Your testimonies are my heritage forever (v. 111). I incline my heart to perform your statutes forever, to the end (v. 112).
verseByVerse.theology: The word is light for the next step on a dark road, not a floodlight on the whole journey.

verseByVerse.quote: Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path. I have sworn an oath and confirmed it, to keep your righteous rules. I am severely afflicted; give me life, O LORD, according to your word! Accept my freewill offerings of praise, O LORD, and teach me your rules. I hold my life in my hand continually, but I do not forget your law. The wicked have laid a snare for me, but I do not stray from your precepts. Your testimonies are my heritage forever, for they are the joy of my heart. I incline my heart to perform your statutes forever, to the end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.

The best-known verse in the psalm rewards noticing exactly what it says. A lamp in the ancient world was a small clay oil lamp that threw a pool of light a few steps ahead. It did not light up the whole road. It lit the next step.

That is how God's word usually guides. It does not always show the whole shape of your future. It shows you what to do next — the next act of obedience, the next step of trust — and then the next. The commandment is a lamp and the teaching a light (Prov 6:23), and Peter says we do well to pay attention to it as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns (2 Pet 1:19). The lamp is for the dark. And the dark will not last forever.

I have sworn an oath and confirmed it, to keep your righteous rules. I am severely afflicted; give me life, O LORD, according to your word!

The lamp does not mean the road is easy. I am severely afflicted. He needs light precisely because it is dark.

Accept my freewill offerings of praise, O LORD, and teach me your rules. I hold my life in my hand continually, but I do not forget your law. The wicked have laid a snare for me, but I do not stray from your precepts.

I hold my life in my hand — a phrase for living in constant danger, as if carrying your life around exposed, liable to be dropped. And still he does not forget and does not stray.

Your testimonies are my heritage forever, for they are the joy of my heart. I incline my heart to perform your statutes forever, to the end.

His inheritance is God's word, and it is the joy of my heart. And his heart leans toward obeying forever, to the end — the ESV notes it may mean "the reward is eternal".

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 113–120 — Samekh: You Are My Hiding Place
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I hate the double-minded, but I love your law (v. 113). You are my hiding place and my shield; I hope in your word (v. 114). Hold me up, that I may be safe (v. 117). My flesh trembles for fear of you, and I am afraid of your judgments (v. 120).
verseByVerse.theology: A single-hearted man hides in God — and trembles before him.

verseByVerse.quote: I hate the double-minded, but I love your law. You are my hiding place and my shield; I hope in your word. Depart from me, you evildoers, that I may keep the commandments of my God. Uphold me according to your promise, that I may live, and let me not be put to shame in my hope! Hold me up, that I may be safe and have regard for your statutes continually! You spurn all who go astray from your statutes, for their cunning is in vain. All the wicked of the earth you discard like dross, therefore I love your testimonies. My flesh trembles for fear of you, and I am afraid of your judgments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I hate the double-minded, but I love your law.

The double-minded are the divided — people who try to love God and something else equally, keeping a foot in each world. James says such a man is unstable in all his ways (Jas 1:8). What the singer hates is that divided loyalty, and against it he sets a single love: I love your law. The prayer of 86:11, unite my heart, has been answered in him.

You are my hiding place and my shield; I hope in your word.

Two pictures of safety: a place to hide from danger, and a shield to hold against it. Both are God himself, and the way into them is his word.

Depart from me, you evildoers, that I may keep the commandments of my God. Uphold me according to your promise, that I may live, and let me not be put to shame in my hope! Hold me up, that I may be safe and have regard for your statutes continually!

Uphold me ... Hold me up. Twice. He does not trust his own strength to keep his hope from collapsing. He needs God's hands under him.

You spurn all who go astray from your statutes, for their cunning is in vain. All the wicked of the earth you discard like dross, therefore I love your testimonies.

Dross is the scum skimmed off molten metal and thrown away. That is what the wicked are in God's eyes. Their cleverness is in vain.

My flesh trembles for fear of you, and I am afraid of your judgments.

And the stanza ends with trembling. The man who hides in God (v. 114) shakes before him. These are not opposites. The God who is our hiding place is the God whose judgments throw the wicked away like dross, and a believer who loves him never loses a holy fear of him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 121–128 — Ayin: It Is Time for the LORD to Act
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Give your servant a pledge of good; let not the insolent oppress me (v. 122). It is time for the LORD to act, for your law has been broken (v. 126). Therefore I love your commandments above gold, above fine gold (v. 127). I hate every false way (v. 128).
verseByVerse.theology: When God's law is trampled around him, the believer loves it more, not less.

verseByVerse.quote: I have done what is just and right; do not leave me to my oppressors. Give your servant a pledge of good; let not the insolent oppress me. My eyes long for your salvation and for the fulfillment of your righteous promise. Deal with your servant according to your steadfast love, and teach me your statutes. I am your servant; give me understanding, that I may know your testimonies! It is time for the LORD to act, for your law has been broken. Therefore I love your commandments above gold, above fine gold. Therefore I consider all your precepts to be right; I hate every false way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have done what is just and right; do not leave me to my oppressors. Give your servant a pledge of good; let not the insolent oppress me.

He appeals to God as a man in the right being mistreated. And he asks for something unusual: a pledge of good. A pledge is what a guarantor gives when he stands surety for another person's debt with his own resources. He asks God to stand guarantor for him, to put himself on the line for his servant. That is precisely what God did in Christ.

My eyes long for your salvation and for the fulfillment of your righteous promise. Deal with your servant according to your steadfast love, and teach me your statutes. I am your servant; give me understanding, that I may know your testimonies!

Three times in three verses, your servant. And the request is to be dealt with according to your steadfast love — not according to what he deserves.

It is time for the LORD to act, for your law has been broken.

A cry that every generation of believers has prayed. When God's law is openly despised — when what he calls good is mocked and what he calls evil is celebrated — the believer is allowed to say: it is time for the LORD to act. Not to take matters into his own hands, but to call on God to take them into his.

Therefore I love your commandments above gold, above fine gold. Therefore I consider all your precepts to be right; I hate every false way.

Look at the surprising logic. Your law has been broken — therefore I love your commandments. You might expect the opposite: when everyone ignores God's word, it is easy to drift with them. The psalm does the reverse. The more the world tramples God's law, the more precious it becomes to the one who loves it — above fine gold. A culture's contempt for Scripture can sharpen a believer's love for it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 129–136 — Pe: The Unfolding of Your Words Gives Light
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Your testimonies are wonderful (v. 129). The unfolding of your words gives light; it imparts understanding to the simple (v. 130). Make your face shine upon your servant (v. 135). My eyes shed streams of tears, because people do not keep your law (v. 136).
verseByVerse.theology: God's word, unfolded, lets in light — and a man who loves it weeps for those who ignore it.

verseByVerse.quote: Your testimonies are wonderful; therefore my soul keeps them. The unfolding of your words gives light; it imparts understanding to the simple. I open my mouth and pant, because I long for your commandments. Turn to me and be gracious to me, as is your way with those who love your name. Keep steady my steps according to your promise, and let no iniquity get dominion over me. Redeem me from man's oppression, that I may keep your precepts. Make your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your statutes. My eyes shed streams of tears, because people do not keep your law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your testimonies are wonderful; therefore my soul keeps them.

He keeps God's word not because he is forced to, but because it is wonderful. Obedience flows from wonder.

The unfolding of your words gives light; it imparts understanding to the simple.

The unfolding — the word means an opening, like a door swung open or a scroll unrolled — lets light in. And the light is for the simple: not the educated elite, but ordinary, unsophisticated people. The Bible is not a puzzle for scholars. When God opens it, a plain person can understand it.

I open my mouth and pant, because I long for your commandments.

The picture is of an animal gasping for water, mouth open. God said in Psalm 81, Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it (81:10). Here is a man with his mouth open, panting for God's word.

Turn to me and be gracious to me, as is your way with those who love your name. Keep steady my steps according to your promise, and let no iniquity get dominion over me. Redeem me from man's oppression, that I may keep your precepts.

Let no iniquity get dominion over me. He is not only afraid of oppressors outside. He is afraid of sin inside, ruling him like a tyrant. He asks God to break its reign.

Make your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your statutes.

The priestly blessing — the LORD make his face to shine upon you (Num 6:25) — turned into a personal prayer.

My eyes shed streams of tears, because people do not keep your law.

And the stanza ends in tears. Not for himself, but for others. He weeps streams because people ignore God's word. Love for Scripture does not make a person proud or harsh toward those who reject it. It makes him weep for them. Jesus wept over Jerusalem. Do we ever weep over those who do not know God's word?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 137–144 — Tsadhe: Your Law Is True
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Righteous are you, O LORD, and right are your rules (v. 137). My zeal consumes me, because my foes forget your words (v. 139). I am small and despised, yet I do not forget your precepts (v. 141). Your righteousness is righteous forever, and your law is true (v. 142); trouble and anguish have found me out, but your commandments are my delight (v. 143).
verseByVerse.theology: Small and despised, the believer rests on a righteousness and a truth that last forever.

verseByVerse.quote: Righteous are you, O LORD, and right are your rules. You have appointed your testimonies in righteousness and in all faithfulness. My zeal consumes me, because my foes forget your words. Your promise is well tried, and your servant loves it. I am small and despised, yet I do not forget your precepts. Your righteousness is righteous forever, and your law is true. Trouble and anguish have found me out, but your commandments are my delight. Your testimonies are righteous forever; give me understanding that I may live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Righteous are you, O LORD, and right are your rules. You have appointed your testimonies in righteousness and in all faithfulness.

This stanza is built on the word righteous. God is righteous, his rules are right, his testimonies were appointed in righteousness. What God says flows from what God is. Paul says the same: the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good (Rom 7:12).

My zeal consumes me, because my foes forget your words. Your promise is well tried, and your servant loves it.

My zeal consumes me — like the man in Psalm 69 who said, zeal for your house has consumed me (69:9). It burns him up that people forget God's words.

Your promise is well tried — refined, like metal tested in the fire and found pure. God's promises have been through every test for thousands of years and have never failed. That is why his servant loves them.

I am small and despised, yet I do not forget your precepts. Your righteousness is righteous forever, and your law is true.

Small and despised. He has no status, no influence, no respect. And yet he holds on to something that is righteous forever and true. The smallness of the believer does not reduce the size of what he believes. On the night before he died, Jesus prayed for his small, frightened disciples, Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth (John 17:17).

Trouble and anguish have found me out, but your commandments are my delight. Your testimonies are righteous forever; give me understanding that I may live.

Trouble and anguish have found me out — tracked him down like hunters. But your commandments are my delight. Trouble and delight in the same verse. That is the Christian life as this psalm describes it: not trouble instead of delight, or delight instead of trouble, but both at once.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 145–152 — Qoph: But You Are Near, O LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With my whole heart I cry; answer me, O LORD! (v. 145). I rise before dawn and cry for help (v. 147). They draw near who persecute me with evil purpose; But you are near, O LORD, and all your commandments are true (vv. 150-151). You have founded them forever (v. 152).
verseByVerse.theology: Enemies come near — and God is nearer.

verseByVerse.quote: With my whole heart I cry; answer me, O LORD! I will keep your statutes. I call to you; save me, that I may observe your testimonies. I rise before dawn and cry for help; I hope in your words. My eyes are awake before the watches of the night, that I may meditate on your promise. Hear my voice according to your steadfast love; O LORD, according to your justice give me life. They draw near who persecute me with evil purpose; they are far from your law. But you are near, O LORD, and all your commandments are true. Long have I known from your testimonies that you have founded them forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With my whole heart I cry; answer me, O LORD! I will keep your statutes. I call to you; save me, that I may observe your testimonies.

The nineteenth stanza is a stanza of prayer, urgent and repeated: I cry, I call, I cry for help. And every request for rescue is joined to a purpose: that I may observe your testimonies. He wants to be saved in order to obey.

I rise before dawn and cry for help; I hope in your words. My eyes are awake before the watches of the night, that I may meditate on your promise.

Before dawn, and before the night watches. He is praying before anyone else is awake, and lying awake meditating when others sleep. For the anxious believer who cannot sleep, this is a model: use the wakeful hours to think over God's promises.

Hear my voice according to your steadfast love; O LORD, according to your justice give me life.

They draw near who persecute me with evil purpose; they are far from your law. But you are near, O LORD, and all your commandments are true.

Here is the heart of the stanza, built on two words: near and far. The persecutors draw near to him — closing in. But they are far from your law. And then: But you are near, O LORD. The enemies are close. God is closer. Whatever is approaching you with evil purpose, the LORD is nearer than it is.

Long have I known from your testimonies that you have founded them forever.

Not a new discovery. Long have I known. A lifetime of reading God's word has taught him that it is founded forever. Experience confirms Scripture.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 153–160 — Resh: Plead My Cause and Redeem Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Look on my affliction and deliver me (v. 153). Plead my cause and redeem me; give me life according to your promise! (v. 154). Great is your mercy, O LORD (v. 156). The sum of your word is truth, and every one of your righteous rules endures forever (v. 160).
verseByVerse.theology: The afflicted man asks God to be his advocate and redeemer, and rests on the whole of his word.

verseByVerse.quote: Look on my affliction and deliver me, for I do not forget your law. Plead my cause and redeem me; give me life according to your promise! Salvation is far from the wicked, for they do not seek your statutes. Great is your mercy, O LORD; give me life according to your rules. Many are my persecutors and my adversaries, but I do not swerve from your testimonies. I look at the faithless with disgust, because they do not keep your commands. Consider how I love your precepts! Give me life, O LORD, according to your steadfast love. The sum of your word is truth, and every one of your righteous rules endures forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look on my affliction and deliver me, for I do not forget your law. Plead my cause and redeem me; give me life according to your promise!

Two legal pictures. Plead my cause — be my advocate in court, argue my case. Redeem me — the word for a kinsman who buys back a relative from debt or slavery. He asks God to be both his lawyer and his next of kin.

That is exactly who Christ is for his people. We have an advocate with the Father, and he is the kinsman who became flesh and blood in order to redeem us.

Salvation is far from the wicked, for they do not seek your statutes. Great is your mercy, O LORD; give me life according to your rules.

Salvation is far from those who do not seek God's word — the same near-and-far picture as the last stanza. And his hope is not his own goodness but great is your mercy.

Many are my persecutors and my adversaries, but I do not swerve from your testimonies. I look at the faithless with disgust, because they do not keep your commands. Consider how I love your precepts! Give me life, O LORD, according to your steadfast love.

Three times in this stanza he asks, give me life (vv. 154, 156, 159) — according to God's promise, rules and steadfast love. The life he needs comes from God's word and God's character together.

The sum of your word is truth, and every one of your righteous rules endures forever.

The sum — the whole of it, added up. Not merely that God's word contains truth, or is mostly true, but that the total is truth. And every one of his rules endures. Nothing in it expires. A believer can trust not just the parts of Scripture he likes, but the sum.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 161–168 — Sin and Shin: Like One Who Finds Great Spoil
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Princes persecute me without cause, but my heart stands in awe of your words (v. 161). I rejoice at your word like one who finds great spoil (v. 162). Seven times a day I praise you (v. 164). Great peace have those who love your law; nothing can make them stumble (v. 165). All my ways are before you (v. 168).
verseByVerse.theology: A man who fears God's words more than princes finds treasure, peace and praise seven times a day.

verseByVerse.quote: Princes persecute me without cause, but my heart stands in awe of your words. I rejoice at your word like one who finds great spoil. I hate and abhor falsehood, but I love your law. Seven times a day I praise you for your righteous rules. Great peace have those who love your law; nothing can make them stumble. I hope for your salvation, O LORD, and I do your commandments. My soul keeps your testimonies; I love them exceedingly. I keep your precepts and testimonies, for all my ways are before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Princes persecute me without cause, but my heart stands in awe of your words.

Powerful men persecute him. He should be terrified of them. But his heart stands in awe — trembles — before something else: God's words. The fear of God drives out the fear of princes. Whoever fears God's word most will fear everything else less.

I rejoice at your word like one who finds great spoil.

The picture is of a soldier after battle stumbling on a great treasure left behind by the enemy. Sudden, unexpected, overwhelming joy. Jesus described the kingdom that way: like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has (Matt 13:44). A believer reading Scripture can have that experience again and again — a verse read a hundred times suddenly opening like a chest of gold.

I hate and abhor falsehood, but I love your law. Seven times a day I praise you for your righteous rules.

Seven times a day — the number of completeness. Praise woven through the whole day, not reserved for one hour a week.

Great peace have those who love your law; nothing can make them stumble.

Not small peace; great peace. And not because nothing bad happens — this psalm is full of persecution and affliction — but because nothing can make them stumble. Their footing is sure, because it rests on the word that is fixed in the heavens.

I hope for your salvation, O LORD, and I do your commandments. My soul keeps your testimonies; I love them exceedingly. I keep your precepts and testimonies, for all my ways are before you.

All my ways are before you. He lives openly before God, hiding nothing. That is not a claim to perfection — the final stanza will make that plain — but a life lived in God's sight.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Let my cry come before you, O LORD (v. 169). My lips will pour forth praise (v. 171). Let my soul live and praise you (v. 175). I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant, for I do not forget your commandments (v. 176).
verseByVerse.theology: The longest psalm ends not with a boast of obedience but with a lost sheep asking to be found.

verseByVerse.quote: Let my cry come before you, O LORD; give me understanding according to your word! Let my plea come before you; deliver me according to your word. My lips will pour forth praise, for you teach me your statutes. My tongue will sing of your word, for all your commandments are right. Let your hand be ready to help me, for I have chosen your precepts. I long for your salvation, O LORD, and your law is my delight. Let my soul live and praise you, and let your rules help me. I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant, for I do not forget your commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let my cry come before you, O LORD; give me understanding according to your word! Let my plea come before you; deliver me according to your word.

The last stanza gathers up the whole psalm into prayer. Cry, plea, understanding, deliverance — all according to your word.

My lips will pour forth praise, for you teach me your statutes. My tongue will sing of your word, for all your commandments are right.

Lips and tongue: the word taken in comes out as song. The end of Bible reading is not only knowledge but worship.

Let your hand be ready to help me, for I have chosen your precepts. I long for your salvation, O LORD, and your law is my delight. Let my soul live and praise you, and let your rules help me.

A final triple request: help me, save me, let me live. And why does he want to live? To praise God: let my soul live and praise you.

I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant, for I do not forget your commandments.

And here is the last verse of the longest psalm in the Bible, and it is astonishing. After 175 verses of love for God's law — delight, meditation, obedience, zeal, tears — the singer does not end with a claim to have kept it all. He ends with a confession: I have gone astray like a lost sheep.

That changes how the whole psalm should be read. This is not a proud man listing his achievements. It is a man who loves God's word with all his heart and still wanders, and knows it. He does not say "I will find my way back". He says seek your servant. The sheep cannot find the shepherd. The shepherd has to come looking.

And the shepherd did. Jesus told of a man who, having a hundred sheep and losing one, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing (Luke 15:4-5). The psalm that is all about God's word ends by asking for the Word made flesh — the Good Shepherd who seeks and carries home every lost sheep who cries, seek your servant.

119.title: Your Word Is a Lamp to My Feet
119.overview:
The longest psalm is an acrostic of twenty-two stanzas, each of eight verses beginning with the same Hebrew letter, and almost every verse speaks of God's word under its many names: law, testimonies, precepts, statutes, commandments, rules, word, promise. It opens with a blessing on those who walk in the law (vv. 1-8) and moves through a young man keeping his way pure by the word stored in his heart (vv. 9-16), a sojourner asking for opened eyes (vv. 17-24), a soul in the dust given life and set running (vv. 25-32), and prayers for a heart inclined to God and eyes turned from worthless things (vv. 33-40).

The singer walks in a wide place (vv. 41-48), sings God's statutes in the house of his sojourning (vv. 49-56), calls the LORD his portion (vv. 57-64), finds affliction good and faithful (vv. 65-80), and nearly perishes like a wineskin in the smoke (vv. 81-88) before confessing that God's word is fixed forever in heaven (vv. 89-96). He loves the law and tastes it like honey (vv. 97-104), walks by its lamp (vv. 105-112), hides in God and trembles before him (vv. 113-120), loves the law more as it is broken (vv. 121-128), weeps for those who ignore it (vv. 129-136), rests on its truth (vv. 137-144), finds God nearer than his enemies (vv. 145-152), asks God to plead his cause (vv. 153-160), and rejoices in the word like one who finds great spoil (vv. 161-168). It ends: I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant (v. 176).
119.theology:
God's word, in all its forms, is the expression of his righteous, faithful character (vv. 137-138; Rom 7:12), fixed forever (v. 89; Isa 40:8), true in its sum (v. 160; John 17:17), and life-giving (vv. 25, 50, 93; Deut 8:3; Matt 4:4).

Love for the law is not legalism: its commands lead to God himself (v. 2), bring freedom (v. 45; Jas 1:25), and are kept out of love (vv. 47-48, 97; John 14:15). Understanding requires God to open the eyes (v. 18; Luke 24:45), and Scripture stored in the heart guards against sin (v. 11; Col 3:16).

Affliction is God's faithful teaching (vv. 67, 71, 75; Heb 12:11). The word guides step by step (v. 105; 2 Pet 1:19), gives wisdom to the simple (vv. 98-100, 130; 2 Tim 3:16), and great peace to those who love it (v. 165).

The psalm ends not in self-righteousness but in confession and dependence: the lost sheep must be sought (v. 176), as the Good Shepherd does (Luke 15:4-6).
119.examples:
A love song to God's word from A to Z.

Scripture stored up like treasure, there when temptation comes.

Open my eyes — before you open your Bible.

From clinging to the dust to clinging to the word.

Commands that turn out to be open country.

Statutes sung like songs of home at an inn.

It was good for me that I was afflicted — said from the other side.

A wineskin shrivelled in the smoke, contents kept.

A lamp that lights the next step, not the whole road.

The enemies are near; God is nearer.

Treasure found after the battle.

The longest psalm ends: seek your servant.

120.text: A Song of Ascents. 1In my distress I called to the LORD, and he answered me.2Deliver me, O LORD, from lying lips, from a deceitful tongue.3What shall be given to you, and what more shall be done to you, you deceitful tongue?4A warrior's sharp arrows, with glowing coals of the broom tree!5Woe to me, that I sojourn in Meshech, that I dwell among the tents of Kedar!6Too long have I had my dwelling among those who hate peace.7I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Deliver Me from Lying Lips
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In my distress I called to the LORD, and he answered me (v. 1). Deliver me, O LORD, from lying lips, from a deceitful tongue (v. 2). What shall be given to you, and what more shall be done to you, you deceitful tongue? A warrior's sharp arrows, with glowing coals of the broom tree! (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: The first song of the pilgrim road begins with a man surrounded by lies.

verseByVerse.quote: In my distress I called to the LORD, and he answered me. Deliver me, O LORD, from lying lips, from a deceitful tongue.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In my distress I called to the LORD, and he answered me.

With this psalm a new group begins. Fifteen psalms in a row (120-134) carry the title A Song of Ascents. Jerusalem stood on a hill, and everyone going to it went up; Psalm 122 speaks of the city to which the tribes go up (122:4). These were very probably the songs pilgrims sang on the road to the festivals — short, memorable, full of the journey.

And the first song of the journey does not begin in Jerusalem. It begins as far from Jerusalem as the singer can imagine, in trouble. Every pilgrimage to God starts with some dissatisfaction with where you are.

He begins with a memory: In my distress I called to the LORD, and he answered me. He has prayed before and been heard. That past answer is the ground for the prayer he is about to pray.

Deliver me, O LORD, from lying lips, from a deceitful tongue.

The trouble is words. Lies, deceit, slander. It does not sound as dramatic as an army, but anyone who has been lied about at work, in a family or in a church knows how deeply it wounds, and how helpless it makes you feel. You cannot answer every lie. You can bring them to God.

verseByVerse.quote: What shall be given to you, and what more shall be done to you, you deceitful tongue? A warrior's sharp arrows, with glowing coals of the broom tree!
verseByVerse.commentary:
What shall be given to you, and what more shall be done to you, you deceitful tongue?

Now he turns and speaks directly to the tongue itself, as if it were a person. What will your punishment be?

A warrior's sharp arrows, with glowing coals of the broom tree!

The punishment fits the crime. A lying tongue shoots words like arrows and sets things on fire, so God's judgment will be arrows and fire in return. The broom tree grows in the desert, and its wood makes charcoal that burns long and very hot. James says the same of the tongue: the tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness ... setting on fire the entire course of life, and set on fire by hell (Jas 3:6).

The singer does not shoot back. He leaves the arrows and the coals to God. That is the believer's freedom when slandered: the deceitful tongue will be answered, and you do not have to be the one who answers it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–7 — Among Those Who Hate Peace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Woe to me, that I sojourn in Meshech, that I dwell among the tents of Kedar! (v. 5). Too long have I had my dwelling among those who hate peace (v. 6). I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war! (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The journey to God's city begins with the ache of living among people who want a fight.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to me, that I sojourn in Meshech, that I dwell among the tents of Kedar! Too long have I had my dwelling among those who hate peace. I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to me, that I sojourn in Meshech, that I dwell among the tents of Kedar!

Two place names, and they point in opposite directions. Meshech was one of the sons of Japheth (Gen 10:2), a people of the far north. Kedar was a son of Ishmael (Gen 25:13), the ancestor of desert tribes to the south and east. No one could live in both places at once. The singer is not giving his address. He is describing his company: he feels like a foreigner stranded among wild, distant, hostile peoples.

Too long have I had my dwelling among those who hate peace.

That is what Meshech and Kedar mean to him: people who hate peace. And he has lived among them too long. The weariness is real.

I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war!

In Hebrew the first half is almost just "I — peace". That is who he is. But the moment he opens his mouth, they reach for weapons. Some people cannot be reconciled with however gently you speak.

Paul's instruction fits exactly: If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Rom 12:18). If possible — because sometimes it is not. So far as it depends on you — because your part is to be for peace, even when they are for war.

And the psalm ends there, unresolved, in Meshech. It does not reach Jerusalem. That is how the pilgrimage begins: not with arrival, but with longing — a person who is tired of the tents of Kedar and has started to look toward the city of peace. The next psalm lifts its eyes to the hills.

120.title: I Am for Peace
120.overview: The first Song of Ascents. The psalmist, answered by God in past distress, asks to be delivered from lying lips and a deceitful tongue (vv. 1-2), and declares that the tongue will be repaid with a warrior's arrows and burning coals (vv. 3-4). He laments that he lives as a stranger in Meshech and Kedar among people who hate peace: I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war! (vv. 5-7).
120.theology:
The Songs of Ascents (120-134) were probably sung on pilgrimage to Jerusalem; this first one begins far from Zion, in distress, as every journey toward God begins in discontent with where one is.

Past answers to prayer ground present petitions (v. 1). Lying tongues are fire and will be judged in kind (vv. 3-4; Jas 3:6), and vengeance is left to God.

Meshech and Kedar describe hostile company rather than a literal address (v. 5; Gen 10:2; 25:13). The believer is to be for peace even when others are for war (v. 7; Rom 12:18).
120.examples:
Fifteen songs for the road up to Jerusalem.

A pilgrimage that begins with being tired of where you are.

Lied about, and unable to answer every lie.

Broom-tree charcoal: a fire that burns long.

Two addresses no one could have at once.

I am for peace — and they reach for weapons.

So far as it depends on you.

121.text: A Song of Ascents. 1I lift up my eyes to the hills. From where does my help come?2My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth.3He will not let your foot be moved; he who keeps you will not slumber.4Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.5The LORD is your keeper; the LORD is your shade on your right hand.6The sun shall not strike you by day, nor the moon by night.7The LORD will keep you from all evil; he will keep your life.8The LORD will keep your going out and your coming in from this time forth and forevermore.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — I Lift Up My Eyes to the Hills
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I lift up my eyes to the hills. From where does my help come? (v. 1). My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth (v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology: A pilgrim looks up at the hills and asks where help will come from — and answers with the Maker of the hills.

verseByVerse.quote: I lift up my eyes to the hills. From where does my help come? My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I lift up my eyes to the hills. From where does my help come?

The second Song of Ascents, and the pilgrim is on the road. Ahead of him are the hills — the hill country of Judah, with Jerusalem somewhere among them. He lifts his eyes and asks a question.

The hills can be read two ways, and both help. They were dangerous: steep paths, ravines, robbers waiting in the rocks, exhausting climbs in the heat. Looking up at them, a traveller would feel his need. And the hilltops were where the shrines of other gods stood, the high places where people went looking for help. Either way, the question is the same: From where does my help come? Not from the hills themselves.

My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth.

The answer looks past the hills to the one who made them. Whatever is on the hilltops — danger or false gods — was made by the LORD, or is nothing at all. The traveller's help comes from the Maker of every hill he must climb. The same confession returns in Psalm 124, in the plural: Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth (124:8).

This is where every believer's security has to start. Not with the size of the problem ahead, but with the size of the God who made it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–8 — He Who Keeps Israel Will Neither Slumber nor Sleep
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He will not let your foot be moved; he who keeps you will not slumber (v. 3). Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep (v. 4). The LORD is your keeper; the LORD is your shade on your right hand (v. 5), by day and night (v. 6). The LORD will keep you from all evil; he will keep your life. The LORD will keep your going out and your coming in from this time forth and forevermore (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Six times in six verses: the LORD keeps — awake all night, at every step, for the whole journey of life.

verseByVerse.quote: He will not let your foot be moved; he who keeps you will not slumber. Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will not let your foot be moved; he who keeps you will not slumber.

Now a different voice answers. The first two verses said my help; from here to the end it is your keeper, keep you. It may be a priest blessing the pilgrims, or a fellow traveller, or the singer preaching to himself. Either way, the promise comes from outside him, as a word to hold on to.

He will not let your foot be moved. On a rocky mountain path, one slip could be fatal. God watches every step.

Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.

Pilgrims camped at night on the road, and someone had to stay awake to watch. Human watchmen doze off. God does not. When Elijah faced the prophets of Baal, he mocked their god: perhaps he is asleep and must be awakened (1 Kgs 18:27). The LORD is not like that. He does not faint or grow weary (Isa 40:28).

That is a verse for the night. When you lie awake at 3 a.m. with everything you cannot control, there is no need for you to stay on watch. Someone else is awake. You can sleep because he does not.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is your keeper; the LORD is your shade on your right hand. The sun shall not strike you by day, nor the moon by night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is your keeper; the LORD is your shade on your right hand.

Here is the heart of the psalm in four words: The LORD is your keeper. The word keep is the psalm's great word. Count it through verses 3 to 8: keeps you, keeps Israel, your keeper, keep you, keep your life, keep your going out. Six times in six verses. A keeper is a guard, a watchman, a shepherd — someone responsible for your safety.

And he is your shade on your right hand. On a road in the Judean summer, shade was life. The right hand is the side of help and protection. God walks beside the traveller like a moving shadow, keeping the sun off him.

The sun shall not strike you by day, nor the moon by night.

The sun could kill a traveller with heatstroke. The moon was also feared in the ancient world, as though it could harm people sleeping in the open. The psalm covers both: every danger of the day, every fear of the night. There is no hour when the keeper is off duty.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD will keep you from all evil; he will keep your life. The LORD will keep your going out and your coming in from this time forth and forevermore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD will keep you from all evil; he will keep your life.

From all evil. This does not mean a believer will never suffer — the Psalms are full of suffering believers. It means that no evil will ever get past God to destroy the life he keeps. He will keep your life — your soul, your self. Jesus said of his disciples, I kept them in your name ... and not one of them has been lost (John 17:12). Peter says believers are by God's power ... being guarded through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed (1 Pet 1:5). And Jude closes his letter with praise to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24).

The LORD will keep your going out and your coming in from this time forth and forevermore.

Going out and coming in is a Hebrew way of saying everything: leaving home in the morning and coming back at night, setting out on the pilgrimage and returning, starting a job and finishing it, being born and dying. All of it kept. And not for a season: from this time forth and forevermore.

God said the same to Jacob when he set out alone on a long journey, afraid and far from home: Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back (Gen 28:15). Every believer is on a journey like that. You will go out tomorrow and come in tomorrow night, and one day you will go out of this world. The same keeper watches over every step of it, and he will bring you home.

121.title: The LORD Is Your Keeper
121.overview: A pilgrim lifts his eyes to the hills and asks where his help comes from: from the LORD, who made heaven and earth (vv. 1-2). A second voice answers: the LORD will not let his foot slip; the keeper of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps (vv. 3-4). The LORD is your keeper, his shade at his right hand, so that neither sun nor moon will strike him (vv. 5-6). The LORD will keep him from all evil and keep his life, his going out and coming in, forever (vv. 7-8).
121.theology:
Help comes not from the hills, whether dangers or shrines, but from their Maker (vv. 1-2; 124:8).

God is the ever-watchful keeper, unlike idols that sleep (vv. 3-4; 1 Kgs 18:27; Isa 40:28). The word keep dominates the psalm, covering every step, every hour, day and night (vv. 3-6).

Keeping from all evil means that no evil can destroy the life God keeps, not that suffering never comes (v. 7). The keeping extends to the whole course of life and beyond (v. 8; Gen 28:15), fulfilled in Christ's keeping of his own (John 17:12; 1 Pet 1:5; Jude 24).
121.examples:
Looking at the hills, and past them to their Maker.

The size of the God who made the problem.

A watchman who never dozes off.

You can sleep because he does not.

A moving shadow on the right hand in the summer heat.

Six times: keep.

Going out tomorrow, coming in tomorrow night — kept.

122.text: A Song of Ascents. Of David. 1I was glad when they said to me, "Let us go to the house of the LORD!"2Our feet have been standing within your gates, O Jerusalem!3Jerusalem— built as a city that is bound firmly together,4to which the tribes go up, the tribes of the LORD, as was decreed for Israel, to give thanks to the name of the LORD.5There thrones for judgment were set, the thrones of the house of David.6Pray for the peace of Jerusalem! "May they be secure who love you!7Peace be within your walls and security within your towers!"8For my brothers and companions' sake I will say, "Peace be within you!"9For the sake of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek your good.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Let Us Go to the House of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I was glad when they said to me, Let us go to the house of the LORD! (v. 1). Our feet have been standing within your gates, O Jerusalem! (v. 2). The city is bound firmly together, where the tribes go up to give thanks (vv. 3-4), and where thrones for judgment were set, the thrones of the house of David (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The pilgrim arrives, remembers the invitation that started the journey, and looks around the city with joy.

verseByVerse.quote: I was glad when they said to me, "Let us go to the house of the LORD!" Our feet have been standing within your gates, O Jerusalem!
verseByVerse.commentary:
I was glad when they said to me, Let us go to the house of the LORD!

The third Song of Ascents, and the pilgrim has arrived. He looks back to the moment the journey began: someone came to him and said, Let us go. And he was glad.

Notice two things. The invitation came from others — they said to me. Worship is not a private hobby; believers call one another to it. And the response was gladness, not duty. Going to God's house was the thing he wanted to do.

That is a fair test of a heart. When someone says, "Let's go to church," or "Let's pray together," or "Let's open the Bible", what rises in you first? Gladness, reluctance, or boredom? This psalm describes a person for whom the answer is gladness, and it invites every believer to ask God for that heart.

Our feet have been standing within your gates, O Jerusalem!

After days on the road, dusty and tired, the pilgrims are standing inside the gates. The journey is over. He savours it: our feet — plural — are here, together.

verseByVerse.quote: Jerusalem— built as a city that is bound firmly together, to which the tribes go up, the tribes of the LORD, as was decreed for Israel, to give thanks to the name of the LORD. There thrones for judgment were set, the thrones of the house of David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem — built as a city that is bound firmly together, to which the tribes go up, the tribes of the LORD, as was decreed for Israel, to give thanks to the name of the LORD.

He looks around at the city. It is bound firmly together — compact, its houses and walls joined closely, a picture of solidity and unity. And that fits its purpose: it is where the tribes, scattered across the country, all come up together. Twelve tribes, often at odds with one another, gathered in one city for one reason: to give thanks to the name of the LORD. (The ESV notes the phrase as was decreed for may be read "as a testimony for".)

That is what God's people become when they gather to worship: a scattered people bound firmly together. Paul says Christ has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility (Eph 2:14).

There thrones for judgment were set, the thrones of the house of David.

Jerusalem was also the seat of justice, where David's line judged the people. Worship and justice lived in the same city. A place where people give thanks to God should also be a place where wrongs are set right.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — Peace Be Within Your Walls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem! May they be secure who love you! (v. 6). Peace be within your walls and security within your towers! (v. 7). For my brothers and companions' sake I will say, Peace be within you! (v. 8). For the sake of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek your good (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Standing in the city, the pilgrim prays for its peace — for his brothers' sake, and for God's house.

verseByVerse.quote: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem! "May they be secure who love you! Peace be within your walls and security within your towers!" For my brothers and companions' sake I will say, "Peace be within you!" For the sake of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek your good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pray for the peace of Jerusalem! May they be secure who love you!
