Now the pilgrim turns from looking to praying. Pray for the peace of Jerusalem. The word peace comes three times in three verses (vv. 6, 7, 8), and the city was once the Salem where Melchizedek was king (Gen 14:18) — king of Salem, that is, king of peace (Heb 7:2). The city of peace is to be prayed for, because it so seldom had any.

Peace here is more than the absence of war. It is wholeness, well-being, everything as it should be. And may they be secure who love you — prosperity and safety for those who love God's city.

Peace be within your walls and security within your towers!

Walls and towers were the city's defences. He prays that inside them there will be peace, not just strength.

For my brothers and companions' sake I will say, Peace be within you! For the sake of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek your good.

And two reasons for the prayer. First, for my brothers and companions' sake — the people he travelled with, who live there, who will be there next year. Love for the city is love for the people in it. Second, for the sake of the house of the LORD our God — because God put his name there. He will not only wish the city well; he will seek your good, work for it.

Jesus came to this city and wept over it: Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! (Luke 19:42). The earthly Jerusalem rejected its King. But believers have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22), and the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother (Gal 4:26).

So how does a Christian pray this psalm? By praying for the peace of God's people — the church, gathered in congregations all over the world, the city of God on earth. Pray for peace within its walls: for unity, for sound teaching, for love between brothers. For your companions' sake, and for the sake of the house of the LORD, seek its good.

122.title: Pray for the Peace of Jerusalem
122.overview: The psalmist remembers his gladness when others invited him to go to the house of the LORD, and now stands within Jerusalem's gates (vv. 1-2). The city is firmly bound together, the place where the tribes go up to give thanks to the LORD's name and where David's thrones of judgment stand (vv. 3-5). He calls for prayer for Jerusalem's peace and the security of those who love her, blesses her with peace for the sake of his brothers, and resolves to seek her good for the sake of the LORD's house (vv. 6-9).
122.theology:
Worship is a shared joy to which believers invite one another (v. 1). God's city binds together a scattered people in thanksgiving (vv. 3-4; Eph 2:14), and justice belongs beside worship (v. 5).

Prayer for the peace of God's city (vv. 6-8) flows from love for fellow believers and for God's house (vv. 8-9). The earthly city missed the things that make for peace (Luke 19:42); Christians belong to the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22; Gal 4:26) and pray for the peace and good of the church.
122.examples:
Someone said, "Let's go" — and he was glad.

Dusty feet standing inside the gates.

Twelve quarrelsome tribes bound into one city.

Worship and justice in the same streets.

The city of peace, prayed for because it so seldom had any.

For my brothers' sake.

Praying for peace within the walls of the church.

123.text: A Song of Ascents. 1To you I lift up my eyes, O you who are enthroned in the heavens!2Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master, as the eyes of a maidservant to the hand of her mistress, so our eyes look to the LORD our God, till he has mercy upon us.3Have mercy upon us, O LORD, have mercy upon us, for we have had more than enough of contempt.4Our soul has had more than enough of the scorn of those who are at ease, of the contempt of the proud.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Till He Has Mercy upon Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To you I lift up my eyes, O you who are enthroned in the heavens! (v. 1). As the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master ... so our eyes look to the LORD our God, till he has mercy upon us (v. 2). Have mercy upon us, O LORD, have mercy upon us, for we have had more than enough of contempt (v. 3), of the contempt of the proud (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: A people worn out by contempt fix their eyes on God's hand and wait for mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: To you I lift up my eyes, O you who are enthroned in the heavens! Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master, as the eyes of a maidservant to the hand of her mistress, so our eyes look to the LORD our God, till he has mercy upon us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To you I lift up my eyes, O you who are enthroned in the heavens!

Two psalms ago the pilgrim lifted his eyes to the hills (121:1). Now he lifts them higher: to you ... enthroned in the heavens. The first look was a question about where help might come from. This one goes straight to the throne.

Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master, as the eyes of a maidservant to the hand of her mistress, so our eyes look to the LORD our God, till he has mercy upon us.

The picture comes from any large household of the time. Servants stood silently at the edge of the room, their eyes fixed on the master's hand. A gesture of that hand told them everything: bring the food, clear the table, you may go, come here. Their whole day depended on watching it. And the same was true of a maidservant watching her mistress.

That is how the psalm says God's people look to him. Not casually, not now and then, but steadily, attentively, waiting for his signal. And waiting till he has mercy upon us. The word till matters. They do not look away when the answer does not come at once. They keep watching the hand.

The Canaanite woman in the Gospels did exactly this. When Jesus seemed to refuse her, she said, Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table (Matt 15:27). Her eyes were on the master's hand, and she would not look away until mercy came. It came. The writer to the Hebrews gives the same instruction for the whole Christian life: looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith (Heb 12:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Have mercy upon us, O LORD, have mercy upon us, for we have had more than enough of contempt. Our soul has had more than enough of the scorn of those who are at ease, of the contempt of the proud.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have mercy upon us, O LORD, have mercy upon us, for we have had more than enough of contempt.

Now the reason for the watching. Have mercy, twice, and then the need: we have had more than enough of contempt. The Hebrew picture is of being filled to the full, glutted, fed until you cannot take any more. They have eaten contempt until they are sick of it.

Our soul has had more than enough of the scorn of those who are at ease, of the contempt of the proud.

And the people pouring the scorn are described precisely: those who are at ease and the proud. Comfortable people, secure, successful, untroubled, looking down on believers who are struggling. Their contempt is the sneer of those who have never needed mercy and cannot imagine why anyone would wait on God for it.

Many Christians know this experience. It is not persecution with prisons and swords; it is the quieter, wearing contempt of a culture that finds faith naive, a colleague who smirks, a family member who treats belief as a weakness. It can wear you down more than open hostility.

The psalm does not answer the scorners. It does not argue with them or try to win their respect. It turns its eyes to the master's hand and asks for mercy. And the New Testament adds a surprising word: If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you (1 Pet 4:14). The contempt of the comfortable is not the last word. The mercy of the one enthroned in the heavens is.

The psalm ends there, still waiting, still watching. Four verses, and no answer yet. That is honest. Some seasons of the Christian life are simply this: eyes on the hand, and till he has mercy.

123.title: Our Eyes Look to the LORD
123.overview: The psalmist lifts his eyes to God enthroned in heaven (v. 1). As servants watch their master's hand and a maidservant her mistress's, so God's people look to the LORD until he shows mercy (v. 2). They plead for mercy, for they have had more than enough of the scorn of the comfortable and the contempt of the proud (vv. 3-4).
123.theology:
Dependence on God is steady, attentive watching of his hand, persisting till he shows mercy (v. 2; Matt 15:27; Heb 12:2).

Believers may be glutted with the contempt of the comfortable and proud (vv. 3-4). The response is not argument but a plea for mercy, and those insulted for Christ's name are blessed (1 Pet 4:14).
123.examples:
From the hills to the throne.

Servants at the edge of the room, watching the hand.

The Canaanite woman who would not look away.

Fed on contempt until sick of it.

The smirk of the comfortable.

Four verses, and still waiting.

124.text: A Song of Ascents. Of David. 1If it had not been the LORD who was on our side— let Israel now say—2if it had not been the LORD who was on our side when people rose up against us,3then they would have swallowed us up alive, when their anger was kindled against us;4then the flood would have swept us away, the torrent would have gone over us;5then over us would have gone the raging waters.6Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as prey to their teeth!7We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we have escaped!8Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — If It Had Not Been the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If it had not been the LORD who was on our side — let Israel now say — if it had not been the LORD who was on our side when people rose up against us, then they would have swallowed us up alive (vv. 1-3); then the flood would have swept us away (v. 4); then over us would have gone the raging waters (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: A people look back at how close they came to being destroyed, and see only one reason they survived.

verseByVerse.quote: If it had not been the LORD who was on our side— let Israel now say— if it had not been the LORD who was on our side when people rose up against us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
If it had not been the LORD who was on our side — let Israel now say —

This Song of Ascents begins with a leader calling out a line and then telling the crowd to say it back: let Israel now say. And the people repeat it: if it had not been the LORD who was on our side.

if it had not been the LORD who was on our side when people rose up against us,

The whole psalm hangs on one word: if. It looks back at a moment of terrible danger and imagines the alternative. What would have happened if the LORD had not been on our side? It is a healthy exercise. Most of us remember our rescues vaguely and forget how close we came. This psalm makes the congregation stop and trace the other road — the one where God was not there.

Paul asked the same question the other way round: If God is for us, who can be against us? (Rom 8:31). The psalm answers from experience: people rose up against us, and they could not win, because the LORD was on our side.

verseByVerse.quote: then they would have swallowed us up alive, when their anger was kindled against us; then the flood would have swept us away, the torrent would have gone over us; then over us would have gone the raging waters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
then they would have swallowed us up alive, when their anger was kindled against us;

Now the three thens — three pictures of what would have happened. First, the enemy as a monster with an open mouth, or the earth itself opening: swallowed us up alive. Israel remembered the day the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the rebels in the wilderness (Num 16:32). Without God, that would have been them.

then the flood would have swept us away, the torrent would have gone over us; then over us would have gone the raging waters.

Then a flash flood — a torrent — tearing down a dry valley after a storm, the kind that sweeps away anything in its path in minutes. Swept away, gone over us, raging waters: the image builds, wave on wave, the way the danger felt.

God promised exactly the opposite through Isaiah: When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you (Isa 43:2). The waters come. They do not overwhelm. Paul described being so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself — and then: He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us (2 Cor 1:8, 10).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–8 — We Have Escaped Like a Bird
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as prey to their teeth! (v. 6). We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we have escaped! (v. 7). Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The trap broke, the bird flew free, and the credit goes to the Maker of heaven and earth.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as prey to their teeth! We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we have escaped!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as prey to their teeth!

A third image of the enemy: wild animals with teeth, and God's people as the prey. But God did not hand them over. And the response to looking back at how close it was is not relief alone, but worship: Blessed be the LORD.

We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we have escaped!

The most vivid picture in the psalm. A small bird caught in a hunter's net or trap — helpless, flapping, waiting for the fowler to come. And then the snare is broken. Notice the grammar. The bird did not break it. Birds cannot break traps. The snare was broken for it, and the bird simply flew.

That is the shape of every true rescue by God, and above all of the gospel. We were caught — in sin, guilt, the power of death — and could not free ourselves. Christ broke the snare. Our part was to fly out of the open trap. We have escaped! — said twice, as if they can hardly believe it.

verseByVerse.quote: Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth.

And the psalm closes with a confession many churches still use to open their worship. Three psalms ago, a single pilgrim said, My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth (121:2). Now the whole congregation says it together: Our help. One person's trust has become a people's testimony.

In the name of the LORD — in who he has revealed himself to be. And he is the one who made heaven and earth. The flood, the teeth, the fowlers, the traps are all inside his creation. The Maker of everything was on our side, so none of it could win.

Try the exercise of this psalm on your own life. Think of the worst moment you have come through. Now say, honestly: "If it had not been the LORD who was on my side" — where would I be? Then say the last verse, and mean it.

124.title: The Snare Is Broken
124.overview: Israel is called to confess that if the LORD had not been on their side when people rose against them, they would have been swallowed alive, swept away by the flood and overwhelmed by raging waters (vv. 1-5). Blessed be the LORD, who did not give them as prey to their enemies' teeth; like a bird, they escaped the fowlers' snare when it was broken (vv. 6-7). Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth (v. 8).
124.theology:
Remembering deliverance includes tracing what would have happened without God (vv. 1-5), so that survival is credited to him alone (Rom 8:31). The waters come, but do not overwhelm those God is with (Isa 43:2; 2 Cor 1:8-10).

Rescue is God's act: the snare is broken for the bird, not by it (v. 7), a picture of the gospel. The personal confession of 121:2 becomes the congregation's: our help is in the name of the Creator (v. 8).
124.examples:
A leader calls out a line; the crowd says it back.

Tracing the other road, where God was not there.

A flash flood down a dry valley.

Birds cannot break traps.

We have escaped! — twice, as if hard to believe.

My help becomes our help.

Where would I be if the LORD had not been on my side?

125.text: A Song of Ascents. 1Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved, but abides forever.2As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds his people, from this time forth and forevermore.3For the scepter of wickedness shall not rest on the land allotted to the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to do wrong.4Do good, O LORD, to those who are good, and to those who are upright in their hearts!5But those who turn aside to their crooked ways the LORD will lead away with evildoers! Peace be upon Israel!

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved, but abides forever (v. 1). As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds his people, from this time forth and forevermore (v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology: Pilgrims see the hills ringing Jerusalem and are told that God surrounds his people like that.

verseByVerse.quote: Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved, but abides forever. As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds his people, from this time forth and forevermore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved, but abides forever.

The pilgrims are near Jerusalem now, and the psalm uses what they can see. Mount Zion stands in front of them — solid rock, unmoved through every storm and every generation. Those who trust in the LORD are like that.

Notice what the comparison is. It is not that believers are strong. It is that those who trust are immovable, because of what they trust. A mountain does not hold itself up. And the stability is forever. The kingdom they belong to cannot be shaken (Heb 12:28).

As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds his people, from this time forth and forevermore.

Now the pilgrim lifts his eyes from the city to the hills around it. Jerusalem sat in a ring of higher ground — the Mount of Olives to the east, ridges on the other sides — like a city held in cupped hands. So the LORD surrounds his people.

Elisha's servant once woke to find an army surrounding their town, and panicked. Elisha prayed, O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see, and the young man saw the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha (2 Kgs 6:17). The enemy surrounded the city; God surrounded the enemy.

And even mountains are only a picture. God said through Isaiah, the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but my steadfast love shall not depart from you (Isa 54:10). The hills around Jerusalem are the best image a pilgrim could see. God's surrounding care is more permanent than they are.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For the scepter of wickedness shall not rest on the land allotted to the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to do wrong (v. 3). Do good, O LORD, to those who are good (v. 4). But those who turn aside to their crooked ways the LORD will lead away with evildoers! Peace be upon Israel! (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: God sets a limit to the rule of the wicked, so that it does not bend the righteous out of shape.

verseByVerse.quote: For the scepter of wickedness shall not rest on the land allotted to the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to do wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the scepter of wickedness shall not rest on the land allotted to the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to do wrong.

This is one of the most perceptive verses in the Songs of Ascents. The scepter of wickedness is the rule of evil people — oppression, injustice in power. It may come on God's people for a time. But it will not rest there, settle permanently. God sets a limit.

And the reason is striking: lest the righteous stretch out their hands to do wrong. God knows that if good people live long enough under bad rule, they begin to compromise. They start to cut corners, to go along, to fight dirty, to despair of doing right. Long oppression does not only hurt the righteous; it tempts them. So God, knowing the frailty of his people, will not let the pressure last beyond what they can bear.

That is a comfort for anyone living under a harsh boss, a corrupt system, or a hostile culture. God sees not only the injustice but the temptation it creates, and he has set its limit.

verseByVerse.quote: Do good, O LORD, to those who are good, and to those who are upright in their hearts! But those who turn aside to their crooked ways the LORD will lead away with evildoers! Peace be upon Israel!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do good, O LORD, to those who are good, and to those who are upright in their hearts!

A prayer for those who have stayed upright under pressure — and the upright are defined by their hearts, not merely their outward conduct.

But those who turn aside to their crooked ways the LORD will lead away with evildoers!

And a warning. These are people who were once on the road and turn aside — who took the crooked path when the pressure came. The very temptation of verse 3 has claimed them. They will be led away with the evildoers they joined. The pilgrimage road has exits, and the psalm warns against taking them.

Peace be upon Israel!

The psalm ends with a blessing, and the same words close Psalm 128 (128:6). Paul ended his letter to the Galatians with an echo of them: peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God (Gal 6:16). Those who trust in the LORD, surrounded by him, kept from crooked ways, receive this peace.

125.title: The LORD Surrounds His People
125.overview: Those who trust the LORD are like Mount Zion, unmovable and lasting forever; as the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds his people forever (vv. 1-2). The rule of the wicked will not remain on the land of the righteous, lest they be drawn into wrongdoing (v. 3). The psalmist asks God to do good to the upright, warns that those who turn to crooked ways will be led away with evildoers, and pronounces peace on Israel (vv. 4-5).
125.theology:
Stability belongs to those who trust, because of the one they trust (v. 1; Heb 12:28). God surrounds his people like the hills around Jerusalem (v. 2; 2 Kgs 6:17), with a love more lasting than mountains (Isa 54:10).

God limits the duration of oppression because prolonged wicked rule tempts the righteous to compromise (v. 3). Those who turn aside share the fate of evildoers (v. 5). Peace rests on the people of God (v. 5; Gal 6:16).
125.examples:
A mountain does not hold itself up.

A city held in cupped hands.

The enemy surrounded the town; God surrounded the enemy.

Long oppression hurts the righteous — and tempts them.

God sees the temptation as well as the injustice.

The pilgrim road has exits.

126.text: A Song of Ascents. 1When the LORD restored the fortunes of Zion, we were like those who dream.2Then our mouth was filled with laughter, and our tongue with shouts of joy; then they said among the nations, "The LORD has done great things for them."3The LORD has done great things for us; we are glad.4Restore our fortunes, O LORD, like streams in the Negeb!5Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy!6He who goes out weeping, bearing the seed for sowing, shall come home with shouts of joy, bringing his sheaves with him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The LORD Has Done Great Things for Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the LORD restored the fortunes of Zion, we were like those who dream (v. 1). Then our mouth was filled with laughter, and our tongue with shouts of joy; then they said among the nations, The LORD has done great things for them (v. 2). The LORD has done great things for us; we are glad (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: A restoration so great it felt like a dream — and even the nations noticed.

verseByVerse.quote: When the LORD restored the fortunes of Zion, we were like those who dream. Then our mouth was filled with laughter, and our tongue with shouts of joy; then they said among the nations, "The LORD has done great things for them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the LORD restored the fortunes of Zion, we were like those who dream.

The psalm opens with a memory. Something happened that was so good, so unexpected, that the people could not believe it was real. We were like those who dream. The likeliest setting is the return from exile, when the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia to send the captives home (Ezra 1:1) — after seventy years, the gates opened.

Many believers know the feeling. An answer to prayer so large that you keep waking up expecting it to be gone. A prodigal child come home. A diagnosis reversed. A marriage restored. Like those who dream.

Then our mouth was filled with laughter, and our tongue with shouts of joy; then they said among the nations, The LORD has done great things for them.

The joy could not be kept in. Laughter — not polite happiness, but the helpless laughter of relief. Shouts of joy. And the effect reached the surrounding nations. People who worshipped other gods looked at Israel coming home and said: their God did this. The LORD has done great things for them. God's rescue of his people is a testimony to the watching world.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD has done great things for us; we are glad.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD has done great things for us; we are glad.

Listen to what Israel does here. The nations had just said, The LORD has done great things for them. And Israel picks up the very same words and makes them their own: The LORD has done great things for us. They agree with the outsiders' verdict. It is a beautiful moment — the testimony of unbelievers echoed back as the confession of believers.

Mary sang the same thing when she carried the Christ: he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name (Luke 1:49). We are glad — simple, and enough.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–6 — Like Streams in the Negeb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Restore our fortunes, O LORD, like streams in the Negeb! (v. 4). Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy! (v. 5). He who goes out weeping, bearing the seed for sowing, shall come home with shouts of joy, bringing his sheaves with him (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Remembering past joy, the people ask for it again — and learn that tears sown in faith come up as harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: Restore our fortunes, O LORD, like streams in the Negeb!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Restore our fortunes, O LORD, like streams in the Negeb!

And then, suddenly, a prayer. The restoration of verse 1 was real, but it was not complete. The people who came home from Babylon found ruins, drought and hardship. So the psalm that began with a memory of restoration turns to ask for restoration again — exactly as Psalm 85 did (85:1-4).

The picture is precise. The Negeb is the dry southern desert of Judah. Most of the year its stream beds (wadis) are empty channels of dust and stones. But when the winter rains come, water rushes down them almost overnight, and the desert blooms. That is what they ask for: not a slow improvement, but a sudden flood of God's goodness into dry places.

If your life, or your church, feels like a dry stream bed — the memory of past blessing, and dust now — this is your prayer. God has done it before. Ask him to send the water again.

verseByVerse.quote: Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy! He who goes out weeping, bearing the seed for sowing, shall come home with shouts of joy, bringing his sheaves with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy!

And the answer to the prayer comes as a promise, drawn from farming. In a time of famine, seed grain was precious. A farmer who took his last seed out to sow it was taking food his family could have eaten. He planted it in hope, and often in tears — the ground was hard, the future uncertain, the children hungry. But the seed he buried came up. Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy.

He who goes out weeping, bearing the seed for sowing, shall come home with shouts of joy, bringing his sheaves with him.

Look at the picture. He goes out weeping, carrying a small bag of seed. He comes home shouting, arms full of sheaves. The same road, the same man, the tears turned into harvest. The shouts of joy at the end of this verse are the same shouts of joy as verse 2. What God did once, he will do again.

This promise covers far more than grain. It is for the parent praying for years for a wayward child. For the Sunday-school teacher who sees no fruit. For the missionary in hard soil. For the grieving, who plant their tears in faith. Paul says, let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up (Gal 6:9). Jesus said, Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh (Luke 6:21), and, You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy (John 16:20).

Notice that the tears are not wasted. They are sown. Faith does not pretend there are no tears; it plants them, and waits for the harvest God has promised. And the final harvest is coming: the ransomed of the LORD shall return and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads (Isa 35:10).

126.title: Those Who Sow in Tears
126.overview: When the LORD restored Zion's fortunes, it was like a dream: mouths filled with laughter and shouts of joy, while the nations said the LORD had done great things for them, and Israel agreed — The LORD has done great things for us; we are glad (vv. 1-3). Now they pray for restoration again, like desert streams in flood (v. 4). Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy: the one who goes out weeping with seed will come home rejoicing with sheaves (vv. 5-6).
126.theology:
God's past restorations are so great they seem like a dream, and they testify to the nations, whose verdict God's people gladly echo (vv. 1-3; Luke 1:49).

Remembered grace grounds prayer for renewed grace, pictured as a sudden flood in dry places (v. 4; cf. 85:1-7).

Faithful sowing in sorrow leads to joyful harvest (vv. 5-6): tears are not wasted but planted (Gal 6:9; 2 Cor 9:6), and sorrow will turn into joy (Luke 6:21; John 16:20-22), consummated when the ransomed come to Zion with everlasting joy (Isa 35:10).
126.examples:
Waking up expecting the answer to be gone.

Laughter that could not be kept in.

The outsiders' verdict echoed as confession.

A dry stream bed flooding overnight.

The last seed, sown in tears.

Going out with a small bag; coming home with arms full.

Tears planted, not wasted.

127.text: A Song of Ascents. Of Solomon. 1Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman stays awake in vain.2It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep.3Behold, children are a heritage from the LORD, the fruit of the womb a reward.4Like arrows in the hand of a warrior are the children of one's youth.5Blessed is the man who fills his quiver with them! He shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — He Gives to His Beloved Sleep
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman stays awake in vain (v. 1). It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep (v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology: All human effort without God is wasted — and God gives rest to those he loves.

verseByVerse.quote: Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman stays awake in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman stays awake in vain.

This is the only Song of Ascents that bears Solomon's name — the king who built the temple, the greatest building project in Israel's history. And the man who built the house of God writes: Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain.

House in the Bible means more than a building. It means a household, a family, a dynasty — God had promised to build David a house of descendants. So the verse covers everything: the literal house, the family inside it, the church, a business, a life. Without God, all the work that goes into it is in vain — empty, wasted, nothing.

And the same is true of security. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman stays awake in vain. The guard on the wall can do his job perfectly and still fail, if God is not guarding the city. Jesus said the house that stands in the storm is the one built ... on the rock (Matt 7:24-25).

This does not mean the builders should stop building or the watchman go to sleep. It means they should build and watch as people who know that the outcome rests with God. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Cor 3:6). Apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:5).

verseByVerse.quote: It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil;

Here is a portrait of many modern lives. Up before dawn, working late into the night, eating meals in a hurry, shoulders tight with worry. The bread of anxious toil — food eaten with anxiety, earned by exhausting labour that never feels like enough. The psalm calls it in vain. Not because work is wrong, but because anxious overwork assumes that everything depends on you. It does not.

for he gives to his beloved sleep.

And the alternative: he gives to his beloved sleep. The people God loves can lie down and rest, because he does not. The watchman of Psalm 121 will neither slumber nor sleep (121:4). His beloved can.

There may be a quiet signature here. When Solomon was born, God sent a message through Nathan, So he called his name Jedidiah, because of the LORD (2 Sam 12:25) — a name that means "beloved of the LORD". The man called God's beloved writes that God gives his beloved sleep.

Jesus told a parable of a farmer who scatters seed, and then he sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how (Mark 4:26-27). The growth happens while he sleeps. The blessing of the LORD makes rich, and he adds no sorrow with it (Prov 10:22). If you cannot sleep for worry about your work, your family or your future, this verse is an invitation to trust the one who is awake.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–5 — Children Are a Heritage from the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behold, children are a heritage from the LORD, the fruit of the womb a reward (v. 3). Like arrows in the hand of a warrior are the children of one's youth (v. 4). Blessed is the man who fills his quiver with them! (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The house God builds includes a household, and children are his gift, not a man's achievement.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, children are a heritage from the LORD, the fruit of the womb a reward. Like arrows in the hand of a warrior are the children of one's youth. Blessed is the man who fills his quiver with them! He shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, children are a heritage from the LORD, the fruit of the womb a reward.

Now the psalm turns from building houses to building households. And the first word is behold — look at this. Children are a heritage from the LORD. Not a human achievement, not a lifestyle choice, not a burden. A heritage, an inheritance given by God. A reward, a gift.

This belongs with the first half of the psalm. Parents can do everything right and still find that their children do not turn out as hoped; they can struggle for years to have children and find none. Children, like everything else, come from God. That frees parents from both pride and despair. And for those who long for children and have none, it must be read with the same care as 113:9 — God's pattern of blessing, not a verdict on any person's worth to God.

Like arrows in the hand of a warrior are the children of one's youth.

Arrows are shaped, straightened and aimed — and then released, to go where the archer cannot. Children are raised and then sent out into a future their parents will not see. (The ESV notes the word may be sons.)

Blessed is the man who fills his quiver with them! He shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate.

The city gate was the place of legal disputes and public business. A man with grown children standing with him was not easily pushed around there. (The ESV notes the last line may refer to the children themselves speaking with enemies in the gate.) A family God has built is a strength, not only a joy.

The next psalm continues the thought, and answers this one. Here, labour without God is anxious toil. In Psalm 128, the one who fears the LORD shall eat the fruit of the labor of your hands (128:2). Same work; different God at the centre.

127.title: Unless the LORD Builds the House
127.overview: Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labour in vain; unless he guards the city, the watchman watches in vain (v. 1). Rising early and working late with anxious toil is futile, for God gives sleep to those he loves (v. 2). Children are a heritage and reward from the LORD, like arrows in a warrior's hand; blessed is the man whose quiver is full, who will not be shamed when he contends in the gate (vv. 3-5).
127.theology:
All human building, guarding and working is futile without God (vv. 1-2; Matt 7:24-25; John 15:5; 1 Cor 3:6). Anxious overwork assumes everything depends on us; God gives rest to his beloved (v. 2; Mark 4:26-27; Prov 10:22), perhaps with an echo of Solomon's name Jedidiah (2 Sam 12:25).

Children are God's gift, not human achievement (v. 3), raised and then sent like arrows (v. 4), and a strength to a household (v. 5). The psalm pairs with 128, where labour under the fear of the LORD bears fruit.
127.examples:
The temple-builder: unless the LORD builds.

A house, a household, a church, a life.

The bread of anxious toil.

You can sleep because the watchman does not.

The seed grows while the farmer sleeps.

Arrows sent where the archer cannot go.

Same work; a different God at the centre.

128.text: A Song of Ascents. 1Blessed is everyone who fears the LORD, who walks in his ways!2You shall eat the fruit of the labor of your hands; you shall be blessed, and it shall be well with you.3Your wife will be like a fruitful vine within your house; your children will be like olive shoots around your table.4Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the LORD.5The LORD bless you from Zion! May you see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life!6May you see your children's children! Peace be upon Israel!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Blessed Is Everyone Who Fears the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Blessed is everyone who fears the LORD, who walks in his ways! (v. 1). You shall eat the fruit of the labor of your hands (v. 2). Your wife will be like a fruitful vine within your house; your children will be like olive shoots around your table (v. 3). Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the LORD (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The fear of the LORD turns anxious toil into fruitful work and a house into a home.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is everyone who fears the LORD, who walks in his ways! You shall eat the fruit of the labor of your hands; you shall be blessed, and it shall be well with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is everyone who fears the LORD, who walks in his ways!

Everyone. Not only kings, priests or the wealthy — every person, man or woman, rich or poor, who fears the LORD. And the fear of the LORD is not an inner feeling only; it shows itself in the feet: who walks in his ways. It is the same blessing that opened Psalm 112 (112:1).

You shall eat the fruit of the labor of your hands; you shall be blessed, and it shall be well with you.

Read this beside the psalm before it. Psalm 127 described people eating the bread of anxious toil, working late and early in vain (127:2). This psalm describes the same work — labour, hands, bread — but now it bears fruit, and the worker gets to eat it. What has changed? Not the job. The fear of the LORD is at the centre. The two psalms are a pair: 127 is work without God, 128 is work under God.

That is a practical word for anyone whose work feels futile. The answer may not be a different job, but a different relation to God in the same job.

verseByVerse.quote: Your wife will be like a fruitful vine within your house; your children will be like olive shoots around your table. Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your wife will be like a fruitful vine within your house; your children will be like olive shoots around your table.

And then the scene moves indoors, to the family meal. Two pictures from the farm. The wife is like a fruitful vine within your house — full of life, beauty and fruitfulness, at the heart of the home. The children are like olive shoots around your table — young shoots springing up around an old olive tree, which lives for generations. The family around the table is a small grove, growing.

It is a picture of ordinary domestic happiness, and the Bible treats it as a real blessing from God. A shared meal, a wife who flourishes, children growing up at the table. Not spectacular, and not small either.

Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the LORD.

Behold — look. This is what the blessing of fearing God looks like: not only in heaven, but at the kitchen table.

As with Psalm 112, this must be read as the pattern of God's world, not as a guarantee for every home. Some who fear God are single, widowed or childless; some faithful families face terrible loss. The psalm describes the kind of goodness that tends to grow where God is feared. It does not promise that no believer's table will ever be empty.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–6 — May You See Your Children's Children
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD bless you from Zion! May you see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life! (v. 5). May you see your children's children! Peace be upon Israel! (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The blessing on one household widens to the city of God and reaches the grandchildren.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD bless you from Zion! May you see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life! May you see your children's children! Peace be upon Israel!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD bless you from Zion! May you see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life!

Now the blessing is spoken over the pilgrim, perhaps by a priest. And it widens. The blessing comes from Zion, where God dwells. And the man's private happiness is tied to the good of God's city: may you see the prosperity of Jerusalem. A believer's family life and the health of God's people belong together. You cannot flourish in a corner while the church withers.

May you see your children's children! Peace be upon Israel!

And it reaches forward in time. Your children's children. To live long enough to see grandchildren was a great blessing, a sign that the family God built was lasting. Faith that is lived at the table is passed down the generations.

And the last words are the same as the last words of Psalm 125: Peace be upon Israel! (125:5). The blessing of one God-fearing home flows out into peace for all God's people. Paul closed Galatians with a blessing of peace and mercy ... upon the Israel of God (Gal 6:16) — the whole family of those who belong to Christ.

128.title: Olive Shoots Around Your Table
128.overview: Blessed is everyone who fears the LORD and walks in his ways: they will eat the fruit of their labour and it will be well with them (vv. 1-2). A wife like a fruitful vine in the house and children like olive shoots around the table are the blessing of the man who fears the LORD (vv. 3-4). May the LORD bless him from Zion, may he see Jerusalem's prosperity all his life and see his grandchildren; peace be upon Israel (vv. 5-6).
128.theology:
The fear of the LORD, shown in walking in his ways, brings blessing to every kind of person (v. 1; 112:1). Paired with 127, it turns anxious toil into fruitful labour (v. 2).

Ordinary family life is a real blessing from God (vv. 3-4), though as a pattern rather than a guarantee. Household blessing is tied to the good of God's people and extends across generations (vv. 5-6), ending in peace on Israel (125:5; Gal 6:16).
128.examples:
Everyone — not only kings and priests.

The same job; God at the centre.

A small grove around the kitchen table.

The blessing of fearing God, at dinner.

A pattern, not a guarantee against an empty chair.

You cannot flourish in a corner while the church withers.

Faith lived at the table, passed to the grandchildren.

129.text: A Song of Ascents. 1"Greatly have they afflicted me from my youth"— let Israel now say—2"Greatly have they afflicted me from my youth, yet they have not prevailed against me.3The plowers plowed upon my back; they made long their furrows."4The LORD is righteous; he has cut the cords of the wicked.5May all who hate Zion be put to shame and turned backward!6Let them be like the grass on the housetops, which withers before it grows up,7with which the reaper does not fill his hand nor the binder of sheaves his arms,8nor do those who pass by say, "The blessing of the LORD be upon you! We bless you in the name of the LORD!"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Yet They Have Not Prevailed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Greatly have they afflicted me from my youth — let Israel now say (v. 1) — yet they have not prevailed against me (v. 2). The plowers plowed upon my back; they made long their furrows (v. 3). The LORD is righteous; he has cut the cords of the wicked (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel looks back over a history of suffering that cut deep, and sees that it never won.

verseByVerse.quote: "Greatly have they afflicted me from my youth"— let Israel now say— "Greatly have they afflicted me from my youth, yet they have not prevailed against me. The plowers plowed upon my back; they made long their furrows."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greatly have they afflicted me from my youth — let Israel now say —

Another call and response, like Psalm 124: a leader speaks a line and tells the congregation to repeat it. And the line is a summary of Israel's whole history. From my youth — from the nation's childhood in Egypt, through wilderness, judges, invasions and exile — they have been attacked. (The ESV notes greatly may mean "often".)

Greatly have they afflicted me from my youth, yet they have not prevailed against me.

The line is repeated, and this time it has an ending: yet they have not prevailed against me. Pharaoh, the Philistines, Assyria, Babylon — every one of them tried to destroy God's people, and every one of them is gone. Israel is still singing.

That is the story of the church as well. Paul described his own life in the same shape: We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed (2 Cor 4:8-9). Greatly afflicted — yet not overcome.

The plowers plowed upon my back; they made long their furrows.

A shocking image. Israel's back is a field, and the enemies have driven a plough across it, cutting long furrows. It is the picture of a whip — the long, deep wounds of a flogging, laid in rows like ploughed ground.

A Christian cannot read that line without thinking of the servant who said, I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard (Isa 50:6) — and of the Roman scourge on the back of Jesus. The suffering of God's people through the ages was gathered up in the suffering of their King, whose back was ploughed for them.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is righteous; he has cut the cords of the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is righteous; he has cut the cords of the wicked.

And here the image turns. A plough was pulled by animals harnessed with cords — ropes. If the ropes are cut, the plough stops dead in the middle of the field. The furrows go no further.

That is what God did. The LORD is righteous, and he would not let the ploughing go on forever. He cut the harness. The oppressors could wound Israel's back, but they could not finish the field.

There is comfort here for anyone who feels ploughed — a long illness, a persecution, a grief that keeps cutting. The ploughing is real, and the furrows are long. But the righteous God holds a knife over the cords, and he will cut them at the time he chooses. The suffering has a limit, as Psalm 125 said (125:3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — Like Grass on the Housetops
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: May all who hate Zion be put to shame and turned backward! (v. 5). Let them be like the grass on the housetops, which withers before it grows up (v. 6), with no harvest for the reaper and no blessing from those who pass by (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who hate God's people will be like weeds on a roof: quick, shallow, and never harvested.

verseByVerse.quote: May all who hate Zion be put to shame and turned backward! Let them be like the grass on the housetops, which withers before it grows up, with which the reaper does not fill his hand nor the binder of sheaves his arms, nor do those who pass by say, "The blessing of the LORD be upon you! We bless you in the name of the LORD!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
May all who hate Zion be put to shame and turned backward!

Now a prayer against those who hate God's people. Turned backward — their attack reversed, their advance halted.

Let them be like the grass on the housetops, which withers before it grows up, with which the reaper does not fill his hand nor the binder of sheaves his arms,

Israelite houses had flat roofs of packed earth. After rain, grass would sprout up there — bright green, quick, and doomed. There was no depth of soil. As soon as the sun came out, it withered before it could grow. No farmer ever harvested his roof.

That is the fate the psalm asks for those who hate Zion. They may spring up fast and look impressive. But they have no roots, and they will wither, leaving nothing behind — no harvest, nothing to gather.

nor do those who pass by say, The blessing of the LORD be upon you! We bless you in the name of the LORD!

And one more detail from the fields. At harvest time, passers-by would greet the reapers with a blessing, and the reapers would answer. When Boaz came out to his fields, he said to the reapers, The LORD be with you! And they answered, The LORD bless you (Ruth 2:4). But no one stops to bless a man harvesting the grass on his roof, because there is nothing to harvest. The enemies of God's people will end without the blessing of the LORD.

The contrast with the psalms around this one is plain. Those who sow in tears come home with sheaves (126:6). Those who hate Zion have no sheaves at all.

129.title: The Plowers Plowed upon My Back
129.overview: Israel is called to say that enemies have greatly afflicted it from its youth, yet have not prevailed (vv. 1-2). They ploughed its back with long furrows, but the righteous LORD cut the cords of the wicked (vv. 3-4). The psalmist prays that all who hate Zion be shamed and turned back, like grass on a roof that withers before it grows, never harvested and never blessed by passers-by (vv. 5-8).
129.theology:
God's people suffer greatly throughout their history but are not overcome (vv. 1-2; 2 Cor 4:8-9). The ploughed back (v. 3) is gathered up in the Servant who gave his back to the smiters (Isa 50:6).

The righteous God sets a limit to oppression by cutting the harness of the wicked (v. 4; cf. 125:3). Those who hate Zion are rootless and fruitless, without the harvest blessing (vv. 5-8; Ruth 2:4), in contrast to those who sow in tears (126:6).
129.examples:
A whole national history in one line.

Greatly afflicted — yet not overcome.

Furrows laid on a back like a field.

Cut the ropes and the plough stops mid-field.

Grass on a flat roof: green, quick, doomed.

No one blesses a man harvesting his roof.

130.text: A Song of Ascents. 1Out of the depths I cry to you, O LORD!2O Lord, hear my voice! Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my pleas for mercy!3If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand?4But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared.5I wait for the LORD, my soul waits, and in his word I hope;6my soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen for the morning, more than watchmen for the morning.7O Israel, hope in the LORD! For with the LORD there is steadfast love, and with him is plentiful redemption.8And he will redeem Israel from all his iniquities.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — With You There Is Forgiveness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Out of the depths I cry to you, O LORD! O Lord, hear my voice! (vv. 1-2). If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: From the bottom of the pit, a sinner learns that God keeps no record against those he forgives.

verseByVerse.quote: Out of the depths I cry to you, O LORD! O Lord, hear my voice! Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my pleas for mercy!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of the depths I cry to you, O LORD!

This is one of the most loved psalms in the Bible, and it begins at the bottom. The depths are the deep waters, the place where a drowning man sinks — the image of being overwhelmed, far from help, with the weight of water overhead. The psalm will show that what has dragged him down is not only trouble, but sin.

And from there, he cries. The depths are not too deep for prayer. There is no place so low that a cry from it cannot reach God.

O Lord, hear my voice! Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my pleas for mercy!

What he asks for is mercy. Not justice, not vindication. A man who asks for mercy knows he does not deserve what he is asking for. That is the right way to begin with God. Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need (Heb 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand?

Now the real depths appear. If you ... should mark iniquities — if God kept a record, noted every sin, stored them up against us — who could stand? The answer is: no one. Not the psalmist, not the priests, not the most devout pilgrim on the road to Jerusalem. If God kept the books, every one of us would fall at the judgment.

This is the honest heart of true religion. Before we can understand grace, we must understand that on our own record, we cannot stand before God.

But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared.

But. Here is the turn, and it is one of the great verses of the Old Testament. God does not keep that record against those he forgives. With you there is forgiveness. Paul quotes David's word for it: Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin (Rom 4:7-8). If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us (1 John 1:9).

And then the surprise: that you may be feared. You might expect forgiveness to make people careless — if God forgives, why worry about sin? The psalm says the opposite. Forgiveness produces fear, reverent awe. A person who has really been forgiven, who knows what the record would have held, does not treat God lightly afterwards. He trembles with gratitude before the God who wiped it out. Cheap forgiveness breeds presumption. Real forgiveness breeds worship.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — More Than Watchmen for the Morning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I wait for the LORD, my soul waits, and in his word I hope; my soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen for the morning (vv. 5-6). O Israel, hope in the LORD! For with the LORD there is steadfast love, and with him is plentiful redemption. And he will redeem Israel from all his iniquities (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: A forgiven man waits for God like a night watchman for dawn, and calls the whole nation to hope.

verseByVerse.quote: I wait for the LORD, my soul waits, and in his word I hope; my soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen for the morning, more than watchmen for the morning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I wait for the LORD, my soul waits, and in his word I hope;

Forgiven, he now waits. I wait ... my soul waits. The whole person leans forward toward God. And the waiting is not vague: in his word I hope. He is waiting for God to do what God has said.

my soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen for the morning, more than watchmen for the morning.

A night watchman on the city wall spends the long dark hours staring east, cold, tired, alert for danger, longing for the first grey light that means his watch is over. And he knows one thing for certain: the morning will come. It always does.

More than watchmen for the morning — and the psalm says it twice, the way a tired man repeats himself at 4 a.m. His soul longs for God more than that. And his hope is as sure as theirs. Dawn is not in doubt; it is only a matter of time.

The LORD is good to those who wait for him ... It is good that one should wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD (Lam 3:25-26). And the whole church waits like this now: we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies (Rom 8:23). If you are in the long night, the dawn is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: O Israel, hope in the LORD! For with the LORD there is steadfast love, and with him is plentiful redemption. And he will redeem Israel from all his iniquities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O Israel, hope in the LORD! For with the LORD there is steadfast love, and with him is plentiful redemption.

And now the psalm turns outward. For six verses it has been I and my soul. Now it is O Israel. The man who has been forgiven in the depths turns to the whole people and tells them to hope. Personal experience of grace becomes a call to the congregation. That is how testimony works.

And the grounds for hope are two. With the LORD there is steadfast love — covenant love that does not quit. And with him is plentiful redemption — not scarce, not rationed, not barely enough. Plentiful. More than sufficient for every sinner who cries from the depths.

And he will redeem Israel from all his iniquities.

The last line is a promise, and its scope is total: from all his iniquities. Not merely from the consequences of sin, or from enemies, but from the sins themselves.

An angel told Joseph the name of the one who would keep that promise: you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins (Matt 1:21). He gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness (Titus 2:14). In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace (Eph 1:7). The psalm that began in the depths ends with a Redeemer who went down into them himself, so that no one who cries from there need stay.

130.title: Out of the Depths
130.overview: Out of the depths the psalmist cries to the LORD for mercy (vv. 1-2). If God kept a record of iniquities, no one could stand, but with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared (vv. 3-4). He waits for the LORD, hoping in his word, more than watchmen wait for the morning (vv. 5-6). He calls Israel to hope in the LORD, with whom is steadfast love and plentiful redemption, for he will redeem Israel from all its iniquities (vv. 7-8).
130.theology:
No one can stand if God marks iniquities (v. 3), but God forgives, not counting sin against the forgiven (v. 4; Rom 4:7-8; 1 John 1:9). Forgiveness produces reverent fear rather than presumption (v. 4).

The forgiven wait for God with sure hope, like watchmen for dawn (vv. 5-6; Lam 3:25-26; Rom 8:23). Personal experience of grace becomes a call to God's people (v. 7).

God's redemption is plentiful and complete, from all iniquities (vv. 7-8), fulfilled in Jesus who saves his people from their sins (Matt 1:21; Titus 2:14; Eph 1:7). Sinners may approach the throne of grace for mercy (Heb 4:16).
130.examples:
No place too deep for a cry to reach God.

Asking for mercy, not justice.

If God kept the books, who could stand?

Cheap forgiveness breeds presumption; real forgiveness breeds worship.

A watchman at 4 a.m., staring east.

From my soul to O Israel.

Plentiful — not rationed — redemption.

131.text: A Song of Ascents. Of David. 1O LORD, my heart is not lifted up; my eyes are not raised too high; I do not occupy myself with things too great and too marvelous for me.2But I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother; like a weaned child is my soul within me.3O Israel, hope in the LORD from this time forth and forevermore.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — I Have Calmed and Quieted My Soul
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O LORD, my heart is not lifted up; my eyes are not raised too high; I do not occupy myself with things too great and too marvelous for me (v. 1). But I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother (v. 2). O Israel, hope in the LORD from this time forth and forevermore (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The shortest of David's pilgrim songs: a proud heart laid down, and a soul resting like a child against its mother.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, my heart is not lifted up; my eyes are not raised too high; I do not occupy myself with things too great and too marvelous for me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD, my heart is not lifted up; my eyes are not raised too high; I do not occupy myself with things too great and too marvelous for me.

Three verses, and one of the most beautiful pictures of the soul in Scripture. David — a king, a warrior, a man with every reason for ambition — begins by telling God what he is not.

My heart is not lifted up. Pride starts inside, in the heart that swells with its own importance. My eyes are not raised too high. It shows in the eyes — the look that sizes people up and looks down on them, the gaze always fixed on the next rung of the ladder. I do not occupy myself with things too great and too marvelous for me. And it shows in what a person busies himself with: questions he is not meant to answer, positions he is not meant to hold, plans that belong to God.

This is not a refusal to think or to work hard. It is a refusal to pretend to be God. There are things too great for us — why God allows what he allows, how every piece of providence fits, what tomorrow holds. A proud soul frets over them and demands answers. A humble soul leaves them with God. Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Never be wise in your own sight (Rom 12:16). And the one who was greatest of all said, I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matt 11:29).

verseByVerse.quote: But I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother; like a weaned child is my soul within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother; like a weaned child is my soul within me.

Here is the picture. Not a nursing baby, but a weaned child. A baby at the breast cries and struggles and demands to be fed; its mother means food, and it wants her for what she gives. A weaned child — perhaps two or three years old in that culture — has gone through the hard struggle of giving that up. And now it can sit quietly in its mother's lap, not demanding anything, simply content to be with her.

That is the soul David describes. It used to come to God crying, grasping, demanding things. It has been weaned. Now it rests against God, content with him, not only with what he gives.

And notice the verbs: I have calmed and quieted my soul. Weaning is not easy, for the child or the soul. It is something David has done, with effort — telling his restless soul to be still, again and again, until it learned. Paul described the same schooling: I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content (Phil 4:11). Contentment is learned.

Jesus put a child in the middle of his arguing disciples and said, unless you turn and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest (Matt 18:3-4). If your prayers are all requests and your soul is always restless for the next thing, this psalm is an invitation: be weaned. Sit with God, and want him.

verseByVerse.quote: O Israel, hope in the LORD from this time forth and forevermore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O Israel, hope in the LORD from this time forth and forevermore.

And from his own quiet soul, David turns to the whole people. O Israel, hope in the LORD — exactly the words that closed the psalm before this one (130:7). There, hope came after forgiveness from the depths. Here, hope comes after pride has been laid down and the soul has been stilled.

The humble, contented soul is a hopeful one. When you stop occupying yourself with things too great for you, you are free to hope in the one for whom nothing is too great. From this time forth and forevermore — not a mood for a quiet afternoon, but a settled posture for the rest of life. A child on its mother's lap, all the way home.

131.title: Like a Weaned Child
131.overview: David tells the LORD that his heart is not proud, his eyes are not haughty, and he does not concern himself with matters too great for him (v. 1). He has calmed and quieted his soul like a weaned child resting with its mother (v. 2). He calls Israel to hope in the LORD now and forever (v. 3).
131.theology:
Humility refuses the pride of heart, eye and ambition that would take God's place (v. 1; Rom 12:16), following the lowliness of Christ (Matt 11:29).

Contentment is learned by stilling the soul until it rests in God himself rather than demanding his gifts, like a weaned child (v. 2; Phil 4:11); such childlikeness is the way into the kingdom (Matt 18:3-4). The humble soul becomes a hopeful one and calls God's people to hope (v. 3; 130:7).
131.examples:
A king telling God what he is not.

Pride in the heart, the eyes and the schedule.

Refusing to pretend to be God.

The nursing baby demands; the weaned child rests.

Wanting God, not only what he gives.

Contentment is learned.

A child on its mother's lap, all the way home.

132.text: A Song of Ascents. 1Remember, O LORD, in David's favor, all the hardships he endured,2how he swore to the LORD and vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob,3"I will not enter my house or get into my bed,4I will not give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids,5until I find a place for the LORD, a dwelling place for the Mighty One of Jacob."6Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah; we found it in the fields of Jaar.7"Let us go to his dwelling place; let us worship at his footstool!"8Arise, O LORD, and go to your resting place, you and the ark of your might.9Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let your saints shout for joy.10For the sake of your servant David, do not turn away the face of your anointed one.11The LORD swore to David a sure oath from which he will not turn back: "One of the sons of your body I will set on your throne.12If your sons keep my covenant and my testimonies that I shall teach them, their sons also forever shall sit on your throne."13For the LORD has chosen Zion; he has desired it for his dwelling place:14"This is my resting place forever; here I will dwell, for I have desired it.15I will abundantly bless her provisions; I will satisfy her poor with bread.16Her priests I will clothe with salvation, and her saints will shout for joy.17There I will make a horn to sprout for David; I have prepared a lamp for my anointed.18His enemies I will clothe with shame, but on him his crown will shine."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Remember David and All His Hardships
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Remember, O LORD, in David's favor, all the hardships he endured, how he swore to the LORD (vv. 1-2): he would not sleep until I find a place for the LORD, a dwelling place for the Mighty One of Jacob (vv. 3-5). Let us go to his dwelling place; let us worship at his footstool! (v. 7). Arise, O LORD, and go to your resting place, you and the ark of your might (v. 8). For the sake of your servant David, do not turn away the face of your anointed one (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: A king who would not rest until God had a home — and a people who pray for God to come and rest among them.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember, O LORD, in David's favor, all the hardships he endured, how he swore to the LORD and vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob, "I will not enter my house or get into my bed, I will not give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the LORD, a dwelling place for the Mighty One of Jacob."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember, O LORD, in David's favor, all the hardships he endured, how he swore to the LORD and vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob,

This is the longest of the Songs of Ascents, and it tells a story about a vow. The pilgrims coming up to the temple remember how the temple came to exist at all. It began with a king who could not rest.

I will not enter my house or get into my bed, I will not give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the LORD, a dwelling place for the Mighty One of Jacob.

Once David was settled in his palace, it troubled him that God's ark was still in a tent. He said to Nathan, See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent (2 Sam 7:2). The psalm puts that restlessness in the form of a vow: no comfortable bed, no sleep, until God has a home.

It is a picture of zeal for God's presence among his people. David cared more about God's house than his own. There is a question here for any believer who has made their own life comfortable: does it trouble us that God's work, God's people, God's worship might be neglected while we live in houses of cedar?

And notice what David refused himself: I will not give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids. The psalms around this one speak of sleep as God's gift — he gives to his beloved sleep (127:2) — and of the God who will neither slumber nor sleep (121:4). David would not take the gift until God had a resting place. The psalm will end with God answering: This is my resting place forever (v. 14).

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah; we found it in the fields of Jaar. "Let us go to his dwelling place; let us worship at his footstool!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah; we found it in the fields of Jaar.

Two place names, and they tell a small story. Ephrathah is Bethlehem — Bethlehem Ephrathah (Mic 5:2), David's home town. That is where they heard about the ark, perhaps as a story from long ago. The fields of Jaar seems to be Kiriath-jearim, the town where the ark had been left. After the Philistines returned it, the men of Kiriath-jearim came and took up the ark of the LORD, and a long time passed, some twenty years (1 Sam 7:1-2). The ark of God's presence sat almost forgotten in a village house for a generation. David went and found it.

Let us go to his dwelling place; let us worship at his footstool!

And having found it, the call goes out: let us go and worship. The ark was God's footstool (99:5) — the place where the King of heaven, so to speak, set his feet on earth.

verseByVerse.quote: Arise, O LORD, and go to your resting place, you and the ark of your might. Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let your saints shout for joy. For the sake of your servant David, do not turn away the face of your anointed one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Arise, O LORD, and go to your resting place, you and the ark of your might.

These verses were prayed again when the temple was finished. Solomon ended his dedication prayer with almost the same words: And now arise, O LORD God, and go to your resting place, you and the ark of your might (2 Chr 6:41). What David vowed, Solomon completed, and the pilgrims sang both.

Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let your saints shout for joy. For the sake of your servant David, do not turn away the face of your anointed one.

Three requests: that God come to his resting place; that the priests be clothed with righteousness and the people rejoice; and that God not turn away from his anointed one, the king of David's line. Hold on to those three requests. The second half of the psalm will answer each one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — The LORD Swore to David a Sure Oath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD swore to David a sure oath from which he will not turn back: One of the sons of your body I will set on your throne (v. 11). For the LORD has chosen Zion: This is my resting place forever; here I will dwell (vv. 13-14). He will bless her, clothe her priests with salvation (vv. 15-16). There I will make a horn to sprout for David; I have prepared a lamp for my anointed (v. 17); on him his crown will shine (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: David's vow to build God a house is answered by God's oath to build David a house — and every request is granted more fully than it was asked.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD swore to David a sure oath from which he will not turn back: "One of the sons of your body I will set on your throne. If your sons keep my covenant and my testimonies that I shall teach them, their sons also forever shall sit on your throne."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD swore to David a sure oath from which he will not turn back: One of the sons of your body I will set on your throne.

Here is the hinge of the psalm. In verse 2, David swore to the LORD. In verse 11, the LORD swore to David. David vowed to build God a house. God answered with an oath to build David a house — a dynasty. And God's oath is sure, from which he will not turn back. (The ESV notes the Hebrew for sons of your body is "of your fruit of the womb".)

That is always how it goes with God. Whatever we offer him, he answers with something far greater. David offered a building; God promised a King who would reign forever. Peter preached at Pentecost that David knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne, spoke of the resurrection of Christ (Acts 2:30).

If your sons keep my covenant and my testimonies that I shall teach them, their sons also forever shall sit on your throne.

And there is a condition. David's sons must keep the covenant. Many of them did not, and the throne was lost to exile. Psalm 89 held the same tension — sons who sin will be disciplined, yet the steadfast love will not be removed (89:30-33). The condition was finally met by one Son of David who kept the covenant perfectly, and his throne is forever.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD has chosen Zion; he has desired it for his dwelling place: "This is my resting place forever; here I will dwell, for I have desired it. I will abundantly bless her provisions; I will satisfy her poor with bread. Her priests I will clothe with salvation, and her saints will shout for joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the LORD has chosen Zion; he has desired it for his dwelling place: This is my resting place forever; here I will dwell, for I have desired it.

Now God speaks, and he answers the first request. The people prayed, Arise, O LORD, and go to your resting place (v. 8). God says: This is my resting place forever; here I will dwell. Not a temporary stop, like the tent or the village house. Forever. And the reason is desire: for I have desired it. God wants to dwell among his people.

I will abundantly bless her provisions; I will satisfy her poor with bread.

Where God dwells, there is provision — and especially for the poor. The God of Zion feeds the hungry. It is not accidental that the King who fulfilled this psalm was born in Ephrathah, Bethlehem, and called himself the bread of life.

Her priests I will clothe with salvation, and her saints will shout for joy.

And the second request is answered — and more. They asked for priests clothed with righteousness (v. 9). God promises priests clothed with salvation — which is the very word Solomon used when he prayed it (2 Chr 6:41). And the saints who were asked to shout for joy (v. 9) will shout for joy. God does not merely grant the request; he answers it in fuller terms than it was asked.

verseByVerse.quote: There I will make a horn to sprout for David; I have prepared a lamp for my anointed. His enemies I will clothe with shame, but on him his crown will shine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There I will make a horn to sprout for David; I have prepared a lamp for my anointed.

And the third request. They asked God not to turn away from your anointed one (v. 10). God answers with two pictures. A horn — the symbol of strength — will sprout, grow up like a branch, from David's line. And a lamp is prepared for the anointed, a light that will not go out. God told Solomon's successor that he would keep one tribe that David my servant may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem (1 Kgs 11:36).

Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, filled with the Spirit at the birth of his son, praised God because he has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David (Luke 1:69). The horn had sprouted.

His enemies I will clothe with shame, but on him his crown will shine.

The clothing theme finishes the psalm. Priests clothed with righteousness (v. 9), priests clothed with salvation (v. 16), and now enemies clothed with shame. And on the anointed King, his crown will shine.

The psalm ends with a crown that shines. The King it looks for says of himself at the very end of the Bible, I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star (Rev 22:16). David would not rest until God had a home. God has made his home with his people forever, in the Son of David whose crown will never dim.

132.title: A Lamp for My Anointed
132.overview: The psalmist asks God to remember David's hardships and his vow not to rest until he had found a dwelling for the LORD (vv. 1-5). They heard of the ark in Ephrathah and found it in the fields of Jaar, and went to worship at God's footstool (vv. 6-7). Arise, O LORD, and go to your resting place; clothe your priests with righteousness; do not turn from your anointed (vv. 8-10). The LORD swore a sure oath to set David's son on his throne, on condition of covenant faithfulness (vv. 11-12).
