He has chosen Zion as his resting place forever, will bless her provisions, satisfy her poor, clothe her priests with salvation and make her saints shout for joy (vv. 13-16). There he will make a horn sprout for David and prepare a lamp for his anointed, clothing his enemies with shame while his crown shines (vv. 17-18).
132.theology:
Zeal for God's dwelling among his people moved David to vow (vv. 1-5; 2 Sam 7:2). The neglected ark was found and brought to Zion (vv. 6-7; 1 Sam 7:1-2).

The people's prayer (vv. 8-10; 2 Chr 6:41-42) is answered point by point and more fully (vv. 14, 16, 17). David's vow to build God a house is met by God's sure oath to build David's house (v. 11; Acts 2:30), conditioned on covenant faithfulness (v. 12; cf. 89:30-33) and fulfilled in the one Son who kept it.

God desires to dwell with his people forever (vv. 13-14), providing for the poor (v. 15). The horn and lamp of David (v. 17; 1 Kgs 11:36) are fulfilled in Christ, the horn of salvation (Luke 1:69) and root of David (Rev 22:16).
132.examples:
A king who could not sleep while God lived in a tent.

The ark forgotten twenty years in a village.

What David vowed, Solomon prayed, and the pilgrims sang.

David swore to God; God swore to David.

Offer God a building; receive an everlasting King.

Asked for righteousness; promised salvation.

A lamp that would not go out, and a crown that shines.

133.text: A Song of Ascents. Of David. 1Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell in unity!2It is like the precious oil on the head, running down on the beard, on the beard of Aaron, running down on the collar of his robes!3It is like the dew of Hermon, which falls on the mountains of Zion! For there the LORD has commanded the blessing, life forevermore.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Like the Dew of Hermon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell in unity! (v. 1). It is like the precious oil on the head, running down on the beard, on the beard of Aaron (v. 2). It is like the dew of Hermon, which falls on the mountains of Zion! For there the LORD has commanded the blessing, life forevermore (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The unity of God's people is holy like anointing oil and life-giving like mountain dew — and both come from above.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell in unity!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell in unity!

Pilgrims came up to Jerusalem from every tribe and every town — northerners and southerners, farmers and shepherds, rich and poor, families with old feuds. For a few days at the festival they camped together, ate together and worshipped together. And someone looked around and said, Behold — look at this — how good and pleasant it is.

Good — right, as God intends. Pleasant — sweet, delightful to experience. Unity among God's people is both. It is not merely a duty to be maintained; it is a joy to be enjoyed. (The ESV notes the phrase may be dwell together: living side by side, not only agreeing in principle.)

Anyone who has been in a church split knows how bitter the opposite is. And anyone who has been in a congregation where people genuinely love each other across every difference knows that this verse is simply true. Jesus prayed for it the night before he died: that they may all be one ... so that the world may believe that you have sent me (John 17:21).

verseByVerse.quote: It is like the precious oil on the head, running down on the beard, on the beard of Aaron, running down on the collar of his robes!
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is like the precious oil on the head, running down on the beard, on the beard of Aaron, running down on the collar of his robes!

The first picture is the anointing of the high priest. God told Moses, You shall anoint Aaron and his sons, and consecrate them, that they may serve me as priests (Exod 30:30). The oil was poured on Aaron's head — lavishly, fragrantly — and it ran down his beard and onto the collar of his robes.

Notice the direction: running down, twice. The oil begins on the head and flows downward over the whole man. That is how unity among God's people works. It does not start at the bottom, by everyone working very hard to get along. It flows down from the head. For Christians, the head is Christ, anointed with the Spirit, and the unity of his body flows down from him. Paul tells believers to be eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph 4:3) — not to manufacture it, but to keep what the Spirit has given.

And the oil was precious and holy — the oil that set Aaron apart for God. Unity among believers is not merely pleasant social harmony. It is a holy thing, consecrated, fragrant before God.

verseByVerse.quote: It is like the dew of Hermon, which falls on the mountains of Zion! For there the LORD has commanded the blessing, life forevermore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is like the dew of Hermon, which falls on the mountains of Zion!

The second picture. Mount Hermon is the great snow-topped mountain in the far north of the land, and the heavy dew on its slopes kept the vegetation green through the dry summer. Zion lies far to the south. Hermon's dew does not literally fall on Jerusalem. That is the point of the image: unity is like refreshing moisture brought from somewhere else, from above, falling on dry ground and making it live.

Both pictures in this psalm are of something that comes down from above — oil from the head, dew from the heights. Unity is a gift before it is a task.

For there the LORD has commanded the blessing, life forevermore.

And the psalm ends with the reason unity matters so much. There — where brothers dwell together in unity, in God's city — the LORD has commanded the blessing. God chooses to pour out blessing where his people are one. And the blessing is life forevermore.

That is a sobering and hopeful word for any church. Division does not only make a congregation unpleasant; it hinders the blessing. Unity does not only make a congregation happy; it is where God has commanded life. If you are in a church right now where there is tension, pray for the oil and the dew, and do what you can to maintain the unity of the Spirit.

133.title: When Brothers Dwell in Unity
133.overview: How good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in unity (v. 1)! It is like the precious anointing oil poured on Aaron's head, running down his beard and robes (v. 2), and like the dew of Hermon falling on the mountains of Zion, for there the LORD has commanded the blessing of life forevermore (v. 3).
133.theology:
Unity among God's people is both good and pleasant (v. 1), the object of Christ's prayer (John 17:21).

It is holy and flows down from the anointed head (v. 2; Exod 30:30), and it is refreshing life brought from above (v. 3): a gift of the Spirit to be maintained rather than manufactured (Eph 4:3). God commands his blessing of eternal life where his people dwell in unity (v. 3).
133.examples:
Old family feuds camping side by side at the festival.

Good and pleasant — a duty and a joy.

Oil running down, twice.

Unity flows from the head; it is not built from the bottom.

Dew from a mountain a long way off.

A gift before it is a task.

Where God has commanded life.

134.text: A Song of Ascents. 1Come, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD, who stand by night in the house of the LORD!2Lift up your hands to the holy place and bless the LORD!3May the LORD bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — May the LORD Bless You from Zion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Come, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD, who stand by night in the house of the LORD! (v. 1). Lift up your hands to the holy place and bless the LORD! (v. 2). May the LORD bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth! (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The pilgrim songs end at night in the temple, with blessing given to God and blessing given back.

verseByVerse.quote: Come, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD, who stand by night in the house of the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Come, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD, who stand by night in the house of the LORD!

This is the last of the fifteen Songs of Ascents. The journey that began in Meshech and Kedar, far from Zion and surrounded by liars (120:5), ends here: inside the house of the LORD, at night.

It is addressed to servants of the LORD, who stand by night. When the festival crowds had gone to sleep, the Levites kept watch in the temple. The Chronicler describes singers who were on duty day and night (1 Chr 9:33). Perhaps the departing pilgrims called this out to them as they left; perhaps it was the evening call to the night shift. Either way, the psalm honours the people who serve God when no one is watching.

Every church has them — the ones who stay late to clean, who pray through the night for others, who serve in unnoticed ways long after the crowd has gone home. This psalm is for them. And it tells them what their real work is: not only guarding the building, but blessing the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: Lift up your hands to the holy place and bless the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lift up your hands to the holy place and bless the LORD!

Lifted hands were the posture of prayer and praise — empty, open, reaching toward God. The holy place is the inner sanctuary where God's presence dwelt. In the dark, in the quiet, the night servants are to turn toward God and bless him.

There is something especially fitting about praise at night. It is praise without an audience, praise when you are tired, praise in the dark. John saw the redeemed in heaven doing what these Levites did: they serve him day and night in his temple (Rev 7:15). The night watch in Jerusalem was a small picture of that endless worship.

verseByVerse.quote: May the LORD bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth!
verseByVerse.commentary:
May the LORD bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth!

And then the blessing comes back. The servants have been told to bless the LORD, twice. Now a voice — perhaps the night servants answering the pilgrims, perhaps a priest — pronounces the LORD's blessing on you. Worship goes up; blessing comes down. It is the same exchange the priests spoke over Israel: The LORD bless you and keep you (Num 6:24).

And listen to how the whole collection is gathered up in this last line. Bless you from Zion — the words spoken over the God-fearing household in 128:5. He who made heaven and earth — the words of the pilgrim who lifted his eyes to the hills (121:2) and of the people who escaped the snare (124:8). The songs that began with a man far from home, crying out in distress, end with a blessing from the Maker of everything, pronounced in his own house.

That is the shape of the Christian life too. It begins far off, among the tents of Kedar. It travels up, through trouble, tears and waiting. And it ends in the presence of God, blessing him and being blessed by him, forever. The next psalm opens with the same call — O servants of the LORD, who stand in the house of the LORD (135:1-2) — as if the praise, once begun, will not stop.

134.title: Bless the LORD by Night
134.overview: The last Song of Ascents calls the servants of the LORD who stand by night in his house to bless him (v. 1) and to lift their hands toward the holy place in praise (v. 2). It closes with a blessing: May the LORD bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth! (v. 3).
134.theology:
The pilgrim songs end inside God's house at night, honouring those who serve unseen (v. 1; 1 Chr 9:33). Their chief work is blessing the LORD, with lifted hands (v. 2), a foretaste of the day-and-night worship of heaven (Rev 7:15).

Worship ascends and blessing descends (v. 3; Num 6:24). The final line gathers phrases from earlier Ascents (121:2; 124:8; 128:5): the journey that began far off in distress ends in blessing from the Creator in Zion.
134.examples:
From the tents of Kedar to the temple at night.

The night shift of the house of God.

Serving when no one is watching.

Praise without an audience.

Blessing goes up; blessing comes down.

Fifteen songs gathered into one last line.

135.text: <sup>1</sup>Praise the LORD! Praise the name of the LORD, give praise, O servants of the LORD,<sup>2</sup>who stand in the house of the LORD, in the courts of the house of our God!<sup>3</sup>Praise the LORD, for the LORD is good; sing to his name, for it is pleasant!<sup>4</sup>For the LORD has chosen Jacob for himself, Israel as his own possession.<sup>5</sup>For I know that the LORD is great, and that our Lord is above all gods.<sup>6</sup>Whatever the LORD pleases, he does, in heaven and on earth, in the seas and all deeps.<sup>7</sup>He it is who makes the clouds rise at the end of the earth, who makes lightnings for the rain and brings forth the wind from his storehouses.<sup>8</sup>He it was who struck down the firstborn of Egypt, both of man and of beast;<sup>9</sup>who in your midst, O Egypt, sent signs and wonders against Pharaoh and all his servants;<sup>10</sup>who struck down many nations and killed mighty kings,<sup>11</sup>Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan,<sup>12</sup>and gave their land as a heritage, a heritage to his people Israel.<sup>13</sup>Your name, O LORD, endures forever, your renown, O LORD, throughout all ages.<sup>14</sup>For the LORD will vindicate his people and have compassion on his servants.<sup>15</sup>The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands.<sup>16</sup>They have mouths, but do not speak; they have eyes, but do not see;<sup>17</sup>they have ears, but do not hear, nor is there any breath in their mouths.<sup>18</sup>Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them.<sup>19</sup>O house of Israel, bless the LORD! O house of Aaron, bless the LORD!<sup>20</sup>O house of Levi, bless the LORD! You who fear the LORD, bless the LORD!<sup>21</sup>Blessed be the LORD from Zion, he who dwells in Jerusalem! Praise the LORD!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Praise the Name of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Praise the LORD! Praise the name of the LORD, give praise, O servants of the LORD, who stand in the house of the LORD (vv. 1-2). Praise the LORD, for the LORD is good; sing to his name, for it is pleasant! (v. 3). For the LORD has chosen Jacob for himself, Israel as his own possession (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The servants in God's house are called to praise, because he chose a people for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD! Praise the name of the LORD, give praise, O servants of the LORD, who stand in the house of the LORD, in the courts of the house of our God! Praise the LORD, for the LORD is good; sing to his name, for it is pleasant! For the LORD has chosen Jacob for himself, Israel as his own possession.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Praise the LORD! Praise the name of the LORD, give praise, O servants of the LORD, who stand in the house of the LORD, in the courts of the house of our God!

The last Song of Ascents ended by calling servants of the LORD, who stand by night in the house of the LORD to bless him (134:1). This psalm picks up exactly there, as if the praise, once begun, keeps going.

Psalm 135 is unusual. Much of it is made from other parts of Scripture — lines from other psalms, from the prophets, from the law — woven together into a new song. It is a psalm by someone who knew the Bible so well that his praise came out in its words. That is a good thing for a believer to aim at.

Praise the LORD, for the LORD is good; sing to his name, for it is pleasant!

Two reasons to praise: God is good, and singing to his name is pleasant. (The ESV notes it may be "for he is beautiful".) Worship is not a chore. It is delightful.

For the LORD has chosen Jacob for himself, Israel as his own possession.

The deepest reason: election. God chose a people for himself. Moses told Israel, The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth (Deut 7:6). Peter says the same of the church: you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you (1 Pet 2:9). Chosen people praise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–14 — Whatever the LORD Pleases, He Does
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For I know that the LORD is great, and that our Lord is above all gods. Whatever the LORD pleases, he does, in heaven and on earth (vv. 5-6). He rules clouds, lightning and wind (v. 7), struck Egypt and the kings of Canaan and gave their land to Israel (vv. 8-12). Your name, O LORD, endures forever (v. 13). For the LORD will vindicate his people and have compassion on his servants (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who does whatever he pleases in the storm and in history has pleased to keep his people.

verseByVerse.quote: For I know that the LORD is great, and that our Lord is above all gods. Whatever the LORD pleases, he does, in heaven and on earth, in the seas and all deeps. He it is who makes the clouds rise at the end of the earth, who makes lightnings for the rain and brings forth the wind from his storehouses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I know that the LORD is great, and that our Lord is above all gods. Whatever the LORD pleases, he does, in heaven and on earth, in the seas and all deeps.

I know. Not "I hope" or "I feel". The psalmist states it as settled knowledge. And the proof of God's greatness is his freedom: Whatever the LORD pleases, he does — the same confession Psalm 115 made against the powerless idols (115:3). In heaven, on earth, in the sea, in the depths: nowhere is outside his will.

He it is who makes the clouds rise at the end of the earth, who makes lightnings for the rain and brings forth the wind from his storehouses.

This verse is almost word for word from Jeremiah: he makes the mist rise from the ends of the earth. He makes lightning for the rain, and he brings forth the wind from his storehouses (Jer 10:13). The neighbouring nations worshipped storm gods. The psalm says the storm belongs to the LORD. The clouds, the lightning and the wind come out of his storerooms.

verseByVerse.quote: He it was who struck down the firstborn of Egypt, both of man and of beast; who in your midst, O Egypt, sent signs and wonders against Pharaoh and all his servants; who struck down many nations and killed mighty kings, Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan, and gave their land as a heritage, a heritage to his people Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He it was who struck down the firstborn of Egypt, both of man and of beast; who in your midst, O Egypt, sent signs and wonders against Pharaoh and all his servants;

From the storm to history. The God who does whatever he pleases in the sky did what he pleased in Egypt.

who struck down many nations and killed mighty kings, Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan, and gave their land as a heritage, a heritage to his people Israel.

Sihon and Og were the two kings east of the Jordan who blocked Israel's way into the land, and their defeat became a byword for God's power. The next psalm names them again (136:19-20). The history told at length in Psalms 78 and 105 is here compressed into a few lines: Egypt struck, kings defeated, the land given as a heritage.

verseByVerse.quote: Your name, O LORD, endures forever, your renown, O LORD, throughout all ages. For the LORD will vindicate his people and have compassion on his servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your name, O LORD, endures forever, your renown, O LORD, throughout all ages.

The ESV notes renown may be remembrance. The line echoes what God said to Moses at the burning bush: This is my name forever, and thus I am to be remembered throughout all generations (Exod 3:15). The name God revealed then has not changed. Empires that seemed permanent have been forgotten; the name of the LORD is still remembered.

For the LORD will vindicate his people and have compassion on his servants.

And this line is from the Song of Moses: For the LORD will vindicate his people and have compassion on his servants (Deut 32:36). The God who struck down Pharaoh and Og will do right by his people again. He will vindicate them — show them to be in the right — and have compassion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–21 — Those Who Make Them Become Like Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands (v. 15), mouths that do not speak and nor is there any breath in their mouths (vv. 16-17). Those who make them become like them (v. 18). O house of Israel, bless the LORD! O house of Aaron, bless the LORD! O house of Levi, bless the LORD! (vv. 19-20). Blessed be the LORD from Zion (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: Breathless idols against the living God, and every group of his people called to bless him.

verseByVerse.quote: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, but do not speak; they have eyes, but do not see; they have ears, but do not hear, nor is there any breath in their mouths. Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, but do not speak; they have eyes, but do not see; they have ears, but do not hear, nor is there any breath in their mouths.

Now the psalm quotes Psalm 115 (115:4-8), with one change. Psalm 115 went on to noses, hands, feet and throats. This psalm cuts that list short and adds a single devastating line: nor is there any breath in their mouths. The idol is not merely silent. It is not alive. It has no breath. The God of verse 7 brings the wind out of his storehouses; the idol cannot draw one breath.

Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them.

And the same warning as Psalm 115: worshippers become like what they worship. Breathless gods make spiritually breathless people.

verseByVerse.quote: O house of Israel, bless the LORD! O house of Aaron, bless the LORD! O house of Levi, bless the LORD! You who fear the LORD, bless the LORD! Blessed be the LORD from Zion, he who dwells in Jerusalem! Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
O house of Israel, bless the LORD! O house of Aaron, bless the LORD! O house of Levi, bless the LORD! You who fear the LORD, bless the LORD!

Psalm 115 called three groups to trust the LORD: Israel, the house of Aaron, and those who fear him (115:9-11). This psalm calls four groups to bless him, adding the house of Levi — the Levites who served in the temple, the night servants of the previous psalm. The whole of God's people, from the priests to the ordinary God-fearer, is summoned.

Blessed be the LORD from Zion, he who dwells in Jerusalem! Praise the LORD!

The Songs of Ascents ended with the LORD blessing his people from Zion (134:3). Here the people bless the LORD from Zion. And the psalm closes as it opened: Praise the LORD! The next psalm will take up the refrain and repeat it twenty-six times.

135.title: Your Name, O LORD, Endures Forever
135.overview: The servants in the LORD's house are called to praise his good and pleasant name, for he chose Israel as his own possession (vv. 1-4). The LORD is great and does whatever he pleases in heaven, earth and sea, commanding clouds, lightning and wind (vv. 5-7); he struck Egypt, defeated Sihon, Og and the kings of Canaan, and gave their land to Israel (vv. 8-12). His name endures forever, and he will vindicate his people (vv. 13-14). The nations' idols are lifeless handiwork without breath, and their makers become like them (vv. 15-18). Israel, Aaron, Levi and all who fear the LORD are to bless him from Zion (vv. 19-21).
135.theology:
Praise is grounded in God's goodness and his choice of a people for himself (vv. 3-4; Deut 7:6; 1 Pet 2:9). His sovereignty extends over creation, storm and history (vv. 5-12; Jer 10:13).

His name endures as revealed to Moses (v. 13; Exod 3:15), and he will vindicate his servants (v. 14; Deut 32:36). Idols are breathless and make their worshippers like them (vv. 15-18; cf. 115:4-8), while all God's people are called to bless the living God (vv. 19-21).

The psalm is woven from earlier Scripture, praise shaped by a mind full of the Bible; see the fuller treatments at Psalms 78, 105, 115 and 136.
135.examples:
The praise of the night servants, carried on.

A song made from Scripture by someone who knew it by heart.

Not "I hope" — I know.

The storm god's weather, in the LORD's storeroom.

A name remembered after the empires are forgotten.

Not only silent: no breath.

Four houses called to bless.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Give Thanks to the God of Gods
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever (v. 1). Give thanks to the God of gods (v. 2). Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his steadfast love endures forever (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: A call to thanks with an answer the congregation will give twenty-six times.

verseByVerse.quote: Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever. Give thanks to the God of gods, for his steadfast love endures forever. Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his steadfast love endures forever;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever.

This psalm was made to be sung in two voices. A leader, or a choir, sings the first half of each line, and the whole congregation answers with the second: for his steadfast love endures forever. When the foundation of the second temple was laid, they sang responsively, praising and giving thanks to the LORD, For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever toward Israel (Ezra 3:11). When fire came down at the dedication of Solomon's temple, the people bowed to the ground and said the same words (2 Chr 7:3).

The answer comes in every one of the twenty-six verses. Count it; it never misses a line. Nothing in the psalm — creation, rescue, judgment, provision — is left without it.

Give thanks to the God of gods, for his steadfast love endures forever. Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his steadfast love endures forever;

Three calls to thanks, three names. The LORD — the covenant name. The God of gods — supreme over every power people worship. The Lord of lords — ruler over every ruler. And behind all three the same reason: his steadfast love. The God above all gods is not a remote supreme being. He is loyal love that never ends.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — To Him Who Made the Great Lights
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To him who alone does great wonders (v. 4); to him who by understanding made the heavens (v. 5), spread out the earth (v. 6), made the great lights (v. 7), the sun to rule over the day (v. 8), the moon and stars to rule over the night, for his steadfast love endures forever (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Every sunrise and every starry night is an act of God's steadfast love.

verseByVerse.quote: to him who alone does great wonders, for his steadfast love endures forever; to him who by understanding made the heavens, for his steadfast love endures forever; to him who spread out the earth above the waters, for his steadfast love endures forever; to him who made the great lights, for his steadfast love endures forever; the sun to rule over the day, for his steadfast love endures forever; the moon and stars to rule over the night, for his steadfast love endures forever;
verseByVerse.commentary:
to him who alone does great wonders, for his steadfast love endures forever; to him who by understanding made the heavens, for his steadfast love endures forever; to him who spread out the earth above the waters, for his steadfast love endures forever;

Now the psalm tells the story from the very beginning: creation. God made the heavens by understanding — with wisdom and design. He spread out the dry land above the waters. And after each act, the congregation answers: for his steadfast love endures forever. Creation itself is an expression of God's covenant love.

to him who made the great lights, for his steadfast love endures forever; the sun to rule over the day, for his steadfast love endures forever; the moon and stars to rule over the night, for his steadfast love endures forever;

The words come from Genesis: God made the two great lights — the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night — and the stars (Gen 1:16). And the psalm puts the refrain after the sun, and again after the moon.

Think about that. Tomorrow morning, when the sun comes up, that is God's steadfast love. Tonight, when the moon rises, that is his steadfast love. The ordinary, reliable rhythms of day and night, which we barely notice, are daily evidence that God keeps faith with his world. Every sunrise is a line of this psalm.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–22 — To Him Who Divided the Red Sea
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To him who struck down the firstborn of Egypt (v. 10) and brought Israel out with a strong hand and an outstretched arm (vv. 11-12); to him who divided the Red Sea in two (v. 13), led his people through the wilderness (v. 16), struck down Sihon and Og (vv. 17-20), and gave their land as a heritage (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole history of rescue, from Egypt to the land, told one line at a time — each followed by the same answer.

verseByVerse.quote: to him who struck down the firstborn of Egypt, for his steadfast love endures forever; and brought Israel out from among them, for his steadfast love endures forever; with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, for his steadfast love endures forever; to him who divided the Red Sea in two, for his steadfast love endures forever; and made Israel pass through the midst of it, for his steadfast love endures forever; but overthrew Pharaoh and his host in the Red Sea, for his steadfast love endures forever;
verseByVerse.commentary:
to him who struck down the firstborn of Egypt, for his steadfast love endures forever; and brought Israel out from among them, for his steadfast love endures forever; with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, for his steadfast love endures forever;

From creation to redemption. And here the refrain does something that can startle a modern reader. To him who struck down the firstborn of Egypt — for his steadfast love endures forever. God's love follows a line of judgment.

That is not cruelty. God's steadfast love is his covenant love for his people, and loving the enslaved meant breaking the power of the slaver. The judgment on Egypt was the rescue of Israel. A love that never judged oppressors would not be love for the oppressed.

to him who divided the Red Sea in two, for his steadfast love endures forever; and made Israel pass through the midst of it, for his steadfast love endures forever; but overthrew Pharaoh and his host in the Red Sea, for his steadfast love endures forever;

The sea split, the people walked through, and Pharaoh's army went under. The ESV notes that overthrew is literally "shook off" — the way a man shakes something off his hand. Exodus says the LORD threw the Egyptians into the midst of the sea (Exod 14:27). Three acts: divide, lead through, overthrow. Three times, the same answer.

verseByVerse.quote: to him who led his people through the wilderness, for his steadfast love endures forever; to him who struck down great kings, for his steadfast love endures forever; and killed mighty kings, for his steadfast love endures forever; Sihon, king of the Amorites, for his steadfast love endures forever; and Og, king of Bashan, for his steadfast love endures forever; and gave their land as a heritage, for his steadfast love endures forever; a heritage to Israel his servant, for his steadfast love endures forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
to him who led his people through the wilderness, for his steadfast love endures forever;

Forty years in the wilderness compressed into one line — and not a word about Israel's grumbling. This is not forgetfulness; Psalm 106 has already told that side. This psalm is looking only at what God did: he led.

to him who struck down great kings, for his steadfast love endures forever; and killed mighty kings, for his steadfast love endures forever; Sihon, king of the Amorites, for his steadfast love endures forever; and Og, king of Bashan, for his steadfast love endures forever;

Sihon and Og again, as in the previous psalm (135:11). Great kings who stood in the way of God's people, and each one named and followed by the refrain.

and gave their land as a heritage, for his steadfast love endures forever; a heritage to Israel his servant, for his steadfast love endures forever.

And the story of the exodus ends with a gift: the land, a heritage. Everything from the burning bush to the Jordan was love keeping a promise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — He Remembered Us in Our Low Estate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: It is he who remembered us in our low estate, for his steadfast love endures forever; and rescued us from our foes (vv. 23-24); he who gives food to all flesh (v. 25). Give thanks to the God of heaven, for his steadfast love endures forever (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: The great history comes home to us: remembered when we were low, rescued, and fed.

verseByVerse.quote: It is he who remembered us in our low estate, for his steadfast love endures forever; and rescued us from our foes, for his steadfast love endures forever; he who gives food to all flesh, for his steadfast love endures forever. Give thanks to the God of heaven, for his steadfast love endures forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is he who remembered us in our low estate, for his steadfast love endures forever; and rescued us from our foes, for his steadfast love endures forever;

And now the psalm comes home. For twenty-two verses it has been him who did great things in the past. Now it is us. He remembered us in our low estate. Perhaps the singers were the returned exiles, poor and humbled. Whoever they were, the great history of creation and exodus has become their own story.

Mary sang the same thing when God chose her: he has looked on the humble estate of his servant (Luke 1:48). That is where God's steadfast love finds people — low. Not at their best, but at their lowest.

he who gives food to all flesh, for his steadfast love endures forever.

And the psalm widens to the whole living world. All flesh — every creature — is fed by God. Jesus pointed to the birds that neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them (Matt 6:26). Every meal is a line of this psalm.

Give thanks to the God of heaven, for his steadfast love endures forever.

And the psalm ends where it began, with thanks. For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen (Rom 11:36).

Here is a way to pray this psalm. Take the events of your own life — your birth, your family, the day you came to Christ, the time God brought you through, this morning's breakfast — and after each one, say the refrain. For his steadfast love endures forever. You will find it fits every line.

136.title: His Steadfast Love Endures Forever
136.overview: A responsive song in which every verse ends for his steadfast love endures forever. Give thanks to the LORD, the God of gods and Lord of lords (vv. 1-3), who alone does wonders and made the heavens, the earth, the great lights, the sun for the day and the moon and stars for the night (vv. 4-9); who struck Egypt's firstborn, brought Israel out, divided the Red Sea, led them through it and overthrew Pharaoh (vv. 10-15); who led his people through the wilderness, struck down great kings including Sihon and Og, and gave their land as a heritage to Israel (vv. 16-22); who remembered us in our low estate, rescued us from our foes, and gives food to all flesh. Give thanks to the God of heaven (vv. 23-26).
136.theology:
God's steadfast love is the ground of every act in creation, redemption, judgment and providence, confessed after each line (vv. 1-26), as Israel sang at great moments (Ezra 3:11; 2 Chr 7:3; Jer 33:11).

Creation's ordinary rhythms are expressions of covenant love (vv. 7-9; Gen 1:16). God's love for his people includes judgment on their oppressors (vv. 10, 15, 17-20).

The history becomes personal: God remembers his people in their low estate (v. 23; Luke 1:48) and feeds all creatures (v. 25; Matt 6:26). All things are from him and to him (Rom 11:36).
136.examples:
One voice sings the line; the congregation answers.

Twenty-six verses, twenty-six times, never missing.

Tomorrow's sunrise is a line of this psalm.

Love for the enslaved means breaking the slaver.

Pharaoh shaken off like something on a hand.

From him who to us.

Breakfast, and the refrain after it.

137.text: <sup>1</sup>By the waters of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, when we remembered Zion.<sup>2</sup>On the willows there we hung up our lyres.<sup>3</sup>For there our captors required of us songs, and our tormentors, mirth, saying, "Sing us one of the songs of Zion!"<sup>4</sup>How shall we sing the LORD's song in a foreign land?<sup>5</sup>If I forget you, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill!<sup>6</sup>Let my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth, if I do not remember you, if I do not set Jerusalem above my highest joy!<sup>7</sup>Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem, how they said, "Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations!"<sup>8</sup>O daughter of Babylon, doomed to be destroyed, blessed shall he be who repays you with what you have done to us!<sup>9</sup>Blessed shall he be who takes your little ones and dashes them against the rock!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — How Shall We Sing the LORD's Song?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: By the waters of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, when we remembered Zion (v. 1). They hung up their lyres while their captors demanded songs of Zion (vv. 2-3). How shall we sing the LORD's song in a foreign land? (v. 4). If I forget you, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill! (v. 5), if I do not set Jerusalem above my highest joy! (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Exiles refuse to turn the songs of God into entertainment for the people who burned his house.

verseByVerse.quote: By the waters of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, when we remembered Zion. On the willows there we hung up our lyres. For there our captors required of us songs, and our tormentors, mirth, saying, "Sing us one of the songs of Zion!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
By the waters of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, when we remembered Zion.

This psalm has no title and needs none. The setting is in the first line. Jerusalem had been destroyed: the Babylonian commander burned the house of the LORD and the king's house and all the houses of Jerusalem, broke down the walls, and carried the people away (2 Kgs 25:9-11). Now the survivors are hundreds of miles east, in the flat river country of Babylon, among its rivers and canals. And they sit down and weep.

The weeping comes when we remembered Zion. Memory is what hurts. The city, the temple, the festivals, the Songs of Ascents they used to sing on the way up — all gone.

On the willows there we hung up our lyres.

The ESV notes the trees may be poplars. Either way, the harps that once accompanied the temple songs are hung on the branches, unplayed. There is a time when the music stops, and the psalm does not pretend otherwise.

For there our captors required of us songs, and our tormentors, mirth, saying, Sing us one of the songs of Zion!

And then the cruelty. The Babylonians — our captors, our tormentors — demand entertainment. Sing us one of the songs of Zion! Perhaps they meant it as mockery: sing about your God who could not save his city. Perhaps they simply wanted exotic music. Either way, they want the worship of the LORD turned into a show for the people who burned his temple.

verseByVerse.quote: How shall we sing the LORD's song in a foreign land? If I forget you, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill! Let my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth, if I do not remember you, if I do not set Jerusalem above my highest joy!
verseByVerse.commentary:
How shall we sing the LORD's song in a foreign land?

The question is not simply "we are too sad to sing". It is: how can the LORD's songs — songs about Zion, his dwelling, his victories — be performed as amusement for his enemies? Some things are too holy to be turned into entertainment. The exiles refuse.

That refusal is a kind of faithfulness. The world often wants the church's songs without the church's God — the beauty of worship detached from the one it worships. This psalm says no.

If I forget you, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill! Let my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth, if I do not remember you, if I do not set Jerusalem above my highest joy!

And the singer takes an oath against himself. The right hand is the hand that plays the lyre; the tongue is what sings. If I forget Jerusalem, let me lose the very abilities I would use to sing for Babylon. Let my hand go dead and my tongue stick. Better never to make music again than to forget Zion in the land of the captors.

And the heart of the oath: if I do not set Jerusalem above my highest joy. More than any pleasure Babylon can offer, more than comfort or success in exile, the city of God comes first. For a Christian, that is the heavenly Jerusalem and the God who dwells there. Exiles in a foreign land are tempted to settle and forget. The psalm is a vow never to let that happen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–9 — Remember, O LORD, Against the Edomites
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem, how they said, Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations! (v. 7). O daughter of Babylon, doomed to be destroyed, blessed shall he be who repays you with what you have done to us! (v. 8). Blessed shall he be who takes your little ones and dashes them against the rock! (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The rawest words in the Psalter: the grief of people who watched atrocity, handed over to God for judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem, how they said, "Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem, how they said, Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations!

Now the grief turns to anger, and the first target is not Babylon but Edom. The Edomites were descendants of Esau — Jacob's brother. On the day Jerusalem fell, they stood by and cheered: Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations! Strip it to the bedrock.

The prophet Obadiah records the same betrayal: On the day that you stood aloof, on the day that strangers carried off his wealth ... you were like one of them, and warns, do not gloat over the day of your brother in the day of his misfortune (Obad 11-12). Lamentations says the same cup will pass to Edom (Lam 4:21-22). The wound of a relative cheering your destruction goes very deep. The psalmist does not take revenge. He asks God to remember.

verseByVerse.quote: O daughter of Babylon, doomed to be destroyed, blessed shall he be who repays you with what you have done to us! Blessed shall he be who takes your little ones and dashes them against the rock!
verseByVerse.commentary:
O daughter of Babylon, doomed to be destroyed, blessed shall he be who repays you with what you have done to us!

Now Babylon. Doomed to be destroyed — the psalmist knows God has already pronounced judgment on the empire. And blessed — happy, fortunate — will be whoever carries it out, repaying Babylon with what you have done to us. God had said, I will repay Babylon and all the inhabitants of Chaldea before your very eyes for all the evil that they have done in Zion (Jer 51:24).

Blessed shall he be who takes your little ones and dashes them against the rock!

This is the most shocking verse in the Psalms, and it must not be skipped or softened. Several things need to be said honestly.

First, it is repayment in kind — with what you have done to us. Ancient conquering armies killed children, and the psalmist had very probably seen it done to Jerusalem's children. He is not inventing a cruelty. He is asking that the cruelty Babylon committed come back on Babylon.

Second, God had already announced this exact judgment. Isaiah's oracle against Babylon said, Their infants will be dashed in pieces before their eyes (Isa 13:16). The psalmist is praying for what God had said he would do.

Third, the psalmist does not do it, and does not ask to. He hands the justice to God and to whoever God uses. Christians are commanded, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Rom 12:19). This verse is never a licence for violence. It is the cry of people who have seen atrocity, spoken honestly to the only one who can judge it.

137.title: By the Waters of Babylon
137.overview: By the rivers of Babylon the exiles sat and wept at the memory of Zion, hanging up their lyres when their captors demanded songs of Zion (vv. 1-3). How could they sing the LORD's song in a foreign land? The psalmist vows that his hand may lose its skill and his tongue cleave to his mouth if he forgets Jerusalem or sets it below his highest joy (vv. 4-6). He asks the LORD to remember Edom, who cried for Jerusalem to be razed (v. 7), and pronounces blessing on the one who repays doomed Babylon for what it did, even to dashing its little ones against the rock (vv. 8-9).
137.theology:
Grief for the loss of God's dwelling is right (vv. 1-2). The LORD's song must not be turned into entertainment for his enemies (vv. 3-4), and God's city is to be set above every joy (vv. 5-6).

The imprecations (vv. 7-9) are the cry of victims of atrocity, asking for judgment God had already announced (Isa 13:16; Jer 51:24; Obad 10-12; Lam 4:21-22), repayment in kind, handed to God rather than taken (Rom 12:19). Heaven rejoices at the final fall of Babylon (Rev 18:20-21); Jesus wept as he foretold the same fate for Jerusalem (Luke 19:44), and bore judgment himself at the cross.
137.examples:
Memory is what hurts.

Harps hanging unplayed in the trees.

Worship demanded as a show.

The world wants the church's songs without the church's God.

Let my hand go dead before I forget.

A brother cheering the demolition.

The rawest grief, handed to the only just Judge.

138.text: Of David. 1I give you thanks, O LORD, with my whole heart; before the gods I sing your praise;2I bow down toward your holy temple and give thanks to your name for your steadfast love and your faithfulness, for you have exalted above all things your name and your word.3On the day I called, you answered me; my strength of soul you increased.4All the kings of the earth shall give you thanks, O LORD, for they have heard the words of your mouth,5and they shall sing of the ways of the LORD, for great is the glory of the LORD.6For though the LORD is high, he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar.7Though I walk in the midst of trouble, you preserve my life; you stretch out your hand against the wrath of my enemies, and your right hand delivers me.8The LORD will fulfill his purpose for me; your steadfast love, O LORD, endures forever. Do not forsake the work of your hands.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I give you thanks, O LORD, with my whole heart; before the gods I sing your praise (v. 1). He bows toward the temple and gives thanks for God's steadfast love and faithfulness (v. 2). On the day I called, you answered me; my strength of soul you increased (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: Unashamed praise in front of every rival power, for a God who answered and made a weak soul strong.

verseByVerse.quote: I give you thanks, O LORD, with my whole heart; before the gods I sing your praise; I bow down toward your holy temple and give thanks to your name for your steadfast love and your faithfulness, for you have exalted above all things your name and your word.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I give you thanks, O LORD, with my whole heart; before the gods I sing your praise;

This psalm opens the last group of psalms bearing David's name (138-145), and it opens with wholehearted thanks. And it is sung before the gods — in front of every rival power, every idol the nations worshipped, every authority that claimed divine honour. David is not embarrassed to praise the LORD in their presence.

That is still the Christian's calling. We praise God not in a sealed room, but in a world full of other gods — money, status, pleasure, ideologies — and we are not to lower our voices because they are listening.

I bow down toward your holy temple and give thanks to your name for your steadfast love and your faithfulness, for you have exalted above all things your name and your word.

The two great covenant words again: steadfast love and faithfulness. And God has exalted your name and your word above everything. (The ESV notes another reading: "you have exalted your word above all your name".) Either way, God's word stands at the very top — he has staked his own name on keeping what he has said. That is why a believer can trust Scripture: God's reputation is bound up with it.

verseByVerse.quote: On the day I called, you answered me; my strength of soul you increased.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the day I called, you answered me; my strength of soul you increased.

A simple testimony. He called; God answered. And notice what the answer was. Not necessarily the removal of the trouble, but this: my strength of soul you increased. The ESV notes the Hebrew is vivid: "you made me bold in my soul with strength".

Sometimes God answers prayer by changing the circumstances. Often he answers by changing the person — giving courage and inner strength to face what has not yet changed. A believer who prays for the storm to stop and finds instead that he has been made brave in it has been answered.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All the kings of the earth shall give you thanks, O LORD (v. 4). For though the LORD is high, he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar (v. 6). Though I walk in the midst of trouble, you preserve my life (v. 7). The LORD will fulfill his purpose for me; your steadfast love, O LORD, endures forever. Do not forsake the work of your hands (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The high God stoops to the lowly, keeps them alive in trouble, and finishes what he has begun in them.

verseByVerse.quote: All the kings of the earth shall give you thanks, O LORD, for they have heard the words of your mouth, and they shall sing of the ways of the LORD, for great is the glory of the LORD. For though the LORD is high, he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the kings of the earth shall give you thanks, O LORD, for they have heard the words of your mouth, and they shall sing of the ways of the LORD, for great is the glory of the LORD.

From one man's thanks, the psalm leaps to the whole world. The kings of the earth — the rulers before whom he has just sung — will themselves give thanks, for they have heard the words of your mouth. The word God has exalted (v. 2) will go out, and kings will hear it and sing.

For though the LORD is high, he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar.

And here is the heart of the psalm. God is high — above kings, above gods. And yet he regards the lowly — looks closely, pays attention, cares. The same truth as Psalm 113: the one seated on high who stoops to the ash heap (113:5-7).

But the haughty he knows from afar. God knows the proud, but at a distance — they get no closeness, no intimacy. The humble get near. Isaiah heard God say, I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit (Isa 57:15). And Peter: God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (1 Pet 5:5). If you want God close, go low.

verseByVerse.quote: Though I walk in the midst of trouble, you preserve my life; you stretch out your hand against the wrath of my enemies, and your right hand delivers me. The LORD will fulfill his purpose for me; your steadfast love, O LORD, endures forever. Do not forsake the work of your hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though I walk in the midst of trouble, you preserve my life; you stretch out your hand against the wrath of my enemies, and your right hand delivers me.

Not around trouble, not past it — in the midst of it. Faith does not guarantee a route that avoids hardship. It guarantees company and preservation inside it: God's hand stretched out against the enemy, his right hand holding the believer.

The LORD will fulfill his purpose for me; your steadfast love, O LORD, endures forever. Do not forsake the work of your hands.

One of the most reassuring verses in the Psalms. The LORD will fulfill his purpose for me. Whatever God set out to do in a person's life, he will finish. Paul said the same to the Philippians: I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Phil 1:6).

And the reason is the refrain of Psalm 136: your steadfast love, O LORD, endures forever.

Then, strikingly, a prayer right after the promise: Do not forsake the work of your hands. David is sure God will finish — and he still asks. Faith does not stop praying because it is confident; it prays because it is confident. And the argument is beautiful: I am the work of your hands. A craftsman does not abandon a piece he has worked on so long. If you feel half-finished — unsure God will complete what he began in you — pray this verse. You are his work, and he does not leave his work undone.

138.title: Do Not Forsake the Work of Your Hands
138.overview: David gives wholehearted thanks to the LORD before the gods, bowing toward the temple for God's steadfast love and faithfulness, since God has exalted his name and word above all (vv. 1-2). When he called, God answered and strengthened his soul (v. 3). All the kings of the earth will thank the LORD and sing of his glory, for though he is high he regards the lowly and knows the proud from afar (vv. 4-6). Though David walks in trouble, God preserves his life and delivers him; the LORD will fulfil his purpose for him, and David prays that he not forsake the work of his hands (vv. 7-8).
138.theology:
God is to be praised openly before every rival power (v. 1), and he has bound his name to his word (v. 2). He may answer prayer by strengthening the soul rather than removing the trouble (v. 3).

The high God draws near to the lowly and keeps the proud at a distance (v. 6; Isa 57:15; 1 Pet 5:5). He preserves his people in the midst of trouble (v. 7) and will complete his purpose for them (v. 8; Phil 1:6), grounded in his everlasting steadfast love; confidence in that promise still prays.
138.examples:
Praise that does not lower its voice before other gods.

God's reputation bound to his word.

Answered by being made brave.

If you want God close, go low.

In the midst of trouble, not around it.

A craftsman does not abandon his work.

139.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1O LORD, you have searched me and known me!2You know when I sit down and when I rise up; you discern my thoughts from afar.3You search out my path and my lying down and are acquainted with all my ways.4Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O LORD, you know it altogether.5You hem me in, behind and before, and lay your hand upon me.6Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high; I cannot attain it.7Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence?8If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there!9If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea,10even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me.11If I say, "Surely the darkness shall cover me, and the light about me be night,"12even the darkness is not dark to you; the night is bright as the day, for darkness is as light with you.13For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother's womb.14I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Wonderful are your works; my soul knows it very well.15My frame was not hidden from you, when I was being made in secret, intricately woven in the depths of the earth.16Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them.17How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How vast is the sum of them!18If I would count them, they are more than the sand. I awake, and I am still with you.19Oh that you would slay the wicked, O God! O men of blood, depart from me!20They speak against you with malicious intent; your enemies take your name in vain.21Do I not hate those who hate you, O LORD? And do I not loathe those who rise up against you?22I hate them with complete hatred; I count them my enemies.23Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts!24And see if there be any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — You Have Searched Me and Known Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O LORD, you have searched me and known me! (v. 1). He knows when David sits and rises, discerns his thoughts and is acquainted with all his ways (vv. 2-3). Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O LORD, you know it altogether (v. 4). You hem me in, behind and before (v. 5). Such knowledge is too wonderful for me (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: A man discovers that he is completely known — and finds it too wonderful to understand.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, you have searched me and known me! You know when I sit down and when I rise up; you discern my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down and are acquainted with all my ways. Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O LORD, you know it altogether.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD, you have searched me and known me!

This is one of the best-loved psalms in the Bible, and one of the most searching. It begins with a fact: God has searched David — investigated him thoroughly, like a man searching a house — and known him. Not known about him; known him.

You know when I sit down and when I rise up; you discern my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down and are acquainted with all my ways.

Every ordinary movement of the day: sitting down, getting up, going out, lying down. God knows all of it. And not only actions — my thoughts, and from afar. There is no distance at which God loses sight of what is going on inside a person. Acquainted with all my ways — familiar with them, the way you know someone you have lived with for years.

Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O LORD, you know it altogether.

Before a word is spoken, God knows it — altogether, completely, including the motive behind it. No creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account (Heb 4:13).

For some people, that is terrifying. For others, it is the greatest comfort there is. John says, whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything (1 John 3:20). To be completely known and still loved is what every human heart longs for. The psalm will show that David is both.

verseByVerse.quote: You hem me in, behind and before, and lay your hand upon me. Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high; I cannot attain it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You hem me in, behind and before, and lay your hand upon me.

Hem me in could sound like a prison. But the picture is of protection: God behind him, God in front of him, God's hand resting on him. Like a child walking between two parents, a hand on the shoulder. The one who knows everything about him has surrounded him.

Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high; I cannot attain it.

David tries to take in what it means to be known like this, and cannot. It is too wonderful, too high, beyond his reach. Paul reached the same limit: Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! (Rom 11:33). The right response to God's knowledge is not to understand it fully, but to worship.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Where Shall I Flee from Your Presence?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? (v. 7). If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there! (v. 8). At the far edge of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me (vv. 9-10). Even the darkness is not dark to you (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: There is nowhere — up, down, east, west or in the dark — where God is not.

verseByVerse.quote: Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there! If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence?

From knowledge to presence. And David asks the question every person has sometimes wanted to ask: is there anywhere I could get away from God? Jonah tried. He rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD and bought a ticket on a ship (Jonah 1:3). God met him in the storm.

If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there!

Up to the highest heaven — God is there. Down to Sheol, the realm of the dead — God is there too. There is no vertical escape. Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the LORD (Jer 23:24).

If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me.

And no horizontal escape either. The wings of the morning is the dawn, rising in the east. The uttermost parts of the sea is the far west, beyond the Mediterranean. Fly as fast as the sunrise from east to west — and God is there when you land.

But notice what God does when David gets there: your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me. Not arrest — guidance and holding. The person who runs from God finds, at the end of the running, the same hand. Paul told the Athenians that God is actually not far from each one of us, for In him we live and move and have our being (Acts 17:27-28).

verseByVerse.quote: If I say, "Surely the darkness shall cover me, and the light about me be night," even the darkness is not dark to you; the night is bright as the day, for darkness is as light with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I say, Surely the darkness shall cover me, and the light about me be night,

One last hiding place: the dark. People have always thought they could hide in the dark — do there what they would never do in daylight, or disappear into despair where no one can see.

even the darkness is not dark to you; the night is bright as the day, for darkness is as light with you.

God does not need light to see. The dark is as clear to him as noon. That is a warning for anyone who thinks the night hides what they do. And it is a comfort for anyone in the darkness of grief, depression or fear: the darkness that hides everything from you hides nothing from God, including you. He sees you there as clearly as in daylight.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother's womb (v. 13). I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made (v. 14). Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me (vv. 15-16). How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! (v. 17). I awake, and I am still with you (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Before anyone saw him, God was knitting him together and writing his days in a book.

verseByVerse.quote: For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother's womb. I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Wonderful are your works; my soul knows it very well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother's womb.

Now David explains why God knows him so completely: God made him. You formed my inward parts — the deepest, hidden organs. You knitted me together in my mother's womb. The picture is of weaving or knitting — bones, muscle and sinew worked together by a craftsman. Job used the same image: You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews (Job 10:11).

Every human being, before birth, was being made by God. This is why Christians have always held that life in the womb is precious. The unborn child is not a thing; it is someone God is knitting.

I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Wonderful are your works; my soul knows it very well.

Fearfully and wonderfully made — made in a way that inspires awe. (The ESV notes it may be "fearfully set apart".) And David's response is praise. Many people struggle to say this about themselves. They dislike their bodies, their faces, their weaknesses, their disabilities. This verse does not say every body is perfect in a fallen world. It says every person was made with awe-inspiring care by God, and that this is a reason to praise him, not to despise ourselves.

verseByVerse.quote: My frame was not hidden from you, when I was being made in secret, intricately woven in the depths of the earth. Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My frame was not hidden from you, when I was being made in secret, intricately woven in the depths of the earth.

The womb is described as secret and as the depths of the earth — a poetic way of saying hidden, dark, beyond human sight. No one could see a child forming. God could. Intricately woven — like fine embroidery.

Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them.

My unformed substance — the embryo, before it had any recognisable shape. God's eyes were on it. And before any of David's days had happened, every one of them was written in God's book. God told Jeremiah, Before I formed you in the womb I knew you (Jer 1:5), and Paul says God chose us in him before the foundation of the world (Eph 1:4).

That means no believer's life is an accident, and no day of it is unplanned by God — including the hard days. The number of your days is written. That is not fatalism; it is the security of being in the hands of a God who knew you before you were.

verseByVerse.quote: How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How vast is the sum of them! If I would count them, they are more than the sand. I awake, and I am still with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How vast is the sum of them! If I would count them, they are more than the sand.

God has been thinking about David since before he was formed. And David, overwhelmed, calls those thoughts precious — and uncountable. Try counting the grains of sand on a beach. God's thoughts toward his people are more than that.

I awake, and I am still with you.

A lovely line. Perhaps he fell asleep counting God's thoughts, and woke up — and God was still there. Every morning, a believer wakes into the presence of the God who never left during the night. And one day believers will wake from death itself, and find him still with them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–24 — Search Me, O God, and Know My Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Oh that you would slay the wicked, O God! (v. 19). They speak against God; I hate them with complete hatred (vv. 20-22). Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts! And see if there be any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting! (vv. 23-24).
verseByVerse.theology: Zeal against God's enemies turns at once into a prayer that God would examine his own heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh that you would slay the wicked, O God! O men of blood, depart from me! They speak against you with malicious intent; your enemies take your name in vain. Do I not hate those who hate you, O LORD? And do I not loathe those who rise up against you? I hate them with complete hatred; I count them my enemies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh that you would slay the wicked, O God! O men of blood, depart from me! They speak against you with malicious intent; your enemies take your name in vain.

After such tender verses, this turn is abrupt, and readers often wish it were not there. But it is connected. A man who has just been overwhelmed by the goodness of God cannot be neutral toward those who speak against that God with malicious intent. (The ESV notes the Hebrew lacks the words your name.) The more you love God, the more his enemies' contempt for him grieves you.

Do I not hate those who hate you, O LORD? And do I not loathe those who rise up against you? I hate them with complete hatred; I count them my enemies.

This is not personal spite — David does not say they have wronged him. It is loyalty. He takes God's side completely: God's enemies are his enemies. It is the same instinct as O you who love the LORD, hate evil! (97:10).

How does a Christian hold this? The New Testament keeps both edges. Abhor what is evil (Rom 12:9) — never make peace with rebellion against God. And Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them (Rom 12:14) — love the persons, pray for their salvation. The hatred of this psalm is directed at settled, bloody opposition to God. And it is immediately followed by something that keeps it from turning into self-righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts! And see if there be any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts!

Here is that something. The moment David declares his hatred of the wicked, he turns the searchlight on himself. The psalm began, you have searched me and known me (v. 1). It ends by asking for exactly that: Search me ... and know my heart. What was a fact at the start has become a prayer.

That is the safeguard against self-righteousness. It is easy to see the wickedness of others. It takes the searching of God to see our own. And David invites it — try me, test me like metal in fire; know my thoughts (the ESV notes the word may mean cares, anxious thoughts).

And see if there be any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting!

Any grievous way — any path of pain, any hurtful habit, anything that grieves God or wounds others. David does not assume he is clean. He asks God to find what he cannot see. And then, lead me in the way everlasting (or, the ESV notes, "in the ancient way", compare Jeremiah 6:16) — the old road that leads to life.

This is a prayer to pray regularly. It takes courage, because God answers it. But the God who searches is the God who knitted you together, whose thoughts toward you outnumber the sand, and whose hand holds you at the far side of the sea. To be searched by him is to be healed by him. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known (1 Cor 13:12). Better still, as Paul says, the greatest thing is not that we have come to know God, but that we are known by God (Gal 4:9).

139.title: Search Me, O God
139.overview: David confesses that the LORD has searched and known him: his sitting and rising, his thoughts, his path, every word before it is spoken; God hems him in and lays his hand on him, knowledge too wonderful to grasp (vv. 1-6). There is no fleeing God's presence: in heaven or Sheol, at the dawn's rising or the farthest sea, God's hand leads and holds him, and darkness is as light to him (vv. 7-12). God formed his inward parts and knitted him in the womb; he is fearfully and wonderfully made; God saw his unformed substance and wrote all his days in his book, and God's precious thoughts toward him outnumber the sand (vv. 13-18). David longs for God to slay the wicked who speak against him, and counts God's enemies his own (vv. 19-22). Then he prays: Search me, O God, and know my heart! ... and lead me in the way everlasting! (vv. 23-24).
139.theology:
God knows every person exhaustively, thoughts and words included (vv. 1-4; Heb 4:13), a knowledge that surrounds and protects his people (v. 5) and exceeds understanding (v. 6; Rom 11:33). He is present everywhere, so there is no escape from him and no darkness that hides from him (vv. 7-12; Jonah 1:3; Jer 23:23-24; Acts 17:27-28).

God forms each person in the womb with awe-inspiring care (vv. 13-15; Job 10:11), knows them before birth, and has written their days (v. 16; Jer 1:5; Eph 1:4). His thoughts toward his people are innumerable and his presence constant (vv. 17-18).

Loyal hatred of settled rebellion against God (vv. 19-22) is held together with love for enemies (Rom 12:9, 14) and guarded by a prayer to be searched oneself (vv. 23-24). To be known by God is the believer's security (1 Cor 13:12; Gal 4:9).
139.examples:
Known, not just known about.

Completely known and still loved.

Hemmed in like a child between two parents.

Jonah's ticket to Tarshish.

Fly with the sunrise east to west, and God is there when you land.

The dark that hides nothing from God — including you.

Someone God is knitting.

Falling asleep counting God's thoughts, and waking with him.

The searchlight turned on oneself.

140.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1Deliver me, O LORD, from evil men; preserve me from violent men,2who plan evil things in their heart and stir up wars continually.3They make their tongue sharp as a serpent's, and under their lips is the venom of asps. Selah4Guard me, O LORD, from the hands of the wicked; preserve me from violent men, who have planned to trip up my feet.5The arrogant have hidden a trap for me, and with cords they have spread a net; beside the way they have set snares for me. Selah6I say to the LORD, You are my God; give ear to the voice of my pleas for mercy, O LORD!7O LORD, my Lord, the strength of my salvation, you have covered my head in the day of battle.8Grant not, O LORD, the desires of the wicked; do not further their evil plot, or they will be exalted! Selah9As for the head of those who surround me, let the mischief of their lips overwhelm them!10Let burning coals fall upon them! Let them be cast into fire, into miry pits, no more to rise!11Let not the slanderer be established in the land; let evil hunt down the violent man speedily!12I know that the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted, and will execute justice for the needy.13Surely the righteous shall give thanks to your name; the upright shall dwell in your presence.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Deliver Me from Violent Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Deliver me, O LORD, from evil men; preserve me from violent men, who plan evil and stir up wars (vv. 1-2). They make their tongue sharp as a serpent's, and under their lips is the venom of asps (v. 3). Guard me, O LORD, from the hands of the wicked (v. 4); the arrogant have hidden a trap for me (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: A man hunted by violent schemers with poisonous tongues asks God to guard him.

verseByVerse.quote: Deliver me, O LORD, from evil men; preserve me from violent men, who plan evil things in their heart and stir up wars continually. They make their tongue sharp as a serpent's, and under their lips is the venom of asps. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Deliver me, O LORD, from evil men; preserve me from violent men, who plan evil things in their heart and stir up wars continually.

The enemies in this psalm are organised. They plan evil in their hearts — it is not impulsive, but calculated. And they stir up wars continually — always making trouble, setting people against one another. Some people seem to live for conflict. David asks to be delivered from them.

They make their tongue sharp as a serpent's, and under their lips is the venom of asps.

Their main weapon is the tongue — sharpened like a snake's, and behind the lips, poison. Words that look harmless carry venom: slander, lies, insinuations that spread and kill reputations.

Paul quoted this very line, and did something startling with it. In Romans he gathers verses from the Psalms to describe not a few wicked men, but the whole human race: Their throat is an open grave; they use their tongues to deceive. The venom of asps is under their lips (Rom 3:13). James agrees: the tongue is a restless evil, full of deadly poison (Jas 3:8). The psalmist prays against poisonous tongues; the New Testament reminds us that every human mouth is capable of the same venom — including ours.

verseByVerse.quote: Guard me, O LORD, from the hands of the wicked; preserve me from violent men, who have planned to trip up my feet. The arrogant have hidden a trap for me, and with cords they have spread a net; beside the way they have set snares for me. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Guard me, O LORD, from the hands of the wicked; preserve me from violent men, who have planned to trip up my feet.

The request is repeated almost word for word from verse 1, as troubled prayers often are. The enemies want to trip up my feet — to make him fall, morally or literally.

The arrogant have hidden a trap for me, and with cords they have spread a net; beside the way they have set snares for me.

Trap, net, snares — the language of a hunter. (The ESV notes it may read "they have spread cords as a net".) The danger is hidden and set beside the way, on the path he has to walk. A believer in a hostile workplace or community often feels exactly this: every conversation might be a trap.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — The LORD Will Maintain the Cause of the Afflicted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I say to the LORD, You are my God (v. 6). O LORD, my Lord, the strength of my salvation, you have covered my head in the day of battle (v. 7). Let their own mischief overwhelm them (vv. 8-11). I know that the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted, and will execute justice for the needy (v. 12). The upright shall dwell in your presence (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: God is the helmet in battle and the advocate of the afflicted, and the wicked are caught in their own snares.

verseByVerse.quote: I say to the LORD, You are my God; give ear to the voice of my pleas for mercy, O LORD! O LORD, my Lord, the strength of my salvation, you have covered my head in the day of battle. Grant not, O LORD, the desires of the wicked; do not further their evil plot, or they will be exalted! Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
I say to the LORD, You are my God; give ear to the voice of my pleas for mercy, O LORD!

The turning point is a confession: You are my God. Before any rescue, David reaffirms whose he is. That is where prayer in danger begins.

O LORD, my Lord, the strength of my salvation, you have covered my head in the day of battle.
